Problem & Motivation: The work addresses text-to-image generation under information-dense prompts, especially prompts requiring multiple objects, precise counts, attributes, spatial relations, layouts, world knowledge, and rendered text. The relevant users are developers of generative-image systems and researchers studying captioned-image training. The paper argues that token count is a poor proxy for conditioning quality: natural-language captions can become longer while preserving the same entities and relations, whereas omitted or ambiguously expressed image content provides weak supervision to the diffuser. It targets the gap between prior long-caption or recaptioning approaches and a representation that exposes image-grounded variables—particularly geometry, object-level attributes, scene context, and relations—in a consistent, addressable form. Key Idea: The core insight is that useful scaling occurs with image-grounded information, not with raw prompt length, and that a typed structured representation makes this information both easier for the diffuser to learn and easier for an LLM to generate or edit. The paper separates this into diffusability—the ability of a caption interface to expose organized image supervision—and promptability—the ability of an image-free LLM to instantiate that interface from a user request. The proposed Diffusability × Promptability expression is explicitly described as a conceptual decomposition, not a fitted multiplicative law. Methodology: The system has three major stages. First, an image-to-structured-prompt pipeline uses Seed-VL for global and cropped per-element semantics, Sapiens pose overlays for human geometry, DepthAnything V2 for relative depth, and SAM 2.1 for masks and occlusion; a final VLM assembles a JSON record containing global fields, elements with attributes/actions/bounding boxes/depth, and cross-element relations. Deterministic masking creates levels L5–L10, ranging from approximately 447 to 1,374 tokens. Second, the paper runs a 15-condition controlled sweep—three natural-language conditions, six nested structured levels, three grid-location variants, and three field ablations—using the same images, initialization, architecture, optimization recipe, and 2.84 × 10^10 cumulative image-token budget for separate BAGEL runs. It measures Grounded Perplexity Gain, GPG = sum of image-conditioned versus image-free token log-likelihood gains under a frozen VLM, and Effective Detailness, ED = F0.5 of caption-attribute precision and image-attribute recall from VLM-extracted tuples; it fits MSE = 0.4549 − 8.45 × 10^−5 GPG and MSE = 0.4200 ED^−0.2073. Third, it trains Qwen-Image on a mixture of structured and natural-language supervision, while training a Qwen3.5-397B-A17B LoRA prompter through approximately 333,000-example SFT, 50,182 filtered cold-start traces, and RFT over 10,003 image-caption pairs. The RFT objective applies token-level KL distillation from an image-conditioned teacher only on rollouts accepted by a structure/alignment/aesthetic verifier. At inference, the system either uses one prompter call followed by one diffusion render or an iterative refine–render–judge loop. Important design decisions are the explicit field hierarchy, deterministic field masking, and verifier-gated OPSD. The hierarchy is supported by field ablations and transfer results, but the paper does not isolate JSON syntax from richer content and organization; deterministic masking improves control but does not remove annotation/model bias; and verifier gating is motivated by precision concerns but inherits VLM-judge errors. Key Results: In the controlled BAGEL sweep, GPG and ED rank caption configurations with Spearman ρ = 0.96, while the fitted correlations with converged MSE are −0.984 for GPG and −0.971 for ED. A configuration-level holdout predicts excluded spatial and field variants with mean absolute MSE errors of 5.0 × 10^−4 using GPG and 8.1 × 10^−4 using ED. The structured field ladder improves BAGEL GenEval2 GM from 46.79 at L5 to 57.70 at L10, with a 26.0% GSB preference over L5. Removing scene context increases MSE by 35.3 × 10^−4 and removing bounding boxes by 14.4 × 10^−4; depth, relations, and atmosphere/lighting change MSE by at most 1.5 × 10^−4. For zero-shot prompter scaling, thinking-mode GenEval++ increases from 46.4% with a 0.8B Qwen3.5 prompter to 86.8% with the 397B model. In the main comparison, the proposed system scores GenEval = 0.94, GenEval2 = 90.6/72.5 AM/GM, DPG-Bench = 90.71, TIIF = 89.1/89.2 short/long, WISE = 0.89, and CoReBench = 85.2. The matched natural-language control scores 0.91, 84.5/56.2, 87.80, 88.5/88.0, 0.84, and 76.1, respectively; the official Qwen-Image prompt enhancer scores 82.4/52.8 GenEval2 and 74.7 CoReBench. Against evaluated baselines, the proposed system exceeds Qwen-Image with official enhancement on all listed metrics and exceeds Nano Banana on GenEval, GenEval2, DPG-Bench, TIIF where reported, and CoReBench, but ties or slightly trails Nano Banana on WISE (0.89 versus 0.89) and trails it on some CoReBench subcategories such as multi-instance composition and text rendering. Prompter ablations show structure score increasing from 4.860 at the base model to 6.273 after SFT, 6.753 after cold-start, and 7.600 after verifier-gated OPSD; GSB reaches 42.0%. The refinement loop raises trained-prompter GSB from 42.0% at one round to 54.7% at eight rounds, while average rounds consumed are only 2.31, indicating rapid saturation. The results are large, but many end-to-end evaluations use GPT-5.4, Gemini, or legacy VLM-based scoring, and published baseline protocols are not uniformly matched. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION, NEW METHOD, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL. The strongest genuine contribution is the controlled formulation of caption informativeness as a recipe-specific predictor of diffusion training loss together with the diffusability/promptability decomposition; the structured JSON interface, VLM recaptioning, specialist annotation, SFT, distillation, verifier gating, and iterative refinement are individually related to prior structured-caption, recaptioning, prompt-enhancement, and inference-time-scaling techniques, so the end-to-end system is primarily a substantial integration and empirical demonstration rather than an entirely new primitive. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper includes unusually detailed protocols, full equations, field ladders, matched natural-language controls, field ablations, spatial serialization variants, prompter-stage ablations, judge/extractor robustness checks, budget refits, and exact evaluator prompts. GPG rankings remain strong across alternative judges, with r from −0.91 to −0.996 after coordinate compatibility, and ED rankings remain stable across image-side extractors, although absolute ED agreement is low. However, each of the 15 scaling configurations is trained only once, so there are no independent seeds, run-level confidence intervals, or significance tests for the central loss relation; reported resampling bands quantify selected-setting sensitivity rather than optimization uncertainty. The calibration is performed on a 7B BAGEL backbone using an in-house continued-training checkpoint, while the main system uses Qwen-Image and does not refit the GPG–loss relation on that backbone. The GPG masking and canonicalization recipe was finalized during metric development on the same controlled sweep, creating a potential metric-selection/Goodhart concern, and ED relies on multiple proprietary API models for extraction and matching. Code is linked at https://github.com/heheyas/context-scaling, models at https://huggingface.co/collections/heheyas/context-scaling, and a demo is linked at https://heheyas-context-scaling.hf.space/; the report also states that Seed-VL is internal and API-only. Reproduction remains constrained by proprietary evaluators, internal annotation components, an in-house BAGEL checkpoint, large multi-GPU training budgets, and noncommercial dependencies such as Sapiens and DepthAnything V2. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS, because the paper delivers and evaluates a trained prompter–diffuser system, an annotation pipeline, editing interface, and optional iterative inference loop. * Practical: The authors provide code, model links, and a demo, and the core single-shot path can run on available accelerator hardware, but the reported training pipeline uses up to 512 GPUs for Qwen-Image and a 397B-parameter prompter, while the annotation and evaluation stack depends on proprietary VLM APIs and noncommercial components. * Efficient: The single-shot path adds one long-form LLM generation before the 50-step diffusion render; the optional loop costs approximately 20–35 seconds per round and invokes three Gemini judge calls per round, with average trained-prompter usage of 2.31 rounds at an eight-round cap, so the paper demonstrates quality gains but not favorable cost or latency relative to simpler prompt enhancement. * Effective: Evidence supports better compositional alignment, attribute binding, world-knowledge generation, reasoning benchmarks, and VLM-judged structure relative to matched controls, but it primarily measures benchmark and model-judge proxies rather than human preference, production reliability, safety, or robustness to adversarial and out-of-distribution prompts. * Scalable: The method scales prompter quality from 0.8B to 397B and tests a 397B prompter with a Qwen-Image diffuser, but it does not test 10×–100× more images, objects, schema fields, video/3D outputs, or deployment traffic; the authors explicitly leave automatic schema discovery and video/3D extension open. The work delivers a software and model artifact: a public code repository, Hugging Face model collection, demo, project page, structured-prompt schema, annotation/training procedures, trained prompter components, and an optional field-level editing/refinement system. It does not deliver a standalone benchmark dataset or a universal theorem about information scaling. Strengths: - The 15-condition matched-budget sweep directly separates caption length from caption content and includes natural-language controls, nested structured levels, spatial encodings, and field ablations rather than relying only on end-to-end image quality. - The two independent information measures provide convergent evidence: a likelihood-based GPG measure and a black-box attribute-based ED measure produce similar configuration rankings, and the paper openly limits the resulting relations to empirical, recipe-specific calibrations. - The matched natural-language retraining control is important: it shows that additional training and the same Qwen-Image architecture do not reproduce the structured-interface gains, with 56.2 versus 72.5 GenEval2 GM and 76.1 versus 85.2 CoReBench. - The prompter analysis isolates scale, reasoning mode, SFT, cold-start data, verifier reward, OPSD, and inference-time refinement, yielding actionable evidence about where quality improvements arise and where additional inference compute saturates. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that GPG and ED depend on image-conditioned measurement models and that fitted relations may shift across judges and extractors. They acknowledge that agreement between the metrics does not eliminate shared evaluator bias, that the schema is hand-designed, that video and 3D generation are not evaluated, and that the structured path increases prompter latency. They also explicitly state that the scaling calibration is backbone-specific, that each sweep setting is trained once, and that resampling bands are not training-run confidence intervals. These limitations are confronted directly rather than hidden, although their practical consequences for cost, privacy, API dependence, and broad deployment are not quantified in detail. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The central causal claim remains confounded between added information and the particular organization/serialization used: the experiment does not compare equally informative structured and natural-language representations with matched semantic coverage and equivalent access to geometry. The scaling-law evidence relies on 15 deliberately designed points, one seed per point, a single in-house BAGEL checkpoint, and metrics whose masking and aggregation choices were selected during development on the same sweep; a preregistered or independently held-out caption family with repeated runs would materially strengthen it. The main end-to-end comparisons are not uniformly matched for training data, compute, sampler, prompt-enhancement budget, or evaluator provenance, and several strongest baselines are closed systems with vendor or leaderboard numbers. The paper does not report human studies, confidence intervals for the 150-prompt GSB comparisons, inter-rater agreement for VLM judges, or robustness across domains, languages, unsafe prompts, long-tail object categories, and substantially larger element counts. It also does not quantify annotation cost, API cost, carbon/compute cost, memory usage, throughput, failure rates, schema-validity rates, or quality degradation when proprietary teachers and judges are replaced by open models. Finally, structured prompts may introduce a strong learned layout prior that improves benchmark alignment while reducing diversity or user control; the paper measures fidelity gains but does not evaluate this tradeoff. Bottom Line: This is a technically substantial and practically relevant report worth reading for its controlled evidence that image-grounded structured conditioning can outperform mere prompt lengthening, but its strongest scaling-law claims should be treated as promising single-recipe correlations rather than general scaling laws, and its deployment value is limited by very high compute, latency, annotation, and proprietary-model costs.

MosaicJoin: Compact Semantic Sketches for Value-Level Join Discovery

G Fan, E Wu, M Daliri, J Freire · arxiv.org · 10 new citations to your articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces MosaicJoin, a training-free semantic join-discovery system that represents each candidate column with a compact value-embedding sketch and ranks columns using sketch-based Chamfer similarity. - Why it's important: It targets the latency and memory bottleneck of semantic join search in data lakes, where exhaustive value comparisons become impractical for columns with tens of thousands to one million values. - How it does it: It selects diverse observed value embeddings with farthest-first k-center sampling, compares query values against the resulting 64-vector sketches, and randomly subsamples up to 1,024 query values for bounded-cost scoring. - The good: Across six benchmark variants, it reports better retrieval quality than the evaluated published baselines while reducing value-level search latency to 0.040–0.322 seconds on the reported base benchmarks, compared with up to 15.646 seconds for exhaustive semantic matching. - The missing: The theoretical guarantee concerns estimation error for a fixed candidate score, not preservation of the top-k ranking, and the paper does not provide a formal approximation bound for replacing a full candidate column with a k-center sketch. - Read it or not: Data-management researchers and practitioners building semantic table search should read it for the practical sketching design and empirical trade-offs, but readers seeking a stronger end-to-end retrieval theory should treat the claims as primarily empirical.
Why this rank

Rigor (78) is supported by diverse benchmarks, relevant named baselines, latency and memory measurements, and component ablations, though confidence intervals, significance tests, label quality, and some baseline comparisons are incomplete. Problem & Motivation: Data-lake users need to discover columns that can be semantically joined with a query column despite aliases, abbreviations, formatting differences, and misspellings. Exact overlap methods miss such matches, while column-level embeddings efficiently retrieve candidates but collapse away the value-level alignments that determine whether a join is actually possible. Exhaustive value-level semantic comparison captures those alignments but scales with both query and candidate cardinality, creating unacceptable latency and memory costs for high-cardinality columns and large repositories. Key Idea: The central insight is to approximate the candidate-side set of value embeddings with a fixed-size subset chosen to minimize worst-case embedding-space coverage radius, then retain a value-level directed best-match score over that subset. This combines late-interaction-style fine-grained matching with bounded candidate representation size. Query-side random subsampling further makes scoring cost independent of query-column cardinality, although it can miss rare joinable values. Methodology: Offline, MosaicJoin embeds every value in each data-lake column with a shared embedding function, ℓ2-normalizes the vectors, and constructs a sketch of size \(m\) using farthest-first traversal: it initializes with the point nearest the column centroid and repeatedly adds the value farthest from its nearest selected representative. The stated k-center objective minimizes the maximum distance from any column embedding to its nearest sketch point; the greedy procedure gives the usual constant-factor approximation when the distance is metric, although the paper does not derive a bound on the resulting joinability-score error. Online, it embeds the query values, samples \(b\) values uniformly with replacement, computes the maximum dot product between each sampled query vector and every candidate sketch vector, averages those matches, and maintains a top-k heap. The primary conceptual score is directed Chamfer similarity, but the experiments use the average of query-to-sketch and sketch-to-query Chamfer scores after finding comparable ablation performance. The default choices are EmbeddingGemma with 128 dimensions, sketch size \(m=64\), query sample size \(b=1024\), and score threshold τ=0.1. The k-center choice is empirically supported against k-means, while the embedding and sketch-size choices are justified by accuracy/runtime measurements; the use of average Chamfer rather than directed Chamfer is only weakly justified because the measured difference is small. Key Results: The evaluation uses Auto-FuzzyJoin, Webtables, and Freyja, plus WDC-augmented variants; the largest setting contains 99,020 columns and candidate columns with up to 1,048,575 values, while query columns contain up to 57,793 values. On the base benchmarks, MosaicJoin reports Recall@20/NDCG@20 of 1.000/0.945 on Auto-FuzzyJoin, 1.000/0.569 on Webtables, and Precision@20/Recall@20/NDCG@20 of 0.829/0.543/0.848 on Freyja. Against DeepJoin, Snoopy, and PEXESO, the reported NDCG@20 improvements reach 17.6% on Webtables and 9.1% over DeepJoin on Freyja; the paper also reports up to 135.7% Precision@10 improvement on Webtables+WDC. On the WDC-expanded settings, MosaicJoin obtains Precision@10/NDCG@10 of 0.630/0.819 on Auto-FuzzyJoin+WDC, 0.066/0.423 on Webtables+WDC, and 0.428/0.562 on Freyja+WDC. Average search times are 0.080, 0.040, and 0.322 seconds on the three base benchmarks, versus 0.507, 0.060, and 15.646 seconds for the exhaustive ESJ variant; MosaicJoin is reported as 2–66 times faster than PEXESO and 2–49 times faster than ESJ. It is not uniformly more accurate than ESJ: ESJ wins on Webtables, Webtables+WDC, and Freyja+WDC, whereas MosaicJoin wins on Auto-FuzzyJoin and Auto-FuzzyJoin+WDC. The default ablation reaches Freyja NDCG@10 0.885; k-means falls to 0.482, \(m=32\) gives 0.848, \(m=128\) gives 0.888, and BGE-768 gives 0.909 at substantially higher search time (0.931 seconds versus 0.080 for EmbeddingGemma-128). These results are standard-scale data-lake experiments rather than 10×–100× stress tests beyond the reported corpus sizes. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING: the contribution is a domain-specific combination of k-center representative sampling, Chamfer-style multivector scoring, and query subsampling for semantic join retrieval, with the main novelty lying in the integration and evaluation of these ideas for high-cardinality data-lake columns rather than in a fundamentally new clustering, embedding, or multivector-retrieval primitive. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper includes component ablations for k-center versus k-means, directed/inverse/bidirectional Chamfer, sketch size, embedding model, and query-sample size, plus comparisons across query sizes and indexing configurations. It evaluates several relevant baselines, including DeepJoin, Snoopy, PEXESO, KOIOS, SILKMOTH, TOPJoin, and an exhaustive ESJ implementation. However, it reports no error bars, multiple random seeds, confidence intervals for retrieval metrics, or significance tests for the main method comparisons. The expanded-benchmark labels rely on Gemini 2.5 Pro with confidence filtering and an annotation pool formed from the union of methods' top-50 results; 200 positive pairs were audited by multiple models and humans, but negative-label quality and recall of unobserved positives are not established. The authors reimplemented KOIOS and SILKMOTH, PEXESO timed out on expanded benchmarks, TabSketchFM was omitted because weights were unavailable, and the strongest embedding model was not used as the default because of latency. Source code, data, and artifacts are stated to be available at https://github.com/VIDA-NYU/MosaicJoin. The formal sampling result is a standard unbiased Hoeffding bound for one fixed candidate score; it does not establish reliable top-k retrieval, simultaneous guarantees over all candidates, or robustness to rare-value distributions. The paper also reports an optional FAISS index for a comparison, but the main Algorithm 2 still scans all candidate sketches, so the claimed asymptotic online procedure remains linear in the number of candidate columns. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS and EMPIRICAL, because the paper builds and benchmarks a retrieval system while reporting experimental results. - Practical: The system runs on commercially available hardware; the experiments use one NVIDIA L40S GPU, 128 GB RAM, and eight CPU cores, and the authors report 2.48 seconds and about 52 MB per newly ingested Freyja column. - Efficient: With 128-dimensional embeddings, \(m=64\), and \(b=1024\), it uses 2.39 GB peak RAM and 2.13 GB peak GPU memory online on Freyja, versus 9.06 GB and 6.09 GB for ESJ; however, the default implementation still computes \(O(Nbmd)\) work across all candidates and stores roughly 68.65 GB for the full Freyja preprocessing setup. - Effective: The evidence shows improved ranking and precision over the tested baselines on the six reported benchmark variants, but the task remains a proxy for successful downstream join execution and the LLM-generated expanded labels may not fully represent production join correctness. - Scalable: It is tested up to 99K columns, 1M candidate values, and 57K query values, but no 10×–100× larger experiment is provided; the authors explicitly leave approximate nearest-neighbor indexing over sketches for future work, and subsampling accuracy declines as the sampled fraction becomes very small. The work delivers an open-source software artifact and associated data; it does not deliver a generally reusable proof technique beyond standard k-center and concentration arguments. Strengths: - The sketch representation directly addresses the key systems trade-off: it retains observed value-level evidence while making candidate-side comparison independent of candidate-column cardinality. - The method models directed, many-to-one semantic coverage, which is better aligned with denormalized and fuzzy joins than exact maximum-bipartite-matching objectives; the Auto-FuzzyJoin comparison with ESJ provides evidence that sketching can sometimes improve robustness to redundant variations. - The evaluation covers heterogeneous base benchmarks, WDC-expanded search spaces, high-cardinality queries, preprocessing cost, memory, latency, and several relevant method families rather than only reporting accuracy. - The strongest practical result is the accuracy/latency operating point: on Freyja, MosaicJoin reaches NDCG@20 0.848 and about 0.322 seconds per query, compared with ESJ's 0.834 and 15.646 seconds, while requiring substantially less online memory. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge the sketch-size versus accuracy trade-off, dependence on embedding quality and sketch construction, possible omission of rare joinable values under query subsampling, the lack of metadata, semantic types, and table context, and the absence of approximate-nearest-neighbor indexing over sketch representations. They also acknowledge that ESJ can achieve higher accuracy on some benchmarks and that value-only matching cannot resolve all contextual ambiguities. These limitations are discussed directly, although the conclusion still uses broad language about capturing the full semantics of high-cardinality columns that is stronger than the empirical and theoretical evidence supports. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The paper does not quantify the probability of top-k ranking errors induced jointly by candidate sketching and query subsampling, nor does it provide a formal relationship between k-center covering radius and Chamfer-score distortion. Uniform sampling is poorly matched to the explicitly acknowledged long-tail and rare-value failure mode; importance sampling, stratification, or recall of rare join-critical values is not evaluated. The expanded labels are generated only for retrieved candidate pools, which creates a selection-dependent evaluation and prevents measuring false negatives outside the union of top-50 lists. The reported gains also depend on the chosen embedding model and values-only setting; no evaluation tests metadata-rich baselines under their intended input conditions or compares against stronger contemporary multivector ANN implementations. There is no end-to-end join execution evaluation, no throughput/concurrency experiment, no latency distribution or indexing-at-scale result, and no study of embedding-model drift or incremental sketch maintenance beyond single-column ingestion. Reimplementation and timeout-based exclusion of baselines reduce confidence in some cross-system speed comparisons, especially when methods use different indexing and execution architectures. Bottom Line: MosaicJoin is a useful and reproducible systems contribution for fast value-level semantic join discovery, with convincing latency gains and generally strong benchmark results, but its novelty is mainly a well-executed integration of known sketching and late-interaction ideas and its ranking guarantees and large-scale deployment claims remain empirically incomplete.

Teaching Nemotron Greek: Mining a Corpus, Adapting Retrieval, and Grounding Generation for Modern Greek across Specialist Domains (17 ▲ )

Ayoub Kirouane, Christos Petrocheilos · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 7 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper builds and releases Greek-adapted Nemotron embedding, reranking, and grounded-reader models, together with the HERA multi-passage RAG benchmark and supporting evaluation artifacts. - Why it's important: Greek is absent from major retrieval benchmarks and from the supported-language coverage of the evaluated Nemotron retrieval models, while specialist Greek documents are a plausible production target for RAG systems. - How it does it: It mines and filters synthetic Greek retrieval pairs, trains a 1B contrastive embedder and cross-encoder with hard negatives, LoRA-tunes a 30B-A3B reader on citation-and-abstention supervision, and evaluates lexical, dense, hybrid, reranking, and reading components separately. - The good: On 5,830 held-out synthetic queries, adapted 1B retrieval improves macro nDCG@10 from 0.362 to 0.835 and exceeds BM25 by +0.080, while hybrid BM25+dense fusion also improves over either component in both in-domain and general-domain evaluations. - The missing: The paper does not evaluate the reader end to end on retrieved contexts, does not compare against Multilingual E5 or Greek-adapted reader baselines, and relies heavily on synthetic queries and LLM-generated benchmark labels. - Read it or not: Read it for evidence that language exposure, rather than model scale, can dominate Greek specialist retrieval and for its unusually explicit failure analysis; treat its reader-quality claims as provisional until human-audited and end-to-end evaluations appear.
Why this rank
Scored using the Systems profile. Practical Impact (82) is the largest strength because the paper releases adapted embedding, reranking, reader, benchmark, and evaluation artifacts, while also demonstrating useful index compression and hybrid retrieval behavior. Novelty (78) and Non-Obviousness (82) come from the released Greek specialist-domain stack and the well-supported finding that language/domain exposure can matter more than model scale, especially relative to BM25 and off-the-shelf dense models. Rigor (72) is reasonably strong due to bootstrap intervals, reruns, negative findings, decontamination checks, and detailed failure analysis, but is limited by synthetic queries and labels, missing standard multilingual and Greek-reader baselines, and no complete retrieved-context evaluation. Completeness (82) is unusually good because the paper explicitly acknowledges synthetic-data optimism, abstention failure, judge confounding, English regression, and the missing end-to-end experiment; Resilience (75) remains constrained by those unresolved validity threats. Weighted composite: 0.15*78 + 0.15*72 + 0.10*82 + 0.15*82 + 0.15*75 + 0.30*82 = 79.

Problem & Motivation: The work addresses retrieval-augmented generation for Modern Greek, especially long, jargon-dense legal, energy, financial, medical, and official documents. Greek is absent from BEIR and MIRACL and is not supported by the evaluated Nemotron retrieval models, leaving both model behavior and benchmark performance largely unmeasured. The specific prior-art gap is not general Greek generation—Meltemi and Llama-Krikri already target that problem—but Greek retrieval, multi-passage grounded reading, citation behavior, and abstention. Existing Greek reading resources such as Belebele and XQuAD use single-passage or translated settings; they do not provide the multi-passage distractors, citation targets, and unanswerable cases needed for RAG evaluation. The paper also investigates whether adapting a smaller model to Greek can outperform larger off-the-shelf multilingual models and whether gains transfer from specialist training domains to general Greek. Key Idea: The central insight is that language and domain exposure are the binding constraints for Greek retrieval, not parameter count, and that lexical and dense retrievers should be combined rather than treated as mutually exclusive. A 1B Nemotron model that is fine-tuned on Greek retrieval pairs outperforms an unadapted 8B multilingual embedder on specialist-domain queries, while its advantage over BM25 reverses on general Greek; reciprocal-rank fusion exploits the complementary failure modes. For grounded generation, the analogous insight is that adapting the reader to citation, context use, and abstention is more important than relying on an off-the-shelf model or merely increasing model scale. Methodology: The pipeline starts with 407,053 raw query-document-label-domain pairs and produces 65,773 per-query records across validation/general, energy, legal, finance, and medical data. Queries are synthetically generated—Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B for the general slice and GLM-5.2 for domain slices—using few-shot production-query conditioning, grounding constraints, and deliberate difficulty variation. The source chunk is treated as the positive without human relevance labels; hard negatives are mined with asymmetric Qwen3-Embedding-8B cosine k-nearest-neighbor search within each domain, with top-rank and similarity-cap filtering. The resulting embedder is a fully fine-tuned Nemotron-3-Embed-1B trained with InfoNCE over the positive, in-batch positives, and seven mined negatives per query; GradCache supports a logical batch of 256 at 4,096 tokens. A pointwise cross-encoder is trained with binary cross-entropy on 394,579 positive/negative pairs and reranks the top 50 candidates. RRF combines BM25 and dense rankings over the top 100 with k=60. The reader is trained from 40,000 teacher-generated citation-and-abstention examples mixed with a 206,909-row Greek instruction pool, using LoRA rank 16 on attention, MLP, and Mamba input projections of Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B; the adapter has 439M trainable parameters and is trained for one epoch on four B200 GPUs. HERA contains 4,946 Greek Wikipedia items, including 3,712 answerable and 1,234 unanswerable questions, 1,145 multi-hop items, 8–40 passages per context, and L1–L5 difficulty. Qwen3.5-122B generates benchmark items and GLM-5.2 verifies them. The main design decisions—4,096-token training rather than the common 512-token limit, domain-matched hard-negative mining, and explicit abstention/citation supervision—are empirically motivated, although the paper does not isolate every choice with a complete ablation matrix. Key Results: On 5,830 held-out synthetic retrieval queries, the adapted Nemotron 1B reaches macro-over-sets nDCG@10 of 0.8352 versus 0.3617 for its base model, 0.7571 for BM25, 0.6801 for Qwen3-Embedding-8B, 0.6843 for Qwen3-Embedding-4B, and 0.6140 for Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B. The adapted model beats BM25 by +0.080 with a 95% paired-bootstrap interval of [+0.072,+0.089]; per-domain adapted scores are 0.8755 on validation, 0.7937 on energy, 0.9497 on legal, and 0.7218 on finance. On the separate medical set of 650 queries over 24,812 passages, it scores 0.6867 nDCG@10 versus 0.6602 for BM25 and 0.5936 for Qwen3-8B, but the +0.027 margin over BM25 has a 95% interval touching zero. On general Greek HERA retrieval over 4,946 queries and 300,000 passages, the adapted Nemotron 1B scores 0.5637 versus 0.1651 for its base, but BM25 scores 0.6442 and Qwen3-4B scores 0.6182; adaptation transfers language competence but not the in-domain dense-over-lexical advantage. BM25+dense RRF reaches 0.6715, versus 0.6442 for BM25 alone, with Recall@10 increasing from 0.7326 to 0.7823. The 512-dimensional truncated embedding scores 0.823 in-domain, 98.5% of the full-dimensional score, and reduces index size by 4x. In reranking, the adapted Nemotron cross-encoder improves over its no-rerank floor by +0.047 on the initial 750-query evaluation and by +0.061 on the larger 2,580-query evaluation; the off-the-shelf reranker is initially indistinguishable from the floor but later improves it by +0.032, demonstrating sample sensitivity. Swapping both retrieval stages raises end-to-end retrieval nDCG@10 from 0.559 to 0.848 and Recall@10 from 0.624 to 0.955, although the paper does not run the reader on these retrieved contexts. On gold-provided HERA contexts, LoRA adaptation increases LLM-judged answer correctness from 29.4% to 66.9%, faithfulness from 25.2% to 84.5%, citation F1 from approximately 23% to 67.8%, and exact citation-set match to 56.5%; abstention recall improves from 1.2% to 30.5% but remains poor. When refusals on answerable items count as wrong, correctness is 28.7% versus 64.3%, reducing the apparent gain by roughly 2.6 points. The reader's English MMLU score drops by 0.098 and English ARC-Challenge by 0.094, while Greek benchmark performance improves on six of eight reported tasks. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and an adapted NEW METHOD in the narrow setting of Modern Greek RAG; the individual techniques—BM25, contrastive embedding fine-tuning, hard-negative mining, pointwise cross-encoder reranking, RRF, LoRA, and LLM-as-judge evaluation—are standard, so the genuine novelty lies in the released Greek specialist-domain stack and HERA benchmark, plus the measured finding that language exposure and hybrid retrieval dominate scale in this setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper reports substantial evaluation detail, paired bootstrap intervals for retrieval comparisons, 10,000 bootstrap draws with seed 42, a larger reranker rerun after an unstable 750-query result, decontamination checks, explicit no-rerank floors, matched-size comparisons, and several honest negative findings. It also reports a 4,096-token truncation audit, corpus statistics, training objectives, LoRA configuration, compute duration, and four instrumentation failures. However, the retrieval corpus is not released, so retraining from scratch is impossible; only models, HERA, the teacher model, and evaluation artifacts are released at the KIEFERSA Hugging Face collection, including https://huggingface.co/collections/KIEFERSA/sophea-nemo-rag and https://huggingface.co/datasets/KIEFERSA/HERA. Retrieval labels are synthetic source-chunk positives rather than human relevance judgments, and all reported retrieval queries are synthetic, with the authors acknowledging that they likely overestimate production performance. HERA is generated and verified by two LLMs with only an unsized human spot-check; its reader judge is from the same Qwen family as the benchmark generator, creating a documented family-preference risk. Reader results are single-run point estimates, although Wilson intervals are reported for judged item proportions. There is no zero-replay control, no systematic ablation of the reader data mixture or LoRA target modules, no comparison with Multilingual E5, and no comparison with Greek-adapted reader models such as Meltemi or Llama-Krikri. The reranker evaluations use different query sets and corpora, and the paper correctly avoids directly composing incompatible absolute scores. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS and EMPIRICAL, because the paper releases runnable embedding, reranking, reader, and benchmark artifacts and evaluates them experimentally. - Practical: The models can run on commercially available GPUs, and the reader training used four B200 GPUs; inference latency, serving throughput, CPU viability, and production integration cost are not reported. - Efficient: The adapted retriever is only 1B parameters, a 0.6B adapted alternative nearly matches it, and 512-dimensional truncation reduces index size by 4x, but end-to-end latency, memory use, reranking cost, and comparison with BM25-only serving are not measured. - Effective: Evidence supports substantial gains for synthetic specialist-domain retrieval and gold-context grounded reading, but the reader's judged correctness is confounded by LLM-generated data and judging, and the paper does not measure the complete retrieved-context RAG system. - Scalable: The evaluation reaches 300,000 passages and contexts of up to 40 passages, but it does not test 10x–100x corpus scale, high query throughput, larger candidate pools, multilingual expansion, or deployment on conversational rather than formal Greek. The work delivers three trained models, HERA, evaluation scripts, and a separately released teacher model; it does not release the retrieval training corpus, preventing full training reproducibility. Strengths: - It identifies and quantifies a non-obvious failure mode: BM25 outperforms every tested off-the-shelf dense embedder, including an 8B model, on all five specialist-domain settings or, in the four-domain main table, three of four sets, while a fine-tuned 1B model substantially surpasses both. - It separates transferable language competence from domain-specific retrieval fit using an out-of-domain Greek Wikipedia evaluation, where the adapted model beats its own base by +0.399 but loses to BM25, preventing an overbroad claim of general superiority. - It evaluates components against meaningful floors and repeats an initially underpowered reranker experiment, revising the claim that the off-the-shelf reranker contributes nothing. - It releases a useful Greek RAG benchmark with unanswerable, multi-hop, long-context, citation, and positional-robustness dimensions, alongside deployable model artifacts and detailed failure disclosures. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly acknowledge synthetic-query optimism, unpublished and weakly documented production-query observations, source-chunk rather than human relevance labels, formal/official corpus bias, translation-heavy instruction data and translationese risk, lack of multi-document citation supervision, canned abstention targets, terse answers, poor abstention recall, same-family generator/judge confounding, unsized human validation, an unlogged HERA candidate acceptance rate, single-run reader estimates, English capability regression, the absence of a zero-replay control, the lack of end-to-end reader evaluation on retrieved contexts, and limited hybrid-retrieval tuning. They also acknowledge missing comparisons with Greek-adapted reader models and Multilingual E5, describing the former as a real gap rather than merely a scope choice. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The largest unresolved issue is that the headline RAG claim is not evaluated as a deployed chain: the paper reports retrieval with one protocol and reading with gold-provided context, but never measures answer correctness, faithfulness, citation quality, or abstention when the reader receives the retrieved top-k passages. The benchmark and training labels are both substantially LLM-generated, while human validation is only an unsized spot-check, so the magnitude of benchmark and supervision artifacts is unknown. The main retrieval gains may be inflated by queries generated from their source passages, a particularly favorable condition for BM25 and source-chunk labeling; real-user evaluation is mentioned but lacks query count, annotation protocol, and published results. The absence of Multilingual E5 is important because it is a standard multilingual retrieval baseline, and the absence of Greek-adapted reader controls makes it difficult to attribute reader gains to the proposed data recipe rather than the selected Nemotron base. The paper does not provide systematic ablations for query synthesis style, 4,096-token length, negative-mining strategy, RRF parameters, reader mixture proportions, replay data, abstention construction, or LoRA target modules. It also does not assess cross-domain contamination or memorization risks in the public-domain specialist corpora, nor does it report serving cost and latency for the proposed two-stage stack. Bottom Line: This is a valuable and unusually candid systems study for Greek RAG, worth reading and deploying as a starting point for specialist-domain retrieval, but its strongest reader and end-to-end claims remain unestablished until human-audited, real-query, retrieved-context evaluations and stronger multilingual and Greek-adapted baselines are added.

#9 — Highly Innovative (79)

OSReward: Instituting Standardized Evaluation for Cross-Platform Computer-Use Reward Models (51 ▲ )

Qiushi Sun, Kanzhi Cheng, Yian Wang, Bowen Yang, Hang Yan, Liheng Chen, Fangzhi Xu, Zichen Ding, Nuo Chen, Jialin Cao, Xingdong Gong, Zehao Li, Kaiming Jin, Xinfeng Yuan, Zhoumianze Liu, Jingyang Gong, Zhangyue Yin, Jiahui Gao, Zhiyong Wu, Tianbao Xie, Jianbing Zhang, Ben Kao, Lingpeng Kong · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 7 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces OSReward, a human-gold cross-platform benchmark for evaluating VLM judges of computer-using-agent trajectories, and releases OS-Shepherd-100K with 9B and 35B open reward models trained to reduce false-success judgments. - Why it's important: Incorrectly rewarding failed computer-use trajectories can corrupt agent evaluation, data filtering, and reinforcement learning, while frontier API judges are too expensive for training-scale use. - How it does it: It combines realistic web, Windows, Ubuntu, and Android trajectories with three-way human annotation, diagnoses a shared leniency bias, filters large-scale pseudo-labeled data by cross-judge agreement, and fine-tunes Qwen3.5 models with SFT followed by GRPO on mined false-success cases. - The good: The 1,019-trajectory benchmark exposes a substantial gap hidden by aggregate accuracy: Claude-Opus-4-8 reaches 89.7% on OSReward but only 69.7% on OSReward-Hard, while OS-Shepherd-9B reaches 60.2% on the hard set at an estimated $1.36 per benchmark pass. - The missing: The paper does not evaluate whether OS-Shepherd rewards actually improve downstream CUA training, and its 100K training labels are selected from models that share the very leniency bias the benchmark diagnoses. - Read it or not: CUA researchers building evaluators, reward models, or RL pipelines should read it for the benchmark and failure analysis; readers seeking a new judge architecture rather than an evaluation-and-distillation study can largely skip it.
Why this rank
Scored using the Empirical profile. Novelty (78) and Non-Obviousness (78) are driven by the cross-platform human-gold benchmark, the hard-case diagnosis of false-success judgments, and the finding that action/reasoning text matters more than additional screenshots. Rigor (82) is strong because of fresh trajectories, three-way annotation, senior adjudication, agreement statistics, 27 judge comparisons, controlled input ablations, and released benchmark/model artifacts. Completeness (80) benefits from directly acknowledging weak quality grading, correlated judge errors, and imperfect external verifiers, while Resilience (73) is reduced by circular pseudo-label supervision, distribution-specific hard-set sampling, and the absence of downstream RL validation. Impact (82) reflects a practical open benchmark and self-hostable 9B/35B reward models, although their effect on agent training and reward hacking remains unshown. Weighted composite: 0.20*78 + 0.25*82 + 0.15*78 + 0.15*80 + 0.15*73 + 0.10*82 = 79.

Problem & Motivation: Computer-using agents operate across browsers, mobile applications, and desktop software, producing long multimodal trajectories whose success must be verified for evaluation, data curation, rejection sampling, and reinforcement learning. Hand-written verifiers cover only fixed tasks and do not apply to open-ended or historical trajectories, while human annotation is too expensive at scale. The specific gap is reliable trajectory-level judgment: a judge must determine whether the environment actually reached the instructed goal, distinguish completed tasks from plausible narratives, and tolerate valid detours without accepting incomplete work. Existing CUA reward studies are described as narrow, platform-specific, or dependent on reused trajectories and noisy benchmark verifiers. Key Idea: The central insight is that CUA judges share a systematic false-success failure mode because they rely more heavily on the agent’s action and reasoning narrative than on decisive visual or environmental evidence. The paper turns this diagnosis into a data and training strategy: use fresh human-gold trajectories to measure the bias, retain only high-agreement judgments from diverse strong judges for large-scale supervision, and use a short RL stage focused on false-success cases to move an open model toward a more balanced success/failure operating point. Methodology: OSReward constructs realistic environments on web, Windows, Ubuntu, and Android, including initialized files, application state, accounts, distractors, live websites, and GUI-only or GUI+CLI action spaces. Annotators explore the environments, write and peer-screen approximately 1,500 grounded instructions, and retain roughly 800 for rollout; agents from Claude, Gemini, Kimi, and Qwen families execute them. A pre-filter removes crashes, persistent blocks, and infrastructure failures. Each surviving trajectory is independently labeled by three annotators; disagreements receive deliberative review by two senior reviewers, and residual-quality items are discarded. The final benchmark contains 1,019 trajectories with binary success/failure labels, a 284-item OSReward-Hard subset selected largely from annotator disagreements and re-verified, and OSReward-Multi labels for alignment and efficiency on 440 successful trajectories. Judges receive the instruction, the last five screenshots by default, and interleaved action and reasoning text, then emit a binary verdict and optional quality ratings. Evaluation reports accuracy, success recall, fail recall, balanced accuracy, macro-recall, and AUC. For OS-Shepherd, approximately 321,631 judge instances from self-collected and public trajectories are filtered by cross-model agreement into 96.6K SFT samples plus roughly 3.1K RL samples. The models start from Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, undergo one-epoch supervised fine-tuning, then approximately 150 GRPO steps with eight rollouts per example, a learning rate of 1e-6, a KL coefficient of 0.001, and 32 NVIDIA H200 GPUs. The main design decisions—fresh human-gold data, hard-case isolation, and false-success-focused RL—are well motivated; however, the choice to use agreement-filtered model judgments as large-scale labels is only partially justified because agreement does not imply correctness when judges share correlated errors. Key Results: On the full 1,019-trajectory OSReward set, Claude-Opus-4-8 achieves 89.7% accuracy and 90.0% balanced accuracy, GPT-5.5 achieves 89.5% and 89.8%, and the best open baseline, Kimi-K2.5, achieves 85.9% and 87.3%. On OSReward-Hard, the best judge reaches only 69.7% accuracy and balanced accuracy; GPT-5.5 reaches 67.3% accuracy and 67.0% balanced accuracy, while the mean judge falls to approximately 52%. The dominant error is over-accepting incomplete tasks, accounting for roughly two-thirds of errors in the reported analysis; pooled over-accepts outnumber over-rejects about three to one. Removing action and reasoning text reduces accuracy by an average of 7.2 percentage points, whereas removing or changing screenshot selections changes accuracy by less than about 0.5–1.2 points on average; 22.7% of individual verdicts flip when text is removed. On OSReward-Multi, the best quality-rating results are only in the low 60s: GPT-5.5 reaches 63.5% mean macro-recall and 66.7% AUC, while OS-Shepherd-35B reaches 56.8% macro-recall and 60.7% AUC. OS-Shepherd-9B improves over Qwen3.5-9B from 76.7% to 86.1% full-set accuracy and from 39.4% to 60.2% hard-set accuracy; OS-Shepherd-35B reaches 85.6% and 62.7%, respectively. The 9B model is estimated at $1.36 per full-set evaluation, versus approximately $45.44 for GPT-5.5 and $86.04 for Claude-Opus-4-8, though open-model costs are estimated from market rates. On OSWorld, WebArena, and AndroidWorld, OS-Shepherd-9B obtains reported accuracies of 73%, 81%, and 83% against benchmark-specific human-written verifiers, respectively; these are agreement measurements, not independent ground-truth accuracy. The main surprising findings are the collapse from roughly 90% aggregate accuracy to near-chance hard-case performance, the weak effect of additional screenshots, and the fact that the 35B model provides only a 2.4-point hard-set balanced-accuracy gain over the 9B model. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION; the benchmark’s cross-platform human-gold construction, hard-case view, systematic leniency analysis, and released OS-Shepherd corpus/models are the substantive contributions, while the underlying SFT-plus-GRPO training recipe and VLM-as-judge setup are standard components applied to CUA reward modeling. Rigor & Reproducibility: The benchmark construction is stronger than typical reused-trajectory evaluations: 1,128 pre-filtered trajectories receive three independent labels, initial unanimous agreement is 75%, pairwise agreement is 83.3%, Krippendorff’s alpha is 0.797, disagreements receive senior meta-review, and 109 items are discarded rather than forcibly labeled. The hard subset receives an additional review and corrects 18 labels. The study evaluates 27 reference VLMs under a common protocol, includes input, reasoning-effort, screenshot-count, temperature, and ensemble analyses, and reports a base-to-SFT-to-RL comparison for OS-Shepherd. The paper states that code, benchmark data, training data, and model checkpoints are released through the OSReward Homepage, but the parsed text does not provide a direct URL. It does not report conventional multiple-training-seed variation, confidence intervals, statistical significance tests, or per-item uncertainty intervals for the headline comparisons. The largest concern is label provenance for OS-Shepherd-100K: high-agreement strong judges supply most labels, yet the paper shows that judges have correlated errors with Cohen’s kappa around 0.71 and a shared leniency bias. Agreement filtering removes ambiguous cases but cannot guarantee correctness on systematic false successes. External-benchmark results compare against human-written verifiers that the authors acknowledge are imperfect, so they demonstrate transfer of operating-point calibration rather than verified ground-truth accuracy. Costs for open models are estimates rather than measured deployment costs. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL, with a released software/data/model artifact rather than only a paper-form result. * Practical: OS-Shepherd is open-weight, self-hostable, and based on 9B and 35B models that can run on commercially available GPU hardware, although the reported training run used 32 NVIDIA H200 GPUs. * Efficient: The 9B model is estimated to cost $1.36 to judge the full benchmark and about 30–60× less than frontier commercial judges at the paper’s illustrative training-call volume; actual local serving throughput, latency, memory use, and hardware requirements are not reported. * Effective: Evidence shows substantially improved benchmark judgment and failure recall over the untuned Qwen3.5 bases, with transfer to three existing benchmarks, but it does not show improved downstream agent learning, safer behavior, or better task success when OS-Shepherd is used as an RL reward. * Scalable: The data pipeline reaches roughly 82K filtered trajectories and 321K judge instances, and the authors claim training-scale affordability, but they do not test 10×–100× larger inference or RL workloads, nor establish that the model remains calibrated as task distributions, applications, trajectory lengths, or platforms expand. The work delivers OSReward benchmark data, OSReward-Hard and OSReward-Multi subsets, the OS-Shepherd-100K training corpus, OS-Shepherd-9B and OS-Shepherd-35B-A3B checkpoints, and associated code according to the paper; the direct repository or homepage URL is not stated in the parsed text. Strengths: - The paper identifies a concrete and actionable failure mechanism—acceptance of incomplete tasks based on agent self-narration—and supports it with error taxonomies, case studies, text-removal ablations, platform breakdowns, and external-benchmark analysis. - The benchmark construction addresses several common evaluation confounds through fresh trajectories, realistic initialized environments, diverse agent backbones, multi-stage human review, explicit grounding rules, and removal of infrastructure-corrupted runs. - OSReward-Hard is diagnostically useful: it prevents the 43/57 full-set class mix from masking failure detection and reveals that even the strongest judges fall to approximately 67–70% balanced performance. - The released OS-Shepherd models show a meaningful cost–accuracy tradeoff: OS-Shepherd-9B improves hard-set accuracy by 20.8 percentage points over its base while operating at a reported cost comparable to small open judges and far below frontier APIs. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that OSReward-Multi is exploratory and applies only to successful trajectories, that quality grading remains weak and miscalibrated, that OS-Shepherd does not yet match frontier accuracy, and that external benchmark comparisons use imperfect human-written verifiers rather than independent gold labels. They also acknowledge that majority-vote ensembling does not resolve correlated judge errors, that soft-label or confidence-weighted modeling is left for future work, and that prompting judges to verify completion explicitly is not evaluated. These limitations are generally confronted directly rather than hidden, although the conclusion still describes the reward signal as reliable at training scale without a downstream training experiment. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The strongest unaddressed issue is circularity in OS-Shepherd supervision: the agreement filter preferentially retains cases on which strong judges agree, potentially excluding precisely the difficult, correlated-error cases that OSReward-Hard exposes. The paper does not quantify label accuracy of the 100K corpus independently of the judge ensemble, nor compare against human-labeled samples at training scale. It also lacks downstream experiments showing that OS-Shepherd improves CUA policy success, reduces reward hacking, or changes RL outcomes relative to commercial judges, hand-written verifiers, or simpler calibrated baselines. The hard-set sampling procedure deliberately increases failures to 70%, so its raw accuracy and cost comparisons are distribution-specific; performance under natural success/failure rates and across unseen applications, languages, resolutions, and longer-than-100-step trajectories is not established. No confidence intervals or repeated-seed results are reported for model training, and the paper does not test simple alternatives suggested by its diagnosis, such as explicit completion-verification prompts, full-trajectory state summarization, outcome-specific tools, or calibrated thresholding. Finally, the benchmark’s human-gold standard inherits annotator subjectivity, especially for open-ended tasks and efficiency/alignment judgments, despite the relatively strong agreement statistics. Bottom Line: This is a valuable benchmark and empirical diagnosis for CUA reward-model research, and OS-Shepherd is a credible low-cost baseline, but practitioners should not treat it as a validated replacement for task verifiers until downstream RL effects and independent evaluation of its pseudo-labels are demonstrated.

Measuring the Dependency Gap: Diagnosing Inter-Column Fidelity in Tabular Generative Models

J Zhang · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces an interaction-sensitive XGB-C2ST diagnostic that decomposes tabular-generation fidelity into marginal, dependency, and numerical–categorical cross components using fully factorized and real-data oracle references. - Why it's important: Common linear C2ST and pairwise Trend metrics can certify synthetic tables that preserve column marginals while destroying the inter-column structure needed for minority-class prediction. - How it does it: It compares gradient-boosted discriminator performance before and after independently permuting columns or swapping numerical and categorical blocks, then interprets the resulting contrasts against zero-dependency and real-data references. - The good: Across four quantitative benchmarks, TabbyFlow exhibits statistically positive dependency gaps, while the fully factorized reference receives near-perfect linear-C2ST scores despite destroying all dependencies; the effect replicates on TabDiff for adult and default. - The missing: The diagnostic is not calibrated to a known amount or type of dependency loss, and the paper does not directly test the proposed remedy of adding dependency-sensitive supervision to the training objective. - Read it or not: Read it if you evaluate or design tabular generators and need to distinguish marginal fidelity from higher-order joint fidelity; skip it if you need a deployable generator, a calibrated universal metric, or production-scale evidence.
Why this rank
Scored using the Empirical profile. Novelty (83) and Non-Obviousness (85) are high because the paper formulates a dependency-sensitive diagnostic that exposes how factorized data can appear faithful under linear C2ST and reports informative negative evidence against simple capacity fixes. Rigor (78) is strong for the held-out evaluation, five-seed experiments, oracle and factorized controls, confidence intervals, and replication on a second generator, though it is reduced by the preprint status, limited inferential power, discriminator dependence, and lack of broader current baselines. Completeness (88) is a major strength: the authors directly acknowledge the lack of calibration, the operational nature of the measure, limited datasets, and failure to test dependency-supervised training. Resilience (82) is good because claims are carefully bounded, while Impact (45) reflects a valuable diagnostic methodology without a released implementation or validated training intervention. Weighted composite: 0.20*83 + 0.25*78 + 0.15*85 + 0.15*88 + 0.15*82 + 0.10*45 = 78.85, rounded to 79.

Problem & Motivation: Synthetic tabular data must preserve joint structure, not merely per-column distributions, because interactions often carry minority-class signal in fraud, marketing, and clinical-risk applications. Existing evaluation practice commonly relies on logistic-regression C2ST and pairwise Trend metrics, which can be insensitive to high-order inter-column dependencies. The paper targets the resulting certification gap: a fully factorized synthetic reference that independently resamples every column receives linear-C2ST detection scores of 0.995–1.000 and Trend scores of 0.69–0.78 despite having zero dependency. The practical concern is that evaluators may conclude that a generator is faithful even when its joint distribution has been substantially damaged. Key Idea: Use controlled permutation interventions on the inputs to the same interaction-sensitive discriminator to localize how much distinguishability comes from marginal mismatch versus joint-dependency mismatch. Independent column permutation preserves marginals while destroying all inter-column structure, so the difference between the unpermuted and permuted XGB-C2ST scores estimates an operational dependency component. A second block permutation preserves within-numerical and within-categorical structure while removing numerical–categorical coupling. The central insight is diagnostic rather than generative: read these contrasts only relative to a zero-dependency fully factorized reference and a real-data oracle, rather than treating them as absolute divergence measures. Methodology: The pipeline splits each real dataset into training and held-out test sets, trains a generator only on the training split, and evaluates synthetic samples against the held-out real test data. For each balanced real-versus-synthetic two-sample set, it trains a gradient-boosted-tree discriminator with 300 estimators, maximum depth 6, and five-fold stratified cross-validation; the reported XGB-C2ST is the canonicalized out-of-fold AUC, where 0.5 indicates indistinguishability and 1.0 complete separability. Let full be the discriminator score on the original samples and marg the score after independently permuting every column within each sample set; the paper defines dep = full − marg. It defines depcross by independently pairing the numerical block from one row with the categorical block from another and subtracting the resulting score from full. The diagnostic is anchored by a fully factorized reference that independently resamples each empirical marginal and by a real-data oracle formed from a fresh real-data subsample. The primary generators are TabbyFlow/EF-VFM, whose objective uses a factorized variational posterior and per-column moment matching, and TabDiff, a mixed-type diffusion model with an additive column-wise denoising objective. Critical design decisions are the use of tree discriminators instead of linear classifiers, the permutation-based decomposition, and the fixed FF/oracle references; the first two are motivated by prior evidence and controlled sanity checks, while the paper acknowledges that the resulting components depend on discriminator capacity and are not algebraic divergences. Additional experiments test an XOR task, a width sweep from 10.6M to 168M parameters, a discrete-aware cross-coupling head, a Gaussian-copula post-processing route, and SMOTE as an orthogonal utility baseline. Key Results: On adult, default, bank, and magic, TabbyFlow's dependency components are respectively +0.050 ± 0.007, +0.077 ± 0.012, +0.038 ± 0.014, and +0.025 ± 0.016, with five seeds and 95% confidence intervals excluding zero; shoppers shows +0.017 ± 0.016, but its interval [−0.004, +0.037] includes zero. TabbyFlow's full XGB-C2ST is 0.607 on adult versus 0.503 for the oracle and 0.991 for the fully factorized reference; corresponding full scores are 0.613/0.506/1.000 on default, 0.562/0.504/0.956 on bank, and 0.551/0.509/0.995 on magic. The zero-dependency reference collapses minority-class F1 to 0.102, 0.087, 0.016, and 0.224 on adult, default, bank, and magic, compared with TabbyFlow's 0.663, 0.452, 0.514, and 0.825 and the oracle's 0.709, 0.467, 0.533, and 0.837. This supports the necessity of dependency for utility, but the residual generator-to-oracle F1 shortfall does not track the measured dependency component: default has the largest dependency gap but only a 0.015 F1 shortfall, while adult's 0.046 shortfall is the only one statistically resolved. TabDiff reproduces comparable dependency gaps on adult (+0.054, 95% CI [0.049, 0.059]) and default (+0.055, 95% CI [0.042, 0.068]); its minority F1 is 0.671 and 0.440. The XOR control satisfies the three-way relation at 0.98 with five sampling steps and 1.00 with twenty. Increasing TabbyFlow from 10.6M to 168M parameters does not significantly reduce dependency on adult or bank; adult's 4×−1× interval is [−0.002, +0.019], excluding reductions larger than 0.002, while magic is inconclusive and directionally compatible with improvement. The added cross-coupling head produces no significant benefit: adult depcross changes by +0.002 ± 0.003, bank by −0.006 ± 0.006, and default by +0.003 ± 0.009. These are standard public datasets at roughly 12,000–49,000 rows, not stress-scale or production-scale evaluations; the compared generators are representative flow-matching and diffusion systems rather than a broad contemporary benchmark. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION, NEW METHOD, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING: the paper contributes a permutation-based decomposition of one interaction-sensitive two-sample score, an empirical finding that standard linear detection metrics miss complete dependency destruction and that modern flow/diffusion generators retain higher-order dependency gaps, and negative evidence against simple capacity or architectural fixes. The underlying ingredients—classifier two-sample tests, boosted-tree discriminators, permutation interventions, and fully factorized references—are established; the paper's distinct contribution is their controlled combination and interpretation as a dependency diagnostic for mixed-type tabular generation. Rigor & Reproducibility: The study uses held-out real test sets, fixed splits, balanced discriminator samples, five random seeds for most experiments, paired comparisons for interventions, explicit convergence checks for the width sweep, and confidence intervals alongside parametric tests. It includes useful controls: a fully factorized reference, a real-data oracle, a numerical-only dataset, discriminator-strength variation, an XOR higher-order-dependency task, and a sampler-level check that the added module affects generated samples. However, the central diagnostic is operational and discriminator-dependent; its magnitude has no calibrated units, and the paper does not show a controlled curve relating dep to a known quantity of destroyed dependency. Five seeds give limited inferential power, and the use of parametric t intervals with four degrees of freedom remains fragile despite the authors' disclosure. The evaluation omits several potentially relevant generator families and does not compare against a broad set of current tabular synthesizers. Code and configuration files are promised upon acceptance, but no repository URL, model weights, or released dataset artifact is provided in the paper; the document is an arXiv preprint (v3, dated 5 August 2026), not a reported peer-reviewed final version. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL. Practical: The diagnostic uses conventional gradient-boosted trees and the generators use standard neural architectures, but the paper does not report hardware, wall-clock time, memory use, or an end-to-end deployment procedure, so commercial-hardware feasibility is not measured. Efficient: No runtime or compute comparison against linear C2ST, existing fidelity suites, or alternative discriminators is reported; the 168M-parameter sweep indicates that substantially larger models were run, but not at what cost. Effective: The evidence establishes that the diagnostic detects known zero-dependency corruption and that dependency is necessary for the tested TSTR minority-F1 utility, but it does not establish that the numerical size of the residual diagnostic gap predicts downstream performance. Scalable: The study covers datasets up to 48,842 rows and models up to 168M parameters, with a 16× parameter increase tested only on selected datasets; it does not evaluate 10×–100× larger tables, feature counts, sample counts, or production workloads. The work delivers a diagnostic methodology and promised code/configuration artifact, but no currently accessible software repository, CLI, library, trained model, or deployment artifact is stated. Strengths: - The fully factorized-reference experiment makes the metric-blindness failure concrete: linear C2ST scores of 0.995–1.000 can coexist with complete destruction of inter-column dependency. - The FF/oracle bracketing gives the operational decomposition an interpretable reference frame and avoids presenting discriminator contrasts as calibrated statistical divergences. - The paper separates dependency necessity for minority utility from the much weaker claim that residual dependency loss explains the generator's remaining utility shortfall; this prevents an overclaim that the measurements do not support. - The negative experiments are unusually informative: the paper reports that a 16× parameter increase and a discrete-aware cross-coupling module do not close the gap, while carefully excluding the under-optimized default width sweep and the inconclusive magic result from stronger claims. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that the decomposition is operational, discriminator-dependent, not necessarily non-negative, and not a fraction of a statistical divergence. They acknowledge that the diagnostic lacks calibration against controlled dependency destruction, that production-scale financial and clinical validation is absent, that the second-generator replication covers only two datasets, and that cross-component ordering is not stable across generators and datasets. They also state that the capacity conclusion rests mainly on adult and more weakly bank, that magic is inconclusive, that default fails the matched-optimization premise, that sampling discretization was not tested on real datasets, that H3 is supported by elimination rather than a direct dependency-supervision intervention, and that the method does not characterize which dependency structures are hard to recover or at what rate. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The strongest unresolved issue is construct validity: XGB-C2ST is itself a learned proxy whose dependency component may reflect classifier capacity, finite-sample artifacts, or interactions unrelated to downstream utility, and the paper does not compare it with kernel tests, higher-order moment/cumulant measures, mutual-information estimates, calibration tasks, or controlled synthetic distributions with known dependency strength. The evaluation uses only five public binary-classification datasets, with the strongest conclusions concentrated on adult and default, so generalization to high-cardinality categorical schemas, longitudinal tables, relational data, rare-event regimes, or privacy-constrained generation remains untested. The paper does not include a direct dependency-supervised objective, which is the proposed causal explanation and practical next step; consequently, the conclusion that the objective lacks gradient pressure remains plausible but not identified. The width sweep starts from an already 10.6M-parameter model and does not probe smaller capacities, training budgets, sampling NFEs, or alternative optimization schedules systematically. The comparison set also excludes many established tabular generators and does not report statistical comparisons across a broad set of strong baselines. Finally, the oracle is a real-data subsample and the fully factorized reference is empirical-marginal resampling; the paper does not quantify how finite reference sample size, discriminator retraining variability, or sample-size matching affects the reported decomposition. Bottom Line: This is a valuable diagnostic and empirical caution for tabular-generation evaluation, with credible evidence that common linear metrics miss dependency loss, but it stops short of a calibrated fidelity measure or a validated training intervention and should be read primarily by researchers auditing synthetic-data metrics rather than practitioners seeking a ready-to-deploy generator.

Co-Evolving Graph and Text Memory for Training-Free Multi-Hop Question Answering

H Man, TH Nguyen · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Co-E, a training-free multi-hop question-answering system that maintains and synchronizes textual and graph memories during inference. - Why it's important: Multi-hop answers often require later retrieval to depend on entities and relations discovered earlier, which static RAG contexts and fixed candidate graphs do not reliably support. - How it does it: Co-E alternates sub-question generation, dual-stream text/knowledge-graph retrieval, intermediate answer generation, and bidirectional memory synchronization that extracts text-to-graph triples and injects graph facts back into text memory. - The good: On six benchmarks, the Qwen3-8B MCTS variant reaches 72.6 EM on 2WikiMultiHopQA, 70.0 EM on Bamboogle, 52.5 EM on MuSiQue, and 74.9 Hits@1 on CWQ, with large Bamboogle ablation drops when synchronization or active maintenance is removed. - The missing: The evaluation lacks repeated-seed variability, cost-normalized comparisons, broad backbone sensitivity, and component ablations across more than one benchmark; MCTS also requires 204.1 LLM calls and 27.0K output tokens per Bamboogle question. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on training-free agentic RAG, multi-hop QA, or graph-text memory, but treat the practical advantage over strong competing systems cautiously because comparisons use heterogeneous backbones, metrics, and evaluation protocols.
Why this rank
Scored using the Systems profile. Novelty (82) and Non-Obviousness (85) are high because bidirectional synchronization of actively maintained graph and text memories provides a coherent answer to the problem of later-hop retrieval depending on earlier discoveries. Rigor (72) benefits from released code, multiple QA and KGQA benchmarks, explicit cost accounting, full-Wikidata testing, and informative synchronization ablations, but is reduced by heterogeneous baselines, no uncertainty estimates, limited cross-dataset ablations, and benchmark-provided topic subgraphs. Completeness (82) is strong because the authors quantify retrieval gaps, entity-linking failures, inference cost, and MCTS limitations; Resilience (72) is lower because matched backbone comparisons, branch-local memory controls, and cost-normalized evaluations are absent. Impact (78) reflects a reusable released system and a potentially influential training-free design, tempered by 204 LLM calls per question for MCTS and unclear production scalability. Weighted composite: 0.15*82 + 0.15*72 + 0.10*85 + 0.15*82 + 0.15*72 + 0.30*78 = 78.
