Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: The work addresses multi-hop question answering over unstructured text and structured knowledge graphs, where solving a later hop may require an entity, relation, or constraint uncovered during an earlier hop. Standard RAG typically fixes its retrieved context before reasoning, while graph-augmented RAG and KGQA often search a pre-built corpus graph or a benchmark-provided topic subgraph. These designs can fail to preserve bridge entities, revise noisy relational hypotheses, or expose graph-derived constraints to subsequent textual retrieval and generation. The target users are researchers and practitioners building knowledge-intensive QA systems that must combine corpus evidence with knowledge-base structure without task-specific fine-tuning. Key Idea: The central insight is to treat graph and text as a single shared, actively maintained working state rather than as independent retrieval channels. Textual evidence expands and revises the graph frontier through entity linking and relation extraction, while surviving graph triples are verbalized and written back into textual memory so that the next query and generation step can use explicit relational constraints. The contribution is therefore more specific than simply combining RAG with a knowledge graph: it makes bidirectional synchronization, consolidation, pruning, and re-injection occur within every reasoning step. Methodology: Given question q, Co-E maintains memory M(t) = (T(t), G(t)), where T stores self-contained retrieved snippets, intermediate answers, verifier feedback, and graph-derived statements, and G is a directed entity-relation graph containing canonical KB triples and open-vocabulary text-derived triples. Each iteration performs four stages: (1) request generation produces a focused sub-question conditioned on q and M(t); (2) corpus retrieval uses generated search queries with dense retrieval over Wiki23 or web search, followed by an LLM extractor that converts documents into atomic snippets, while graph retrieval links entities and issues k-hop SPARQL queries, reranks candidates, and retains up to 128 triples; (3) response generation produces an intermediate answer or reasoning state; and (4) synchronization first consolidates textual evidence, then links entities and extracts relations into G, prunes irrelevant, redundant, contradictory, or isolated edges, textualizes surviving graph facts, and runs a second textual consolidation pass. CoT uses this loop sequentially, whereas MCTS explores reasoning trajectories using a PUCT-style score, verifier rewards from no-context, text-memory, and graph-memory views, shared global memory, backpropagation, and up to 20 iterations with maximum depth 10. Critical design choices are the paired shared memory, bidirectional propagation, and active maintenance; the ablations support their importance, although the paper does not isolate the contribution of each individual prompt, reranker, extractor, verifier, or retrieval configuration beyond selected component removals. Key Results: On KGQA under the standard Freebase topic-subgraph protocol, Co-E MCTS obtains 85.5 Hits@1 on WebQSP and 74.9 on CWQ; CoT obtains 85.3 and 70.1. On text QA, MCTS obtains 61.8 EM on HotpotQA, 72.6 on 2WikiMultiHopQA, 52.5 on MuSiQue, and 70.0 on Bamboogle; CoT obtains 59.6, 70.1, 49.3, and 66.4. The reported comparisons include training-free and trained systems with 3B–70B or closed-source backbones, so the strongest comparisons are not always matched. Co-E MCTS exceeds the listed open-backbone baselines on the four text-QA datasets and is competitive with stronger or trained systems; on CWQ it slightly exceeds PoG at 74.9 versus 74.7 but remains below PoG on WebQSP at 85.5 versus 93.9. On Bamboogle, removing bidirectional synchronization reduces MCTS EM from 70.0 to 61.1, removing text-to-graph or graph-to-text propagation reduces it to 64.0 or 63.1, removing active maintenance reduces it to 49.5, and removing graph memory or textual memory reduces it to 54.8 or 55.0. The full-Wikidata stress test lowers MCTS from 85.5 to 78.6 on WebQSP and from 74.9 to 73.4 on CWQ. The system is computationally expensive: on Bamboogle it averages 204.1 LLM calls and 27.0K output tokens per question in MCTS mode, versus 58.0 calls and 7.8K tokens for CoT and 9.3 calls and 1.2K tokens for IR-CoT. A Qwen3.5-4B check on Bamboogle loses 1.8 EM for MCTS and 3.3 EM for CoT. The paper reports no uncertainty intervals or statistical tests. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION, NEW METHOD, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely distinctive contribution is the within-inference bidirectional synchronization of a textual working memory and a graph working memory with active consolidation and pruning; MCTS, dense retrieval, SPARQL querying, entity linking, relation extraction, and prompt-based verification are established components combined in this framework rather than individually new algorithms. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper provides useful implementation details, prompt templates, hyperparameters, role-level cost accounting, and an openly stated codebase at https://github.com/hieum98/wemg. It evaluates four text-QA and two KGQA benchmarks, includes CoT-versus-MCTS comparisons, modality and synchronization ablations, a full-Wikidata stress test, failure analysis, and one smaller-backbone check. However, ablations are concentrated on Bamboogle, with no systematic component study across datasets; multiple random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, and variance across stochastic LLM calls are not stated. The evaluation relies heavily on heterogeneous published baselines with different backbones, training regimes, retrieval sources, and metrics; some baselines report F1 rather than EM, and the supplementary Acc metric uses an LLM judge. The main KGQA results use benchmark-provided Freebase topic subgraphs, which materially constrain the retrieval problem, while the full-Wikidata experiment changes KB schema, identifiers, and aliases and is explicitly not a matched replacement. The public Wikidata endpoint, prompt-based extraction and consolidation, and numerous role-specific LLM calls introduce reproducibility and latency sensitivity. The system is not trained on the evaluation benchmarks according to the paper, but the extent to which prompts or hyperparameters were selected against these benchmarks is not stated. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS, because the paper builds and evaluates an inference-time QA system and releases a codebase. Practical: The system runs on commercially available hardware; the reported setup uses four NVIDIA A100 80GB GPUs, with Qwen3-8B served on two GPUs, FAISS and CPU evaluation locally, and either a local Virtuoso endpoint or public Wikidata. Efficient: It is substantially more expensive than ordinary iterative RAG: Bamboogle requires 204.1 LLM calls and 27.0K output tokens for MCTS, 3.5 times CoT output tokens and approximately 22 times IR-CoT output tokens; caching reduces repeated work but does not remove the underlying call count. Effective: The benchmark evidence shows improved exact-match or Hits@1 performance over the selected open-backbone comparisons, especially on compositional datasets, but 44.8% of manually inspected Bamboogle failures are retrieval gaps that synchronization cannot repair, so effectiveness remains dependent on evidence quality. Scalable: The paper tests standard benchmark sizes and a full-Wikidata retrieval setting, but it does not evaluate 10x–100x workload, graph, corpus, or concurrency scaling; the number of calls and SPARQL operations suggests that MCTS cost may grow substantially with reasoning depth. The work delivers a reusable software system and codebase, but no new dataset, trained model, or standalone library specification is reported. Strengths: - The paper identifies a concrete failure mode in existing multi-hop RAG—later retrieval cannot reliably use relational state discovered earlier—and maps it to a coherent graph-text memory design rather than merely adding graph retrieval. - The four-way synchronization cycle is operationally explicit: consolidation, text-to-graph propagation, graph-to-text propagation, and re-consolidation. This makes the proposed mechanism implementable and testable. - The Bamboogle ablations provide strong evidence that the reported gains are not explained solely by MCTS: removing bidirectional synchronization costs 8.9 EM for MCTS and 13.9 EM for CoT, while removing active maintenance costs 20.5 EM. - The paper reports both benchmark performance and failure/cost analyses. The finding that retrieval gaps account for 44.8% of Bamboogle MCTS failures usefully limits the claim that memory alone solves multi-hop reasoning, and the full-Wikidata experiment probes robustness beyond the standard topic-subgraph setup. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that synchronization cannot correct repeatedly retrieved false facts, with retrieval gaps accounting for 45% of Bamboogle errors; they also report incomplete chains at 21%, wrong entity linking at 14%, synthesis errors at 14%, and surface-form mismatch at 7%. They acknowledge dependence on entity linking and path selection, the absence of rollback semantics because MCTS shares global memory across branches, the high inference cost of MCTS, and the limited backbone study centered primarily on Qwen3-8B with a Qwen3.5-4B check only on Bamboogle. They propose cross-source checking, better disambiguation, hop constraints, chain verification, branch-local memory, early stopping, caching, adaptive CoT/MCTS routing, and broader backbone evaluation as future work. These limitations are confronted directly rather than omitted. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The strongest evidence for the core mechanism comes from one ablation benchmark, Bamboogle; the paper does not establish whether the same component effects hold on HotpotQA, MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA, WebQSP, or CWQ. - The system is compared against baselines with different model sizes, training data, retrieval sources, and metric conventions, making the claimed advantage difficult to attribute to memory synchronization rather than backbone or infrastructure differences. A matched Qwen3-8B baseline with the same retrieval budget and role prompts is not reported for every relevant alternative. - No wall-clock latency, dollar cost, peak memory, SPARQL query count, or throughput comparison is provided, despite the very high LLM-call count. Caching is described, but cache hit rates and end-to-end latency are not stated. - The shared-memory MCTS design can allow errors from one branch to influence other branches; the authors acknowledge the absence of rollback, but do not quantify contamination or compare against branch-local memory. - The training-free claim does not eliminate benchmark-specific engineering risk: prompts, thresholds, hop limits, top-k values, and the 128-triple pruning budget may have been selected using evaluation behavior, and tuning methodology is not documented. - The full-Wikidata test is informative but changes knowledge-base schema and answer normalization, so it cannot establish a clean improvement over the Freebase protocol or demonstrate open-domain robustness at genuinely large-scale graph retrieval. Bottom Line: Co-E is a useful and technically concrete contribution for researchers studying graph-text memory in training-free multi-hop QA, but its main practical claim is weakened by extreme MCTS inference cost, heterogeneous baselines, limited cross-dataset ablations, and the absence of variance and cost-normalized evaluation.

PG-LLM: Benchmarking General-Purpose Language Models for Protein Variant Ranking

RK Arora, LT Chen, M Du, D Marks, G Church · biorxiv.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces PG-LLM, a benchmark that evaluates 13 general-purpose language models on ranking protein variants and compares them with 95 published protein predictors across 217 ProteinGym assays. - Why it's important: Reliable variant prioritization can reduce the number of protein designs requiring expensive wet-lab testing, but it is unclear whether general-purpose models can substitute for specialized protein predictors. - How it does it: Each model receives an assay description, a wild-type sequence, and a shuffled set of 50 full-length mutant sequences, then produces a joint ranking without alignments, structures, retrieval, or external tools. - The good: Claude Opus 5 reaches nested-macro Spearman ρ = 0.406, exceeding 41 of 46 sequence-only predictors and 49 of 95 published comparators, while the post-knowledge-cutoff evaluation provides evidence that the result is not solely benchmark memorization. - The missing: The benchmark evaluates stratified samples of at most 50 variants rather than complete assays or prospective wet-lab hit rates, and the comparison gives specialist predictors additional inputs that LLMs do not receive. - Read it or not: Protein-design researchers and LLM-evaluation practitioners should read it for the benchmark design, contamination analysis, and candidate-list/test-time scaling results; readers seeking a deployable variant-effect predictor can skip it because specialist methods still perform better and the benchmark is a preprint.

Scored using the Empirical profile. Novelty (75) is strong for introducing a focused listwise benchmark and contamination-aware comparison of general-purpose LLMs with 95 protein predictors, while Non-Obviousness (78) comes from showing that tool-free LLM ranking is moderately competitive but degrades sharply with larger candidate lists. Rigor (82) is a major strength: the study spans 217 assays, 13 models, extensive specialist baselines, temporal evaluation, parser checks, scaling analyses, and released code and predictions, although the paper is a preprint and uncertainty relies mainly on three candidate draws. Problem & Motivation: Protein engineering requires prioritizing a small number of variants for experimental testing from large sequence libraries. Deep mutational scanning provides measured variant-function maps across activity, binding, expression, stability, and organismal fitness, but specialist predictors generally rely on protein-specific inputs such as multiple-sequence alignments, structures, retrieval, or family models. The unresolved question is whether general-purpose language models can interpret an assay objective and jointly rank candidate sequences without a dedicated protein-modeling pipeline. The paper targets this evaluation gap rather than a specific clinical variant-calling application; it does not evaluate clinical pathogenicity, indels, or iterative wet-lab optimization. Key Idea: The central insight is to test general-purpose LLMs through a listwise ranking interface rather than by converting them into conventional per-variant scoring models. The model must infer the assay objective, identify sequence differences, reason about biochemical and structural plausibility, and compare all candidates jointly. The benchmark uses identical candidate sets and the same nested-macro Spearman metric for LLMs and published predictors, while explicitly preserving the informational asymmetry between tool-free LLM inputs and specialist-model inputs. Methodology: PG-LLM uses all 217 substitution assays covering 186 proteins in ProteinGym v1.3, including 148 single-substitution and 69 multi-mutant assays. For each assay, variants are sorted by measured fitness, divided into ten fitness bins, sampled approximately evenly across those bins, shuffled, assigned opaque identifiers, and presented in sets of N = 10, 50, or 100; an exploratory condition uses N = 500 with one draw. Each prompt contains protein and organism names, a short assay description, the direction of better performance, the complete wild-type sequence, and complete mutant sequences, but no mutation notation, source publication, measurements, alignments, structures, retrieval, or programmatic tools. The 13 evaluated models are Claude Opus 5/4.8/4.7, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-5.5, GPT-5.4 mini/nano, Gemini 3.6 Flash, Gemini 3.5 Flash, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite, GLM-5.2, and Kimi K3, each evaluated at a provider-supported reasoning setting; the paper also reports within-family test-time-compute sweeps. Models return a JSON permutation, and rankings are scored with Spearman correlation against experimental fitness. The primary score is ProteinGym's nested-macro aggregation: assays are averaged within protein-functional-category cells, proteins within categories, and the five functional-category means receive equal weight; three fixed candidate draws provide the primary uncertainty estimate. The authors rescore 95 published predictors—46 sequence-only and 49 alignment/structure-based—on the same selected variants. Critical design decisions are fitness-stratified candidate sampling, listwise rather than independent variant scoring, and equalized nested-macro aggregation. These choices are reasonably motivated for comparing candidate-ranking behavior, but the authors acknowledge that they make absolute scores non-interchangeable with standard full-assay ProteinGym results. Key Results: At N = 50, Claude Opus 5 leads the raw LLM leaderboard with ρ = 0.406, standard error 0.002 across three draws, followed by GPT-5.6 Sol at 0.402, Claude Opus 4.8 at 0.356, Gemini 3.5 Flash at 0.343, GPT-5.5 at 0.336, and Gemini 3.1 Pro at 0.328. The apparent top-two ordering is coverage-sensitive: on 180 assays scored by both, Sol reaches 0.409 versus Opus 5 at 0.400; on 156 assays scored in all three draws, Sol reaches 0.415 versus 0.400. Opus 5 exceeds 41 of 46 sequence-only predictors and 8 of 49 alignment/structure predictors, but remains below the sequence-only median of 0.374? Actually its 0.406 exceeds that median, remains slightly below ESM2-650M at 0.411, below the alignment/structure median of 0.435, and well below VenusREM at 0.523. It beats ESM2-650M on 65 of 188 shared assays and VenusREM on 40; an oracle that selects the better model per assay improves over VenusREM by only 0.014, from 0.533 to 0.547. Candidate-list length substantially affects LLMs: GPT-5.6 Sol falls from ρ = 0.423 at N = 10 to 0.375 at N = 100, Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite falls from 0.300 to 0.083, and in the exploratory N = 500 condition Gemini 3.5 Flash and Gemini 3.1 Pro reach only 0.175 and 0.166, while Flash-Lite reaches −0.002; specialist references remain nearly flat across list sizes. Test-time compute improves all four reported model-family sweeps but with tapering gains: Sol rises from 0.322 at low effort to 0.402 at maximum effort, Opus 4.8 from 0.209 to 0.356, GPT-5.5 from 0.248 to 0.336, and Gemini 3.5 Flash from 0.254 to 0.343. Across 180 assays, LLM performance is nearly unchanged across low, medium, and high MSA-depth strata (0.313, 0.301, and 0.311), whereas sequence-only predictors rise from 0.309 to 0.380 to 0.411. Source-study recognition appears in 88% of Sol traces, 57% of Opus 4.8 traces, 45% of GPT-5.5 traces, and 9% of Gemini 3.5 Flash traces, but is not consistently associated with higher accuracy. In the 59-assay, 19-study post-1-February-2026 panel, Sol improves from 0.271 at low effort to 0.332 at maximum effort, slightly exceeding VespaG v2 at 0.323; Opus 4.8 reaches 0.290 at xhigh and Gemini 3.5 Flash reaches 0.255 at high effort. These temporal-holdout results support similar performance trends but do not establish absence of contamination for all models or all benchmark data. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, with a limited NEW EVALUATION FORMULATION: the main contribution is a public, listwise benchmark and controlled analysis of general-purpose LLMs against protein predictors, while the prompting, Spearman evaluation, ProteinGym data, and specialist baselines are largely existing components applied in a new comparative setting rather than a new prediction algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility: The study uses 217 assays, three fixed candidate draws for the primary benchmark, 13 LLMs, 95 published predictors, shared candidate sets, nested-macro aggregation, provider-coverage analyses, parser sensitivity checks, candidate-size sweeps, test-time-compute sweeps, protein-cluster bootstrap intervals, and a temporally separated 59-assay panel. The primary N = 50 outputs contained all identifiers, so strict and permissive parsers produced identical results; at N = 100, padding occurred in 37 of 6,790 cells and changed scores by at most 0.0033, whereas N = 500 required padding in 301 of 581 cells and was appropriately treated as exploratory. The paper does not report conventional multiple independent model-training seeds because the evaluated systems are fixed commercial or external APIs; uncertainty is primarily based on three candidate draws, and several top-model comparisons are affected by provider refusals or safety blocks. The source-recognition audit relies on one unvalidated LLM judge, and visible reasoning traces cannot establish the models' actual internal information sources. Published predictors retain alignments or structures while LLMs do not, so the comparison is matched in candidates and metric but not in inputs. Aggregate results, assay-level predictions, traces, scoring code, temporal-source metadata, and audit records are released at https://www.proteingymllm.com/ and through the PG-LLM GitHub repository; data assets for the 59 recent assays are available from the authors upon request rather than fully public. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL. Practical: The benchmark can be queried using commercially available hosted models and standard protein-prediction software, but per-query cost, latency, API availability, and hardware requirements are not reported. Efficient: The method can consume tens of thousands of output tokens at high reasoning settings and requires joint processing of all candidates, while no systematic cost, memory, throughput, or compute comparison with specialist predictors is provided. Effective: Evidence shows moderate ranking correlation on measured DMS candidate sets—up to ρ = 0.406 for Opus 5 and 0.332 for Sol on the recent-assay panel—but does not measure prospective wet-lab hit rate, calibration, absolute fitness prediction, or improvement in an engineering campaign. Scalable: Performance degrades as candidate lists grow, with Sol dropping from 0.423 at N = 10 to 0.375 at N = 100 and tested Gemini models reaching 0.166–0.175 at exploratory N = 500; behavior at 10×–100× larger lists or complete assays is not demonstrated. The work delivers a reusable benchmark, codebase, evaluation data, traces, and leaderboard rather than a standalone trained model or production variant-ranking tool. Strengths: - The benchmark isolates a meaningful capability—joint ranking from assay context and raw sequences—rather than relying on a generic biological question-answering score. - The comparison spans 13 general-purpose models and 95 protein predictors, with matched candidate sets and a protein/category-balanced aggregation that reduces domination by heavily represented proteins. - The candidate-list and test-time-compute experiments expose an important operational limitation: LLMs gain from reasoning but lose substantially when the ranking set becomes larger, unlike specialist predictors. - The temporal evaluation and source-recognition audit directly address contamination concerns, and the authors distinguish explicit source recognition from evidence of causal memorization. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that PG-LLM uses controlled, fitness-stratified samples rather than complete assays, so its scores are not interchangeable with standard full-assay ProteinGym scores. They acknowledge unequal model inputs and interfaces, possible ProteinGym exposure during pretraining, inability of trace audits to establish or exclude silent recall, provider refusals and changing coverage, parser padding problems in N = 500, and the limited scope to measured substitution variants. They explicitly note that the benchmark does not evaluate indels, clinical pathogenicity, wet-lab hit rate, or iterative engineering campaigns, and call for private evaluations on unpublished score tables. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The main unresolved issue is external validity: fitness-stratified sets of 50 candidates may make broad ordering easier than ranking all variants in a real library, and the paper does not report top-k enrichment, precision at experimentally affordable budgets, calibration, or prospective wet-lab validation. The specialist comparison is informative but not capability-matched because protein predictors receive alignments and structures while LLMs are deliberately denied them; controlled add-one-tool experiments would be needed to separate general reasoning from missing biological inputs. The primary uncertainty estimate uses only three candidate draws and does not provide confidence intervals or significance tests for most pairwise model differences, making the 0.406 versus 0.402 top ranking practically indistinguishable. API refusals create substantial missingness for the leading Claude and GPT models, and although shared-set analyses mitigate this, the missingness mechanism may still be correlated with assay content. The recent-assay panel is useful but small, includes two assays released before Sol's stated cutoff as boundary exceptions, and does not release all data publicly. Finally, the paper does not quantify inference cost or latency, both of which may dominate deployment decisions when high-reasoning runs consume tens of thousands of tokens. Bottom Line: This is a valuable and unusually careful benchmark study showing that tool-free general-purpose LLMs capture moderate protein-variant signal and outperform many sequence-only predictors, but practitioners should still use specialist protein models for reliable large-scale prioritization until full-assay, cost-aware, contamination-controlled, and prospective evaluations show otherwise.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a formal transformation from typed, case-associated message logs into prefix-closed global event logs and distributed communicating alphabets suitable for synthesising Petri-net-based Industry nets. - Why it's important: Organisations can often access inter-organisational message exchanges more readily than the private internal event logs needed for cross-organisational process mining, while message correlation and causal ordering remain difficult. - How it does it: It orders same-case message events using per-process timestamps and send/receive edges, enumerates finite downward-closed conversations and their linear extensions, then applies a finitely valued action function that preserves process roles and message complements. - The good: The formal correspondence is precise: for each finite conversation, the message-preserving assignment function induces an occurrence-level partial order isomorphic to the original message-event poset (Theorem 6), and the derived event log satisfies the required input-before-output-counting prefix property (Theorem 5). - The missing: The paper does not evaluate the construction on real message logs, quantify computational cost, compare discovered Industry nets with alternatives, or explain how action functions and case identifiers are obtained when they are unavailable or noisy. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on formal distributed process discovery or Petri-net semantics; practitioners seeking an evaluated mining system can skip it until the assumptions and construction are tested on operational data.

Problem & Motivation The work addresses cross-organisational process mining for distributed business processes whose component organisations exchange asynchronous typed messages. The target users are process analysts and researchers who cannot obtain private local event logs from all participating organisations and who therefore rely on message-service records, such as EDI or financial-services exchanges. Prior message-mining approaches generally reconstruct event logs operationally or analyse a particular middleware, protocol, or case study, but do not provide a general formal account of how message identities, local ordering, case boundaries, and asynchronous communication jointly determine a global event language suitable for distributed process discovery. The paper focuses on preserving causal relations rather than recovering unobserved internal actions. Key Idea The central insight is to treat a message log as a partially ordered set of message events and to represent its behaviour by all finite linear extensions of finite downward-closed same-case subsets, called conversations. A constrained action function then abstracts repeated message events into finitely many input/output action labels while preserving process partitioning and the complement relation between sending and receiving events. Message-preserving assignment functions recover the correspondence between abstract input and output occurrences; this allows the paper to prove that the causal order in the original message log survives abstraction. The idea is a formal composition of partial-order semantics, action relabelling, and asynchronous-channel assignment functions, rather than a statistical or data-driven inference mechanism. Methodology A message log K consists of a set of paired output/input events, with case, message type, process, and per-process natural-number time attributes. First, the paper defines an event relation that orders same-case events on the same process by local time and orders each message output before its corresponding input. It requires the log to be sound, meaning this relation is acyclic, and takes its reflexive-transitive closure as a partial order. Second, it defines a conversation as a same-case downward-closed subset of this poset and defines the event language EL(K) as the union of the linear extensions of all finite conversations. Theorems 1 and 2 establish that infinite conversations are represented through limits of finite prefixes and that EL(K) is finitary and prefix-closed. Third, an action function alpha maps message events to finitely many labels while satisfying disjointness across processes and input/output roles and a complement condition that maps paired events consistently. A message-labelling function with the channel property yields such an action function by event extension (Theorem 3), and together with a compatible type function produces an n-dimensional distributed communicating alphabet (Theorem 4). Fourth, the labelled event log alpha(EL(K)) is shown to satisfy the prefix property. Assignment functions match input occurrences with earlier complementary output occurrences; the message-preserving assignment function theta_C is defined for each finite conversation, and the induced occurrence-level order is proved isomorphic to the original conversation poset. Finally, the paper invokes the prior Industry-net synthesis procedure: if each projected local language belongs to the input family of a process-discovery algorithm, the resulting Industry net contains the derived global event log; equality additionally requires FIFO message preservation and completeness. The key design decisions—same-case ordering, downward closure, and finite action abstraction—are formally motivated, but their suitability for noisy or incomplete operational logs is not empirically justified. Key Results The paper reports formal results rather than experimental measurements. It proves that every infinite conversation is the limit of the finite languages of its finite subconversations (Theorem 1), that the event language EL(K) is finitary and prefix-closed (Theorem 2), and that a channel-consistent message labelling induces a valid distributed communicating alphabet (Theorem 4). The derived action language has the input/output prefix property (Theorem 5). For each finite conversation C, the message-preserving assignment function theta_C induces an occurrence partial order isomorphic to the original message-event poset (Theorem 6), and the labelled sequences from C equal the theta_C-linearisations and are contained in the less restrictive FIFO linearisations (Theorem 7). Under local-language membership assumptions, the prior synthesis procedure yields an Industry net whose language contains the derived event log (Theorem 8); equality is conditional on FIFO being message-preserving and on completeness (Theorem 9). Examples use two-process OTC settlement traces with two message types and two or four messages, but no benchmark, dataset, runtime, model-size, accuracy, conformance, or scalability numbers are provided. The baselines are not empirical methods; the paper mainly compares message-preserving and FIFO assignment semantics. Novelty Classification NEW FORMULATION, NEW METHOD, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING: none. The genuine contribution is a formal method and set of correctness theorems for translating paired message logs into causal global event languages and then applying existing distributed Petri-net synthesis; the construction reuses Enterprise/Industry nets, action languages, and synthesis machinery from the authors' prior work rather than introducing a new discovery algorithm or dataset. Rigor & Reproducibility The paper gives explicit definitions, assumptions, examples, and proofs for its central lemmas and theorems, including an appendix proof for the infinite-poset limit result. The central causal-preservation argument is stronger than an illustrative claim because Theorem 6 establishes poset isomorphism for each finite conversation. However, there are no experiments, ablations, complexity analyses, error bars, multiple seeds, statistical tests, implementation details, or public code/data/model releases mentioned. Reproducibility is therefore limited to reconstructing the mathematics from the paper. The method assumes that every message has correctly paired output and input events, case assignments are known and accurate, per-process timestamps are unique and causally consistent, the log is sound, and a suitable finite action function is already available. It does not address action-label discovery, missing or duplicated messages, clock errors, mis-correlation across cases, or noisy logs. The claimed Industry-net synthesis is also conditional on local projections belonging to the discovery algorithm's language family and, for exact equality, on completeness; these conditions are not checked on data. Deployability: (4-property check) Profile: THEORETICAL. The paper's primary contribution consists of definitions, formal languages, and proofs, with no primary experimental or deployed-system claim. - Sound: The main results are stated with explicit assumptions such as acyclicity, finite process dimension, paired message events, and compatible action/type functions; the presented proofs cover the principal claims, although the practical validity of the assumptions is not tested. - General: The framework applies to finite or countably infinite logs with asynchronous bilateral channels, but remains restrictive about complete pairing, reliable case identifiers, unique local timestamps, and a fixed finite action abstraction. - Tight: The causal-preservation theorem is an exact isomorphism for message-preserving assignments, while the FIFO result is only an inclusion and can admit additional linearisations; no lower-bound or complexity-tightness analysis is provided. - Implementable: The definitions suggest an implementable pipeline and can feed the prior synthesis algorithm, but the paper provides no implementation, complexity bound, or evidence that action-function construction and language enumeration are tractable at operational scale. The work stops primarily at paper form: it delivers a reusable formal construction and proof framework, not a released library, CLI, dataset, trained model, or evaluated mining tool. Strengths - It isolates a precise semantic problem—preserving causality when message identities are abstracted into repeated input/output actions—and proves the relationship rather than relying on informal trace diagrams. - The use of finite downward-closed conversations gives a coherent treatment of potentially infinite message logs while retaining the finitary, prefix-closed language expected by the downstream Petri-net synthesis framework. - The distinction between message-preserving assignment functions and FIFO assignment functions exposes exactly what causal information is lost during abstraction: the former reproduces the original conversation poset, whereas the latter permits additional reorderings. - The construction composes cleanly with prior Enterprise/Industry-net discovery results and states explicit sufficient conditions for language inclusion and equality instead of claiming unconditional exact recovery. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly note that the derived global event logs contain no internal actions, that infinite conversations are handled through finite prefixes, that action functions must use finitely many labels, and that abstraction removes message identities so causal relations must be represented through assignment functions or channel policies. They also state that equality between the derived language and the synthesised Industry-net language requires FIFO to be message-preserving and the event log to be complete. The discussion presents these as scope conditions, but does not experimentally investigate their frequency, consequences, or failure modes in real logs. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The action function is an input to the method, yet identifying which messages represent occurrences of the same local action is likely the main practical mining problem; the paper offers a consistency criterion but no inference algorithm or evaluation. - The sound-log assumption excludes precisely the data-quality issues common in distributed logging, including missing receives, duplicate records, inconsistent case IDs, clock anomalies, and cross-case event interleavings; no repair or uncertainty model is provided. - There is no complexity or scalability analysis for enumerating finite conversations, linear extensions, labelled languages, or assignment functions; these sets can grow combinatorially even for small traces. - The paper does not compare its formal pipeline with existing EDI/web-service process-mining systems, event-correlation techniques, partial-order mining methods, or alternative distributed process models. - The Industry-net result is inherited conditionally from prior work and guarantees language inclusion rather than measured discovery quality, conformance, precision, or usefulness; no real organisational case study demonstrates practical impact. - The construction uses local timestamps to order all same-case events on a process, while the paper acknowledges that execution order may be coincidental rather than causally required; the resulting over-ordering is not quantified or mitigated. Bottom Line This is a rigorous formal extension of the authors' distributed Petri-net synthesis framework to message-log inputs and is worth reading for researchers studying causal semantics and distributed process discovery, but it is not yet a practically validated process-mining method and offers no evidence that it outperforms existing message-log tooling.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces JAXBench, a 50-workload TPU v6e benchmark suite and evaluation harness for measuring LLM-generated Pallas kernel correctness and speed relative to XLA and hand-tuned TPU kernels. - Why it's important: TPU kernel optimization lacks a shared, production-relevant target, limiting reproducible comparison and slowing progress on hardware-specific ML performance engineering. - How it does it: It combines production operators from MaxText with translated fused operators from KernelBench, sizes workloads for high MXU utilization, and evaluates generated kernels through compilation, bf16 correctness checks, and device-side profiling with iterative or beam-search feedback. - The good: With Gemini 3 Flash, TPU-specific documentation raises per-sample correctness from 5.8% to 37.3%, while Autocomp reaches 1.36× geometric-mean speedup over XLA and solves 45 of 50 benchmarks. - The missing: The evaluation uses one TPU v6e chip, a single primary model, fixed 144-sample budgets, and no multi-chip, cross-hardware, cost-normalized, statistical, or strong-agent comparison. - Read it or not: TPU/JAX systems researchers and developers of accelerator-code agents should read it for the benchmark and failure analysis; readers seeking a new kernel-generation algorithm can largely skip it because the main contribution is infrastructure and empirical characterization.

Problem & Motivation: ML workloads increasingly depend on low-level kernels tuned to specific accelerator architectures, but TPU kernel optimization has no GPU-benchmark analogue with production-scale workloads, saturated hardware, and expert references. The target users are researchers building autonomous code-generation agents and engineers optimizing JAX workloads on Google TPUs. Existing GPU-oriented suites do not transfer directly because TPU execution, Pallas/Mosaic programming, memory spaces, systolic tiling, prefetch scheduling, and grid traversal differ substantially from CUDA/Triton. The paper argues that prior Pallas benchmarks are insufficiently representative: MultiKernelBench uses TPU v2-8, does not target JAX or production LLM operators, and employs shapes that may be too small to saturate the MXU. Key Idea: The central insight is to benchmark TPU kernel agents in the compute-relevant regime while explicitly separating two bottlenecks: TPU-specific information needed to produce correct Pallas code and search structure needed to improve a correct kernel. JAXBench operationalizes this by choosing the smallest per-workload shapes whose XLA baseline reaches at least 60% MXU utilization, then comparing documentation-conditioned iterative search with Autocomp's translation-plus-optimization beam search. Methodology: JAXBench contains 17 priority operators extracted from MaxText implementations of Llama-3.1, DeepSeek-V3, Mixtral, Mamba-2, RetNet, and AlphaFold2, plus 33 fused operators translated from KernelBench Level 2 into idiomatic JAX. The translated workloads are validated against their PyTorch references on matched bf16 inputs using `jnp.allclose` with `atol = rtol = 10^-2`; failed translations are regenerated or repaired before inclusion. Candidate implementations are Pallas kernels generated from the XLA/JAX reference. The harness JIT-compiles each workload, runs five warmups and 50 profiled iterations, extracts device-side `jit_*()` timings from `jax.profiler`/Perfetto traces, and reports median latency. Candidates must first compile and pass numerical correctness; incorrect or missing candidates receive a 1× aggregate speedup floor. The baseline is XLA-compiled JAX, with eight of the 17 priority workloads also compared against Tokamax Pallas kernels whose block sizes were tuned over 203 configurations. Four agent strategies are evaluated: independent best-of-N sampling, iterative refinement using compiler/correctness/profiler feedback, iterative refinement augmented with Autocomp's TPU documentation context, and Autocomp's two-phase beam-search pipeline. The primary evaluation uses Gemini 3 Flash with 144 samples per benchmark; a five-kernel model-capacity ablation uses Gemini 3.1 Pro. The 60% MXU-utilization threshold is a consequential design choice and is motivated by avoiding launch-bound tasks, but it biases the suite toward large, compute-oriented shapes. The bf16 tolerance is practical but does not establish broader numerical robustness. The use of an LLM to translate and select KernelBench workloads is described, although the paper does not quantify translation-selection bias. Key Results: On all 50 workloads with Gemini 3 Flash, best-of-N obtains 1.01× geomean speedup and correct kernels on 13/50 benchmarks; plain iterative refinement obtains 1.18× and 32/50; iterative refinement with TPU context obtains 1.28× and 48/50; and Autocomp obtains 1.36× and 45/50. Autocomp causes 76% of benchmarks to beat XLA at the final budget, while the context-only iterative method solves more benchmarks but spends more samples on correctness recovery. Across pooled samples, TPU context raises per-sample correctness from 5.8% to 37.3%; API/runtime failures remain 59.8% for iterative-plus-context and 55.8% for Autocomp. On eight workloads with hand-tuned Tokamax references, the hand-tuned kernels reach a 2.08× floor-1 geomean over XLA, compared with 1.60× for Autocomp and 1.34× for iterative-plus-context. Autocomp fails correctness on paged and ragged-paged attention, while it exceeds the hand-tuned reference on sparse attention and Megablox GMM in the reported configurations; these comparisons are workload-specific and do not establish superiority over expert kernels generally. The hand-tuned references achieve particularly large gains for memory-bound attention, including 6.91× on ragged-paged attention and 3.91× on flash attention, whereas GEMM shows no gain over XLA at 0.96×, consistent with XLA already saturating compute. On the five-kernel Gemini 3.1 Pro ablation, geomean speedups are 1.07× for best-of-N, 2.43× for iterative, 3.82× for iterative-plus-context, and 3.79× for Autocomp; the latter two methods produce correct kernels on all five tasks. This ablation is too small to support a general model-scaling conclusion. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING; the benchmark and profiler-grounded TPU harness are the primary original contributions, while the evaluated agents combine existing iterative-feedback, documentation-conditioning, and beam-search techniques rather than introducing a new kernel-generation algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility: The study provides a standardized workload interface, explicit prompts in the appendix, device-side timing intended to exclude host dispatch overhead, 50 timing iterations per workload, correctness gates, XLA baselines, and expert Pallas references for eight tasks. Code, the benchmark, evaluation harness, and baseline results are stated to be released at https://github.com/AI-Hypercomputer/accelerator-agents/tree/main/JAXBench. The paper reports no multiple random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, significance tests, or repeated runs across independent TPU devices. It uses a single primary LLM, Gemini 3 Flash, and compares against only a limited set of agent baselines; AlphaEvolve and KernelEvolve are explicitly left for future work. The 144-sample budget is equalized for most methods, but Autocomp early-stops and can use fewer samples, complicating strict compute-budget comparisons. The benchmark construction uses Gemini for PyTorch-to-JAX translation and an LLM-based filter for context selection, creating possible model- or prompt-dependent bias. XLA and Tokamax are relevant baselines, but the hand-tuned references cover only eight workloads and are not necessarily optimal for every exact shape or sparsity pattern. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS, because the paper releases a runnable benchmark and evaluation harness and evaluates generated kernels on TPU hardware. Practical: The workloads and harness run on commercially available Google Cloud TPU v6e hardware, but deployment requires TPU access, JAX/Pallas/Mosaic compatibility, and a cloud-hosted Gemini model for the reported agent results. Efficient: The generated kernels can improve device latency by 1.36× geomean over XLA with Gemini 3 Flash and up to 1.60× on the eight-reference subset, but the paper does not report LLM inference cost, TPU compilation cost, total search time, energy, or cost-normalized performance. Effective: The evidence shows meaningful single-device latency gains on selected JAX operators, especially memory-bound attention, but does not demonstrate end-to-end model throughput, training time, inference service performance, or quality-preserving behavior beyond the stated bf16 pointwise tolerance. Scalable: The paper evaluates only one TPU v6e chip and explicitly excludes multi-chip sharding, collectives, communication overlap, and topology-aware scheduling; behavior at 10×–100× workload or device scale is not measured. The work delivers a reusable benchmark, dataset-like workload suite, profiling/evaluation tool, baseline kernels, and reported results rather than a generally deployable autonomous optimizer. Strengths: - Establishes a TPU-native benchmark with 50 workloads spanning production LLM operators, emerging sequence-model and scientific operators, and fused standard operators rather than merely porting small GPU tasks. - Uses per-workload shape selection and roofline/MXU analysis to avoid evaluating predominantly launch-bound workloads; the stated 60–95% MXU-utilization range for many fused workloads makes the speedup target more technically meaningful. - Provides a useful decomposition of agent failure: documentation materially improves Pallas correctness, while Autocomp's search allocation improves optimization after a correct seed exists. - Uses device-side profiling and includes eight tuned Tokamax references, allowing generated kernels to be compared both with a reproducible compiler baseline and with expert-written implementations. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that all workloads run on a single TPU v6e chip, that multi-chip sharding and collective communication are out of scope, that hand-tuned references exist for only eight of 17 priority operators, and that the Gemini 3.1 Pro study covers only five kernels. They identify multi-TPU evaluation, collective-aware optimization, fine-tuning or reinforcement learning from execution feedback, and hybrid search controllers as future work. They also acknowledge that the Pro results are preliminary and that generated methods still trail expert kernels on important attention workloads. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The paper does not test robustness across TPU generations, chip instances, compiler/JAX versions, input distributions, or shape variants, so the benchmark may reward tuning to one v6e configuration and one fixed shape per operator. The 60% MXU-utilization construction rule can exclude memory-bound or small-shape workloads where production latency may still matter, while the reported geometric means floor incorrect and slower results at 1×, masking failure severity and potentially overstating aggregate utility. The use of a single vendor model and vendor-linked TPU documentation leaves open whether the findings generalize to open models or independently authored context. There is no cost-normalized comparison of Autocomp versus iterative refinement, no variance analysis over model sampling, and no end-to-end validation that operator speedups translate into application-level gains. The paper also does not report whether generated kernels remain correct over broader numerical ranges, multiple dtypes, noncanonical masks, or dynamic shapes, nor does it compare against a human optimization time budget or stronger general-purpose search agents. Bottom Line: JAXBench is a useful and likely reusable evaluation foundation for TPU kernel-generation research, with credible evidence that documentation and search allocation matter, but its single-v6e, single-model, single-shape evaluation makes the empirical conclusions narrower than the paper's broader claims about autonomous TPU optimization.

Problem & Motivation The work addresses the gap between generating code that passes functional tests and generating code that is fast under realistic workloads. The problem affects code-generation models used for competitive programming, automated software engineering, and performance-sensitive programming: standard RL with verifiable rewards primarily optimizes a binary correctness signal and does not reliably teach algorithm selection, data-structure choice, or implementation efficiency. The paper cites external evidence that correctness and efficiency diverge, including an 81% correctness rate but only 4.1% of expert speedup on SWE-fficiency, and large drops from pure-correctness to complexity-constrained scores on Venus and BigO(Bench. Its specific research gap is not merely the absence of a timing reward; it is the lack of a training-compatible timing signal that remains informative under noisy execution, weak or short test suites, sparse rewards, reference-distribution mismatch, and unstable policy optimization. The authors frame optimization RL as a coupled measurement, reward-design, and optimizer-stability problem in a one-shot generation setting, where the model must produce an optimized solution from the problem statement without iterative execution feedback. Key Idea The central insight is that execution time becomes learnable only when the entire transformation from program to policy update is engineered as a reliable signal. The paper therefore treats test construction, timing infrastructure, environment intervention point, reward composition, and GRPO statistics as one system rather than adding raw runtime to an existing correctness reward. The most consequential conceptual choice is to separate correctness tests from large-input optimization tests, then condition optimization credit on correctness and compare timing to problem-specific human references instead of using absolute seconds. The main online result comes from post-execution per-test percentile ranking with a binary top-30% gate, although pre-execution filtering and ranked timeout environments also work. This is a system-level synthesis of known ingredients more than a single new algorithmic primitive. Methodology The pipeline starts from 12,275 DeepMind Code Contests problems and retains Python tasks with both correct and incorrect human submissions. The authors re-execute human solutions, de-duplicate against evaluation benchmarks, generate additional correctness and optimization tests using a CWM 32B input-generator model, infer expected outputs through agreement among verified human solutions, and filter tests, solutions, and problems for false positives, failures, exceptions, timeouts, and positive-control attrition. This yields 2,723 cleaned problems, of which 1,302 satisfy a duration-filterability criterion based on robust coefficient of variation at least 0.3; the final RL split contains 1,000 training and 302 test problems. Correctness tests enforce semantic validity, while larger optimization tests aim to create runtime spread. Candidate code is executed through CES, a dedicated remote sandbox with a 1 GB memory limit and 10-second cap. Stored human-reference durations are mapped to the current CES state using an affine calibration, d_fresh = 0.6306 d_stored + 0.0529, estimated with leave-one-problem-out validation. The authors compare three environment families: pre-execution filtering of optimization tests by absolute duration, relative duration, or character length; intra-execution time limits, including absolute, relative, and ranked-reference limits; and post-execution ranking using per-test percentiles or a leaderboard percentile against human solutions. Rewards consume correctness, an optimization gate, and optionally a graded quality signal. The principal reward choices are correctness-gated binary collapsed rewards and two-gate rewards; additive blends, optimization-only rewards, multitask objectives, continuous quality scores, and bucketed variants are ablated. An offline simulator replays human solutions and stored durations through the same environment code path to screen candidate configurations using AUC, steepness, monotonicity, deviation from the diagonal, and noise. Online training uses asynchronous GRPO. Critical modifications include more same-prompt rollouts, larger training batches, centering but not standard-deviation-normalizing group returns, a token-weighted prompt baseline, fixed 32,768-token loss normalization, a 30-step freshness cutoff, and no replay buffer. These choices are empirically motivated by zero-advantage groups, timing noise, stale service states, and long incorrect trajectories, although several are supported mainly by targeted ablations rather than a unified theoretical analysis. Key Results On DMC-Optim, standard RLVR with the original tests reaches 43.5% p100, 18.0% p50, 7.7% p30, and 1.9% p10 pass@1 for Qwen 2.5 7B. The strongest post-execution per-test percentile reward reaches 46.2%, 31.3%, 19.1%, and 6.0%, respectively; relative to the p30 baseline this is approximately a 150% improvement, while p100 remains close. For Qwen 2.5 32B, standard RLVR reaches 54.8%, 21.1%, 9.4%, and 2.4%, while the same configuration reaches 55.7%, 39.6%, 24.2%, and 8.5%, corresponding to relative improvements of 88%, 157%, and 254% at p50, p30, and p10. For CWM 32B, standard RLVR reaches 69.8%, 30.7%, 13.7%, and 3.3%; the post-execution top-30% configuration reaches 70.2%, 50.4%, 30.9%, and 9.8%, giving 64% and 126% relative gains at p50 and p30. Pass@10 also improves, indicating that the change is not solely a pass@1 selection effect: for Qwen 2.5 7B, p50 pass@10 rises from 41.1% under standard RLVR to 56.1% under the strongest post-execution configuration. Naive raw-duration rewards are much weaker: on optimization tests they improve p30 by only 17.2–19.4% relative to the enriched correctness baseline and remain roughly 42% below the ranked p30 reward; on base tests they reduce p30 by 10.8%. Relative-timeout environments improve strict scores but reduce p100 correctness by roughly 17–27% in the reported ablations. On out-of-distribution LiveCodeBench, timeout-based percentile evaluation is too insensitive, so the paper reports speed win rates against each model's standard-RLVR baseline. CWM 32B reaches up to 83.0% median-passing-sample speed wins and 66.3–68.1% best-passing-sample wins, with p@1 declining from 56.4% for standard RLVR to approximately 53.8–54.2% for the strongest post-execution configurations. The model-analysis study uses GPT-OSS 120B to classify blinded code pairs; among 174 classifiable optimization-RL versus RLVR pairs, optimization RL wins 89% of speed-win comparisons, with 47% attributed to I/O improvements, 34% to constant-factor changes, 6% to algorithm refinements, 6% to mathematical shortcuts, 2% to data-structure changes, and 1% to full algorithm changes. The judge identifies complexity improvements in 13% of optimization-RL wins over RLVR, versus 22% for humans; optimization RL beats the fastest available human in 33% of classified speed-win cases and does so with a complexity improvement in 7% of cases. These latter classifications are weaker evidence because 22% of model-versus-RLVR speed wins are unclassifiable and the judge identifies the faster program with only 68% accuracy overall, although manual checking of classifiable complexity labels reports 94.8% accuracy. Novelty Classification The contribution is best classified as NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and an ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION, with a partial NEW METHOD classification: DMC-Optim, its test-generation and duration-filterability pipeline, the CES calibration protocol, the offline environment simulator, and the demonstrated recipe for stable timing-based GRPO are new as a combined artifact and empirical methodology, whereas the individual components—GRPO, correctness-gated rewards, human-relative runtime ranking, remote execution, and batch stabilization—are largely existing ideas recombined for one-shot code optimization. Rigor & Reproducibility The paper provides unusually extensive ablations across data construction, timing backends, environment families, reward forms, model sizes, evaluation thresholds, calibration parameters, difficulty slices, and sandbox perturbations. It includes comparisons against standard RLVR on base tests, enriched correctness-plus-optimization tests, naive linear/log runtime rewards, multiple pre-/intra-/post-execution environments, and several reward compositions. It reports uncertainty estimates: single-run training-time 95% confidence-interval half-widths are approximately 1.1–1.4 points at p50 for the main 10k-step Qwen 7B/CWM 32B settings, while bootstrap test-set uncertainty for CWM 32B is approximately 4.3 points at p50. The main p50 and p30 improvements exceed the reported training variability by several multiples. However, the asynchronous runs remain stochastic, several headline configurations appear to rely on averaged or selected runs, and the simulator is screened against only 20 online Qwen 7B environments; the authors explicitly state that it is useful for pruning degenerate settings but not validated as a reliable predictor of full learning curves. Qwen models are decontaminated against the relevant benchmarks for SFT, but CWM 32B uses a released SFT checkpoint whose exposure to DMC-derived material cannot be fully controlled. The evaluation is also partly coupled to the training construction: DMC-Optim rankings use human reference solutions and a calibrated sandbox that define both the reward and the primary metric. The paper text lists licenses and dataset/model assets but does not state a public code, dataset, or model-weights URL for the complete reproducible artifact; CES itself is described as pre-existing infrastructure rather than released by this work. Reproduction therefore requires substantial compute, a compatible remote execution service, generated tests, stored human timings, and calibration data. Deployability: (4-property check) Profile: SYSTEMS, with substantial EMPIRICAL evaluation; the paper builds and evaluates a full data-generation, remote-execution, reward, and training stack rather than only proposing an abstract method. Practical: The method can run on commercially available H100-class GPUs and CPU execution infrastructure, but the main runs require 8 H100 nodes for about one day at 7B and 32 H100 nodes for about 1.5 days at 32B, plus a separately provisioned CES service, so it is practical for well-funded research or production teams rather than ordinary developers. Efficient: Optimization-test execution adds about 15% rollout-generation overhead relative to RLVR on the same optimization tests, and optimization RL is within 5% of enriched-test RLVR in wall-clock time; relative to base-test RLVR, the full enriched pipeline costs about 25% more training time, while data construction, calibration, and remote infrastructure remain substantial costs. Effective: The evidence shows improved correctness-gated speed on DMC-Optim and pairwise speed transfer on LCB, with p100 mostly preserved in-domain, but LCB p@1 decreases by up to approximately 3.6 points for Qwen 7B and hard-problem p@1 decreases by about 13% for CWM 32B, so effectiveness is demonstrated for the benchmark proxy rather than production software performance. Scalable: The method transfers from Qwen 7B to Qwen 32B and CWM 32B, but it has not been tested at 10x–100x the prompt pool, model scale, repository size, or execution workload; the RL experiments use only about 1,000 training prompts and roughly 30 passes over that pool, and the authors present scaling beyond this regime as an expectation rather than a measured result. The work delivers a benchmark/data artifact in DMC-Optim, a timing and calibration pipeline, an offline simulator, and a training recipe; the paper does not clearly state that a complete public software repository, CES service, trained checkpoints, or the full 117 GB corpus is released. Strengths - It identifies and empirically isolates a real failure chain: short tests and additive timing noise, incompatible local execution, poorly shaped correctness-speed rewards, sparse GRPO advantages, and stale asynchronous batches. The local-versus-CES study is especially strong: repeated local rankings move by 41.2 percentile points peak-to-peak on average, while local-to-CES correction has negative cross-validated R2 across 36,660 pairs. - The DMC-Optim construction separates semantic correctness from optimization workload and uses verified correct and incorrect human solutions as positive and negative controls. Generated tests reduce mean false-positive rate from 8.27% to 2.11% on a 257-problem diagnostic subset, while explicit filtering acknowledges that augmentation can reduce correct-solution pass rates and can introduce invalid or overly aggressive tests. - The reward study provides a useful empirical result: correctness-gated binary or collapsed objectives outperform raw continuous timing, additive blends, multitask mixtures, and optimization-only rewards in the reported setting. This directly tests the claim that preserving correctness in the reward is more important than exposing a smoother runtime scalar. - The main improvements are large relative to reported training variability, appear across three model starts and two model sizes, persist across difficulty strata and evaluation criteria, and transfer to LCB pairwise speed comparisons. The qualitative analysis also finds some genuine algorithmic and mathematical improvements rather than only faster I/O. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly limit the study to single-file Python competitive-programming problems, fixed human reference pools, noisy wall-clock timing, and short-horizon one-shot generation. They state that DMC-Optim does not cover repository-scale profiling, memory optimization, multi-language systems code, or long-horizon edit loops. They acknowledge the cost of stronger test generation, many sandbox executions, calibration, and large-scale RL. They report that LCB tests are too short for stable absolute timeout evaluation and that optimization RL can remove interface or wrapper code useful to benchmark harnesses, partly because the training setup removes instruction-following rehearsal. They also acknowledge that the judge-based improvement analysis is conditioned on GPT-OSS labels, excludes 22% of speed wins as unclassifiable, and may underrepresent interesting improvements. Finally, they note that fixed human references may not generalize and propose generated, learned, or adversarially refreshed reference distributions as future work. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The primary benchmark, reward, and evaluation all use the same human-reference timing ecosystem, so the strongest DMC-Optim results may partly reflect adaptation to a fixed reference distribution rather than general runtime optimization. The LCB transfer is useful but uses pairwise comparisons against the corresponding standard-RLVR model, not an independent absolute performance standard. - The central duration-filterability threshold, test-generation thresholds, reward percentile choices, and environment-selection procedure are extensively swept. Although the offline simulator reduces online cost, the paper does not provide a fully held-out benchmark for selecting these design choices, leaving some risk of benchmark-specific tuning and Goodhart effects. - The paper does not compare against strong contemporary alternatives on equal compute, such as iterative execution-feedback refinement, performance-aware supervised fine-tuning, preference optimization over slow/fast correct pairs, inference-time search, or other online execution-reward RL systems. The comparison against standard RLVR and naive duration rewards establishes necessity within the proposed framework but does not establish superiority over the broader code-optimization literature. - The main gains are measured through percentile pass@k thresholds defined by the same human pool used to construct timing rewards. Absolute runtime distributions, memory use, CPU architecture sensitivity, language portability, and energy cost are not evaluated. The claim that the approach will transfer to C++ or real repositories is plausible but unmeasured. - The CWM 32B results have weaker contamination control than the Qwen results because the authors cannot verify that the released SFT and midtraining data exclude DMC-derived problems and training prompts. This does not invalidate the within-model comparison, but it reduces confidence in the cross-model interpretation. - Evaluation-time calibration can change strict p10 scores by about 35 percentage points while preserving relative ordering. This is a serious limitation for absolute headline numbers: the method demonstrates robust relative improvements under the tested calibration sweeps, but the reported percentile scale is not an invariant measurement of model quality. - The fallback and service-state analysis reveals bursts where CES-only execution falls to 54.3% and local fallback reaches 41.6% for logged intervals. The paper uses conservative conversions and freshness filtering but does not run a controlled replay study that quantifies how these service events alter policy updates or whether the main gains survive systematically under injected timing noise. - The model-learning analysis relies on an LLM judge to classify optimization mechanisms and selects best-of-20 passing samples. It is therefore descriptive rather than causal, and it does not show how frequently the policy changes algorithmic behavior on ordinary single-sample generation or how those changes behave under unseen input distributions. Bottom Line This is a strong and unusually careful systems/empirical paper for execution-grounded code RL: its benchmark and measurement methodology are valuable, and its large in-domain speed gains are credible relative to the reported baselines, but practitioners should treat it as a well-supported recipe for competitive-programming Python rather than evidence that RL has solved general software-performance optimization.

Learning from Failures: Retrieval-Centric CoT via Hard Negatives for Unified Multimodal Retrieval (26 ▲ )

Zelong Sun, Jun Wang, Kaicheng Yang, Tiancheng Gu, Ziyong Feng, Zhiwu Lu · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 7 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces UniME-R1, an embedder–adviser retrieval system that uses initial retrieval failures to generate Retrieval-Centric Chain-of-Thought (RC-CoT), then either reranks the initial candidates or performs refined full-corpus retrieval. - Why it's important: Fine-grained attributes, relations, temporal events, and document details are often lost by single-pass multimodal embeddings, causing expensive retrieval systems to return semantically plausible but incorrect candidates. - How it does it: A dual-mode Qwen3-VL embedder retrieves an initial top-k set, while a retrieval-aware adviser analyzes each candidate, predicts whether the target is already present, and generates discriminative correction cues when it is not. - The good: On MMEB-V2, UniME-R1 reaches 69.9 with a 2B embedder and 70.3 with a 4B embedder, improving over the strongest reported baselines by 3.1 and 1.4 points, respectively; candidate-side processing is reported as 27× faster than Embed-RL. - The missing: The evaluation does not establish robustness at genuinely large production-scale corpora, and the hard negatives, teacher annotations, rewards, and training data are all derived from MMEB-V2 or model-generated judgments, leaving contamination and judge-induced bias insufficiently tested. - Read it or not: Multimodal retrieval researchers and practitioners evaluating reasoning-augmented embedding pipelines should read it for the failure-conditioned routing design and ablations, while readers seeking deployment evidence beyond benchmark-scale experiments can defer it.
