Problem & Motivation Non-invasive MEG decoders can retrieve short perceived-speech segments from large audio candidate sets, but their learned weights generally do not correspond to identifiable cortical locations, rhythms, or temporal response profiles. This limits the use of decoding models as scientific instruments: high retrieval accuracy does not establish whether the model relies on acoustic envelope cues, phonetic or lexical information, narrative context, or stimulus-locked ocular and cardiac artifacts. The work targets naturalistic perceived-speech decoding in healthy listeners and seeks to close the interpretability gap between flexible deep models and classical electrophysiological source analysis. The prior gap is specifically the lack of a high-performing whole-head MEG speech decoder whose internal spatial and temporal filters can be related to the forward model of cortical sources while also testing which stimulus-associated information affects retrieval. Key Idea The central idea is to make the first decoder stage a collection of jointly learned spatial–temporal branches, with each branch treated as an interpretable source-like component rather than an arbitrary latent channel. A branch's spatial pattern is recovered using the covariance of temporally filtered MEG, rather than by interpreting the raw spatial filter alone; the resulting pattern is then projected into cortical source space. This architecture is paired with matched feature-present and feature-absent MEG substitutions, allowing the authors to separate generic signal replacement damage from the effect of removing MEG associated with a particular speech feature. The novelty lies primarily in combining an existing theoretically motivated factorized interpretation framework with a strong naturalistic, non-invasive MEG retrieval task and a dedicated intervention analysis. Methodology The input is a 3-second, 208-channel MEG segment sampled at 100 Hz, paired with an audio segment beginning 150 ms earlier to account for auditory latency. The authors use 27 English-speaking participants and 49 participant-session recordings from MEG-MASC. Ocular and cardiac ICA components are removed; recordings are resampled, baseline-corrected, robust-scaled, standardized, and clipped. The audio target is a sequence of wav2vec 2.0 Base embeddings with 768 feature channels, and the model is trained with a one-directional MEG-to-audio contrastive cross-entropy objective. Similarities are computed after L2 normalization and division by a learned temperature; duplicate audio targets within a minibatch are handled as one positive target rather than as mutual negatives. The front end first maps 208 sensors to 270 virtual channels using fixed-layout real spherical harmonics up to degree 23, yielding 576 basis functions per virtual channel. A shared 1 × 1 unmixing transformation is followed by a subject-specific projection into K = 25 branches. Each branch then receives a depthwise 15-tap temporal convolution, corresponding to 150 ms at 100 Hz. The main model uses two residual temporal convolutional blocks and a convolutional head that maps the branch representation to the wav2vec trajectory. Three critical design decisions are reasonably motivated: subject-specific projections address inter-subject sensor geometry and anatomy; spherical harmonics encode the approximately spherical MEG helmet geometry; and branch-wise temporal filtering makes source interpretation sensitive to both spatial topography and temporal dynamics. However, the physical superiority of spherical harmonics is supported more by modeling rationale than by a large empirical advantage, since the reported 3D-versus-2D gain is approximately one percentage point. For interpretation, the effective participant-specific spatial filter is the product of the subject, unmixing, and attention matrices. For branch k, the spatial pattern is estimated as g-hat-k proportional to R-h-k w-k, where R-h-k is the covariance of MEG filtered by that branch's temporal kernel. Temporal patterns are computed from the lag-embedded branch signal and its covariance, and spectra are obtained from the temporal-pattern Fourier magnitude. The spatial patterns are mapped with an MNE inverse solution using an fsaverage template, ico4 source space, a boundary-element head model, loose orientation constraints, depth weighting, and fixed regularization. Cross-participant patterns are analyzed with SVD, RAP-MUSIC, and complete-linkage clustering over joint cortical-map and temporal-spectrum similarity. The stimulus-use analysis tests 19 acoustic, phonetic, lexical, and contextual features. For eligible test windows, marked intervals are replaced with real MEG donors from the same participant and session, using matched feature-present and feature-absent donor pairs. Five donor pairs are averaged per query. The primary statistic is the difference in the correct candidate's retrieval rank between feature-absent replacement and feature-present replacement. Participant-level effects are tested with 100,000 sign-flip permutations and one-sided max-T familywise-error correction across features. This design controls some generic replacement effects, but it does not isolate independent causal contributions because feature masks overlap and covary. Key Results The main K = 25, two-block model achieves 39.75 ± 0.34% Top-1 and 70.40 ± 0.31% Top-10 accuracy among 1005 candidates across six independently trained solutions. The seed-42 main checkpoint reports 40.01% Top-1 and 70.60% Top-10 with 486,619 trainable parameters. A K = 15 model reaches 39.51% Top-1 and 70.23% Top-10 with 380,769 parameters. The closest tested high-capacity configuration, K = 270 with five blocks, has 7,210,224 parameters but reaches only 36.41% Top-1 and 67.46% Top-10 under the authors' controlled protocol. The authors compare these figures with Défossez et al.'s 41.3% Top-1 and 70.7% Top-10 among 1363 candidates and Zhang et al.'s reported 39.6–41.9% Top-1 and 69.2–71.1% Top-10 among 1464 candidates, but correctly note that those studies use word-aligned windows and different artifact preprocessing, so the comparisons are not direct. Accuracy rises rapidly from one branch to a plateau around K = 10–25; removing the attention layer costs approximately 4–5 percentage points, replacing spherical-harmonic attention with planar attention costs approximately one point, and removing temporal context costs approximately one point. Subject-specific spatial mapping produces the largest ablation degradation. Retrieval increases with paired segment duration: for the two-block model, Top-1 is 14.37% at 1.5 s, 28.03% at 2.25 s, 39.94% at 3 s, 52.66% at 4 s, and 62.20% at 5 s; corresponding Top-10 values are 41.00%, 59.52%, 70.84%, 80.31%, and 86.33%. This experiment demonstrates the value of longer paired MEG and audio segments, not neural-context integration alone, because both modalities are lengthened together. The feature-compression experiment shows that a learned target projection can reduce the wav2vec feature dimension from 768 to approximately 12 with essentially unchanged retrieval; the seed-42 LinearDR-12 model reports 39.95% Top-1 and 70.54% Top-10. PCA-based reduction performs substantially worse at low dimensions, indicating that high-variance wav2vec directions are not the same as the MEG-relevant directions. Temporal compression behaves differently: reducing the target trajectory to 32 or 8 time points causes clear degradation, while global mean, max, additive-attention, gated-attention, and query-attention pooling produce near-chance retrieval. Thus, the evidence supports a compact feature subspace but not a temporally collapsed segment summary. Paired occlusion yields corrected positive effects for 15 of 19 features. The largest rank differences are silence, 75.62; high loudness, 60.77; vowels, 38.70; and strong acoustic onset, 36.19, all with pFWER < 10^-4 and positive effects in all 27 participants. Additional positive effects occur for fricatives, 12.80; stops, 9.27; sibilants, 7.94; high surprisal, 7.34; pseudowords, 1.71 with pFWER = 0.022; silence offsets, 1.60; liquids/glides, 1.21; nasals, 1.18; word onsets, 1.02; schwa, 0.96; and combined silence edges, 0.91. There is no corrected positive evidence for high predictive entropy, pFWER = 0.069; silence onsets, pFWER = 0.316; rare words, rank difference −2.98; or random word lists, rank difference −17.77. The negative random-word-list effect is counter-intuitive: replacing MEG recorded during random word lists with narrative MEG improves retrieval, suggesting that coherent narrative structure supplies more recoverable information than isolated words, although this remains an interpretation of an intervention contrast rather than a direct measure of semantic processing. Source analyses identify distributed common-template patterns in bilateral auditory and superior temporal regions, posterior/dorsal-stream areas, frontal opercular and inferior frontal regions, and medial temporal regions. Clustering yields 49 spatial–spectral clusters, with the 12 largest showing median within-cluster correlations of 0.51–0.67 for cortical maps and 0.63–0.72 for temporal spectra. Left-lateralized branches show a low-frequency component below 10 Hz plus a weaker approximately 13.3-Hz component, whereas right-lateralized branches are dominated by a roughly 6.6-Hz component. Because the filters contain only 15 samples at 100 Hz, the effective frequency resolution is approximately 6.7 Hz, making the hemispheric spectral interpretation suggestive rather than definitive. Novelty Classification NEW METHOD, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL: the paper combines spherical-harmonic spatial attention, subject-conditioned compact spatial–temporal branches, source-space weight interpretation, and paired MEG occlusion for naturalistic speech retrieval; the individual components largely extend prior factorized neural decoding and contrastive MEG-to-speech methods rather than introducing a fundamentally new learning objective. Rigor & Reproducibility The study provides substantial controlled ablations over branch count, convolutional depth, attention parameterization, subject conditioning, unmixing, temporal filtering, filter support, segment duration, feature-space compression, and temporal compression. The main retrieval result averages six independently trained solutions and reports small seed variability, with Top-1 standard deviation approximately 0.34 percentage points. The paired occlusion analysis is repeated across six seeds, and all 15 positive seed-42 features remain positive and significant under the same criterion in all six models; the negative random-word-list contrast remains negative in all six. The feature analysis uses participant-level sign-flip inference, 100,000 permutations, and max-T familywise-error correction, and it does not treat repeated donor substitutions as independent observations. The evaluation nevertheless has important limits. Most architectural sweeps and compression experiments use seed 42 only, and the paper does not report confidence intervals or multiple-seed results for every ablation. The dataset contains one MEG corpus, 27 participants, and a test set drawn from later pieces of the same Black Willow narrative used in development, so generalization to new speakers, stories, languages, recording sessions, or acquisition sites is not established. Test windows are generated with a fixed stride and may overlap in time, which can reduce the effective independence of candidate segments. The external baselines use different candidate counts, word alignment, preprocessing, and target representations, preventing a clean head-to-head comparison. The authors release code at https://github.com/ivsemenkov/LISA/, the MEG-MASC dataset is publicly available, and ICA components are provided at https://osf.io/3wrft/; the project page is https://ivsemenkov.github.io/LISA/. Model weights are not stated as publicly released. Deployability (4-property check) Profile: EMPIRICAL, because the paper trains and evaluates a neural MEG decoder rather than primarily proving a theorem or reporting a deployed infrastructure system. - Practical: The model trains on a single NVIDIA Tesla V100 32 GB GPU and uses publicly available MEG data and code, so it is runnable on commercially available hardware, although it requires calibrated MEG acquisition and participant-specific recordings. - Efficient: The main decoder has 486,619 trainable parameters, approximately 20× fewer than the compared 9,565,054-parameter decoder, but the paper does not report inference latency, memory use, or end-to-end preprocessing cost. - Effective: The model solves the held-out within-corpus retrieval task with 40.01% Top-1 and 70.60% Top-10 accuracy among 1005 candidates and produces interpretable source-associated patterns, but evidence for actual phoneme, word, semantic, or clinical decoding is indirect because the target is audio-embedding retrieval. - Scalable: The method is tested across 27 participants, 49 recordings, up to 5-second windows, and 1005 candidates, but it is not tested at 10×–100× candidate, participant, narrative, language, or acquisition scale; cross-dataset and cross-session scalability is therefore not demonstrated. The work delivers a reusable software artifact and analysis pipeline, including the LISA codebase and stimulus-occlusion/source-localization procedures, but it does not deliver a validated clinical tool, real-time system, or released trained model. Strengths - It addresses an important interpretability problem at the level of the measurement model: spatial filters are interpreted through temporally filtered covariance and then mapped through an MEG inverse model, rather than ranked solely with post-hoc saliency. - The compact branch bottleneck is empirically supported: K = 15–25 retains nearly the full retrieval score, while the 14.8× larger K = 270, five-block model performs 3.60 Top-1 points worse under the controlled evaluation. - The paired feature-present/feature-absent donor design is more informative than comparing occluded inputs only with unmodified inputs, because it controls for generic damage caused by replacing real MEG segments. - The paper separates feature-axis and temporal-axis compression and obtains a non-obvious result: the decodable target feature space is approximately 12-dimensional, whereas preserving within-window temporal structure remains essential. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly state that the analysis uses a single corpus with 27 participants and does not establish replication on new narratives, architectures, corpora, or evaluation protocols. They acknowledge that the factorized front end cannot represent fully space–time-inseparable cortical waves. They also state that stimulus features overlap and covary, donor substitutions can alter correlated states, and rank differences should not be interpreted as calibrated neural encoding strengths. Finally, they acknowledge that source maps use a common fsaverage anatomy and shared coregistration rather than participant-specific forward models, which limits anatomical precision; individual anatomy was available for only six participants with successful surface reconstruction. Analyst-Identified Gaps The paper does not provide a matched reimplementation of the strongest prior decoder under identical preprocessing, candidate construction, target representation, and window alignment, so the claim of comparable accuracy remains partly protocol-dependent. It also does not evaluate cross-narrative generalization: development and testing use different pieces of Black Willow but remain within the same story, leaving open whether the decoder retrieves novel speech based on neural representations or exploits story-, speaker-, recording-, or acoustic-distribution-specific regularities. The use of fixed-stride, potentially overlapping candidate windows may inflate the effective difficulty or dependence structure relative to independent segment retrieval, and the paper does not quantify this. Source localization is presented as physiologically plausible but lacks participant-specific localization validation, localization uncertainty estimates, or comparison against independently measured auditory responses. The occlusion analysis controls generic donor replacement but does not match donors jointly on all correlated acoustic and linguistic variables, so claims about individual feature reliance remain weaker than the corrected p-values suggest. Finally, the interpretation of 6.6-Hz and 13.3-Hz hemispheric components is under-resolved by the 15-tap filters and is not tested with the longer-filter models or with an independent participant-level replication. Bottom Line This is a strong and useful preprint for interpretable neural decoding because it shows that near-benchmark naturalistic MEG retrieval can coexist with source- and dynamics-aware analysis, but its neuroscientific conclusions should be treated as hypothesis-generating until replicated across narratives, participants, anatomies, and independent datasets.

JoyAI-Video-Edit: Real-Time Open-Ended Video Editing with Autoregressive Diffusion (75 ▲ )

Yicheng Xiao, Wenxun Dai, Xinran Qin, Lin Song, Maoquan Zhang, Hang Xu, Yukang Chen, Yitong Li, Guohui Zhang, Yuan Zhang, Xuying Zhang, Tommy Zhang, Jianlong Yuan, Peihao Li, Shuai Lu, Siming Fu, Chuyang Zhao, Xin Han, Jie Huang, Wenbo Li, Guoqing Ma, Wei Huang, Xiaojuan Qi, Haoyang Huang, Nan Duan · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 5 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces JoyAI-Video-Edit, a 16B-parameter causal autoregressive diffusion system for open-ended instruction-guided video editing that processes incoming 720p video at approximately 30 FPS. - Why it's important: Existing high-quality video editors generally require future frames, fixed-length clips, or expensive iterative denoising, which prevents low-latency editing during live broadcasting, communication, and interactive content creation. - How it does it: The system combines chunk-wise causal attention with bounded KV caching, resampling-based autoregressive training, source-anchored distribution-matching distillation for two-step generation, and long-horizon rollout optimization. - The good: On the authors' one-minute LongV2VBench, it scores 3.30 overall versus 1.71 for the strongest reported streaming baseline and achieves 30.19 FPS at 720×1280 on one Nvidia B200 GPU. - The missing: The long-video benchmark and paired training data are largely author-constructed or synthetically generated, while human evaluation uses only videos shorter than 10 seconds and the paper reports no error bars, multiple-seed variation, or independent evaluation of open-ended streams beyond one minute. - Read it or not: Researchers working on causal video diffusion, streaming generation, or interactive video systems should read it for the source-anchored distillation and deployment design; readers seeking independently validated real-world editing quality should treat the results as preliminary because this is an arXiv preprint with limited external evaluation.

Problem & Motivation The work addresses causal, low-latency video-to-video editing in settings where frames arrive continuously, the total duration is unknown, and the editor must preserve source identity, geometry, motion, and unedited regions while applying an instruction. This problem affects live broadcasting, video communication, interactive entertainment, telepresence, and real-time content creation. Offline diffusion editors can use bidirectional temporal context and iterative denoising, but they cannot emit results before future frames are available and their memory and computation typically grow with clip length. Independently processing short windows causes redundant computation and boundary discontinuities. Causalization introduces a second problem: the model is trained with clean target history but consumes imperfect self-generated history at inference, causing errors and source drift to accumulate. The paper targets the combined gap of causal generation, bounded state, source-faithful few-step inference, and long-horizon stability. Key Idea The central insight is to use the aligned current source chunk as an explicit fidelity anchor during distillation, while using generated history primarily for continuity. Source-Anchored Distribution Matching Distillation applies classifier-free guidance independently along the text-conditioning and source-fidelity axes to construct a source-sharpened teacher target; this guidance is used only during training and is absorbed into a two-step generator, so deployment requires only one conditional branch. The approach combines this with bounded causal history and long-horizon autoregressive optimization to address temporal drift rather than treating streaming as independent short-clip editing. Methodology The system contains an MLLM condition encoder, a causal video VAE, and a multimodal diffusion transformer. The MLLM encodes the first source frame and editing instruction, while the VAE maps source video, optional reference images, and target videos into a shared latent space with temporal compression of 8 and spatial compression of 24×24. Foundation training proceeds through text-to-image pretraining, text-to-video training, image-editing training, and bidirectional V2V/IV2V editing training. The bidirectional editor uses flow matching: for target latent z0, noise epsilon, and noise level sigma, it forms z_sigma=(1-sigma)z0+sigma epsilon and trains with the squared velocity loss ||v_theta(z_sigma,sigma;c,z_s,z_r)-(epsilon-z0)||². The model is then adapted to chunk-wise autoregression, using one latent frame or eight video frames per chunk, bidirectional attention within a chunk, causal attention across chunks, a fixed sliding history window, and the first chunk as a global sink. Training initially uses clean-history teacher forcing and then resampling forcing, which regenerates detached historical chunks with model predictions to approximate the inference history distribution. For acceleration, DMD uses a causal generator, trainable fake-score model, and frozen real-score model; SA-DMD modifies the real-score target as v_cond + w_txt(v_cond-v_-txt) + w_src(v_cond-v_-src), where the source-free branch omits the aligned source latent. The distilled generator uses two denoising steps. Long-Horizon Autoregressive Distillation performs segmented SA-DMD optimization over extended rollouts, clearing graphs between clips while accumulating gradients; mirror looping extends conditioning when rollouts exceed source-video length. Deployment uses FP8 quantization, operator fusion, compilation, optimized VAE execution, pipelining, pseudo-encoding, and cached clean KV states. The fixed context, source anchor, and two-step distillation are the key design decisions; the paper motivates each, but does not provide extensive sensitivity studies for window size, source-guidance weight, chunk length, or rollout horizon. Key Results On OpenVE-Bench, a Gemini multimodal judge scores the 720×1280 system 3.60/5 overall. It outperforms streaming baselines SANA-Streaming at 2.62, LiveEdit at 2.00, Xmax-X2.0 at 1.87, and StreamDiffusionV2 at 1.23, while remaining close to offline systems such as Bernini-R at 3.72 and Kling-3.0 Omni at 3.64. JoyAI-Video-Edit scores 4.47 on local change and 4.06 on local removal, matching the best reported local-change result and exceeding all listed methods on local removal, but it does not lead on background change, where SANA-Streaming reports 3.20 versus 2.90. The authors construct LongV2VBench with 229 one-minute editing tasks across background change, global style, local addition, local modification, and local removal. On this benchmark, JoyAI-Video-Edit scores 3.30 overall, compared with 1.71 for Xmax-X2.0, 1.64 for SANA-Streaming, 1.23 for LiveEdit, and 1.21 for StreamDiffusionV2; it ranks first in every category. Its full-pipeline throughput is 30.19 FPS at 720×1280, compared with 20.90 FPS for Xmax-X2.0 at 832×1440, 14.51 FPS for SANA-Streaming at 704×1280, 15.45 FPS for LiveEdit, and 18.07 FPS for StreamDiffusionV2. On an 81-frame input, full-pipeline latency is 2.68 seconds, with 2.18 seconds attributed to the DiT and 0.405 seconds to the VAE; the reported per-chunk request-to-response latency is 226 ms and the complete cycle is 266 ms. Human pairwise evaluation uses single-shot videos shorter than 10 seconds: JoyAI-Video-Edit receives 90%, 87%, 81%, and 87% preference against LiveEdit, SANA-Streaming, Xmax-X2.0, and StreamDiffusionV2, respectively, but only 48% against Bernini-R versus 44% for Bernini-R, and 35% and 34% against Seedance 2.0 and Kling-3.0 Omni, respectively, versus 56% for each competitor. The ablation reports that SA-DMD raises LongV2VBench overall from 2.81 to 3.23 and global style from 3.61 to 4.24, LHAD raises overall to 3.06, and combining both reaches 3.30. The strongest evidence is therefore against relatively weak streaming baselines and on an author-created benchmark; comparisons across resolutions, hardware, implementation maturity, and model size limit direct interpretation. Novelty Classification NEW METHOD, NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely new methodological element is the source-anchored use of independent text and source-fidelity guidance inside autoregressive DMD, combined with segmented long-horizon distillation for video editing; bounded causal attention, resampling forcing, DMD, KV caching, quantization, and VAE optimization are established ideas adapted and integrated into this setting. LongV2VBench is a new one-minute benchmark, although its construction and independence from the authors' training pipeline require closer scrutiny. Rigor & Reproducibility The paper includes a component ablation for SA-DMD and LHAD, and it reports automatic, human, quality, latency, and throughput evaluations. However, it reports no confidence intervals, standard deviations, multiple random seeds, statistical tests, evaluator counts, judge prompts, or human-study protocol details beyond pairwise voting. The authors use a Gemini multimodal judge for OpenVE-Bench and a benchmark whose long-video data are constructed by the authors; the paired editing training data are also synthesized through keyframe propagation, latent-shared I2V, filtering, and MLLM recaptioning. This creates potential evaluator and data-construction bias and makes independent generalization difficult to assess. Streaming baselines are evaluated at different resolutions and, for SANA-Streaming, the authors explicitly use a public implementation that is slower than the original paper's reported implementation. The paper states that code is available at https://github.com/jd-opensource/JoyAI-Video-Edit, but it does not state that model weights, training data, LongV2VBench, evaluator code, or complete deployment configurations are released. The paper also lacks ablations for history-window size, global-sink design, source-guidance weight, two-step versus more-step inference, FP8 effects, synthetic versus real paired data, and training-horizon length. Deployability: (4-property check) Profile: EMPIRICAL and SYSTEMS. Practical: The authors demonstrate execution on commercially obtainable but high-end Nvidia B200 hardware, but do not report requirements, performance, or quality on less expensive GPUs or multi-user serving configurations. Efficient: The system reaches 30.19 FPS end to end at 720×1280 with a 16B model, two-step denoising, FP8 execution, bounded KV caching, and optimized VAE paths; the comparison is favorable against the reported streaming implementations, although hardware and optimization parity are not fully established. Effective: Automatic scores, ablations, and short-video human preferences support improved editing quality and source preservation, but the main long-horizon evidence relies on a new author-built benchmark and the human study does not test sustained streams. Scalable: The architecture keeps per-chunk computation and cache size bounded with stream duration, but the paper directly evaluates only one-minute videos and does not measure behavior at 10×–100× longer durations, higher concurrency, changing instructions, dropped frames, or distribution shifts. The work delivers an open-source code artifact and a trained 16B system according to the paper; release of weights and benchmark data is not stated. Strengths - It addresses a concrete systems bottleneck—causal, source-faithful editing under bounded latency—rather than merely applying an offline editor to independent windows. - SA-DMD identifies and operationalizes a meaningful tension between generated-history continuity and source fidelity, and the ablation shows substantial gains, especially for global style and local change. - The method integrates algorithmic and systems contributions coherently: causal chunking, source anchoring, long-horizon training, KV reuse, FP8 inference, and VAE optimization jointly produce a measured 30.19 FPS pipeline. - The evaluation includes a sustained one-minute benchmark and compares against both streaming and offline systems, exposing a long-horizon failure mode that standard sub-10-second benchmarks miss. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The paper does not contain a dedicated limitations section. It implicitly acknowledges that paired video-editing data are difficult to collect and therefore uses synthetic construction and filtering, and it limits the principal long-video evaluation to one-minute videos. It does not explicitly discuss failure cases, quality degradation beyond one minute, hardware cost, source-guidance trade-offs, benchmark bias, or the limitations of automated and short-video human evaluation. Analyst-Identified Gaps The largest concern is evaluation independence: both the paired training data and LongV2VBench are author-constructed, while the benchmark's generation and filtering pipeline uses related editing models and MLLM-based quality checks. The paper does not establish that LongV2VBench is held out from model development or that its prompts and content are free of leakage. Human evaluation covers only clips shorter than 10 seconds, so the claim of long-term consistency is supported mainly by Gemini scores on the authors' benchmark rather than by human judgments over sustained streams. The paper omits error bars and statistical reliability for all headline quality results, does not report the number or demographics of human evaluators, and gives insufficient detail for reproducing the judge evaluation. Baseline comparisons are confounded by different resolutions, model sizes, hardware, and deployment implementations; closed-source vendor results are particularly difficult to audit. The claimed open-ended behavior is not tested at substantially longer durations, under instruction changes during a stream, or under source videos with difficult motion, occlusion, text, or camera cuts. Finally, the paper does not quantify memory consumption, power use, cost per processed minute, or quality loss from FP8 quantization and two-step distillation. Bottom Line This is a technically substantial systems paper with a credible source-anchored distillation idea and strong reported streaming results, but its practical and scientific claims should be accepted provisionally until independent datasets, longer human evaluations, reproducible baselines, and statistically supported experiments validate performance beyond the authors' one-minute benchmark.

#23 — Highly Innovative (76)

Linear representations of grammaticality in neural language models

J Li, N Kim · arxiv.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a mass-mean linear probing framework for detecting grammaticality in the hidden sentence representations of pretrained neural language models and evaluates it across 25 models, 67 BLiMP datasets, additional English benchmarks, and five non-English languages. - Why it's important: It addresses whether apparent syntactic competence in language models reflects an internal grammaticality distinction rather than only sentence likelihood, plausibility, lexical frequency, or other acceptability-related factors. - How it does it: It subtracts the mean hidden representation of ungrammatical examples from that of grammatical examples to form a single probe direction, then tests held-out classification, cross-phenomenon transfer, probability-controlled fitting, acceptability controls, and cross-linguistic transfer. - The good: The strongest evidence is that probes trained on one grammaticality dataset generalize across phenomena and remain successful after probability-related manipulations, with model-level success increasing strongly with scale and reaching 94.0% of BLiMP datasets for Qwen3-14B. - The missing: The experiments do not establish that the decoded direction is a causal or syntactic representation rather than a robust correlational feature induced by benchmark construction, training-data artifacts, or residual acceptability cues. - Read it or not: Researchers studying probing, syntactic generalization, or computational models of grammar should read it for its deconfounding design, while readers seeking evidence of human-like grammatical competence should treat the conclusions as substantially stronger than the measurements warrant.
Why this rank
Scored using the Empirical profile. Novelty (76) and Non-Obviousness (78) are strong because the work turns grammaticality into a transferable representation-level diagnostic and systematically tests probability, plausibility, phenomenon, and language confounds. Rigor (82) is supported by 25 models, 67 BLiMP datasets, held-out transfer, repeated fitting subsets, shuffled nulls, localization controls, and released code, although preprint status, possible benchmark contamination, and limited uncertainty reporting reduce confidence. Completeness (84) and Resilience (76) are helped by unusually candid acknowledgment that linear decodability is not causal syntactic competence, but the claims remain vulnerable to template artifacts, residual acceptability cues, layer-selection assumptions, and benchmark dependence. Impact (48) is moderate because the method is a useful research diagnostic but does not improve model behavior or provide a production artifact; the weighted composite is approximately 76.

Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: The work addresses the long-standing question of whether neural language models distinguish grammatical from ungrammatical strings as an internal property, rather than merely assigning higher probability to strings that are more frequent, plausible, familiar, or compatible with world knowledge. This matters to computational linguistics and cognitive science because probability-based targeted syntactic evaluation cannot cleanly separate grammaticality from correlated sentence properties, and because claims that language models model human linguistic knowledge presuppose a reliable measure of grammatical competence. The specific gap is an evaluation method that examines internal representations and tests whether a grammaticality signal survives controls for string probability, sentence similarity, semantic plausibility, factuality, imageability, and related acceptability factors. Key Idea: A grammaticality distinction can be tested as a low-complexity geometric property of model representations: if grammatical and ungrammatical sentences differ in their class means, the vector between those means should define a linear direction that classifies held-out examples and transfers across phenomena. The paper’s main interpretive move is to treat successful cross-phenomenon and cross-language transfer, together with resistance to probability and acceptability controls, as evidence for a coherent grammaticality dimension rather than a collection of benchmark-specific cues. This is a plausible diagnostic, but linear decodability alone does not demonstrate that the direction corresponds to a causal mechanism or to syntactic knowledge. Methodology: The authors evaluate 25 publicly available autoregressive models from GPT-2, Llama, OLMo, Pythia, and Qwen3, ranging from 14 million to 14 billion parameters. They use BLiMP and SCaMP for English grammaticality, LI-Adger for fitting mixed acceptability contrasts, DGL, RUBLiMP, ZhoBLiMP, and CLAMS for additional grammaticality tests, and Shades, Drive, and Truth for extra-grammatical controls. For each sentence, they extract hidden states from the final hidden layer, using the critical token span, the token immediately before the critical span, or the final punctuation token; representations are mean-centered by token position. The mass-mean probe computes class means \(\mu_0\) and \(\mu_1\), forms \(\theta = \mu_1-\mu_0\), and classifies an example using \(\sigma(\theta^T x)\), with grammaticality assigned when \(\theta^T x>0\). Most probes use 1,600 fitting sentences and held-out evaluation; each setup is repeated over 100 random fitting subsets. Probe success requires both a Holm-Bonferroni-adjusted Welch test against a label-shuffled null and at least a 5 percentage-point advantage over that null. Experiment 1 tests transfer from LI-Adger to all BLiMP datasets and compares representation-based and probability-based minimal-pair measures. Experiment 2 tests localization at pre-critical, critical, and final regions and 40-by-40 cross-dataset transfer, while regressing accuracy against length, lexical overlap, and representation similarity. Experiment 3 constructs counter and favour fitting sets by selecting from the highest- and lowest-probability sentence subsets. Experiment 4 tests transfer to plausibility, conceivability, factuality, imageability, arousal, and related variables, compares plausible and implausible SCaMP conditions, and removes shared directions through boundary tilting. Experiment 5 tests within- and cross-language transfer across English, German, French, Hebrew, Russian, and Mandarin Chinese. The central design choices—mass-mean probing, held-out transfer, and explicit null/deconfounding conditions—are well motivated; the choices of final-layer representations, benchmark-derived labels, and linear residualization are less fully justified and constrain interpretation. Key Results: In Experiment 1, all 25 models show some successful grammaticality probes, but success varies from 13.4% of the 67 BLiMP datasets for Pythia-14M to 94.0% for Qwen3-14B. Model size correlates with success rate at \(R=0.928\), with global accuracy at \(R=0.950\), and with accuracy conditioned on successful probes at \(R=0.942\). Representation-based minimal-pair accuracy is generally below probability-based accuracy in small models, but the difference ranges from -13.4 to +6.89 percentage points and reverses for some datasets in larger models; the difference correlates with log parameter count at \(R=0.791\), \(p<0.001\). In Experiment 2, probes succeed at the critical and final regions but not the pre-critical control; final-region success ranges from 7.81% for Pythia-14M to 94.38% for Llama-3.1-8B. Model size accounts for 51.5% of variance in critical-region success and 59.0% in final-region success. Removing within-phenomenon transfers reduces success by only 4.06 percentage points in the critical region and 2.20 points in the final region, although within-phenomenon accuracy remains higher by 14.0 and 6.64 points, respectively. Sentence length, word overlap, and representation similarity correlate with accuracy, but regressed estimates remain above the null. In Experiment 3, probability-controlled fitting produces small accuracy changes: the largest reported drop in the counter condition is 3.19 points, and the counter condition generally preserves probe success. In Experiment 4, grammaticality probes transfer to extra-grammatical datasets only 11.2% of the time on average, compared with 55.9% for grammaticality-to-grammaticality transfer; plausible-to-implausible SCaMP transfer loses 1.06 accuracy points on average, with within-model differences ranging from -0.57 to 4.34 points. Boundary tilting against extra-grammatical directions leaves grammaticality performance approximately intact, whereas a control tilt using other grammaticality directions destroys it. In Experiment 5, successful within-language probes have mean accuracy of 66.6% across the selected models and English; cross-language probes average 61.4%. Cross-language success decreases for all five selected models, with relatively small declines for Llama and much larger declines for OLMo-7B and Qwen3-4B. The most surprising result is not uniformly strong multilingual transfer: language-general encoding appears model-dependent rather than a universal property. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and limited NEW FORMULATION: the paper applies an existing low-complexity mass-mean probe to grammaticality, adds a systematic framework for cross-phenomenon, probability-controlled, acceptability-controlled, and cross-language tests, and reports evidence that grammaticality is linearly decodable and partly transferable, while the underlying probe and most datasets are existing techniques and benchmarks rather than new artifacts. Rigor & Reproducibility: The study has broad model coverage, held-out evaluation, 100 random fitting runs for most configurations, label-shuffled null probes, multiple representation regions, cross-dataset tests, and several targeted controls. It reports adjusted significance testing and effect-size thresholds, but it does not report conventional confidence intervals or error bars for all headline comparisons, model-training seeds, or independent replications with newly generated grammaticality items. The regression and boundary-tilting analyses provide useful robustness checks, although the validity of treating shared representational directions as removable nuisance factors depends on strong linear and measurement assumptions. The authors state that code, analyses, and data are available at https://github.com/jane-lisy/linear-gram. The paper is an arXiv preprint, listed as arXiv:2607.15175v1 dated 16 July 2026, rather than a peer-reviewed publication. No trained model or new benchmark is released. Potential benchmark contamination is discussed but not measured: the authors acknowledge that grammaticality benchmarks or metalinguistic material may occur in pretraining, and they avoid chat models, but they do not perform contamination audits or training-data attribution. The models are preselected for above-chance BLiMP probability performance, which is a defensible prerequisite for the stated hypothesis but limits conclusions about models that fail behavioral tests. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL. Practical: The method can run on commercially available hardware for the smaller models, but extracting hidden states from 7B–14B models across hundreds of thousands of benchmark examples requires substantial GPU memory and inference time. Efficient: Mass-mean fitting is computationally cheap and adds only a vector dot product per example, but the dominant cost is hidden-state extraction and the paper does not report runtime, memory, or cost relative to probability-based evaluation. Effective: The evidence supports reliable decoding of benchmark grammaticality labels and some transfer across datasets, but it does not show improved language-model behavior, human judgment prediction beyond the source labels, or causal syntactic competence. Scalable: The study spans 14M–14B parameters and many benchmark items, but it does not test 10x–100x larger models, longer naturalistic discourse, adversarially constructed sentences, or deployment distributions; scalability beyond the tested model families and synthetic/minimal-pair benchmarks is therefore not established. The work delivers reusable code, analyses, and data through the cited GitHub repository, but no standalone library, CLI, trained model, or production system. Strengths: - The paper replaces a single probability-based grammaticality metric with a representation-level diagnostic and tests whether the result transfers to held-out phenomena rather than only fitting and testing on the same contrast. - The critical-region versus pre-critical control provides evidence that the decoded signal emerges when the grammaticality contrast becomes unavoidable, while the final-region results show that the signal is not restricted to a particular local token. - The probability and acceptability analyses are unusually direct for a probing study: counter/favour sampling, plausible-versus-implausible comparisons, extra-grammatical transfer, and boundary tilting all address different versions of the central confound. - The 25-model sweep reveals a substantive scaling pattern—larger models show more successful and more transferable probes—and the multilingual experiment shows that cross-language transfer is heterogeneous rather than being assumed from English-only evidence. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that mass-mean probing is intentionally low-complexity and may under-extract grammaticality information compared with richer probes. They do not tune representation layers and acknowledge that layer choice can materially affect accuracy. They note that grammaticality encoding may not equal syntactic representation, that the mechanism producing the boundary remains unknown, and that specific phenomena can remain undetectable despite strong overall grammaticality signals. They acknowledge uncertainty about pretraining co-occurrence structure, possible metalinguistic information in training data, the need for carefully vetted corpora for cognitive comparisons, and the limited scope of their multilingual analysis. They also note that their phenomenon categories may not correspond to model-internal categories and that future work should test nonce-word and training-development settings. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The central conclusion remains correlational: a linear direction that predicts benchmark labels does not show that models compute grammaticality, that the direction is causally used for prediction, or that it encodes syntactic structure rather than a distributed acceptability or anomaly feature. - The probability manipulation changes the composition of the fitting set but does not fully establish conditional independence between grammaticality, probability, lexical frequency, plausibility, length, and template identity; residual correlations in both fitting and evaluation data remain possible. - The benchmarks are heavily composed of synthetic minimal pairs and repeated templates, and the study does not evaluate independently authored, naturally occurring, adversarial, nonce-word, or long-context items that would more strongly test abstraction beyond benchmark regularities. - The use of the final hidden layer and punctuation representations is not compared systematically with all layers, pooled token states, residual-stream locations, or causal interventions, despite the paper itself noting that layer selection can substantially change results. - The 5% threshold and repeated testing across thousands of model-region-dataset configurations raise a dependence and multiplicity issue that Holm correction may not fully address when success rates and downstream selections are aggregated; the paper does not provide a preregistered analysis or a complete hierarchical model of these outcomes. - Cross-linguistic conclusions are based on only five models selected for strongest English performance, and language benchmarks differ in size, construction, tokenization, and phenomenon coverage; the reported transfer cannot be separated cleanly from model multilingual exposure or dataset-specific lexical/format cues. - The claim that the grammaticality direction is a major organizational principle is stronger than the reported effect sizes support for many models: success means statistically above a shuffled null with a 5-point margin, while successful-probe accuracies are often in the mid-60% range and many phenomenon-model pairs fail. Bottom Line: This is a valuable and unusually careful probing study that establishes robust linear decodability and partial transfer of benchmark grammaticality labels, but it should be read as evidence for a reusable representational diagnostic—not as a resolution of whether neural language models possess human-like grammatical knowledge.

ServerlessT2I: Efficient Text-to-Image Workflow Serving on a Serverless Platform

X Jiang, S Li, S Yao, T Feng, L Yang, D Nie, H Yang… · arxiv.org · inference optimize llm faster inference throughput - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces ServerlessT2I, a serverless text-to-image serving system that decomposes customized diffusion workflows into independently schedulable model functions connected as DAGs. - Why it's important: Customized T2I workflows create large model-loading, GPU-memory, communication, and multi-tenant fairness costs when deployed as monolithic GPU functions. - How it does it: It combines layer-prefix GPU caching with overlapped host-to-GPU loading, NVSHMEM-based callback tensor transfers, virtualized GPU weight placement, and vTime-based fairness scheduling. - The good: On a 32-H800 testbed with production-trace workloads, it maintains at least 90% SLO attainment at up to 1.5× rate scale, uses as few as 8 GPUs where a strong baseline needs 24, and reduces execution loading latency by 90% in a microbenchmark. - The missing: The evaluation does not provide publicly reproducible traces or code, lacks comparisons against several specialized or jointly optimized serving systems, and tests real hardware only up to 32 GPUs; the 256-GPU result is simulation-based. - Read it or not: Systems researchers and operators building multi-tenant diffusion serving should read it for its integration of DAG execution, memory overloading, GPU-resident communication, and fairness, while readers seeking general-purpose serverless inference or video-generation results can skip it.
Why this rank
Profile: systems. Novelty (78) and Non-Obviousness (78) are strong because the paper introduces a coherent serverless-native formulation combining workflow DAG execution, GPU-resident tensor movement, layer-prefix caching, and GPU-time fairness accounting. Problem & Motivation: The paper addresses serverless serving of highly customized and bursty text-to-image workflows, including diffusion models, ControlNet-style tandem adapters, and LoRA-style weight updates. In production traces, the authors report 31,133 distinct workflows over 20 days, T2I accounting for 28% of GPU usage in one March 2026 trace, and 75% of functions having inter-arrival-time coefficients of variation above 1. Existing deployments package each workflow as one opaque GPU function, so autoscaling replicates non-bottleneck components, cold-start loading remains expensive for models of tens of GiB, and users must manage multi-GPU placement and tensor movement for workflow parallelism. Request-count quotas also misrepresent resource consumption because the paper reports up to a 16× spread in workflow inference latency. The target gap is therefore not faster isolated diffusion inference, but efficient, elastic, and fair multi-tenant execution of thousands of heterogeneous workflows. Key Idea: The central insight is to treat a T2I workflow as a DAG of independently executable model functions and use otherwise idle GPU memory as a shared backend data plane. This enables the system to cache only selected model layers, retain tensors on GPUs across function boundaries, and account for actual model-function GPU service rather than requests or denoising-step counts. The most distinctive technical move is the combination of layer-prefix caching and virtualized weight placement: the first layers start inference immediately while later layers load asynchronously, and cached weights can occupy either the PyTorch or NVSHMEM memory region. Methodology: Users implement each model through `setup_io`, `load_model`, and `execute` methods, declare named inputs and outputs, and compose model functions through an orchestrator. The runtime infers a dependency DAG by matching interfaces and topologically sorts it; at request time, it releases ready functions, dispatches them to distributed GPU executors, materializes outputs, and repeats until the image is returned. The data plane uses a three-tier GPU/host/external-storage cache, with LRU eviction and host-memory caching of popular workflows; its loading policy preloads a prefix of model layers into GPU memory and streams the remainder from host memory during inference. The prefix length is selected from profiled per-layer loading and compute times using the paper's latency model, with the stated target of hiding loading when possible. For intermediate tensors, executors reserve NVSHMEM symmetric-heap arenas, use a buddy allocator, publish tensor metadata, and perform one-sided GPU transfers when callback-marked inputs are reached. Model-weight virtualization maps logical layers to physical tensors in either the PyTorch or NVSHMEM region and evicts cached layers under pressure, preserving early layers preferentially. Scheduling charges each tenant measured or estimated GPU wall-clock time for loading, computation, and transfers as vTime; a fairness filter admits tenants within slack Δ of the least-served tenant, and a second score ranks ready functions by normalized waiting time, remaining critical-path work, and execution cost. These choices are motivated by workload measurements and microbenchmarks, but the paper does not fully evaluate sensitivity to profiling error, heterogeneous GPU types, cache-policy alternatives, or scheduler-weight calibration. Key Results: The evaluation uses 32 NVIDIA H800 GPUs, six diffusion base-model families with 6B–12B parameters and 4–50 denoising steps, 5 basic workflows in S1, and 20 workflows including ControlNet and LoRA adapters in S2. Baselines are adapted monolithic deployments of vLLM-Omni for S1 and Diffusers for S2, each with no cache, whole-workflow cache, or model-level cache. At the reported operating points, ServerlessT2I sustains up to 2× higher request rates at the same GPU budget, uses up to 3× fewer GPUs at fixed request rate, meets up to 7× tighter SLO scales, and tolerates up to 2× higher burstiness while maintaining approximately 90% SLO attainment. In S1, it maintains 100% SLO attainment through rate scale 1.5, whereas MCache falls below 90% at rate scale 1.0; it reaches the 90% target with 8 GPUs versus 24 for the strongest vLLM-Omni baseline. In S2, it remains above 90% through rate scale 1.5, reaches 98% attainment with 16 GPUs, and reaches 97% attainment at SLO scale 8, while MCache and WCache require scales 16 and 18 respectively to achieve comparable attainment. Under burst tests, it stays above 96% through CoV scale 4 in S1 and above 90% through scale 5 in S2. The data plane reduces loading latency by 90% and end-to-end latency by 21% relative to pipelined loading without prefix caching; half-prefix retention still reduces loading latency by 62%. ServerlessT2I achieves 84–88% average GPU-memory utilization in selected end-to-end settings, compared with 13–71% for baselines, and adds 3% average execution latency over Diffusers. The scheduler's fairness/efficiency microbenchmark increases SLO attainment from 62% at slack 0 to 84% at slack 20. A 256-GPU, 600-inflight-request experiment is simulation-based and reports 3.3% control/data-plane overhead, not a physical deployment result. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION, NEW METHOD, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely new contribution is the serverless-native integration of model-DAG execution, GPU-resident callback communication, layer-granular weight virtualization, and GPU-time fairness accounting for customized T2I workflows; individual ingredients such as serverless DAGs, model caching, NVSHMEM, LRU eviction, and fairness scheduling are adapted from established systems techniques rather than invented independently here. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper includes component microbenchmarks, end-to-end evaluations, a model-weight-virtualization study, fairness-slack experiments, an execution-overhead comparison, and a scale simulation. It reports concrete workloads, GPU models, cache variants, request-rate and burstiness manipulations, SLO definitions, and parameter/model ranges, and it verifies identical generated images for the compared inference paths. However, it does not report error bars, repeated-run variance, multiple seeds, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests. The production traces appear proprietary; no public dataset, code repository, model weights, or reproducibility URL is stated, although the implementation comprises approximately 4,000 lines of Python for the runtime and 3,000 lines of Python/C++/CUDA for the data plane. The baseline comparison is useful but narrow: vLLM-Omni and Diffusers are adapted monolithic systems, while specialized systems such as Katz, DistriFusion, xDiT, TetriServe, or TridentServe are not evaluated in the same end-to-end multi-tenant setting. The strongest scale result beyond the physical testbed is a simulator calibrated to measured latencies, and the headline gains depend partly on production popularity skew and underutilized host/GPU memory assumptions. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS/EMPIRICAL. Practical: The prototype runs on commercially available NVIDIA H800 GPUs with PyTorch, CUDA, NVSHMEM, FastAPI, and ZeroMQ, but deployment requires specialized NVLink/RDMA-capable infrastructure and integration with the authors' runtime rather than an off-the-shelf cloud platform. Efficient: Evidence shows substantially lower GPU demand and higher memory utilization than monolithic cache baselines, while adding 3% average execution latency over Diffusers; absolute CPU, host-memory, network, scheduler, and energy costs are not reported. Effective: The physical experiments demonstrate improved SLO attainment, loading latency, burst tolerance, and service fairness on 5–20 workflows, but they evaluate serving proxies and latency rather than image-quality, tenant utility, cost, or production customer outcomes. Scalable: The system is physically tested on 32 H800 GPUs and simulated at 256 GPUs with 600 inflight requests; behavior at 10×–100× larger fleets, substantially larger workflow sets, heterogeneous accelerators, or extreme cache churn remains unvalidated. The work delivers a prototype serverless runtime and data plane, but no public software artifact or repository is stated. Strengths: - The paper identifies a coherent systems abstraction—model functions in a workflow DAG—that simultaneously enables independent scaling, transparent data movement, and fine-grained tenant accounting rather than optimizing only one isolated inference kernel. - The layer-prefix caching policy is a concrete response to a measured T2I-specific asymmetry: loading can take 3.2×–13.5× a model's inference time, so ordinary overlap is insufficient. The paper derives a simple selection rule and shows a 90% loading-latency reduction in its microbenchmark. - GPU-resident communication with callback-based fetching matches the timing structure of ControlNet parallelism and avoids host serialization and PCIe transfers; the reported parallel execution approaches the stated theoretical optimum. - The vTime scheduler addresses a real fairness mismatch in which equal request rates can consume radically different GPU service, and it provides an explicit bounded-unfairness argument under an eligible-backlogged condition rather than only presenting a heuristic. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly exclude video generation because its loading/computation ratio and workflow composition differ from T2I. They acknowledge that NVSHMEM regions are statically sized, creating a tension between communication capacity and cache capacity, and address this with model-weight virtualization rather than dynamic region resizing. They also acknowledge that fairness slack trades service balance for SLO efficiency and that DAG tenants may be outstanding but not eligible-backlogged because their work is blocked on dependencies. The paper does not present these boundaries as universal claims, which improves scope clarity. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The main evidence relies on proprietary production traces and author-controlled adaptations of baselines; the absence of public traces, code, and repeated-run statistics makes the headline 2×/3×/7× comparisons difficult to independently verify. - The comparison omits strong specialized T2I workflow systems and does not establish whether ServerlessT2I is complementary to, or superseded by, systems that already provide multi-GPU parallelism, adapter caching, or stage-level scheduling. - The evaluation does not quantify total host-memory footprint, network/interconnect utilization, CPU overhead, energy, monetary cost, cache occupancy, or cold-start behavior including container-image retrieval, despite framing the system as serverless infrastructure. - The fairness guarantee assumes eligible-backlogged tenants and uses estimated vTime before completion; the paper does not test estimation error, tenant churn at scale, adversarial workflow mixes, starvation under blocked DAGs, or fairness metrics beyond pairwise cumulative GPU-time differences. - The system's generality is narrower than the programming abstraction suggests: it is designed around immutable tensors, stateless model functions, fixed seeds for retries, PyTorch execution, transformer-like layers, and T2I workflows whose inference is compute-bound and memory-slack-rich. These assumptions may fail for dynamic control flow, mutable state, video, heterogeneous accelerators, or memory-intensive batches. Bottom Line: This is a technically substantive and practically relevant systems paper whose strongest contribution is the integration of model-DAG scheduling with a GPU-resident memory/data plane; it is worth reading for T2I-serving researchers and cloud operators, but its publication-level claims would be substantially stronger with public artifacts, variance analysis, broader baselines, and physical evaluation beyond 32 GPUs.

AlgMortar: a fully algebraic multiscale mortar preconditioner

LF Santos, FS Sousa, RF Ausas, RT Guiraldello… · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces AlgMortar, an algebraic multiscale mortar preconditioner that constructs domain decomposition, local Dirichlet-like solves, and interface coupling using only an SPD sparse matrix and right-hand side. - Why it's important: Large heterogeneous porous-media systems can contain tens to hundreds of millions of unknowns, while industrial simulators may not expose geometric or discretization metadata needed by geometric multiscale methods. - How it does it: It partitions the matrix graph, modifies each subdomain diagonal to form local SPD operators, represents interface pressure by piecewise-constant edge functions, and enforces a weighted algebraic analogue of weak flux continuity. - The good: On 50M- and 100M-cell SPE11C corner-point problems, AlgMortar is faster than BoomerAMG at relative tolerance 10^-6, and it achieves 0.71 strong-scaling efficiency from 27 to 216 MPI processes on a 110.6M-DOF high-contrast problem. - The missing: The evaluation lacks ablations over partitioning, interface-space dimension, smoothing, and block counts, and it compares against only one AMG configuration rather than a broader set of strong contemporary algebraic and multiscale baselines. - Read it or not: Researchers and practitioners working on parallel Darcy-flow solvers should read it for the algebraic reformulation and large-scale implementation results, but readers seeking evidence of broad black-box robustness beyond TPFA Darcy systems should wait for the proposed extensions.

Problem & Motivation: The work addresses the solution of large sparse SPD systems from second-order elliptic equations, especially finite-volume Darcy-flow discretizations with highly heterogeneous or high-contrast permeability. The target users are reservoir, subsurface-flow, and other scientific-computing practitioners who need scalable Krylov preconditioners but may lack reliable access to geometry, PDE coefficients, grid topology, or discretization-specific information. Existing multiscale mortar methods can provide effective coarse corrections but normally use geometric partitions, local meshes, and mixed finite-element data; algebraic multiscale methods remove that dependency but do not directly reproduce the weak flux-continuity mechanism of MMMFEM. The paper seeks to close this gap by deriving a matrix-only analogue of MMMFEM that can operate on irregular grids and legacy solver matrices. Key Idea: The central insight is to treat nonzero inter-subdomain matrix couplings as algebraic interface edges and introduce an interface variable representing the average of the two endpoint pressures on each edge. For a coupling a_kl, the interface value is (p_k+p_l)/2; the local matrix receives a diagonal correction that converts each subdomain block into a Dirichlet-like operator, while a weighted weak projection of this average onto a low-dimensional mortar space supplies the global coupling. This makes the method an exact rewriting when the full edge space is retained and a multiscale approximation when the interface space is restricted. On uniform Cartesian TPFA systems with homogeneous permeability, the construction exactly recovers MMMFEM. Methodology: The pipeline first builds the adjacency graph of A and partitions its unknowns with METIS/ParMETIS into nonoverlapping subdomains. It identifies cross-partition nonzeros as interface edges, constructs endpoint trace operators L and U, their average M=(L+U)/2, a diagonal edge-weight matrix W containing intersubdomain couplings, and coupling matrices B satisfying B^T=4WM. For subdomain i it defines A_i=A_ii-sum_j D_ij, where D_ij is the diagonal matrix of row sums of A_ij; under SPD A and negative interface couplings, these local operators are SPD. It then solves A_i p_i=f_i for particular solutions and A_i p_i^(k)=-B_i psi_k for multiscale basis functions, using parallel Cholesky factorizations. The interface variable lambda belongs to a mortar space Lambda, normally one piecewise-constant basis function per interface, and satisfies Z^T W(lambda-Mp)=0. Eliminating either variable yields an SPD interface or reduced pressure system, so the result can be used with PCG; in practice the preconditioner applies local solves, assembles and solves the interface system, reconstructs the pressure, and adds symmetric block-Jacobi pre- and post-smoothing. The key design choices—graph partitioning, diagonal local modification, and piecewise-constant interface space—are mathematically connected to the MMMFEM formulation, but the choice of partition quality, interface resolution, and smoothing parameters is primarily justified empirically rather than through systematic sensitivity studies. Key Results: The experiments use TPFA finite-volume Darcy systems, Cartesian grids, the SPE10 permeability benchmark, and SPE11B/SPE11C corner-point grids. On a cross-shaped contrast field with contrast 10^6 and 13.8M to 110.6M DOFs, weak scaling over 27, 64, 125, and 216 MPI processes gives AlgMortar times of 10.31, 12.47, 18.19, and 21.05 seconds, with 38, 37, 38, and 37 outer PCG iterations; AMG takes 8.62, 15.13, 25.47, and 40.02 seconds with 21, 22, 23, and 24 iterations. Strong scaling for the fixed 110.6M-DOF problem reduces time from 119.83 seconds on 27 processes to 21.05 seconds on 216, with speedup 5.69 and efficiency 0.71; PCG iterations fall from 48 to 37. On SPE10, whose reported contrast is 2.80x10^7, AlgMortar takes 26.15 to 39.64 seconds for 10^-11 tolerance over 27 to 216 processes, versus AMG's 10.51 to 42.11 seconds, while at 10^-6 it takes 9.64 to 16.50 seconds versus AMG's 8.73 to 32.62 seconds. Under contrasts from 2.94x10^4 to 2.67x10^10, AlgMortar takes 12.15–19.06 seconds on a 54M-DOF grid and 14.60–18.08 seconds on a 93.3M-DOF grid, remaining faster than AMG but requiring 23–49 versus AMG's 16–17 iterations. On SPE11C, AlgMortar versus AMG takes 25.77 versus 29.72 seconds for 50M cells at 10^-11 and 11.21 versus 23.50 seconds at 10^-6; for 100M cells it takes 38.45 versus 34.84 seconds at 10^-11 and 15.98 versus 25.95 seconds at 10^-6. The most important counterpoint is that AlgMortar often needs substantially more PCG iterations than AMG—184 versus 29 on the smallest SPE10 case at 10^-11—so its advantage comes from parallel setup/application behavior and scaling rather than uniformly better spectral convergence. Novelty Classification: The contribution is primarily a NEW METHOD and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, with a supporting NEW FORMULATION and empirical finding: it algebraically realizes MMMFEM from matrix graph connectivity and values, proves SPD properties under M-matrix-like assumptions, and implements the method in PETSc for large parallel Darcy systems; graph partitioning, local solves, mortar coarse spaces, and smoothing are individually established techniques, so the novelty lies in their specific algebraic mortar construction and equivalence to MMMFEM rather than in any wholly new domain-decomposition primitive. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper gives a formal derivation of the algebraic formulation, proves well-posedness of the coupled system and positive definiteness of the reduced preconditioner when A is SPD and the interface-weight matrix has negative-definite negative, and derives a condition-number bound through the projection error of average interface pressures. It reports weak and strong scaling, residual tolerances of 10^-6 and 10^-11, contrast studies up to 2.67x10^10, and tests reaching approximately 100M active cells. However, it does not report error bars, repeated runs, multiple random seeds, statistical tests, or uncertainty in wall-clock measurements. Ablations are limited: the paper compares direct and iterative interface solves and discusses smoothing choices, but does not systematically isolate the effects of graph partitioning, mortar-space dimension, number of subdomains, block-Jacobi block count, number of smoothing steps, or interface solver tolerance. The baseline is BoomerAMG with parameters taken from prior work rather than a broad comparison against current algebraic multiscale, overlapping Schwarz, adaptive coarse-space, or production reservoir-solver preconditioners. The implementation uses PETSc/petsc4py, MUMPS, ParMETIS, METIS, HYPRE, OPM-derived assembly, and pyopmspe11; PETSc, pyopmspe11, and cited external projects have public URLs, but the authors do not state that AlgMortar source code, exact input files, partition files, or model weights/data are released in a dedicated repository. The experiments are all based on TPFA Darcy matrices, and the strongest claims about arbitrary grids and discretizations are therefore broader than the demonstrated evidence. Deployability (4-property check): EMPIRICAL/SYSTEMS profile. Practical: The method runs on commercially available distributed-memory hardware using MPI, PETSc, sparse local Cholesky solves, and iterative or direct interface solves, although setup requires substantial HPC software dependencies. Efficient: It can outperform the reported BoomerAMG in wall-clock time at larger process counts, but local factorization, graph partitioning, interface construction, 15 pre- and 15 post-smoothing steps, and interface solves create nontrivial setup and memory costs; the interface component becomes a setup bottleneck, and memory scaling is not quantified. Effective: The evidence shows that it reduces time-to-residual for the tested high-contrast TPFA Darcy systems, including 50M–100M-cell corner-point cases, but it does not establish accuracy beyond solving the same linear system or robustness for non-TPFA discretizations, multiphase systems, or general SPD matrices. Scalable: It demonstrates weak scaling to 216 processes and strong scaling of a 110.6M-DOF case to 216 processes, plus a 100M-cell case on 250 processes, but provides no 10x–100x extrapolation, no larger process-count study, and no evidence that the interface system remains scalable at substantially larger subdomain counts. The paper delivers an implemented PETSc PCShell preconditioner and algorithmic procedures, but no dedicated public AlgMortar software artifact is explicitly identified. Strengths: - The algebraic construction is more than a direct combination of standard AMG and domain decomposition: it identifies an interface-edge pressure average and a weighted weak constraint that reproduces MMMFEM exactly in a meaningful Cartesian special case. - The SPD analysis is useful for deployment because it establishes that both the coupled formulation and reduced pressure operator are compatible with PCG under explicit M-matrix-like sign assumptions, and it links spectral clustering to mortar-space approximation error. - The evaluation reaches 110.6M DOFs in controlled scaling tests and approximately 100M active corner-point cells, rather than stopping at small benchmark matrices. - The results expose a credible systems tradeoff: AlgMortar often uses more iterations than AMG but can win in wall-clock time because its setup and application phases scale better in the tested configurations. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly identify future extensions to transient multiphase problems, broader unstructured meshes, non-TPFA discretizations, improved interface spaces, scalable interface solvers, and graph-partitioning strategies. They acknowledge that higher-order interface spaces can reduce PCG iterations but increase interface-system size and cost, and that interface operations and setup become bottlenecks at higher process counts. They also note that partition reuse could reduce overhead for time-dependent problems. These limitations are stated directly, although the paper does not quantify the failure boundary for the present piecewise-constant interface space. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The theoretical assumptions are narrower than the paper's black-box framing: the proofs require SPD A and negative intersubdomain couplings with -W positive definite, while many general SPD discretizations can contain positive off-diagonals or coupling patterns that do not satisfy this structure. The experiments use only TPFA Darcy matrices, so claims about arbitrary grids, mixed-dimensional models, anisotropy, and discretization independence remain untested. The AMG comparison may not be fully reproducible or decisive because only one BoomerAMG setup is used, no tuning parity or memory comparison is reported, and AMG iteration counts are often much lower. The large PCG iteration counts on SPE10 at 10^-11 tolerance suggest that the piecewise-constant mortar space may be inadequate for stringent solves, yet there is no systematic interface-space ablation or comparison with higher-order/adaptive spaces. Wall-clock results lack repeated-run variability, hardware specifications, memory usage, communication volume, and breakdown of total factorization versus storage costs. Finally, the reported iterative interface solve uses an inexact tolerance of 10^-2, but the effect of this inexactness on outer PCG reliability and reproducibility is not analyzed beyond selected timings. Bottom Line: AlgMortar is a technically substantive algebraic reformulation with convincing large-scale MPI evidence for TPFA Darcy systems, and it is worth reading for solver researchers, but its practical superiority over well-tuned modern multilevel methods is not yet established outside the tested benchmarks and parameter choices.

A Poostforoushan, L Vogel, C Binnig · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces TEmBed-T, a diagnostic benchmark extending TEmBed with query-to-table retrieval, structural table shuffling, and header-stripped table type detection for evaluating table-level embeddings. - Why it's important: Table encoders support data discovery, retrieval, schema understanding, and table-centric prediction, but a model that performs well on retrieval may fail to preserve relational structure or infer table semantics from cell values. - How it does it: It evaluates frozen embeddings along three distinct axes using heterogeneous retrieval corpora, value-shuffled triplets that preserve token marginals while breaking row associations, and probe classifiers trained on header-stripped table embeddings. - The good: The controlled shuffling protocol isolates structural encoding effectively: HyTrel reaches 0.8747 triplet accuracy and a 0.59 silhouette score, while transformer and hashing baselines score at or below chance and collapse to 0% on the ECB statistical dataset. - The missing: The study evaluates only five approaches, uses task-specific proxy metrics rather than downstream application outcomes, and does not establish that the proposed properties predict real retrieval, QA, or data-discovery performance beyond the benchmark tasks. - Read it or not: Researchers building or evaluating table encoders should read it for the benchmark design and failure analysis, while practitioners seeking a universally best embedding model will find that the paper does not provide one.
