Problem & Motivation: Table-level embeddings are increasingly used for table retrieval, data-lake discovery, schema understanding, and downstream prediction, but existing evaluations emphasize end-to-end retrieval or individual invariance probes and therefore conflate representation quality with task-specific success. The paper targets the absence of a property-level evaluation that separates cross-domain robustness, structural fidelity, and semantic preservation without headers. The intended users are researchers selecting or designing table encoders for heterogeneous database, enterprise, web, NL2SQL, and table-question-answering settings. Key Idea: Evaluate table embeddings through controlled, complementary perturbations rather than a single retrieval score. The most technically distinctive idea is the shuffling triplet: a structurally faithful positive is produced by permuting rows and columns, while a negative preserves each column's token multiset but independently shuffles values and destroys cross-column row associations. Because the positive and negative retain the same lexical content, successful separation requires sensitivity to relational structure rather than token overlap or surface vocabulary. Methodology: TEmBed-T adds three evaluations to TEmBed. First, it performs query-to-table retrieval over five TARGET corpora—FeTaQA, TabFact, OTT-QA, Spider, and BIRD—with headers only or the first 100 rows, and with markdown or CSV serialization for text encoders; it reports MRR and recall. Second, for each table it constructs an anchor, a positive generated by row/column permutation, and a negative generated by intra-column value shuffling. It measures whether cosine distance satisfies d_pos < d_neg using triplet accuracy and the stated silhouette score, sweeping permutation type, positive and negative perturbation magnitudes, and default, BIG (up to 500 x 80), and SMALL (up to 20 x 8) table windows. Third, it strips headers and trains frozen-embedding probes—XGBoost, MLP, and KNN—to predict one of 10 Schema.org table types using 8,000 training and 1,000 test tables; it reports macro-F1. The evaluated pool contains MiniLM, Granite-R2, GritLM, HyTrel, and a scikit-learn HashingVectorizer baseline, with embedding dimensions described as 32 and 768, although the exact dimension assigned to each model is not fully clarified. Critical design choices are the lexical-control negative in shuffling, the frozen encoders in table type detection, and heterogeneous retrieval corpora; the first is well-motivated, while the relationship between probe recoverability and intrinsic embedding quality is less fully justified because classifier choice materially affects absolute results. Key Results: In retrieval with 100 rows and markdown serialization, average MRR@10 is 0.72 for GritLM, 0.70 for Granite-R2, 0.54 for MiniLM, 0.32 for Hashing, and 0.02 for HyTrel. GritLM leads Wikipedia-derived FeTaQA, OTT-QA, and TabFact, whereas Granite-R2 is strongest on Spider, showing domain-dependent rank reversals. Adding 100 rows increases average MRR@10 from 0.56 to 0.70 for Granite-R2, 0.56 to 0.72 for GritLM, 0.21 to 0.32 for Hashing, 0.02 to 0.02 for HyTrel, and 0.50 to 0.54 for MiniLM. In canonical table shuffling, HyTrel obtains 0.8747 accuracy averaged over six datasets, compared with 0.1802 for GritLM, 0.1286 for Granite-R2, 0.1965 for MiniLM, and 0.0000 for Hashing; HyTrel's silhouette score is 0.59, while Granite-R2, MiniLM, GritLM, and Hashing score -0.53, -0.44, -0.40, and -0.02. On ECB, HyTrel reaches 1.00 accuracy and all other approaches reach 0.00, providing the clearest evidence that lexical-only and order-sensitive text encoders fail the structural probe. For header-stripped type detection with XGBoost, macro-F1 is 0.9252 for Hashing, 0.9103 for Granite-R2, 0.9059 for GritLM, 0.7818 for MiniLM, and 0.6439 for HyTrel; with MLP, GritLM leads at 0.9375 and HyTrel remains lowest at 0.6557. Thus no approach ranks first on more than one task: GritLM leads retrieval, HyTrel leads shuffling, and Hashing leads XGBoost-based type detection. The test scale is standard benchmark scale rather than stress-scale deployment; exact numbers of retrieval queries and shuffling triplets are not stated in the main text. Novelty Classification: NEW BENCHMARK, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and modestly NEW FORMULATION: the main contribution is a benchmark suite that combines existing retrieval and probing ideas with a value-shuffled structural triplet protocol designed to defeat bag-of-words shortcuts; the paper does not introduce a new embedding model or learning algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility: The study includes 15 shuffling variations, perturbation-magnitude sweeps, row-versus-column analyses, table-size ablations, serialization comparisons, three probe classifiers, per-dataset breakdowns, and 10,000-resample bootstrap 95% confidence intervals for retrieval and shuffling. These analyses support the claim that rankings differ across tasks, and classifier-consistent rankings partially support the type-detection comparison. However, the paper does not report multiple random seeds, statistical tests for type-detection differences, full dataset and triplet counts, or confidence intervals for all reported metrics. The baseline pool is small: it includes three text serialization encoders, one structure-aware encoder, and hashing, but no broader set of recent table-specific or multimodal/LLM-based encoders. Spider uses all train, validation, and test splits for evaluation, which may complicate comparison with standard held-out protocols, and the WDC type-detection experiment is subsampled to 800 training and 100 test tables per class. Source code, data, and other artifacts are stated to be available at https://github.com/IBM/table-representation-evals; the paper does not state whether model weights are released. The benchmark itself is designed to reduce lexical shortcuts in shuffling, but its interpretation depends on the assumption that row and column order are semantically irrelevant, which fails for temporally or ordinally sorted tables. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL. Practical: The evaluated encoders and scikit-learn probes can run on commercially available hardware, but the paper does not report hardware, batch size, memory use, or model-serving requirements. Efficient: Granite-R2 offers the reported best cost-quality trade-off, while GritLM has higher pooled quality and Hashing takes approximately 350 seconds in the plotted experiment despite the lowest pooled quality; absolute timing is hardware- and implementation-dependent and the paper provides no normalized throughput or memory comparison. Effective: The evidence demonstrates differentiated performance on retrieval, structural discrimination, and type-probe recoverability, but it does not directly measure end-to-end data-lake discovery, question answering, NL2SQL, or other production outcomes. Scalable: The evaluation includes tables up to the BIG window of 500 x 80 and retrieval inputs capped at 100 rows, but it does not test 10x–100x larger tables, corpora, query loads, or embedding indexes, so scalability beyond the tested windows is not established. The work delivers a reusable benchmark and evaluation code/data artifact, not a new trained embedding model or production system. Strengths: - The value-shuffled negative is a meaningful improvement over simple permutation probes because it preserves token distributions while breaking row-wise associations, making lexical overlap insufficient for success. - The three tasks expose sharply different capability profiles: retrieval favors GritLM, structural fidelity favors HyTrel, and type detection can favor Hashing or dense transformers depending on the probe, directly challenging single-metric model selection. - The evaluation includes controlled perturbation and size/magnitude ablations rather than reporting only one benchmark score; the near-zero transformer performance on ECB and HyTrel's 0.99–1.00 performance on several datasets provide interpretable failure and success cases. - The released artifact and explicit serialization, corpus, and probe dimensions make the benchmark comparatively easy to reuse and extend. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The paper explicitly notes that the permutation-based positive assumes row and column order have no intrinsic semantics, which may not hold for temporally sorted or otherwise ordered tables. It also frames the suite as an initial evaluation and concludes that a model covering all three capabilities remains an open problem. Beyond this caveat, the paper does not provide a dedicated limitations section or systematically discuss dataset representativeness, benchmark-to-application validity, probe leakage, or computational constraints. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The benchmark's structural-fidelity label encodes a particular notion of table semantics: it treats row/column permutations as benign and independent within-column shuffling as destructive, but some tables have meaningful row order, column order, repeated keys, hierarchical layouts, or intentionally independent columns. The type-detection result is also sensitive to the probe: Hashing leads XGBoost at 0.9252 macro-F1 but trails all transformer models with KNN at 0.8017, so the ranking is not purely an encoder property. The paper does not test whether benchmark scores predict downstream task improvements, nor does it compare against stronger contemporary table encoders, cross-encoder retrieval systems, supervised retrieval baselines, or simple serialization and pooling alternatives. The use of all Spider splits and a small balanced WDC subsample may inflate or narrow conclusions, while the pooled cross-task quality and average rank combine non-comparable metrics without a principled weighting. Finally, the cost analysis reports aggregate execution time without hardware, energy, memory, indexing, or per-table throughput, limiting its practical significance. Bottom Line: This is a useful and reproducible diagnostic benchmark paper whose structural triplet protocol and cross-task failure analysis merit attention from table-representation researchers, but its claims should be treated as evidence that evaluation is multi-dimensional—not as a validated prescription for production model choice.

ACM

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Agentic Context Management (ACM), a framework in which an LLM agent autonomously compresses its working context, archives the original messages, and retrieves them on demand through memory tools. - Why it's important: Long-horizon search and coding agents accumulate noisy, redundant tool traces that consume context capacity and can terminate before completing difficult tasks, even with nominally large context windows. - How it does it: ACM exposes `manage_context` and `query_memory` actions, then trains the agent with teacher-guided on-policy distillation that inserts beneficial memory calls and removes premature ones. - The good: On Qwen3.5-9B, ACM post-training raises Pass@1 from 0.570 to 0.727 on BrowseComp-Plus, from 0.367 to 0.425 on DeepSearchQA, and from 0.489 to 0.530 on SWE-Bench Verified while reducing BrowseComp-Plus peak tokens from 63K to 54K. - The missing: The evaluation does not establish end-to-end efficiency because it omits latency, monetary cost, summarizer/querier overhead, storage cost, and strong direct comparisons with closely related learned proactive methods such as AgentFold. - Read it or not: Researchers building long-horizon LLM agents should read it for the lossless external-memory design and training pipeline, but deployment-oriented readers should treat the performance and efficiency claims as preliminary until cost and scale are measured.

Problem & Motivation: Long-horizon web research and repository-level coding agents interleave reasoning, tool calls, observations, failed attempts, and redundant searches until their histories exceed the model's effective context capacity. Existing solutions either increase the nominal window, reduce attention cost, or compress the history using fixed thresholds or external summarizers; these approaches can degrade retrieval quality, discard raw evidence, and trigger compression at times unrelated to the agent's reasoning state. The target users are developers and researchers deploying autonomous agents for multi-step information seeking and software engineering, where context overflow and accumulated noise limit exploration depth and solution reliability. Key Idea: The central insight is to treat context compression as an explicit agent action coupled to reversible external storage: the agent decides when to replace a span of its working history with a summary, while the raw span remains addressable through an identifier and can be selectively queried later. This separates compact short-term working context from persistent per-episode memory. The idea is conceptually close to proactive context folding and memory-augmented agents, so the strongest distinctiveness lies in combining agent-initiated reversible compression with a publicly released teacher-guided policy-training pipeline rather than in the abstract memory separation alone. Methodology: ACM models an agent policy \(\pi_\theta(a_t\mid H_t)\) interacting with tools and environments. The agent receives two tools: `manage_context`, which summarizes all messages since the previous compression boundary, stores the raw messages on disk, and returns a summary with a unique identifier; and `query_memory`, which sends a natural-language query plus the archived raw messages associated with an identifier to a querier LLM and returns extracted information. The training pipeline uses two on-policy rollout conditions. In the no-tool rollout, a teacher identifies an early point where compression or retrieval would help, such as redundant searches or loops, injects the memory action, and resumes the rollout. In the tool-enabled rollout, the teacher removes premature memory calls and replaces them with search, document retrieval, or commitment actions. The student is trained for three epochs using top-20-token on-policy distillation, with loss \(L_{ACM}=-E_\tau\sum_{t\in T_a}\sum_{v\in V}p_T(v\mid s,h_{<t})\log\pi_\theta(v\mid s,h_{<t})\), masking system, user, and tool-output tokens. Training data retains failed student trajectories, filters teacher traces for reference-answer leakage, and mixes annotated data with resampled original rollouts. Critical design decisions are the agent-controlled timing, raw-message archival, and dual-constraint annotation; the paper motivates each behaviorally, but does not isolate the contribution of summary quality, querier quality, storage format, or alternative memory boundaries. Key Results: On Qwen3.5-9B with a 128K context cap, the untrained ACM agent obtains Pass@1 scores of 0.635 on BrowseComp-Plus, 0.405 on DeepSearchQA, and 0.508 on SWE-Bench Verified, compared with ReAct scores of 0.570, 0.367, and 0.489, respectively. ACM post-training raises these to 0.727, 0.425, and 0.530, with average tool calls of 46.2, 58.8, and 79.3 and peak token counts of 54K, 41K, and 50K. Relative to ReAct, these are approximately 27.5%, 15.8%, and 8.4% gains; the paper reports the first two as 27% and 16% and the coding gain as 8%. ReSum, ACON, and ACE score 0.608/0.371/0.475, 0.614/0.380/0.480, and 0.589/0.352/0.494 across the three benchmarks, respectively. The post-trained model nearly matches the much larger Qwen3.5-397B-A17B on BrowseComp-Plus (0.727 versus 0.653) but remains below it on DeepSearchQA (0.425 versus 0.710) and SWE-Bench Verified (0.530 versus 0.682); it also trails Gemini3-Flash on BrowseComp-Plus and coding. In a four-trial BrowseComp-Plus analysis, ReAct has Pass@1 57.0%, Pass@4 73.5%, and consistency Pass^4 34.1%, whereas the third ACM post-training epoch reaches 72.7%, 82.0%, and 59.3%. The reported case study traverses 222K raw tokens while keeping peak actual context at 98K, but it is a single example. The benchmarks are standard-scale rather than stress-scale: BrowseComp-Plus uses 150 evaluation examples, DeepSearchQA is out-of-domain, and SWE-Bench uses SWE-Gym for training; no experiment tests 10x to 100x larger raw histories or substantially larger deployments. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION; reversible agent-initiated context management is a meaningful formulation and system contribution, while the two-tool interface and teacher/student distillation combine several existing ideas from memory agents, context folding, summarization, and on-policy distillation, making the training pipeline and empirical evidence more novel than the underlying memory metaphor. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper includes useful ablations separating GPT5.5 distillation from ACM training and showing that ACM training improves all three tasks, while combined training is best on BrowseComp-Plus and SWE-Bench but not DeepSearchQA. It also reports Pass@4 and consistency, tool-use decomposition, context-growth curves, threshold-sensitivity analysis for query pivots, and a small-model failure study. However, the main tables do not report confidence intervals, statistical tests, or systematic multiple-seed results; four rollout trials are used for some analyses, but the number of independent evaluation seeds is not otherwise clearly stated. The authors reimplemented ReSum, ACON, and ACE because prior results were unavailable on these benchmarks and explicitly acknowledge possible implementation differences. Direct comparisons to AgentFold, SUPO, and Mem1 are omitted from the main evaluation because their released regimes differ, leaving the closest proactive learned competitor insufficiently tested. Training uses benchmark-specific data and reference answers during teacher annotation, and although leakage filters are described, the paper does not quantify their effectiveness or evaluate contamination. Code, training data, rollout annotations, and model checkpoints are stated to be available at https://github.com/lixiaochuan2020/agentic-context-management; the paper is an arXiv preprint, arXiv:2607.23809v1, dated 26 July 2026. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS — the work builds and evaluates an agent framework with external storage, memory tools, model checkpoints, and a training-data pipeline. - Practical: The system can run on commercially available hardware in principle, but each compression and memory query invokes additional LLM inference and requires an external workspace, and the paper does not report hardware, latency, throughput, or operational integration details. - Efficient: ACM reduces measured peak prompt tokens from 63K to 54K on BrowseComp-Plus relative to ReAct and from 68–71K for summary/memory baselines to 54K, but increased search, summarizer, querier, and storage calls mean that KV-cache savings do not establish lower total compute or cost. - Effective: Accuracy improves over ReAct and the reproduced summary/memory baselines on all three tasks, and the case study shows successful recovery of archived evidence; nevertheless, the evidence measures benchmark pass rates rather than reliability, factuality under memory-retrieval errors, or production task completion cost. - Scalable: The system demonstrates one 222K-token raw-history trajectory under a 128K working window, but it does not test 10x–100x larger histories, concurrent agents, storage growth, retrieval contention, or behavior under failures of the summarizer, querier, or external memory. The work delivers a software artifact, public data-generation materials, and model checkpoints through the stated GitHub repository; it does not provide a general formal guarantee that the semantic content returned by summarization and query retrieval is lossless. Strengths: - The separation between compact working context and archived raw messages addresses a real failure mode of long-horizon agents without making compression irreversible at the storage level. - The dual-constraint data-generation procedure teaches both positive and negative memory decisions, avoiding a simpler but potentially harmful policy that merely learns to compress frequently. - The ablation shows that context-management training, rather than generic teacher distillation alone, drives consistent gains across search and coding; GPT5.5 distillation alone lowers BrowseComp-Plus from the 0.635 ACM baseline to 0.623, whereas ACM training reaches 0.727. - The paper connects performance gains to observable behavior: lower peak context, more search and document calls, longer trajectories, and improved consistency, rather than reporting accuracy without mechanism-level analysis. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that ACM requires a sufficiently capable base model with sustained long-horizon reasoning and tool use; weaker models may terminate before context pressure arises. They also acknowledge that ReSum, ACON, and other prior compression baselines were reimplemented because they lacked results on the selected benchmarks, so implementation differences may affect comparisons. They confront both limitations directly, including a Qwen3-4B-thinking study showing two-turn rollouts, 1.2 tool calls, and 3.4% BrowseComp-Plus accuracy versus 19.4 turns, 16.2 calls, and 57.3% for Qwen3.5-9B. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The paper calls the method “lossless,” but only the storage of raw messages is lossless; the agent receives an LLM-generated summary or query answer, so semantic retrieval can still omit, distort, or mis-rank evidence. The efficiency claim focuses on peak context and KV-cache pressure while omitting the extra summarization and querying calls, wall-clock latency, GPU memory, dollar cost, disk usage, and failure recovery. The evaluation does not include a strong head-to-head experiment with AgentFold, which the paper itself identifies as closely related, nor does it test whether a fixed-threshold reversible archive would explain much of the gain. The training teacher is a 397B model and receives reference answers, but the paper does not quantify teacher-call cost, annotation volume, dataset size after filtering, or reference-answer leakage. The positive correlation between tool-call frequency and accuracy is correlational and may reflect more inference budget rather than context management itself; comparisons should therefore control total tool calls or compute. Finally, the use of an LLM querier over archived messages introduces another model-dependent bottleneck whose accuracy, calibration, and adversarial robustness are not evaluated. Bottom Line: This is a worthwhile preprint for researchers working on long-horizon LLM agents because it provides a practical reversible-memory design and reproducible training pipeline with credible benchmark gains, but its deployment and novelty claims remain incomplete until total inference cost, strong proactive baselines, retrieval fidelity, and larger-scale robustness are measured.

Problem & Motivation: The work addresses evaluation of agent self-evolution: whether an agent can use prior interactions to update persistent state and improve on related future tasks. The target domain is economically valuable, rule-governed enterprise work spanning CRM, ERP, finance, healthcare, legal, and data-analysis workflows. The paper identifies three gaps in prior evaluation: limited coverage of enterprise procedures, train–test splits that do not deliberately tie test improvements to transferable capabilities, and static public benchmarks that permit contamination. The intended evaluation problem is therefore not merely task-solving accuracy, but attributable transfer of hidden, deterministic business rules under explicit supervision and cost constraints. Key Idea: The central insight is rule hybridization. Each task group shares an environment and contains atomic business rules that are hidden from the model’s prior knowledge; training tasks expose different subsets of those rules, while held-out tasks recombine them with new entities, evidence, and rule combinations. A performance gain is consequently interpreted as evidence that the agent extracted and reused rules rather than simply memorizing an identical task. This is a benchmark-construction idea rather than a new learning algorithm. Methodology: GDPevo has three construction stages. First, an agent filters public real-work benchmarks such as GDPval, SOP-Bench, JobBench, healthcare, legal, SaaS, SQL, and workplace suites to identify domain-rich, deterministic, long-horizon scenarios. Second, an orchestrator creates a shared environment, ten tasks, reference answers, evaluation scripts, atomic rules, and a train–test rule matrix; an environment builder implements the database, web application, API, or other tools, while ten task builders instantiate five training and five test tasks. Third, calibration agents require roughly 40–60% base test accuracy, a roughly 10–30 percentage-point few-shot lift, and post-evolution accuracy below 80%; six reviewer agents then check completeness, rubric design, diversity, and answer leakage, accepting groups with at least five of six votes. During evaluation, the agent is defined as harness plus model and produces a portable SKILL.md artifact from five training tasks. Four supervision conditions are compared: base with no training, fewshot with training questions and gold answers, self with training questions only, and reflect-3 with training attempts and three rounds of grader feedback. The evolution method is skill distillation, with additional comparisons among five skill creators. Task scores use weighted binary rubric points generated into code-based tests by an LLM and executed deterministically; each test task runs three times, and accuracy, tokens, turns, and monetary cost are recorded. The key design decisions—explicit rule-based train–test construction, isolated Docker workspaces, and deterministic grading—are well motivated for attribution and reproducibility, although the paper does not independently validate all generated rules and graders with human domain experts. Key Results: The released benchmark contains 240 tasks in 24 groups, with 5 training and 5 held-out test tasks per group, across six domains: CRM, ERP, finance, healthcare, legal, and data analysis. On the full benchmark, GPT-5.5/Codex scores 49.37% base, 55.80% self, 57.82% reflect-3, and 64.51% fewshot; Opus-4.8/Claude Code scores 50.63%, 55.05%, 59.27%, and 67.07%, respectively; GLM-5.2/Claude Code scores 46.12%, 50.96%, 55.49%, and 60.09%; and DeepSeek-V4-Pro-Preview/Claude Code scores 43.58%, 46.17%, 47.15%, and 48.79%. Fewshot gains range from 5.21 to 16.44 percentage points, while all supervision conditions improve over the corresponding base configuration by 2.59–16.44 points. GPT-5.5 fewshot reduces test-time cost from $1.29 to $1.02 per task and tokens from 767.9k to 543.9k, but its skill-generation overhead makes amortized end-to-end cost approximately $1.296 per task, nearly equal to the $1.294 base cost. Opus-4.8/fewshot obtains the highest aggregate accuracy, but its amortized cost rises from $1.37 to $1.87 per task. A fully informed human-plus-Codex/GPT-5.5 condition reaches 91.6%, leaving a large gap from the best evolved agent. In a restricted cross-domain experiment using only one CRM, ERP, and finance group, fewshot has five of six off-diagonal transfer effects negative, with a worst case of −5.0 points, whereas reflect-3 has three positive off-diagonal effects and a worst loss of −1.0 point. In the skill-creator comparison, a minimal Naive creator reaches 65.12% for GPT-5.5/Codex versus 60.79–62.69% for the other creators, and 48.01% for DeepSeek versus 46.74–47.84% for the alternatives. The headline findings are plausible but should be interpreted as benchmark-specific: the task suite is synthetic and the baselines are agent configurations rather than established self-evolution algorithms or human business operators. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, NEW FORMULATION, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING—the genuinely distinctive contribution is the rule-hybridization formulation and automated generation pipeline for attributable self-evolution evaluation, while the evaluated skill-based evolution and supervision conditions combine established ideas in a new enterprise-workflow setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper reports three runs per held-out task, standard deviations across task groups, complete task-group breakdowns, rubric-level diagnostics, cost and token measurements, controlled skill-creator comparisons, isolated Docker execution, and case studies of positive, negative, and limited transfer. The pipeline, 240-task benchmark, graders, generated skills, and evaluation results are released at https://github.com/Prism-Shadow/GDPevo. However, it does not report statistical significance tests, confidence intervals beyond task-group standard deviations, or broad multiple-seed analyses of the evaluated models. The six-domain benchmark is generated by agents, and both construction and review rely heavily on GPT-5.5/Codex instances; independent human domain validation of task realism, rule correctness, rubric semantics, and grader agreement is not reported. The benchmark calibrates groups using the same general class of agent behavior that it later evaluates, which may select for particular model capabilities and create a form of benchmark-specific Goodhart pressure. Contamination resistance is argued through rapid regeneration and demonstrated by producing V2 in two days, but the paper does not empirically measure contamination or compare performance before and after exposure. The cross-domain experiment uses only three hand-selected groups and omits self supervision, limiting the strength of its generalization claim. Deployability (4-property check): EMPIRICAL, with a substantial released benchmark and generation pipeline rather than a deployed business system. Practical: The Docker-based environments can run on commercially available hardware, but the reported agents depend on proprietary or preview model and harness versions, and infrastructure requirements are not fully specified. Efficient: Evolution can reduce test-time cost—for example, GPT-5.5 fewshot lowers cost by 20.88%—but skill-generation overhead can erase the saving, and the best Opus configuration increases amortized cost. Effective: The evidence shows improvement on GDPevo’s deterministic proxy tasks, not validated correctness or productivity in live CRM, legal, healthcare, finance, or ERP deployments; the best evolved accuracy remains 67.07%, versus a 91.6% fully informed human-plus-agent reference. Scalable: The pipeline expanded from 120 to 240 tasks in under two days, but the paper does not test evaluation or generation at 10×–100× scale, nor establish that quality, independence, grading validity, or cost remain stable. The work delivers a reusable benchmark, generation pipeline, graders, evaluation traces, and skill artifacts; it does not deliver a production business automation system. Strengths: - Rule hybridization directly addresses the attribution problem in self-evolution evaluation by making the train–test dependency explicit and auditable at the rule level. - The benchmark covers 24 stateful task groups across six enterprise-oriented domains, including healthcare and legal workflows that are underrepresented in many agent-evolution suites. - The evaluation separates accuracy from resource use and includes cost, tokens, turns, rubric-level outcomes, transfer matrices, and failure cases rather than reporting a single aggregate score. - The case studies identify a concrete failure mechanism—skills omit scope conditions and evidence-to-output dependencies—rather than treating negative transfer as unexplained variance. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The paper explicitly acknowledges that the 91.6% oracle is only an approximation because it uses non-expert human operators with Codex/GPT-5.5 rather than domain experts. It also acknowledges that the four case studies use different model–harness configurations and are diagnostic rather than controlled comparisons, that cross-domain transfer is restricted to three V1 domains for tractability, and that current agents remain far below the fully informed ceiling. The paper discusses failure modes including overfitting, dropped scope conditions, limited hidden-rule structure, builder–grader coupling, information leakage, and evaluation-orchestrator errors. It does not provide a broader discussion of synthetic-task validity or human agreement with the generated graders. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The strongest unresolved issue is construct validity: the paper calls the tasks real-business tasks, but the evaluated environments, examples, rules, reference answers, and graders are newly generated and their fidelity is not established through domain-expert review or comparison with outcomes from real operators. The LLM-generated grader is deterministic only after generation; determinism does not guarantee that its tests faithfully encode the intended business rule, and the reported calibration and review agents may share correlated errors with the builders. The evaluation compares only four model–harness pairs, includes no human-only baseline, no strong non-skill memory or parameter-update baseline, and no direct comparison against leading self-evolution systems under matched compute and information budgets. The five-task training budget, calibration thresholds, and fixed skill format may favor fewshot skill distillation and constrain conclusions about self-evolution methods more generally. The contamination argument remains prospective rather than experimentally demonstrated, and the claim that V2 can be regenerated in two days does not quantify quality drift, novelty, or reproducibility across regenerated versions. Finally, the aggregate gains have substantial task-group variability, but the paper does not report per-group statistical tests or uncertainty for the cross-domain matrix, making some transfer conclusions fragile. Bottom Line: GDPevo is worth reading as a useful benchmark-design contribution with an unusually explicit transfer mechanism and actionable failure analysis, but its empirical conclusions about real-world agent self-evolution remain preliminary until independent human validation, stronger algorithmic baselines, and contamination and regeneration studies establish that its synthetic deterministic tasks measure more than benchmark-specific skill extraction.

Problem & Motivation: The work addresses the faithfulness of personalized LLMs that infer, store, and reuse user attributes from sparse conversational evidence. The affected domain includes persistent-memory assistants, recommendation systems, and other personalized agents. Existing memory benchmarks primarily test recall, retrieval, temporal validity, or personalization quality; they do not directly measure whether stored or expressed attributes were supported by what the user actually revealed. The paper isolates over-inference from ordinary factual hallucination and from population-level bias: a model may generate a plausible or stereotypical claim about an individual even when the claim is not licensed by the user’s evidence. The authors focus on an early-interaction setting with exactly three revealed facts, where personalization pressure is high but evidence remains sparse. Key Idea: The central insight is to evaluate personalization as an evidence-to-claim relationship rather than as response usefulness or factual accuracy. Claims are divided into Grounded, Reasonable, Stereotype, and Fabricated categories, with Stereotype and Fabricated jointly defining over-inference. This evidence-only criterion deliberately treats a claim as unsupported even if it is plausible, agrees with the hidden ground-truth profile, or is rhetorically useful for completing the requested task. A second insight is scope-dependent metacognition: a model’s self-audit may rank risky records within that model while remaining badly calibrated for comparing safety across models. Methodology: MirageBench contains 150 personas, each with a 15-attribute ground-truth profile and exactly three first-person revealed facts. The personas comprise 50 stereotypical, 50 counter-stereotypical, and 50 neutral profiles; 8 were hand-crafted, 70 sampled from PersonaMem-v2, and 72 generated by an LLM under coverage constraints. Each model performs six open-ended tasks—dating profile, weekend itinerary, recommendation letter, birthday gift, apartment description, and stress-source identification—using only the three revealed facts. In the Probe stage, the model explicitly lists inferable attributes. In the Task stage, it generates personalized responses and separately audits its own claims. An external Claude Opus 4-7 judge extracts claims and assigns the four taxonomy labels, using the revealed facts as evidence and the hidden profile only for a separate accuracy check. The primary metric is OI Rate = (Stereotype + Fabricated claims) / total claims. The Accum stage runs eight rounds of memory updates and measures stored inferred-attribute counts, linear growth, and removal or revision rates. Critical design decisions include fixing evidence at three facts, separating task context from evidence, and using a constant external judge across models; the first two support controlled measurement but also constrain ecological validity, while the judge choice is only partially justified by a single-human validation study. Generation uses temperature 0.7, judging uses temperature 0.0, and the experiments query 12 models across seven families, including proprietary APIs and one self-hosted Qwen3-8B model. Key Results: Every evaluated model over-infers between 35.1% and 48.7% of claims; the cross-model macro-average is 41.6% and the claim-weighted micro-average is 41.8% over 143,616 claims. Qwen3-8B has the highest judged OI rate at 48.7%, followed by DeepSeek-v4-pro at 45.4% and GPT-4o-mini at 45.1%; Gemini-3.1-pro and Claude Opus 4-6 have the lowest rates at 35.1% and 35.4%, respectively. Fabricated claims dominate stereotypical claims, averaging 31.1% versus 10.5%. OI varies substantially by task: apartment description reaches 57.8%, recommendation letters 48.2%, stress-source identification 39.8%, itineraries 38.7%, dating profiles 28.5%, and gifts 27.0%. Stereotypical personas yield 44.8% OI versus 37.0% for counter-stereotypical personas, a 7.8 percentage-point gap present in all 12 models. At the model level, self-audit OI is negatively rank-correlated with judge OI (Spearman ρ = −0.60, permutation p = 0.044), but the 95% bootstrap interval is [−0.90, +0.06] and the family-clustered interval is [−0.87, +0.14]. Within models, self-audit AUROC for identifying high-OI records ranges from 0.58 to 0.83, with 9 of 12 models above 0.75. Direct Probe elicitation produces only 0.7%–4.6% incorrect inference rates, creating a mean 38.6-point gap from implicit Task-generation OI. In the two-persona, eight-round accumulation pilot, 9 of 12 models show approximately linear growth with R² > 0.90 and slopes of roughly 5–15 attributes per round; GPT-5.5 and GLM-5.1 reach 125.0 and 121.5 inferred attributes by round 8, with removal rates of 0.4% and 1.4%. Novelty Classification: The contribution is primarily NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and NEW FORMULATION, with a secondary NEW SYSTEM/TOOL classification for the evaluation pipeline; the taxonomy and evidence-only metric operationalize an under-measured failure mode, while the model sweep and self-monitoring inversion provide the main empirical novelty, but the pipeline combines standard prompting, claim extraction, LLM judging, and correlation analysis rather than introducing a new learning algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility: The study reports explicit prompts, model snapshots, decoding temperatures, persona construction procedures, metric definitions, per-model and per-task breakdowns, and a blind validation sample. The independent judge agrees with one blind human annotator at 89.8% four-way accuracy with κ = 0.863 and at 95.0% binary accuracy with κ = 0.900; disagreements are mostly between adjacent taxonomy categories. However, there are no reported multi-annotator agreement statistics, confidence intervals for κ, repeated-generation seeds, or significance tests for most model and task comparisons. The judge is a single Claude Opus 4-7 model, and one evaluated model belongs to the same family, leaving judge-backbone and model-family effects unresolved. The self-audit and judge use independent claim extractors, so their record-level comparisons do not match claims one-to-one. The benchmark mixes 70 sampled and 72 LLM-generated personas, which may introduce generation artifacts or stereotype leakage. The paper says MirageBench will be released in full, but no URL, repository, data license, or currently available model artifact is stated. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL. Practical: The evaluation can run on commercially available API-accessible models and was orchestrated from a CPU-only workstation, although the self-hosted Qwen3-8B run used two NVIDIA H20 GPUs. Efficient: The study requires 900 task instances per model plus claim extraction and external judging, so it is substantially more expensive than ordinary single-pass evaluation; the paper does not provide token counts, dollar cost, or latency comparisons. Effective: The benchmark directly measures evidence support for personalized claims and establishes judge-human agreement on a stratified sample, but it does not measure downstream user harm, recommendation quality, satisfaction, privacy outcomes, or whether reducing OI improves utility. Scalable: The main single-turn evaluation uses 150 personas and 6 tasks, while the longitudinal analysis uses only 2 personas and 8 rounds; behavior at 10×–100× the persona, task, turn, or memory scale is not tested. The work delivers a benchmark and evaluation pipeline, with a promised dataset release, but the stated material does not identify a released repository or deployable mitigation system. Strengths: - The evidence-only formulation cleanly separates user-profile faithfulness from world-fact correctness and makes unsupported personalization measurable at the claim level. - The benchmark varies task groundability and persona stereotype alignment, allowing the paper to distinguish generic fabrication from task-induced genre pressure and stereotype-driven inference. - The external-judge validation is stronger than an unvalidated automatic metric: the 400-claim blind comparison reports κ = 0.863 for four classes and κ = 0.900 for binary OI, with 71% of disagreements confined to adjacent categories. - The distinction between within-model self-audit usefulness and cross-model self-audit unreliability is a substantive and practically relevant observation, even though its cross-model statistical support remains limited. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly identify the use of one judge and one human annotator, the absence of a cross-judge robustness check, possible influence of the hidden profile on borderline judge decisions, and the fact that evidence-only scoring can make task-presupposed content count as over-inference. They characterize the self-monitoring inversion as exploratory because it uses only 12 correlated models and a confidence interval containing zero. They also acknowledge that Accum uses only two personas and a prompt instructing retention rather than free pruning, which biases absolute accumulation upward. Finally, they state that they evaluate no mitigation and do not measure downstream recommendation quality or user satisfaction. These limitations are confronted directly, particularly for the accumulation pilot, although the discussion still draws fairly broad design implications from the constrained setup. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The benchmark’s definition of faithfulness is contestable for tasks whose requested output inherently requires hypothetical or creative content; classifying all task-required but evidence-unsupported claims as over-inference measures strict provenance compliance rather than necessarily harmful personalization. The study does not compare this strict metric with a task-aware or uncertainty-expressing alternative, so the reported OI rates may be upper bounds for practical deployments. The model sample is broad but not statistically independent: seven families and 12 snapshots cannot establish a general scaling or capability relationship, and provider-specific prompting, API behavior, and model versions may confound comparisons. The self-monitoring inversion may be driven by differences in label severity, output length, claim extraction, or prompt compliance rather than a general metacognitive phenomenon; the paper’s own strict-versus-lenient explanation is plausible but not experimentally tested with calibration controls or standardized audit prompts. The hidden personas are partly LLM-generated and all evidence sets contain exactly three facts, leaving naturalistic evidence density, multilingual interaction, real user histories, memory implementations, and adversarial or corrective turns untested. The accumulation prompt nearly hard-codes retention, and the analysis does not compare against a neutral pruning prompt, a provenance-aware memory system, or an actual deployed memory architecture. No mitigation experiment demonstrates that provenance tags, external filtering, or abstention reduces OI without degrading personalization utility. Bottom Line: This is a useful and technically concrete benchmark paper for researchers evaluating personalized-memory faithfulness, with credible evidence that unsupported claims are common, but its strongest cross-model and longitudinal conclusions remain exploratory until validated with multiple judges and annotators, naturalistic memory settings, larger longitudinal samples, and tested mitigations.

K-EXAONE 2.0 Technical Report (13 ▲ )

Eunbi Choi, Kibong Choi, Sehyun Chun, Seokhee Hong, Junwon Hwang, Hyojin Jeon, Ahra Jo, Hyunjik Jo, Yeonsik Jo, Minhyeok Jung, Doyoung Kim, Heegyu Kim, Joonkee Kim, Seonghwan Kim, Soyeon Kim, Sunkyoung Kim, Yireun Kim, Yongil Kim, Byungoh Ko, Changhun Lee, Dohaeng Lee, Haeju Lee, Jinsik Lee, Kyungmin Lee, Minwoo Lee, Wonkee Lee, Sangha Park, Sungjune Park, Kwangrok Ryoo, Kijung Seo, Minju Seo, Yongwoo Song, Sejong Yang, Heuiyeen Yeen, Stanley Jungkyu Choi, Yemuk Choi, Yongchan Chun, Jiwon Ham, Dasol Hong, Sujeong Im, Kijeong Jeon, Gerrard Jeongwon Jo, Hyeongjun Jo, Yujin Jo, Jiyeon Jung, Naeun Kang, Daeseong Kim, Euisoon Kim, Hayeon Kim, Hyosang Kim, Myoungshin Kim, Unsol Kim, Youchul Kim, Chaeeun Lee, ChaeYoon Lee, Edward Hwayoung Lee, Honglak Lee, Hwansoo Lee, Minkyung Lee, Sangeun Lee, Solji Lim, Woohyung Lim, Chanwoo Moon, Jueun Mun, Jimin Park, Seojeong Park, Yongmin Park, Hyerin Seo, Donghyeon Shin, Donghyun Son, Eunyong Son, Kaehyun Um, Sihoon Yang, Chang En Yea, Sihyuk Yi, Kyungjae Yoo, Chansik Yoon · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 6 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces K-EXAONE 2.0, an open-weight multilingual Mixture-of-Experts foundation model with 750B total parameters, approximately 37B activated per token, 256K-token context, ten-language coverage, and two self-speculative decoding paths. - Why it's important: The model targets practical sovereign-AI deployment by combining frontier-scale capacity with Korean and multilingual capabilities, long-context processing, agentic coding, safety controls, and an Apache 2.0 release. - How it does it: It upcycles K-EXAONE by expanding depth from 48 to 78 layers and experts from 128 to 256, then applies continual pre-training, staged long-context mid-training, SFT, preference optimization, and DSpark/MTP speculative decoding. - The good: On the authors' evaluations, it improves substantially over K-EXAONE in SWE-Bench Verified (49.4 to 68.2), Terminal-Bench 2.1 (30.3 to 43.8), and OpenAI-MRCR (52.3 to 94.4), while achieving perfect Needle-in-a-Haystack retrieval through 256K tokens. - The missing: The report does not provide compute, wall-clock, memory, or cost comparisons for training and serving, nor controlled full-scale ablations that isolate upcycling, data, mid-training, post-training, and scale effects. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on large multilingual MoE systems, long-context inference, Korean-language AI, or sovereign-model safety; skip it if you seek a narrowly isolated algorithmic contribution rather than a broad, vendor-authored model report.

Problem & Motivation: The work addresses the need for open-weight, frontier-scale language models that can be built and operated within national linguistic, cultural, institutional, and safety contexts. The target users include model developers, infrastructure operators, Korean public- and private-sector organizations, and researchers needing long-context, multilingual, coding-agent, tool-use, and safety capabilities. The stated gap is that existing open-weight models may provide scale or broad capability but do not necessarily combine Korean sociocultural grounding, ten-language coverage, 256K context, agentic workflows, and an openly deployable license. The report also targets the practical cost of replacing a trained model: rather than discarding K-EXAONE's learned parameters and training investment, it seeks to expand and continue training that model. Key Idea: The central insight is to treat frontier-scale model development as an upcycling and capability-direction problem: expand a proven sparse MoE along depth and expert capacity while preserving routing and attention choices, stabilize the enlarged network, and use staged data-centric training to direct the added capacity toward long-context reasoning, agents, multilinguality, and safety. The most technically identifiable sub-idea is block-level depth expansion combined with expert duplication plus norm-preserving random rotation noise, which prevents duplicated experts from remaining gradient-tied. The overall contribution is nevertheless a coordinated system recipe rather than one isolated new learning principle. Methodology: The backbone is a sparse MoE decoder with 78 layers: two dense layers followed by 76 MoE layers, 20 global-attention and 58 sliding-window-attention layers, 256 experts per MoE layer, one shared expert plus top-8 routed experts per token, and 2,048-dimensional experts. The second layer uses a 4,096-token sliding window and other sliding-window layers use 128 tokens; QK normalization, SWA-only RoPE, sigmoid routing, sequence-level load balancing, and dropless routing are inherited from K-EXAONE. Upcycling expands depth from 48 to 78 layers by repeating selected middle LLLG blocks and expands width by duplicating experts and router rows, then applying random rotation noise to break symmetry. The last 16 MoE layers clamp both SwiGLU branches at 7.0 for numerical stability, reducing the reported peak activation from 6,862 without clamping to 48.96 with clamping. Continual pre-training first uses a healing stage and then an additional 8T tokens; it adds Active Reading and latent-thinking synthetic data, Korean institutional data, and data for four additional languages. Mid-training proceeds from 8K to 64K and then 256K context, with 400B tokens in each of two stages and increased emphasis on long documents, repositories, tool trajectories, advanced reasoning, and agent workflows. Post-training uses 350B-token SFT covering reasoning, code, knowledge, chat, and agents, followed by multi-task and safety-aware preference optimization with GROUPER; the router is frozen during SFT. MTP is trained jointly with the backbone using cross-entropy and later refined using an end-to-end total-variation objective intended to optimize rejection-sampling acceptance. DSpark is a separately trained five-layer, block-size-seven semi-autoregressive drafter conditioned on intermediate target hidden states and trained on target-generated data. These design decisions are plausible and supported by limited targeted studies, but most full-scale training choices and their interactions are not experimentally isolated. Key Results: The report evaluates 24 benchmarks across nine categories and compares against K-EXAONE, Qwen3.5, GLM-5.1, and DeepSeek V4 Pro, with some baseline values taken from official reports, blogs, or leaderboards rather than reproduced runs. K-EXAONE 2.0 scores 83.5 on MMLU-Pro, 82.2 on GPQA-Diamond, and 18.3 on HUMANITY'S LAST EXAM; it scores 92.3 on AIME 2026, 78.4 on HMMT FEB 2026, and 78.6 on IMO-ANSWERBENCH. Coding scores are 40.1 on SciCode, 68.2 on SWE-Bench Verified, and 43.8 on Terminal-Bench 2.1, versus 35.6, 49.4, and 30.3 for K-EXAONE. Agent-tool scores are 14.2 on τ3-Bench Banking and 80.0 on Claw-Eval. Instruction-following scores are 92.4 on IFEval and 72.6 on IFBench. Long-context scores are 94.4 on OpenAI-MRCR, 56.2 on AA-LCR, and 89.6 on Ko-LongBench; OpenAI-MRCR improves by 42.1 points over K-EXAONE, although the authors evaluate only through 128K despite the model's 256K context claim. Korean scores are 69.1 on KMMLU-Pro, 84.2 on CLICK, and 91.1 on HRM8K-KSM; multilingual scores are 86.6 on both MMMLU and GlobalMMLU-Lite and 71.3 on POLYMATH. Safety scores are 99.8 on the in-house KGC-SAFETY benchmark and 89.5 on ROK-FORTRESS. Compared with stronger external models, K-EXAONE 2.0 is generally behind Qwen3.5 and DeepSeek V4 Pro on world knowledge, coding, Korean, multilingual, and several reasoning tasks, but exceeds them on the reported KGC-SAFETY score and is competitive or higher on some long-context retrieval measures. DSpark yields 1.81-2.57x end-to-end speedup on 8 H200 GPUs with FP8 and draft budget seven, compared with 1.27-1.77x for MTP; acceptance length improves by 32-66% relative to MTP across the reported math and code tasks. The results are standard-scale benchmark evaluations for a frontier model, with no 10x-100x stress test or production deployment measurement. Novelty Classification: The contribution is primarily NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION, with secondary NEW METHOD elements in the block-level MoE upcycling and DSpark integration; the architecture, continual training, SFT, preference optimization, speculative decoding, and safety taxonomy largely combine established techniques, while the genuinely distinctive contribution is their demonstrated integration into an openly released 750B/37B-activated Korean-centered model. Rigor & Reproducibility: The report includes useful targeted ablations: Active Reading versus textbook-style synthetic data, Korean institutional versus open data, mid-training stage comparisons, MTP versus DSpark decoding, and a clamping analysis. The mid-training study on a small-scale model reports HLE gains of 3.15 for direct SFT, 4.71 for Mid-Stage 2, and 5.66 for Mid-Stage 2 followed by SFT. However, it does not report multiple random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, statistical tests, or per-task variance. It lacks full-scale factorial ablations isolating the effects of depth expansion, width expansion, healing, the 8T continual-training tokens, the two mid-training stages, SFT, GROUPER, safety training, and model scale. Several comparisons use author-run results for K-EXAONE and external official numbers for other models, creating setup and reporting asymmetries; some baselines are larger or use different reasoning configurations. The strongest safety result, KGC-SAFETY, is in-house and closely related to the authors' own safety taxonomy and training process, so it is vulnerable to evaluator/training alignment and Goodhart effects. ROK-FORTRESS uses an ensemble of contemporary judge models, but the report does not provide human agreement, judge calibration, or judge sensitivity analyses. The code repository is listed at https://github.com/LG-AI-EXAONE/K-EXAONE-2.0 and the model at https://huggingface.co/LGAI-EXAONE/K-EXAONE-2.0-750B-A37B; the model is released under Apache 2.0. The report does not establish that the public release contains complete training data, training scripts, checkpoints, or all evaluation harnesses. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL and SYSTEMS, because the report describes and evaluates a released model and inference modules. - Practical: Inference is demonstrated on commercially available H200 GPUs, but a 750B-parameter model still requires substantial multi-GPU memory and distributed serving; the report does not give minimum hardware or quantized deployment requirements. - Efficient: Sparse activation reduces per-token computation to approximately 37B active parameters, and DSpark reports 1.81-2.57x end-to-end speedup over non-speculative decoding on 8 H200 GPUs, but total memory, latency, throughput, energy, and cost relative to dense or competing MoE systems are not reported. - Effective: Benchmark evidence supports improvements in long-context retrieval, repository coding, terminal interaction, instruction following, multilingual math, and Korean-context safety, but it does not directly measure reliability in deployed organizations or open-ended agent failure rates. - Scalable: The model is tested to 256K context and 750B total parameters, but the report does not test 10x-100x larger models, longer contexts, higher concurrency, or failure behavior under production-scale serving; claims about future trillion-parameter scaling remain unvalidated. The work delivers an open-weight trained model, inference-time MTP and DSpark modules, a GitHub code artifact, and evaluation resources, but not a fully reproducible end-to-end training stack or public training corpus. Strengths: - The report demonstrates a credible large-scale upcycling path from 236B to 750B total parameters while increasing activated parameters only from 23B to 37B, addressing both capacity growth and sparse inference cost. - The combination of 256K context training, repository-level coding data, tool-use trajectories, and preserved thinking targets realistic long-horizon workflows rather than only short-form question answering. - The DSpark comparison is concrete and operationally relevant: on identical FP8 targets and draft budgets, it improves acceptance length and reports 1.81-2.57x end-to-end speedups. - The open Apache 2.0 release, Korean institutional grounding, ten-language coverage, and explicit safety-taxonomy development provide practical value beyond a closed vendor model announcement. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that the model can generate inappropriate, harmful, biased, factually false, stale, or syntactically and semantically incorrect responses. They acknowledge that safety evaluation must evolve against increasingly sophisticated risks and that the model does not lead on every benchmark. They also identify the need to scale advanced reasoning-data generation and improve the translation of mid-training gains into post-training performance. These limitations are stated at a high level, but the report does not quantify failure rates, recency limitations, bias, or deployment risk. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The report does not disclose training compute, GPU-hours, energy, financial cost, token mixture sizes beyond selected stages, data provenance at sufficient detail, or contamination audits beyond a description of lexical decontamination. It does not provide full-scale ablations to separate architectural scaling from data and post-training effects, nor does it test whether upcycling is cheaper or better than training a comparable model from scratch. The benchmark suite is partly author-selected and includes in-house Korean and safety tests that may favor the model's training objectives. External baseline scores mix official reports, leaderboard values, and internal evaluations with potentially different prompts, sampling, tool wrappers, and reasoning budgets. Long-context evidence relies heavily on synthetic needle retrieval; the principal MRCR evaluation stops at 128K, and no end-to-end 256K agent or document reasoning study is reported. The perfect NIAH result is not sufficient evidence for robust long-context synthesis, attribution, or resistance to distractors. No robustness evaluation covers prompt injection in tools, API errors, malicious repositories, multi-agent interaction, concurrency, or model degradation under quantization. The safety evaluation lacks independent human annotation details, inter-rater agreement, refusal/helpfulness trade-offs, false-refusal rates, and adversarial transfer tests outside the authors' taxonomy. Finally, the report does not establish that the released artifact can be reproduced from the public materials or that the claimed Apache 2.0 model license resolves underlying training-data copyright and privacy risks. Bottom Line: This is a valuable open model and systems report for researchers and practitioners studying large multilingual MoE upcycling, long-context inference, agentic coding, and Korean-context safety, but its broad engineering achievement is better supported than its causal claims about which ingredients produce the gains.

Entering the Era of Discrete Diffusion Models: A Benchmark for Schrödinger Bridges and Entropic Optimal Transport

X Aramayo Carrasco, G Ksenofontov, A Leonov… · proceedings.iclr.cc · 10 new citations to your articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a discrete-space Schrödinger bridge (SB) and entropic optimal transport (EOT) benchmark with analytically known solutions, together with three discrete solvers: DLightSB, DLightSB-M, and α-CSBM. - Why it's important: Discrete SB methods currently lack ground-truth evaluation, so proxy metrics can conceal whether a solver actually recovers the desired transport process. - How it does it: It constructs target marginals by reweighting a factorizable discrete reference process with a nonnegative CP-decomposed potential, making normalization, sampling, and dynamic transitions tractable in high dimensions. - The good: On the proposed Gaussian-mixture benchmark, DLightSB obtains conditional Shape Scores of 0.85–0.95 and conditional Trend Scores of 0.77–0.97 across dimensions 2, 16, and 64, generally outperforming CSBM, α-CSBM, and DLightSB-M. - The missing: The evaluation is entirely synthetic and structurally aligned with DLightSB's CP parameterization; there is no evidence that the benchmark rankings transfer to real discrete domains or to benchmark distributions outside this construction. - Read it or not: Researchers developing discrete diffusion or SB solvers should read it for the exact-solution benchmark and implementation, but practitioners seeking a deployable solver should treat the reported performance as preliminary because scalability and real-data effectiveness remain untested.

Problem & Motivation The work addresses the difficulty of evaluating generative EOT/SB solvers on discrete spaces such as categorical vectors, text, molecular graphs, protein sequences, and quantized representations. Existing evaluations often use indirect metrics such as FID, reconstruction error, or marginal-matching scores, which do not directly measure recovery of the EOT/SB solution and can be confounded by parameterization and regularization. The specific prior-work gap is the absence of discrete distributions with analytically known optimal SB/EOT couplings and trajectories, combined with a limited supply of practical discrete-space solvers. The intended users are researchers comparing discrete diffusion, flow-matching, and Schrödinger-bridge algorithms rather than end users of a particular application. Key Idea The central insight is to generate benchmark pairs from a known optimal conditional distribution of the form q(x1|x0) proportional to v(x1) q_ref(x1|x0), then define p1 as the resulting second marginal. This construction guarantees that the selected q solves the SB/EOT problem for p0, p1, and q_ref. Representing v with a nonnegative CP decomposition converts otherwise exponential sums over |X| = S^D states into products of one-dimensional sums, with normalization and sampling cost O(KDS). The same representation also yields tractable dynamic SB transitions. The benchmark and DLightSB methods therefore share an inductive bias by construction, which makes DLightSB useful as an oracle-like solver but weakens the benchmark as a neutral test of generalization. Methodology The benchmark operates on X = {0,...,S−1}^D with S = 50 categories, a discretized initial Gaussian p0, and either a uniform or Gaussian-like factorizable Markov reference process with N+1 = 128 time transitions. The target is generated by selecting v(x1) as a mixture of K = 4 rank-one CP components, each using discretized Gaussian cores, and setting p1(x1) = sum_x0 p0(x0)q(x1|x0). For the static solution, the model uses qθ(x1|x0) = vθ(x1)q_ref(x1|x0)/cθ(x0), where vθ has learnable CP weights and cores; DLightSB optimizes the equivalent direct-KL objective L(θ) = E_p0[log cθ(x0)] − E_p1[log vθ(x1)]. DLightSB-M uses the analogous CP parameterization for time-dependent SB transitions and optimizes a Markovian-projection loss. CSBM applies bidirectional discrete iterative Markovian fitting, training factored transition models with either KL or MSE losses; α-CSBM replaces full alternating projections with simultaneous partial updates using a stop-gradient objective and approximately halves the computational burden. Critical design choices are the CP factorization, which is mathematically justified for tractability but restricts benchmark structure; the use of uniform and Gaussian-like reference chains, which probes different category geometries but remains narrow; and infinite independent training samples from p0 and p1, which isolates solver error but removes finite-data effects central to the stated generative task. DLightSB and DLightSB-M use K = 1000 components in experiments, are trained for 100,000 updates, and CSBM-family methods use five fitting iterations with 120,000 updates in the first and 40,000 in later iterations. Key Results The experiments use D ∈ {2, 16, 64}, S = 50, Gaussian references with γ ∈ {0.02, 0.05}, uniform references with γ ∈ {0.005, 0.01}, one A100 GPU for most runs, 20,000 precomputed test pairs, and 1,000 conditional samples for each of 157 test x0 values. DLightSB is the strongest method on the forward benchmark: its conditional Shape Scores range from 0.85 to 0.95 and its conditional Trend Scores from 0.77 to 0.97 across the reported settings, with many values at or above 0.90. DLightSB-M is usually competitive but degrades at D = 64, especially for uniform references, where conditional Shape Scores can fall to 0.49–0.73 and Trend Scores to 0.48–0.83 depending on loss and N. CSBM and α-CSBM are substantially weaker in difficult high-dimensional or low-stochasticity settings; for example, CSBM with KL and N+1 = 16 reaches conditional Shape Scores as low as 0.62–0.79 and Trend Scores as low as 0.35–0.67 at D = 64, while increasing N+1 to 64 generally improves results. KL generally outperforms MSE, consistent with the authors' observation that MSE oversmooths modes. The trajectory KL for DLightSB is near zero in most settings, whereas CSBM can reach 189.1 and DLightSB-M can reach 26.4; reverse trajectory KL is especially unstable for DLightSB-M, reaching 329.7 in a D = 64 uniform-reference setting. The reverse benchmark exposes the construction bias: DLightSB, CSBM, and the tested methods all obtain nearly uninformative C2ST AUC values of roughly 0.90–1.00, so the authors discard that metric. Training takes about 20 minutes for DLightSB at D = 2 and under 7 hours at D = 64, versus under 14 hours for CSBM and nearly two days for DLightSB-M at D = 64 using two A100 GPUs. These numbers demonstrate controlled synthetic recovery, not real-data quality or stress-scale deployment. Novelty Classification NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK, NEW FORMULATION, NEW METHOD, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. The genuinely new contribution is the exact-solution construction for discrete SB/EOT evaluation and its CP-based tractable instantiation; DLightSB and DLightSB-M adapt the existing LightSB framework, while α-CSBM is a relatively direct combination of CSBM with online α-IMF updates rather than a fundamentally new optimization principle. Rigor & Reproducibility The paper provides proofs for the benchmark-construction theorem, tractable CP parameterization, dynamic transitions, the DLightSB loss reformulation, and the DLightSB-M projection result. It reports forward and reverse trajectory KL in addition to dimension-wise and pair-wise marginal metrics, and it includes a reverse-benchmark diagnostic that reveals the forward construction's inductive bias. However, the experiments do not report multiple random seeds, error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Ablations are limited: the paper varies dimension, reference process, stochasticity, fitting-step count, and KL versus MSE, but does not systematically vary CP rank K, initialization, neural-network capacity, or training budget. The benchmark and experiments use infinitely sampled training data, and the principal benchmark distribution is generated using the same CP structure used by DLightSB. DDSBM is discussed but not experimentally compared, and the baseline suite contains mostly simple reference methods rather than strong, independently parameterized discrete diffusion or flow solvers. Code is released at https://github.com/gregkseno/catsbench; the CSBM implementation is linked at https://github.com/gregkseno/csbm. No dataset beyond synthetic benchmark generators or pretrained model weights is stated. Deployability (4-property check) Profile: EMPIRICAL, with a systems/artifact component. Practical: The experiments run on commercially available NVIDIA A100 GPUs, and the released code should permit reproduction, although DLightSB-M at D = 64 requires two A100 GPUs and nearly two days. Efficient: α-CSBM achieves similar conditional scores to CSBM while approximately halving its computational cost, whereas DLightSB has short training times at low dimension but its K = 1000 CP representation creates severe memory and computation costs as D grows. Effective: The methods recover the exact synthetic conditional and trajectory distributions reasonably well in the forward benchmark, but the evidence does not establish effectiveness on real discrete data or beyond the benchmark's low-order marginal metrics. Scalable: The largest tested dimensionality is D = 64 with 50 categories and 128 transitions; no 10×–100× scale experiment is provided, and the authors explicitly report severe high-dimensional memory constraints. The work delivers a reusable benchmark generator, evaluation code, and solver implementations rather than only a paper-form result. Strengths - It identifies a real evaluation deficiency in discrete SB/EOT research and supplies ground truth rather than relying solely on proxy generative metrics. - The benchmark-construction theorem is simple, general for positive reference processes and nonnegative potentials, and directly exposes why the generated pair has a known optimum. - The CP parameterization reduces normalization and sampling from exponential dependence on S^D to O(KDS), enabling exact benchmark generation and direct optimization in dimensions up to 64. - The experiments measure both endpoint conditional fidelity and dynamic trajectory divergence, and the reverse-benchmark analysis openly demonstrates that DLightSB's strong forward results are partly caused by benchmark-method alignment. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly acknowledge that DLightSB and DLightSB-M require large K in high dimensions and therefore face severe memory constraints. They also state that CSBM and α-CSBM are sensitive to parameter choices and require long training times. They recognize that the forward benchmark favors DLightSB(-M) because its CP inductive bias matches the construction, and they attempt to probe this issue with a reverse benchmark. They report that C2ST is uninformative in the reverse setting and discard it. These limitations are confronted directly, although the paper does not resolve them. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The benchmark is entirely synthetic and uses discretized Gaussian mixtures with only two reference-process families; there is no evaluation on text, graphs, molecules, proteins, tabular data, or vector-quantized representations. - The main comparison is structurally favorable to DLightSB because the ground-truth potential is CP-decomposed and the solver uses the same parameterization. The reverse benchmark cannot provide exact conditional metrics, so it does not fully correct this confound. - The experiments use infinite training data sampled independently from p0 and p1, omitting finite-sample estimation, dataset shift, empirical marginal noise, and out-of-sample generalization under realistic data budgets. - The Shape and Trend Scores inspect only one- and two-coordinate marginals; high-dimensional joint errors can remain large while these metrics are high. Trajectory KL is also decomposed using coordinate-wise transitions, which may underrepresent cross-coordinate dependence for some models. - The paper lacks repeated-seed variability, compute-normalized comparisons, parameter counts, memory measurements, convergence curves, and a systematic CP-rank ablation. Consequently, the reported superiority may partly reflect tuning and representation capacity rather than solver quality alone. - Stronger contemporary discrete diffusion, flow-matching, or neural SB baselines are absent or excluded without a direct empirical comparison, limiting the benchmark's ability to establish a field-wide ranking. Bottom Line This is a useful and technically credible first benchmark for exact evaluation of discrete Schrödinger-bridge solvers, worth reading for researchers in discrete diffusion and entropic transport, but its solver ranking should not be treated as general evidence until the benchmark is diversified beyond CP-generated synthetic distributions and evaluated with stronger baselines and statistical controls.
