Problem & Motivation Long-context LLM serving must retain or retrieve large KV caches while supporting high request concurrency. Full GPU-resident KV caches exhaust HBM, whereas dynamic sparse-KV systems offload most entries to host memory but commonly retain GPU-resident landmarks, low-rank keys, quantized representations, or other auxiliary state to reduce retrieval latency. The paper measures this auxiliary residency as a substantial bottleneck: in its motivating measurements it accounts for at least 30% of GPU memory across evaluated configurations and, together with landmarks, can occupy up to 64% of HBM. The resulting batch-size limits reduce throughput and can expose PCIe transfer latency on the decoding critical path. The target domain is online serving of 8B–32B Llama and Qwen models with 64K–512K contexts. Key Idea The central insight is that the sparse retrieval index needed for the next decoding step is predictable from the preceding speculative token and fixed GPU-resident landmarks, even when the exact token prediction is wrong. The paper reports average KV-index prediction accuracy of approximately 88% across its configurations, higher than speculative-token accuracy itself. This converts sparse KV retrieval from a residency problem into a scheduling problem: likely-needed entries can be transferred before attention needs them, while prediction misses are corrected urgently. The conceptual contribution is distinct from simply applying ordinary speculative decoding because the speculative token serves as retrieval guidance rather than as a candidate output whose acceptance determines generation. Methodology DualDecoder is implemented on top of ShadowKV and has three main stages. First, a lightweight pre-decoding step generates the first real output token, which initializes the first speculative token; subsequent decoding co-executes the current/output token and a speculative successor token in shared model kernels, using sequence-dimension packing and a causal mask so the speculative token cannot affect the normal output. Second, the speculative token and fixed K landmarks produce a predicted sparse retrieval index for the next step. A layer-aware scheduler starts prefetching entries for a future layer after an earlier layer's attention completes, thereby overlapping host-to-device transfers with model computation. It places corrections for omitted entries on a high-priority urgent stream and speculative transfers on a lower-priority stream. For layers with consistently poor prediction accuracy, it selectively reconstructs keys from a low-rank GPU-resident representation while still fetching values. Third, a two-layer ping-pong buffer maintains one buffer for current attention and one for incoming transfers, with CUDA events enforcing read/write dependencies. GPU-side assembly kernels gather, reorder, and merge transferred blocks into the sparse attention layout. The principal design decisions are well motivated operationally, but the paper gives limited analytical treatment of scheduler thresholds, buffer sizing, or the cost and selection criteria of adaptive reconstruction. Key Results The experiments use eight NVIDIA Hopper GPUs with 80 GB HBM each, Intel Xeon host CPUs, 1.6 TB host memory, and PCIe 5.0; models are Llama-3 and Qwen-2.5 variants from 8B to 32B, with contexts from 64K to 512K. Against vLLM, SpeCache, and ShadowKV, DualDecoder reports 42 tokens/s for Qwen-2.5-32B at 64K context, exceeding ShadowKV by 1.14x, SpeCache by 9.02x, and vLLM by 3.65x. At 128K and 256K it exceeds ShadowKV by 2.62x and 1.32x, respectively; vLLM is out of memory at both lengths, while SpeCache is out of memory at 256K. Under a synthetic Poisson-arrival workload with a 60-second P99 request-completion target, the paper reports up to 2.51x the tolerable arrival rate of ShadowKV, including 4.8 requests/s versus ShadowKV's 1.92 requests/s for a 32B model at 128K context. At matched batch sizes, memory consumption is reported to be up to 36.4% lower than ShadowKV and 62.0% lower than SpeCache; increasing context from 64K to 512K adds 3.7 GB for DualDecoder versus 17.8 GB for ShadowKV or vLLM failures. KV-index overlap ranges from roughly 82.6% to 97.2% in the shown configurations. Co-batched dual-token execution takes 0.035 ms versus 0.069 ms for two separate passes, and GPU-side gathering reduces one reported retrieval overhead from 49.5 ms to 3.25 ms, a 93.4% reduction. The quality table reports first-generated-token exact-match on four RULER subsets: at 64K/128K, DualDecoder averages 1.00 versus ShadowKV's 0.94/0.74, but QA-2 remains only 0.58/0.43 for DualDecoder. These results indicate strong systems gains on the selected setup, but they do not demonstrate broad generation-quality preservation. Novelty Classification NEW METHOD, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION: the genuinely new element is the observation and exploitation of consecutive-step sparse-KV-index predictability through a speculative token, combined with layer-aware prefetching and constant-depth buffering; the dual-token execution, priority streams, GPU gathering, CUDA event coordination, and selective low-rank reconstruction are largely systems combinations of established mechanisms adapted to this retrieval setting. Rigor & Reproducibility The paper includes component studies for dual-token execution, priority scheduling under 5%–33% miss rates, and GPU versus CPU gathering, as well as memory, throughput, latency, prediction-accuracy, and end-to-end task measurements. It does not report multiple random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, statistical significance tests, or repeated-run variability. The ablations are useful but incomplete: there is no clear end-to-end ablation isolating predictive prefetching, layer-aware timing, ping-pong buffering, adaptive reconstruction, and miss correction on the main throughput metric. Baselines include vLLM, SpeCache, and ShadowKV, with ShadowKV as the implementation substrate; they are relevant and fairly recent, but the comparison omits several potentially direct alternatives in the related work, including systems using learned retrieval heads, remote KV pools, sequence parallelism, or other prefetching designs. Request arrivals are synthesized with a Poisson process rather than taken from production traces. Quality is evaluated on RULER-derived NIAH/QA tasks and mostly via the first generated token, which is insufficient to establish full-output equivalence. No code, dataset, model weights, or repository URL is stated. The paper is an arXiv preprint, identified as version 1 dated 29 July 2026 in the parsed document, so the results should be treated as self-reported pre-publication measurements. There is also an internal naming inconsistency: the appendix refers to the system as “StreamDecoder” rather than DualDecoder. Deployability (4-property check) Profile: SYSTEMS. Practical: The implementation runs on commercially available NVIDIA Hopper GPUs and PCIe-connected host CPUs, but it requires integration with a specific sparse-KV framework, CUDA stream/event coordination, host-side KV storage, and customized attention/gather kernels; portability to other accelerators and interconnects is not evaluated. Efficient: Relative to the reported baselines, it reduces memory by up to 36.4% versus ShadowKV and 62.0% versus SpeCache and reduces a reported gather-transfer cost by 93.4%, while the dual-token kernel study reports lower layer latency; however, total energy, CPU utilization, host-memory bandwidth, preprocessing/profile cost, and overhead under low concurrency are not reported. Effective: The evidence shows higher throughput, larger sustainable arrival rates, and lower memory use on the selected long-context workloads, while the mechanism preserves the sparse-retrieval result when misses are corrected; it does not establish equivalent full-generation quality across broad language tasks, and the reported quality evidence is limited. Scalable: The system is measured through 512K context and 32B models on an eight-GPU server, with memory increasing by only 3.7 GB from 64K to 512K in one comparison, but behavior at 10x–100x request scale, substantially larger models, multi-node deployments, different CPU-GPU links, and contexts beyond 512K is not evaluated. The paper delivers a system implementation and associated CUDA scheduling and memory-management mechanisms, but no public software artifact or reusable benchmark is identified. Strengths - It identifies a concrete and previously underemphasized bottleneck—GPU-resident auxiliary state in sparse-KV systems—and quantifies its impact on memory and batch size rather than treating KV offloading as cost-free. - The predictive-prefetching insight is non-obvious and operationally useful: KV-index overlap can remain high even when token prediction is relatively poor, allowing approximate prediction to improve data movement without changing the final attention semantics. - The design addresses the main systems failure modes jointly: dual-token execution limits prediction overhead, layer-aware scheduling creates transfer overlap, priority queues handle misses, and two-layer ping-pong buffers prevent prefetching from recreating the memory bottleneck. - The evaluation reaches 512K context and 32B models on real GPU hardware and reports both throughput and memory/concurrency effects, not just isolated kernel speedups. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly discuss three engineering challenges: choosing prefetch timing without excessive buffering, avoiding the cost of a second speculative decoding pass, and bounding the prefetched KV buffer. They also acknowledge inevitable prediction misses and address them through urgent transfers and selective key reconstruction. They do not provide a dedicated limitations section identifying workload dependence, benchmark coverage, hardware dependence, or the restricted quality evaluation. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The strongest quality claim is “strictly lossless” relative to ShadowKV, but the table evaluates only the first generated token on four RULER subsets and does not compare against dense full-KV inference over complete generated sequences; this leaves semantic drift and later-token errors largely untested. - Prediction accuracy and overlap are reported without enough detail about sparse budget, chunk size, head/layer selection, per-request variance, distribution tails, or how misses affect latency under adversarial or rapidly changing attention patterns. - The first speculative-token analysis uses the real second output token for initialization through an extra pre-decoding step; the paper measures this overhead only qualitatively and does not evaluate short-generation workloads where the one-step startup cost may be material. - The evaluation is tied to ShadowKV's retrieval formulation and implementation, so it is unclear whether the predictability observation transfers to other sparse-KV selectors, learned retrieval heads, quantized caches, multi-query/grouped-query attention variants, or remote-KV architectures. - The “ideal” throughput comparison in the motivation section scales measured throughput proportionally with batch size rather than measuring an actual implementation, so its lost-throughput percentages are upper-bound estimates rather than deployable baseline results. - There is no production trace evaluation, multi-node experiment, energy/cost analysis, or sensitivity study across PCIe generations and alternative host-memory configurations. The paper also does not report code release or sufficient implementation detail to independently reproduce the scheduler and memory allocator. Bottom Line DualDecoder offers a credible and practically relevant systems idea for sparse-KV long-context serving, with strong single-node throughput and memory results, but its novelty and generality are limited by dependence on ShadowKV and its evidence for quality, workload robustness, and production-scale deployment is not yet sufficient for an unqualified systems claim.

Problem & Motivation: The paper addresses stage-transition stalls in prefill/decode-disaggregated LLM serving, particularly when users self-host models on rented cloud GPUs with limited inter-node bandwidth. Prefill nodes generate KV caches that must reach decoding nodes, but the cache size scales with model size, sequence length, and batch size. On the authors' Alibaba Cloud setup, transferring a 48K-token workload can take 6.5× the prefill-computation time, and the transfer gap reaches 7.1× at 15 Gbps. Existing approaches overlap transfer with prefill computation, but this is insufficient when multiple prefill nodes send caches to a bandwidth-constrained decoding node. The prior-work gap is not KV sparsity itself—dynamic KV selection already exists—but how to use query-dependent sparsity before decoding queries are available, while avoiding a network round-trip on every decoding step. Key Idea: Treat KV entries according to when their importance can be known: universally important entries are identified from an offline positional-importance profile and pushed proactively; context-dependent entries are fetched on demand but in parallel with local KV loading; and remaining entries are transferred speculatively during idle network and CPU periods. The central systems insight is that selective attention and selective data movement can share a KV-index abstraction, allowing the transfer layer to exploit the same sparsity used by decoding without changing the underlying KV-selection algorithm. Methodology: SmartGen first runs offline calibration inference using a selected KV-selection method, such as InfiniGen or HATA, and records how frequently each KV entry is selected. It partitions every layer's sequence dimension into M blocks, assigns each block an average selection frequency, forces the first two layers to be proactive, and chooses the top K_r blocks according to K_r = M(L−1)T_p/T_t, where T_p is profiled prefill time and T_t is full-transfer time; K_r is clipped between 2M and LM. During online prefill, selected blocks are written to the decoding node's host-memory KV pool through one-sided RDMA WRITE, together with a GPU-visible mask recording whether each entry is local or remote. During decoding, an existing selector produces a BH × k KV index; SmartGen indexes the mask, splits the index into local and remote subsets, and loads both lanes concurrently. For remote entries, the decoding node sends indexes to prefill nodes via GPU-direct RDMA, and prefill nodes return selected KV entries directly to GPU memory. SmartGen reorders selected entries so remote entries become contiguous and uses NIC scatter-gather to reduce placement overhead; the paper justifies reordering by noting that positional information is already encoded in the KV representations. Finally, it transfers remaining blocks in the background, limiting each speculative round to 10% of the total blocks. The main design choices—profile-based positional importance, GPU-resident masks, and speculative transfer—are motivated with measurements and component studies, although the profile's stability outside the calibrated prompt-length and workload ranges remains an assumption rather than a demonstrated property. Key Results: The evaluation uses three Alibaba Cloud prefill instances, each with two NVIDIA L20 GPUs, one L20 decoding instance, 15–32 Gbps RDMA, models Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-14B, Gemma-3-12B, and Phi-4-14B, and four LongBench workloads: MultiFieldQA, GovReport, SAMSum, and LCC. Requests use 64 output tokens, with up to 60K batched input tokens by default; a sensitivity test reaches 96K batched tokens. Against full transfer, partial transfer, and HACK's 2-bit quantization, SmartGen lowers TTST by up to 4.3× overall. On Qwen3-14B/MultiFieldQA at batch size 6, SmartGen and HACK achieve 3.7× lower TTST than full transfer, while partial transfer achieves 2.9×; SmartGen has about 1.5× lower TBT than partial transfer and about 1.4× lower TBT than HACK. As batch size increases from 1 to 6, TTST grows 10.4× for full transfer, 4.0× for partial transfer, 1.7× for HACK, and 2.0× for SmartGen. At 15 Gbps, SmartGen's TTST improvement over full transfer is 3.3×, versus 2.5× at 32 Gbps. Across sequence lengths from 6K to 96K batched tokens, TTST increases by 1.0 second for SmartGen versus 3.1 seconds for full transfer. The profile-based selector improves TBT by up to 1.3× over random and 1.2× over sequential selection, and reduces the on-demand ratio by up to 51% and 38%, respectively. Accuracy remains near the full-cache baseline: the reported relative accuracy for SmartGen is generally 96–120% for InfiniGen and 92–107% for HATA across the displayed model/workload combinations, whereas HACK falls as low as 13–77%. SmartGen's results are strongest on standard long-context benchmarks and cloud testbeds, not on stress-scale deployments with hundreds of nodes or very large models. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING; the genuinely new contribution is applying existing dynamic KV sparsity to cross-node KV transfer through a coordinated proactive/on-demand/speculative architecture, while the KV-selection algorithms, RDMA primitives, and attention kernels are standard components reused in a new systems setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper includes component ablations for profile-based transfer, parallel transfer, and speculative transfer on both virtualized Alibaba L20 instances and physical V100S CloudLab servers; it also studies bandwidth, sequence length, KV-block count, selection ratio, speculative ratio, and two KV-selection algorithms. It compares against full transfer, sequential partial transfer, HACK, and proactive-only baselines, and separates a LongBench dataset for calibration. However, it reports no error bars, confidence intervals, multiple-run variance, random-seed analysis, or statistical significance tests. Full-transfer comparisons are implemented on the same inference stack and use local InfiniGen selection, which makes the baseline reasonably competitive for computation but leaves some implementation-level comparability questions. The evaluation assumes a 75% host-memory prefix-cache hit ratio, and several conclusions about profiling stability are inferred from a small set of datasets and prompt-length ranges. The paper is an arXiv preprint (arXiv:2607.28150v1, dated 30 July 2026 in the supplied text), not identified as peer-reviewed. No code, dataset, CLI, library, or model-weight URL is stated. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS, because the work implements and evaluates a transfer engine integrated with an LLM inference system. - Practical: The demonstrated implementation runs on commercially available NVIDIA L20 GPUs and commodity cloud RDMA instances; the paper also describes a fallback for systems without GPU-direct RDMA, although that variant is not experimentally evaluated. - Efficient: SmartGen reduces network-transfer latency and approaches full-transfer TBT, but it adds profiling, KV-mask maintenance, index splitting/reordering, metadata traffic, RDMA control messages, and speculative background transfers; at 15 Gbps, first-layer KV and selector metadata already saturate the link. - Effective: Experiments show lower TTST and near-full-cache LongBench accuracy on five models and four workloads, but the evidence targets the proxy metrics TTST, TBT, CTL, and benchmark scores rather than production SLO attainment, cost per request, throughput under concurrent arrivals, or tail latency. - Scalable: The method is tested up to 96K batched tokens, six prefill processes, one decoding GPU, and 14B models, but behavior at 10×–100× node count, larger models, many decoding nodes, heterogeneous traffic, or network contention is not measured. The work delivers an implemented systems artifact inside the authors' inference stack, but the paper does not state that the implementation is publicly released. Strengths: - It identifies a concrete and consequential bottleneck—stage-transition delay caused by KV movement—and quantifies it under low-bandwidth cloud conditions rather than assuming ideal datacenter networking. - The three-path design addresses distinct temporal problems: prefill-time uncertainty, decoding-time remote fetches, and cumulative later-iteration transfer cost. The GPU mask and RDMA ordering mechanism provide a plausible interface between an existing KV selector and distributed cache state. - The paper evaluates both training-free InfiniGen and training-based HATA across five model families, four task types, two hardware/network environments, and multiple network bandwidths, making the systems claim broader than a single-model prototype. - The component analysis supports the architectural decomposition: parallel fetching reduces TBT by approximately 1.1–1.2×, and speculative transfer contributes a further 1.2–1.3× reduction in the reported settings. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge that metadata and the first two KV layers can saturate the network at 15 Gbps, causing SmartGen to exceed the ideal-case TTST; they leave this overhead for future work. They discuss workload drift and propose periodic or grouped profiling, but do not experimentally evaluate those adaptations. They also note that cloud instances without GDR require CPU-side index splitting and an extra host-to-device copy, claiming PCIe bandwidth makes this acceptable without presenting measurements. The paper acknowledges speculative-transfer interference and selects a 10% ratio as a compromise, with 20% causing up to a 1.4× early-token TBT increase and 5% requiring about 20 iterations to complete. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The paper does not test calibration-to-evaluation distribution shift beyond the selected LongBench setup, even though positional similarity is the key assumption behind proactive transfer. It does not report tail TTST/TBT, request-level throughput, GPU utilization, network utilization, or total serving cost under realistic arrivals, so the claimed practical benefit may differ from the average-latency results. The comparisons omit potentially important combinations such as SmartGen plus KV quantization, despite describing the methods as orthogonal, and do not compare against more recent end-to-end disaggregated serving systems under matched bandwidth and scheduling conditions. The 75% prefix-cache hit assumption may materially affect prefill and transfer overlap, but sensitivity to hit rate is not evaluated. The paper also does not measure the overhead of profiling, mask updates, RPC/control traffic, RDMA memory registration, or multi-prefill-node contention at scale. Accuracy evaluation reports relative benchmark metrics but does not assess generation-level divergence, safety-critical retrieval failures, or longer output lengths; 64-token generations may understate cumulative remote-fetch behavior. Finally, the claim that reordering selected KV entries is always semantically harmless deserves a more explicit treatment for implementation details involving position-dependent kernels, grouped-query attention, or selector-specific indexing conventions. Bottom Line: This is a worthwhile systems paper with a credible cross-layer optimization and strong initial measurements, but its evidence supports adoption for bandwidth-constrained prototype deployments rather than a definitive claim of robust, production-scale disaggregated LLM serving.

Mask2Shield: Strengthening LLM Safety against Neuron-Pruning Attacks

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Mask2Shield (M2S), a masked-forward alignment method that trains open-weight language models to preserve refusal behavior after selected safety-associated FFN channels are functionally removed. - Why it's important: Open-weight LLMs can lose safety alignment when a white-box attacker prunes a small set of internal neurons, creating a deployment risk that ordinary output-level alignment does not address. - How it does it: M2S masks selected safety-related FFN dimensions during harmful-example training, optimizes the remaining computation to produce a refusal, and uses an unmasked frozen-teacher KL loss on benign examples to limit capability drift. - The good: Across ten model configurations, recomputed Safety-Neuron attacks fall from 80–279 successful attacks for base models to 1–44 of 313 for M2S, with transfer to the independent TwinBreak pruning pipeline. - The missing: The evaluation covers only sparse FFN-channel deletion and does not test unrestricted weight editing, attacker retraining, residual-stream direction ablation, stronger adaptive attacks, or scaling beyond the tested models and pruning budgets. - Read it or not: Researchers working on white-box LLM safety and model editing should read it for the training-under-functional-damage idea and extensive cross-model results, while practitioners seeking general jailbreak protection should not treat it as evidence against input-level or unrestricted model attacks.

Problem & Motivation The work addresses safety failure in released open-weight LLMs under white-box neuron-pruning attacks. An attacker with model access can inspect FFN activations, identify dimensions associated with harmful-versus-benign prompt differences, and zero the corresponding channels without retraining the model. Prior alignment methods optimize normal forward-pass behavior and therefore may concentrate refusal in a small removable internal pathway. The target domain is safety-aligned instruction-following models, and the specific gap is robustness to sparse internal computation removal while retaining coherent generation and benign task capability. The paper focuses on selector-identified FFN-channel pruning, not general model tampering or prompt-based jailbreaks. Key Idea The core insight is to make the attack operation a training condition: disable the safety-associated channels during harmful-example forward passes and force the model to learn a refusal through the remaining computation. The paper’s intended mechanism is therefore redistribution or redundancy of refusal support rather than merely strengthening the original safety neurons. The frozen unmasked teacher is a secondary but important complement that prevents the model from solving the masked refusal objective by refusing broadly. Methodology M2S begins with an aligned checkpoint and disjoint harmful and benign probe prompts. For each transformer layer and FFN gate/up projection, it max-pools token activations over valid positions, fits a logistic probe to distinguish harmful from benign prompts, standardizes probe coefficients within each projection, and selects dimensions with positive coefficients and z-score greater than 3.0. During four epochs of full-parameter Adafactor fine-tuning, each update uses one harmful–benign pair. For the harmful example, hooks zero the selected channels for the first 50 response tokens and optimize a response-token refusal cross-entropy, L_ref. For the benign example, the unmasked student matches the frozen original model’s complete answer distribution over valid answer tokens using temperature-1 KL divergence, L_KL. The total objective is L = 5.0 L_ref + 0.5 L_KL, with learning rate 10^-6, no weight decay, gradient clipping at 1.0, and maximum sequence length 384. Three critical decisions are reasonably aligned with the threat model: masking activations rather than freezing parameters directly simulates functional pruning; recomputing attack targets after training tests adaptivity; and teacher distillation on complete benign answers addresses over-refusal. However, the paper does not provide a systematic sensitivity study for the z-score threshold, 50-token mask horizon, loss weights, or optimizer settings. Key Results On 313 StrongREJECT harmful prompts judged by Llama-Guard-3-8B plus a refusal-keyword check, recomputed Safety-Neuron attacks achieve 80–279 successful attacks on base models and 1–44 on M2S models across ten configurations. Representative results include Qwen2.5-7B falling from 279/313 to 35/313, Llama-3-8B from 261/313 to 1/313, Phi-4 from 273/313 to 1/313, and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B from 80/313 to 36/313. M2S also transfers to TwinBreak, which uses a different selector and sequentially removes 1% of candidate parameters for five rounds: at iteration five, M2S reports HarmBench ASRs of 0–15%, AdvBench ASRs of 0–6%, JailbreakBench ASRs of 0–6%, and substantially lower StrongREJECT scores than published base-model rows. In a cumulative deletion study on Llama-3.2-1B, targeted removal produces 1/313, 2/313, 11/313, 18/313, and 16/313 successes at 0.5%, 1%, 2%, 5%, and 10% removal, respectively; output validity is 100% through 2%, 68.05% at 5%, and 0% at 10%, so the 10% result reflects generation collapse rather than selective safety preservation. Capability effects are mixed: M2S improves several Qwen and Llama scores, but reduces Gemma-7B GSM8K from 0.3321 to 0.2645 and Phi-4 GSM8K from 0.9022 to 0.8831; the comparison rows for prior methods are transcribed from SafeNeuron rather than uniformly rerun in this study. Novelty Classification The contribution is primarily NEW METHOD, with a narrower NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING: the paper combines selector-based FFN masking during refusal fine-tuning with unmasked teacher distillation, and shows that this can reduce vulnerability to adaptive sparse neuron-pruning attacks; the selector, distillation, refusal cross-entropy, and pruning attacks themselves are existing ideas or standard components. Rigor & Reproducibility The study uses ten model configurations from Qwen2.5, Llama 3/3.2, Gemma, Phi-4, and DeepSeek families; disjoint defense, probe, attack-selection, and evaluation prompts; recomputed attack targets; an independent TwinBreak transfer test; a targeted-versus-random deletion comparison; and ablations for masking, random masks, and teacher KL. The no-mask and random-mask ablations retain high attack success, while removing KL reduces ASR but causes 27–73 refusal-keyword matches on 100 GSM8K prompts, supporting the role of both components, although the lexical diagnostic is weak evidence of semantic capability. Reported ± values are binomial standard errors over benchmark items, not variation across training seeds; no multiple-seed results, confidence intervals for attack rates, significance tests, or hyperparameter sweeps are reported. The paper releases implementation and evaluation scripts at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MD123, but it does not state that model weights, training data, or exact generated teacher answers are released. Important concerns are that prior-method rows are copied from SafeNeuron, the primary attack and training selector are closely related FFN-channel methods, evaluation relies heavily on automated judges, and the claimed generality beyond sparse FFN pruning remains untested. Deployability: (4-property check) Profile: EMPIRICAL. Practical: The authors report that most full-parameter runs finish within one hour on one NVIDIA PRO 6000 GPU, so the method can run on commercially available hardware, although cost for larger models is not quantified. Efficient: M2S requires full-parameter fine-tuning, activation-probe fitting, and a frozen teacher forward pass, but the paper provides no direct memory, throughput, or compute comparison against SafeNeuron or ordinary safety fine-tuning. Effective: Evidence shows strong robustness against two sparse FFN-channel pruning pipelines while preserving many benchmark scores, but effectiveness against unrestricted weight edits, attacker retraining, residual-direction ablations, or real deployment attacks is not evaluated. Scalable: Models range from 1B to 14B parameters, but no 10×–100× scale experiment or extrapolation measurement is provided; the authors explicitly note increased cost for larger models. The work delivers training and evaluation scripts as a software artifact, but no stated library, CLI, dataset, or released trained model weights. Strengths - It identifies a concrete failure mode—safety concentrated in removable internal channels—and converts that threat into a directly testable training objective rather than relying on ordinary refusal fine-tuning. - The adaptive evaluation recomputes safety-neuron targets after defense training, avoiding the weak protocol of protecting only the originally identified channels. - The experiments cover ten model configurations and include transfer to TwinBreak, whose selector and sequential pruning procedure differ from the NeuroStrike-derived training mask. - The cumulative pruning study distinguishes low attack success from model destruction by measuring output validity, showing that at 10% deletion the model collapses rather than safely answering normally. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly limit the defense to sparse channel deletion and state that it does not establish robustness to unrestricted weight editing, retraining, or all white-box attacks. They acknowledge full-parameter fine-tuning and frozen-teacher costs, the need to tune loss weights for new model families, and dependence of mask quality on the NeuroStrike selector. They also acknowledge architecture-dependent capability trade-offs, particularly for Gemma, and the possibility that better or complementary selectors may improve results. These limitations are confronted directly rather than omitted. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The paper does not evaluate an attacker that jointly optimizes channel selection and pruning for harmful compliance after observing the defended checkpoint, beyond the fixed SafeNeuron recomputation and TwinBreak protocol. - It does not test residual-stream refusal-direction ablation, arbitrary weight perturbations, low-rank edits, fine-tuning-based safety removal, quantization-induced changes, or combined prompt-and-parameter attacks, despite citing work showing that refusal is not confined to discrete FFN channels. - There is no multi-seed analysis or uncertainty over attack success rates, and the capability standard errors do not capture fine-tuning variability. - The primary comparison to SafeNeuron, RLHF-Safety, and SN-Tune relies on rows transcribed from prior work, making cross-method differences less controlled than the table presentation suggests. - The study does not report refusal quality, helpfulness, response length, toxicity severity, or semantic validity beyond automated safety judges and a 100-example lexical GSM8K diagnostic; the teacher KL objective may preserve token distributions without preserving task-level behavior. - The claim that M2S reduces reliance on a safety bottleneck is plausible for the tested selector, but the results could partly reflect making the model more fragile to pruning in a way that causes degradation before harmful compliance; this trade-off is only directly characterized for one Llama-3.2-1B cumulative sweep. Bottom Line This is a useful and technically coherent defense for the narrow but important threat of adaptive sparse FFN-channel pruning, with unusually strong cross-model and cross-attack evidence, but it should not be interpreted as a general solution to white-box LLM safety tampering until broader adaptive attacks, controlled baselines, seed variation, and task-level utility evaluations are added.

See2Think: Do Multimodal Models Really Use Intermediate Visual States?

S Yan, Z Yan, H Xu, P Zhou, J Chen, C Ji, S Cao… · arxiv.org · 10 new citations to your articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces See2Think, an evaluation framework combining a 1,200-sample benchmark and the Visual Action-of-Thought protocol to measure whether multimodal models select, faithfully render, and subsequently use intermediate visual states. - Why it's important: Visual traces and tool calls can create the appearance of reasoning without improving answers, so developers need to distinguish useful visual computation from decorative or misleading intermediate states. - How it does it: It compares textual CoT, action planning without rendering, closed-loop rendered actions, and task-relevant corrupted feedback, while scoring action relevance, render faithfulness, and feedback uptake. - The good: Across 4,800 trajectories, action relevance is near saturation (0.958–0.994 overall by model), whereas render faithfulness is much lower (0.594–0.630), identifying a concrete post-planning bottleneck; corrupted feedback reduces 3D accuracy by 10.3–15.5 percentage points for trajectories with medium or high feedback uptake. - The missing: The process metrics and interventions depend heavily on GPT-5.4 judging and image-rendering quality; only 56.7% of 120 audited WrongRender cases pass all quality criteria, and no statistical uncertainty or repeated-seed analysis is reported. - Read it or not: Researchers building multimodal agents, visual scratchpads, or process benchmarks should read it for its diagnostic framework, while practitioners seeking an accuracy-improving reasoning method can largely skip it because VAoT lowers overall accuracy for three of four evaluated models.
Why this rank
Scored using the Empirical profile. Novelty (82) and Non-Obviousness (80) are high because the action–render–use decomposition and corrupted-feedback intervention provide a useful new diagnostic formulation rather than merely another accuracy benchmark. Rigor (68), Completeness (78), and Resilience (68) are meaningful but constrained by GPT-5.4 judging, fragile WrongRender validity, missing uncertainty estimates, and limited model coverage; Impact (65) reflects a reusable benchmark and protocol rather than an accuracy-improving method. Problem & Motivation: Multimodal models increasingly generate sketches, annotations, crops, and other intermediate visual states, but final-answer accuracy alone cannot establish whether those states are relevant, faithfully executed, or actually used. The problem affects researchers evaluating multimodal reasoning systems and developers deploying visual agents in diagram understanding, 3D scene reasoning, scientific interpretation, and embodied interaction. Existing benchmarks often contain text-solvable examples, rely on oracle visual clues, score aggregate trace quality, or omit matched interventions that test dependence on the returned state. The paper targets the resulting attribution gap: a model may propose a relevant action but receive a faulty rendering, may use a rendered state without gaining accuracy, or may change its answer when the state is corrupted without genuinely benefiting from correct visual feedback. Key Idea: The core insight is to separate visual-state utility from behavioral dependence by treating intermediate visual reasoning as an intervenable three-stage pipeline: action selection, rendering, and downstream feedback use. A model can be evaluated not merely on whether it emits a visual trace, but on whether the action targets relevant evidence, the renderer realizes that action, later reasoning uses information actually present in the result, and behavior changes when task-relevant feedback is corrupted. This decomposition is the paper's main intellectual contribution; the underlying operations—highlighting, cropping, annotating, and drawing—are established techniques. Methodology: See2ThinkBench contains 1,200 samples, exactly 100 in each of 12 categories, organized into six 2D structured categories, two 3D scene categories, and four real-world visual categories. Candidates come from RBench-V, EMMA, M3CoT, PRISM-Bench, CLEVR, Super-CLEVR, VLABench, DROID, and IntPhys2. The construction pipeline generates an image-and-question caption, tests a reasoning model five times using only the question and caption, removes samples answered correctly in at least three trials, rewrites most multiple-choice questions as free-form queries, and performs automatic and manual quality checks. The remaining 1,073 samples use free-form answers and 127 retain structured candidates. VAoT receives image I, question q, textual thought T_t, and structured action A_t; an external renderer applies the action to the current state R_t, returns the result, and the model iterates over the history H_t until answering. Actions include highlighting, annotation, auxiliary-line drawing, cropping, and zooming. Four conditions use the same benchmark and nominal interaction budget: CoT reasons directly over the original image; VAoT-NoRender emits actions without returning rendered states; VAoT executes actions and returns states; and VAoT-WrongRender returns natural-looking states with task-relevant evidence intentionally modified. GPT-5.4 judges answer semantics and, for one selected key step per VAoT trajectory, assigns Action Relevance, Render Faithfulness, and Feedback Uptake on {0, 0.5, 1}. The principal design decisions—caption-only shortcut filtering, constrained external rendering, and matched corrupted-feedback intervention—are well motivated for diagnosis, but their validity depends on the filtering model, renderer behavior, judge reliability, and intervention quality. No training loss or optimization objective is introduced; VAoT is an inference-time evaluation protocol. Key Results: On the full 1,200-sample benchmark, overall accuracy varies by model and setting rather than favoring VAoT universally. GPT-5.5 scores 50.2% with CoT, 48.0% with VAoT-NoRender, 44.6% with VAoT, and 42.3% with WrongRender. GPT-o3 scores 43.5%, 40.8%, 43.8%, and 39.3%, respectively. Gemini 3.5 Flash scores 57.0%, 58.2%, 56.2%, and 53.9%, while Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct scores 38.7%, 37.2%, 35.7%, and 34.8%. Thus CoT is best for GPT-5.5 and Qwen3-VL, closed-loop VAoT is marginally best for GPT-o3, and action planning without rendering is best for Gemini. Averaged across models, 2D accuracy is 47.5% for CoT, 44.5% for VAoT-NoRender, 43.0% for VAoT, and 42.9% for WrongRender; 3D accuracy is 63.4%, 64.9%, 63.6%, and 50.0%; real-world accuracy is 39.1%, 38.9%, 38.8%, and 38.4%. Robot Manipulation is a severe outlier, with 0–4% accuracy across models and settings. Process scores show Action Relevance of 0.976, 0.988, and 0.964 for 2D, 3D, and real-world tasks, versus Render Faithfulness of 0.586, 0.610, and 0.656 and Feedback Uptake of 0.756, 0.838, and 0.822. In paired analyses, completely unfaithful rendering produces net accuracy losses of 6.1 points in 2D and 9.3 points in 3D; at perfect faithfulness, the net transition is -1.2 points in 2D, +0.3 in 3D, and +0.9 in real-world tasks. Under corrupted feedback, the overall VAoT-minus-WrongRender difference is -2.3, +3.4, and +3.1 points for uptake scores 0, 0.5, and 1, while the corresponding 3D differences are +3.5, +10.3, and +15.5 points. WrongRender changes the semantic answer in 32.7–54.2% of samples across models. These results support behavioral sensitivity to visual states, especially in 3D, but do not show that rendered visual reasoning improves accuracy overall. Novelty Classification: NEW BENCHMARK, NEW EVALUATION FORMULATION, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL—the genuinely new contribution is the matched action–render–use diagnostic formulation and corrupted-feedback protocol, while the benchmark combines existing source datasets and the visual operations are standard. Rigor & Reproducibility: The study evaluates all four conditions on all 1,200 samples for four models and retains complete sample-level alignments, enabling paired comparisons rather than only aggregate averages. It includes appendices with source construction, prompts, evaluation rules, paired counts, qualitative cases, a 240-trajectory human audit, and a 120-case WrongRender audit. Human reviewers found the automatic process judgments reasonable or partially reasonable in 94.4% of key-step selections, 96.9% of action-relevance judgments, 92.9% of render-faithfulness judgments, and 95.0% of feedback-uptake judgments. However, strict human agreement is substantially lower for action relevance (74.8%) and render faithfulness (70.2%), the judge is another proprietary model from the same vendor family as one evaluated model, and the answer and process scores remain judge-based for most free-form and trajectory-level evaluations. The WrongRender intervention is especially fragile: only 68/120 audited cases (56.7%) pass all five quality criteria, although 94/120 (78.3%) are acceptable under a one-failure threshold; the strict audited subset shows an 8.82-point accuracy drop, compared with 3.19 points for the relaxed subset. The paper reports no confidence intervals, statistical significance tests, multiple random seeds, per-item variance, or inter-annotator agreement coefficients. A repository and website are provided at https://github.com/CSU-JPG/See2Think and https://sgysy.github.io/seetothink/, but the parsed paper does not specify the exact release contents, licenses, model weights, or whether all source data and renderer implementations are available. The paper is an arXiv preprint, version 1 dated 29 July 2026, not a stated peer-reviewed publication. Deployability (4-property check): EMPIRICAL profile. Practical: The protocol can in principle run on commercially available hardware, but it requires multimodal model inference, an image renderer, repeated interaction, and an external judge, so operational cost is materially higher than ordinary single-pass evaluation. Efficient: The paper reports no latency, token, renderer-call, memory, or monetary-cost measurements, and VAoT does not improve overall accuracy for GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.5 Flash, or Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct. Effective: The evidence supports diagnosis of action relevance, rendering fidelity, and behavioral sensitivity, but it does not demonstrate that VAoT solves visual reasoning better than CoT; the best overall score is 58.2% for Gemini with VAoT-NoRender, versus 57.0% with CoT. Scalable: The benchmark scale is standard rather than stress-scale—1,200 samples and four models—and the paper does not test 10×–100× more tasks, longer trajectories, larger images, more concurrent agents, or substantially larger models. The work delivers a reusable benchmark and inference-time evaluation tool, with code and a website cited, rather than a trained reasoning model or deployed production system. Strengths: - It formulates a useful causal-style diagnostic distinction between visual-state utility and behavioral dependence, avoiding the common inference that emitting a tool call proves genuine visual reasoning. - The action-relevance/render-faithfulness/feedback-uptake decomposition localizes failures more specifically than final accuracy: action selection is near saturation, while rendering is consistently weaker and differs by environment. - The matched VAoT-NoRender, VAoT, and WrongRender comparisons expose non-obvious behavior: models can depend on visual feedback even when correct rendering produces no net accuracy gain, and high feedback uptake does not imply correct use. - The benchmark spans 12 categories and three visual environments, removes many caption-solvable cases, normalizes most tasks to free-form answers, and includes human audits rather than relying exclusively on unvalidated automatic scores. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly limit coverage to four representative multimodal models, acknowledge possible errors from the external renderer and automatic process evaluator despite human validation, and state that WrongRender effects depend on intervention quality. They report that quality-filtered analyses preserve the direction but not a stable magnitude of the accuracy drop. They also identify broader model coverage, learned rendering, and finer-grained process supervision as future work. These limitations are directly acknowledged, although their implications for causal interpretation and statistical confidence are not fully quantified. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The caption-only filtering procedure uses a strong multimodal captioner and a reasoning model, so residual text shortcuts and model-dependent selection bias are not independently measured; the benchmark is also assembled from heterogeneous existing datasets with source-specific distributions and possible overlap with model pretraining. The comparison conditions are prompt-matched but not demonstrably equal in token budget, number of visual reads, renderer latency, or effective information exposure, which complicates interpreting accuracy differences as the effect of visual-state use alone. The single GPT-5.4 judge scores all 4,800 trajectories and free-form answers, yet the paper provides no blinded human reannotation of a representative random sample, no judge-versus-human correlation, and no formal inter-rater reliability statistic. Selecting one key visual step per trajectory may discard multi-step dependencies, while uptake scoring from textual reasoning can conflate genuine use of rendered evidence with post-hoc verbal mention. WrongRender is not a controlled symbolic intervention: it is generated by an image editor instructed to alter key evidence, and its 56.7% strict-pass rate means aggregate sensitivity estimates mix valid corruptions with renderer failures. Finally, the paper does not evaluate naturalistic tools, learned visual scratchpads, longer-horizon agents, additional contemporary open models, or whether training models to improve render faithfulness changes downstream task performance. Bottom Line: This is a worthwhile diagnostic benchmark and protocol for researchers studying multimodal reasoning faithfulness, but its strongest contribution is measurement methodology rather than an accuracy advance, and its conclusions should be treated as preliminary until judge bias, intervention validity, statistical uncertainty, and broader model coverage are addressed.

Reasoning as Search: Bridging Symbolic and Neural Approaches to Artificial Intelligence

L Dionisopoulos · escholarship.org · neural symbolic - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This thesis introduces a dual-system account of intelligence and contributes two studies: an object-centric neurosymbolic solver for ARC-AGI and an empirical analysis of how supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement-learning data shape chess reasoning in a 7B language model. - Why it's important: It addresses the practical tension between symbolic systems that offer precision but become brittle and neural systems that scale better but can be inefficient, unfaithful, and weak out of distribution. - How it does it: It frames reasoning as search, using symbolic program synthesis over a DSL for ARC and post-training over engine-verifiable chess trajectories for language models, then maps both to a shared library-learning framework. - The good: The chess study provides the strongest evidence: 120M-token SFT plus RL raises Predict Move legality from 8% for base Qwen2.5 7B to 98%, average move rank to 0.83, Best Move accuracy to 62%, and Worst Move accuracy to 64%, while multi-step trajectory data preserves more faithful reasoning than single-move data. - The missing: The central unification is conceptual rather than formally derived or experimentally tested, and the empirical study uses one 7B base model, chess-specific tasks, small evaluation sets, no reported multi-seed uncertainty, and an LLM judge for key qualitative metrics. - Read it or not: Read the chess chapter and its released artifacts if you study reasoning-model post-training; read the full thesis mainly for its synthesis of symbolic search, library learning, and neural reasoning rather than for a validated general theory of intelligence.

Problem & Motivation The thesis addresses how to build systems that combine broad knowledge with task-specific composition, which it equates operationally with reasoning or search. The motivating domains are program synthesis and visual abstraction through ARC-AGI, where exact generalization from only 2–7 examples exposes brittleness and sample-efficiency problems, and language-model reasoning in chess, where models must select legal and high-quality moves in a sequential, verifiable environment. It identifies a gap between symbolic approaches, which constrain search and support executable, precise solutions but require manually designed primitives and segmentations, and neural approaches, which absorb knowledge and search heuristics into scalable approximators but may hallucinate, exploit reward proxies, and fail to model underlying mechanisms. The thesis claims that recent reasoning models increasingly resemble library-learning systems, but this claim is primarily a proposed interpretive framework rather than a directly tested hypothesis. Key Idea The core insight is to treat reasoning as traversal through a search space whose effective actions and traversal policy are shaped by learned or engineered knowledge. In symbolic systems, the space consists of typed programs and object transformations; in language models, it consists of token or thought trajectories whose next-token policy implicitly guides search. The thesis further argues that both can be understood as instances of a library-learning loop involving stored knowledge, a search policy, a compression or update mechanism, and online experience. This abstraction is intellectually coherent and useful for comparing otherwise disparate systems, but it is not a new formal theory: the thesis does not define a common mathematical framework that yields new theorems, algorithms, or testable predictions beyond the empirical chess observations. Methodology The thesis has three layers. First, it surveys program synthesis, typed regular tree grammars, top-down and bottom-up enumeration, probabilistic search, and DreamCoder-style library learning. Second, its ARC system parses grids into objects using three segmentation schemes—color, contour-scale, and monochrome contour—and applies a nine-operation DSL containing color, recolor, rotate, flip, delete, translate, copy, copy-translate, and draw-line. A roughly 400K-parameter vision transformer with 64-dimensional embeddings, 10 transformer layers, 8 heads, and an iBOT-inspired self-distillation objective is trained on approximately 200K synthetic examples; an attempted encoder predicts DSL and object distributions to guide A* search, but this component fails, so the final solver uses symbolic object graphs and feature matching. Third, the chess study fine-tunes Qwen2.5 7B-Instruct with several data families—rejection sampling, guided synthetic explanations, factual board QA, verbalized alpha-beta traces, Best Move, and Best Line—then applies Dr. GRPO with Clip-Higher and no KL penalty. The reward is based on engine-verified performance across Predict Move, Best Move, Worst Move, and Legal Moves tasks. Key design choices include dense engine-grounded targets, multitask RL, and 4–6-ply Best Line targets intended to encode transition dynamics and value estimates; the rationale is plausible, but causal isolation between these choices is incomplete. Key Results The ARC implementation solves 16 of 400 training problems and 4 of 400 public evaluation problems, but the neural policy intended to guide A* never learns a useful DSL distribution; these results are therefore a proof of concept for object-centric symbolic search, not evidence of a functioning neurosymbolic neural-guided solver. The chess experiments evaluate 400 examples per principal task and 1,000 unseen factual-board tasks plus 600 out-of-distribution mate tasks. The best 120M-token SFT sequence, starting with Best Move-All and followed by Best Line-All, reaches after RL 98% legal moves and 0.83 average normalized move rank on Predict Move, 0.87 Legal Moves IoU, 62% Best Move accuracy, 64% Worst Move accuracy, 90% referenced-move accuracy, and 4.8/10 average LLM-judged reasoning quality. The 7B model exceeds the reported gpt-oss-120b baseline on several custom tasks but remains far below that baseline on some measures, including Legal Moves IoU (0.87 versus 0.96), Best Move accuracy (0.62 versus 0.57, higher for the thesis model), Worst Move accuracy (0.64 versus 0.79, lower), and out-of-distribution mates (14.8% versus 78.3%). The strongest qualitative finding is that Best Move training produces strong final behavior but markedly unfaithful reasoning after RL, whereas Best Line training yields comparable performance, more stable RL, and higher faithfulness. RL also shifts the median normalized move rank from 0.66 to 0.93 in the principal scaled run and reduces hallucinated board references, although full-game play against OpenAI o3 remains poor. The experiments are standard-scale for academic 7B post-training, not stress-scale deployment or general reasoning evaluation. Novelty Classification The contribution is best classified as NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION, with a weaker NEW FORMULATION claim: the chess work provides a controlled comparison of chess post-training data formats and the Best Move versus Best Line distinction, while the ARC work contributes an object-centric DSL/graph solver and attempted neural-guided search; the broader reasoning-as-search and library-learning unification is largely a synthesis and reinterpretation of existing program-synthesis, DreamCoder, chain-of-thought, and RL ideas rather than a new formal method. Rigor & Reproducibility The chess chapter includes extensive data-inclusion comparisons, scaled runs, held-out task evaluations, out-of-distribution mate tests, training curves, hyperparameters, token budgets, and analyses of hallucination, strategy usage, reasoning quality, and predictive complexity. It reports 400-sample task evaluations, 1,000 factual-board samples, 600 mate samples, regression confidence intervals, and significant correlations between LLM-judge and expert scores. Code, models, evaluations, and data are stated to be released at github.com/lucasdino/lang-chess, with the dataset also identified at huggingface.co/datasets/lucasdino/chess-reasoning-data. However, no multiple random seeds, error bars over independent training runs, or conventional significance tests for most model-to-model performance differences are reported. The main qualitative measures rely on Llama 4 Maverick for parsing and gpt-oss-120b for judging; although expert correlations are reported, the judge remains a possible source of bias. Baseline selection is limited: the main controlled comparison uses only Qwen2.5 7B-Instruct, while the stronger 120B comparator is not matched for training or compute. The custom evaluation tasks and engine-generated training data also create a risk of benchmark-specific optimization, and the ARC results lack meaningful comparisons with strong contemporary ARC solvers. Deployability: (4-property check) Profile: EMPIRICAL, because the thesis primarily evaluates trained models and experimental solvers, although it also releases reusable software and data. Practical: The chess model can run on commercially available GPUs, but the scaled training required approximately 500 H100 hours, making reproduction and further post-training expensive for individual practitioners. Efficient: The deployed model has 7B parameters and outperforms or approaches larger open models on several custom tasks, but the thesis does not provide inference latency, memory consumption, throughput, or a controlled compute-normalized comparison against alternatives. Effective: Engine-verified task scores show substantial improvement on the stated chess proxies, but poor full-game performance against OpenAI o3 and weaknesses on some out-of-distribution tasks limit the claim that it solves general chess reasoning. Scalable: The work scales SFT from 15M to 60M and combines two 60M-token phases, but it does not test 10×–100× larger models, datasets, environments, or task distributions; scalability beyond the 7B single-base-model setting is claimed only indirectly. The work delivers a released chess codebase, training data, evaluations, SFT checkpoints, and RL models. The ARC component appears to provide an implementation and solver code, but the paper does not identify a separately packaged library or stable production tool, and the conceptual framework stops short of a reusable formalism or proof technique. Strengths - The chess chapter separates answer quality from reasoning faithfulness and shows an important failure mode: RL can improve engine-scored decisions while making verbalized reasoning less faithful when SFT trains only direct best-move targets. - The Best Line versus Best Move comparison is a useful, non-obvious intervention that connects multi-step targets to more stable RL and better out-of-distribution behavior; the thesis supports this with training dynamics and held-out evaluations rather than a single headline score. - The study releases code, data, checkpoints, and evaluation procedures, and it documents dataset construction, board representations, hyperparameters, reward design, and supplementary analyses in enough detail to support replication. - The ARC chapter honestly documents a failed neural-guidance component and isolates a smaller symbolic result instead of presenting the intended hybrid architecture as completed; the object-centric DSL and graph representation offer a concrete engineering case study of where symbolic inductive bias becomes brittle. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly acknowledge that the ARC neural embeddings do not support a useful DSL policy, that manual segmentation, DSL design, and argument enumeration create brittleness, and that the completed ARC solver is purely symbolic and solves only 4 of 400 public evaluation cases. For chess, they acknowledge reliance on Qwen2.5 7B-Instruct, lack of replication across base models, limited reward-function tuning, distribution mismatch caused by emphasizing mid- and late-game positions, poor full-game performance against OpenAI o3, and the need for multi-turn RL and broader environments. They also acknowledge that chess information density is a heuristic framework rather than a single validated metric. These limitations are confronted directly, particularly in the ARC discussion and the chess chapter's separation of demonstrated results from proposed future work. Analyst-Identified Gaps The strongest unacknowledged or insufficiently resolved issue is causal attribution: Best Move and Best Line differ simultaneously in output length, target structure, number of engine-grounded actions, valuation tokens, and token efficiency, so the claim that transition-dynamics learning causes improved faithfulness is plausible but not established. The study needs matched-token and matched-information ablations, multiple seeds, confidence intervals for headline comparisons, and experiments across additional base models and model sizes. The LLM-as-judge methodology is vulnerable to evaluator bias and does not establish mechanistic faithfulness; direct engine-based consistency checks, human annotation, or intervention-based tests would strengthen the claim. The custom evaluations are close to the training task and use the same engine family for labels and rewards, so they may reward engine imitation rather than general chess reasoning. The thesis does not report training-data deduplication or contamination checks against pretraining corpora, nor does it provide a compute-normalized comparison with larger baselines. For ARC, the reported 4/400 evaluation result is too weak to support claims about general library learning, and there is no systematic comparison against contemporary symbolic, object-centric, or LLM-based ARC methods under matched compute. Bottom Line The chess study is worth reading and reproducing for its concrete evidence that multi-step, engine-grounded post-training targets can improve the stability and faithfulness of RL-trained reasoning models, while the thesis-wide AGI unification is an interesting perspective piece rather than a validated general theory and the ARC system is not competitive with established benchmark solvers.

AgentOPSD: Recursive Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning (67 ▲ )

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces AgentOPSD, a critic-free turn-level credit-assignment method that recursively converts privileged self-distillation likelihood gaps into bounded per-turn policy advantages for long-horizon agents. - Why it's important: Sparse terminal rewards in multi-turn agent tasks assign the same trajectory-level signal to pivotal and routine actions, making learning increasingly inefficient as interaction horizons grow. - How it does it: It sums token-level teacher–student log-probability gaps within each environment turn, accumulates them as evidence in a log-odds belief state initialized by the group success rate, and uses each belief revision to reshape GRPO advantages. - The good: Across ALFWorld, Search-QA, and WebShop with Qwen2.5-3B/7B, AgentOPSD generally beats GRPO and competing self-distillation RL methods, reaching 89.1% ALFWorld success with Qwen2.5-7B and reducing measured horizon sensitivity to −0.54 success points per additional turn. - The missing: The paper reports no independent training seeds, confidence intervals, or statistical tests for the main benchmark table, so the significance and robustness of several small gains remain unclear. - Read it or not: Researchers working on verifiable-reward LLM agents or long-horizon credit assignment should read it for the recursive evidence construction; readers seeking evidence beyond simulated benchmarks and 3B–7B models can defer it.

Problem & Motivation: The work addresses training language-model agents in interactive environments such as embodied household tasks, web shopping, and search-based question answering, where rewards are usually binary and available only after a full trajectory. GRPO and related group-relative methods broadcast one sequence-level advantage to every token and turn, although some actions determine success while others are redundant, misleading, or merely procedural. Existing self-distillation methods provide denser token- or step-level signals, but token boundaries do not match environment transitions and local signals do not account for evidence accumulated in earlier turns. The targeted gap is therefore history-dependent, environment-aligned credit assignment without a learned critic, reward model, or additional rollouts. Key Idea: A turn should receive credit according to how much it changes the current estimated support for eventual success, rather than according to its self-distillation gap in isolation. AgentOPSD treats the summed privileged-versus-unprivileged action likelihood ratio as evidential input, recursively updates a success belief in log-odds space, and uses the marginal belief revision between consecutive turns as the credit signal. This is a meaningful formulation of sequential credit, although the Bayesian interpretation depends on strong assumptions about the retrieved skill-conditioned branch. Methodology: For each task, the method samples a group of G=8 on-policy trajectories and computes the standard GRPO sequence advantage, A_seq=(R−R_bar)/(sigma_R+epsilon), from binary terminal outcomes. For every turn k, a shared-parameter student and a detached, training-only skill-conditioned teacher score the sampled action token by token; the method computes delta_k,t=log pi(y_k,t|s_k,c+)−log pi(y_k,t|s_k) and sums these gaps into turn evidence e_k. It then initializes B_0 by clipping the group success fraction R_bar to [10^-4,1−10^-4], recursively updates c_k=gamma c_{k−1}+e_k and B_k=sigma(logit(B_0)+c_k), and defines turn credit as Delta B_k=B_k−B_{k−1}. The credit is outcome-aligned with q_k=sign(A_seq)Delta B_k, standardized within each trajectory, converted into a bounded multiplier w_k=clip(1+b z_k,1−b,1+b), and mixed with the original advantage as A_tilde_k=A_seq[(1−lambda)+lambda w_k]. Tokens inherit their turn's reshaped advantage and are optimized with a clipped GRPO/PPO objective plus KL regularization; no separate distillation loss, critic, or extra rollout is used. Critical design choices are turn-boundary aggregation, recursive evidence accumulation with gamma=0.95, and bounded outcome-aligned reshaping with lambda=0.5 and b=0.2. The paper motivates these choices with environment alignment, sequential evidence, and sign preservation, but the success-conditional interpretation of the teacher is assumed rather than empirically validated. Key Results: On Qwen2.5-7B, AgentOPSD obtains 89.1% average ALFWorld success versus 81.2% for GRPO, 85.9% for SDAR, 88.4% for StepOPSD, and 82.0% for RLSD; its per-category ALFWorld results are 91.2/87.5/100/90.5/75.0/84.2 for Pick, Look, Clean, Heat, Cool, and Pick2. On Qwen2.5-3B, it obtains 84.4% ALFWorld success versus 75.0% for GRPO and 84.4% for SDAR. On Search-QA, it reaches 49.2% average accuracy with Qwen2.5-7B versus 42.0% for GRPO, 49.0% for RLSD/SDAR, and 48.2% for StepOPSD; with Qwen2.5-3B it reaches 46.7% versus 36.4% for GRPO and 43.4% for SDAR. On WebShop with Qwen2.5-7B it reports 49.2% normalized score and 79.7% exact accuracy, versus 49.0%/77.3% for RLSD and 49.0%/82.8% for SDAR; thus AgentOPSD improves score but not exact accuracy over SDAR. The ALFWorld horizon-sensitivity slope is −0.54 success points per extra turn for AgentOPSD, compared with −2.91 for GRPO and −3.59 for RLSD. The main evaluations use standard benchmark settings, at most 50 ALFWorld turns, 15 WebShop turns, and 4 Search-QA turns, with 3B and 7B models; they do not test 10×–100× larger models or substantially longer horizons. The strongest counterpoint to the broad improvement claim is that AgentOPSD is not uniformly best on every metric or task category, including WebShop exact accuracy and several ALFWorld subcategories. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION, NEW METHOD, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING; the genuinely new element is the recursive, log-odds belief-revision interpretation and bounded use of turn-level self-distillation evidence, while the underlying ingredients—GRPO, PPO clipping, privileged self-distillation, likelihood-ratio scoring, and advantage reweighting—are established techniques combined for agentic long-horizon RL. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper includes controlled component ablations on ALFWorld/Qwen2.5-7B: full AgentOPSD reaches 89.1%, versus 85.9% for per-token accumulation, 82.8% for raw local gaps, 80.5% without outcome-aligned sign, and 78.9% without the empirical-rate prior. It also sweeps lambda, gamma, and the upper policy-clip bound across three model/environment configurations, with shaded local ±1 standard-deviation bands in training curves. However, the main results do not report the number of independent runs, seed-level variance, error bars, or significance tests, and the ablation appears to be a single reported run. The implementation, algorithm pseudocode, prompts, training settings, and code URL (https://github.com/ZethWang/AgentOPSD) are provided; no separately released dataset or trained weights are mentioned. Evaluation uses a training-only retrieved SkillBank signal, so the comparison is controlled against similarly privileged baselines but still depends on a particular skill-retrieval source and keyword-matching procedure. WebShop uses only 128 fixed validation tasks, and the paper does not establish whether repeated tuning or benchmark-specific choices affected the reported results. The Bayesian approximation rests on assumptions that the skill-conditioned policy approximates success-conditioned behavior and that the unconditioned policy is failure-dominated when success is rare; these assumptions are not directly measured. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL, with a reusable training-code artifact rather than a deployed production system. - Practical: The method can run on commercially available accelerators and uses standard on-policy language-model training, but the reported training setup still uses up to 8 H800 GPUs and requires a privileged skill retriever during training. - Efficient: Relative to GRPO it adds one teacher forward pass per trajectory and elementwise bookkeeping, avoiding critics and extra rollouts, but the paper does not report wall-clock time, memory overhead, or tokens-per-second impact. - Effective: Evidence on three interactive benchmarks shows improved aggregate success or accuracy over GRPO and several self-distillation baselines, but the improvements are benchmark-proxy results and are not validated on real users, production tools, or distribution shifts. - Scalable: The method is evaluated only at Qwen2.5-3B/7B, group size 8, and horizons up to 50 turns; behavior at 10×–100× model, batch, task, or horizon scale is not tested. The work delivers open-source AgentOPSD training code and a reproducible algorithm specification, but no new dataset, model checkpoint, library release, or deployed agent service is reported. Strengths: - The method identifies a concrete mismatch between token-level distillation signals and environment-level actions, then aligns credit with turn boundaries rather than merely renaming token scores as steps. - The recursive revision Delta B_k distinguishes evidence that is decisive early from similar evidence that becomes redundant after prior turns, which is a more specific sequential-credit mechanism than local gap scaling. - The bounded reshaping preserves the sign of the verifier-derived advantage and recovers GRPO at lambda=0, providing a clear safety property and a controlled interpolation to the baseline. - The experiments compare against multiple self-distillation RL formulations under shared backbones, data, and training budgets, and the ablations isolate granularity, recursion, outcome sign, and prior anchoring. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The paper explicitly frames the self-teacher contrast as an approximation rather than a calibrated success probability, and it acknowledges that the method relies on training-only privileged skills. It also notes that the method is intended for long-horizon settings and that its hyperparameters matter less on four-turn Search-QA. It does not present a dedicated limitations section discussing seed variance, fixed-task evaluation, real-world deployment, or the validity of its success-conditional assumptions. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The largest empirical gap is the absence of multi-seed results and uncertainty estimates, especially because several gains over strong baselines are small and the reported curves are noisy. The paper does not compare against reward-based or value-based credit-assignment methods such as GiGPO, GAE-style critics, or additional-rollout methods in the main table, so it does not establish the best trade-off against the broader credit-assignment landscape. The claim that the teacher gap identifies pivotal turns is evaluated only indirectly through final task performance; there is no counterfactual, human, or environment-grounded test of turn-credit accuracy. The Bayesian derivation is also weaker than the presentation suggests: the teacher is assumed to approximate a success-conditioned policy, the marginal policy is treated as failure-dominated in a limited regime, and the algorithm uses both the sign and magnitude of recursive belief revisions even though the appendix emphasizes sign and ranking preservation for the local contrast. Finally, the dependence on SkillBank retrieval and the possible overlap between skill construction, training environments, and evaluation tasks are not stress-tested, leaving uncertainty about transfer when no curated skills exist or when the privileged guidance is mismatched. Bottom Line: AgentOPSD is a worthwhile and technically coherent advance for researchers studying critic-free, long-horizon LLM-agent RL, but its strong practical and novelty claims should be discounted until multi-seed significance tests, credit-quality validation, broader baselines, and scaling experiments are supplied.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces AURORA-LM, a continuous-latent diffusion language model that learns to generate high-capacity, causally ordered text latents and decodes them into discrete tokens. - Why it's important: It targets the central trade-off in continuous language modeling between making latents easy to generate and preserving the information needed for accurate token-level reconstruction. - How it does it: It combines a query-based causal autoencoder, block-causal flow matching over latent blocks, a low-rank noisy-input pathway with full-width clean-latent prediction, width-calibrated noise sampling, and self-trajectory consistency. - The good: At 130M denoiser parameters, it reports Gen-PPL 23.56 and MAUVE 0.890 on 1,024-token OpenWebText generation, and ROUGE-1/2/L scores of 36.6/13.4/28.9 on XSum, exceeding the evaluated baselines. - The missing: The paper does not provide a convincing compute- and latency-normalized comparison against strong contemporary autoregressive or discrete-diffusion models, and its 1B-scale evidence compares only with one released 1.8B latent-diffusion checkpoint. - Read it or not: Researchers working on continuous or diffusion language models should read it for the latent-capacity and trajectory-consistency analyses; readers seeking evidence of deployment advantages over modern autoregressive LMs can likely defer it.
