Problem & Motivation The work addresses the difficulty of converting complex, evolving French maintenance regulations into structured knowledge usable by regulatory-compliance workflows and Computerized Maintenance Management Systems. The target domain is industrial maintenance, where users need to identify actors, actions, affected artifacts, conditions, legal sources, and cross-references for specific obligations. Prior legal information-extraction methods are described as largely dataset-driven and do not provide an end-to-end path from regulatory text to an ontology-grounded knowledge graph. Existing resources such as ELI, SEMLEG, and maintenance ontologies provide general legal, activity, or metadata structure, but do not supply the domain-specific relation vocabulary and domain–range signatures needed for this application. Key Idea The central insight is to use the LLM twice under different structural regimes: first, allow open relation extraction on a representative corpus sample so that maintenance-specific predicates can be discovered; then normalize and formalize those predicates into an ontology whose property signatures constrain extraction from the full corpus. This turns the ontology from a fixed prerequisite into an automatically refined intermediate representation. The paper’s main conceptual observation is that ontology quality must account not only for missing predicates but also for newly observed domain–range combinations of existing predicates. Methodology The pipeline begins with a SEMLEG-based core ontology retaining classes such as Actor, Action, Artifact, Condition, Source, Location, Reason, Situation, and Time, together with compatible object properties. The corpus contains 6,370 official French regulatory articles across 20 topics, retrieved from Légifrance using maintenance-oriented references from an Apave guide. Ontology engineering uses a stratified sample of 1,389 articles, approximately 10% of each domain–document-title pair. For each sampled article, an entity-extraction prompt assigns typed entities using class-guided Turtle Light serialization; a relation-extraction prompt then generates triples without a predefined predicate vocabulary; and a topic-classification prompt retains triples labeled maintenanceActivity while discarding other legal-activity and cross-reference triples for ontology induction. Entity and property labels are embedded and merged when cosine similarity exceeds 0.7, with the most frequent variant selected as canonical; property merging is performed within subject-class/object-class pairs. Five percent of triples per property, with at least one example per signature, are divided into 15 batches and passed to a relation-discovery prompt that proposes object properties with labels, domain, range, evidence, definitions, competency-question alignment, and confidence scores, which are formalized as OWL axioms. Two ontology variants are produced: GPT-4.1/OpenAI and mistral-large-2512/Mistral. Each paired ontology and model then performs closed triple extraction over the complete corpus using admissible properties and signatures as prompt-level constraints. Outputs are fused again, represented in intermediate tables, and lifted to RDF with RML. The graph combines ELI, DCTERMS, CNT, SKOS, PROV, and Web Annotation, and reifies extracted relations as rdf:Statement and semleg:ExtractedRelation to attach evidence and provenance. Critical design decisions include the 0.7 fusion threshold, the open-to-closed transition, and prompt-level rather than formally enforced signature constraints; the paper provides operational rationale for the workflow but does not systematically justify the threshold or compare it with alternatives. Key Results The induced GPT-4.1 ontology contains 75 maintenance-specific properties and 105 signatures, whereas the Mistral ontology contains 44 properties and 59 signatures; the variants share 21 properties and 18 signatures. Over the full corpus, the unfused Mistral graph contains 2,119,485 RDF triples, 74,035 entities, 2,643 object properties, and 4,694 signatures; fusion reduces these to 1,131,066 triples, 20,827 entities, 500 properties, and 1,636 signatures. The unfused OpenAI graph contains 1,507,755 triples, 53,804 entities, 2,649 properties, and 4,374 signatures; fusion produces 1,311,916 triples, 38,339 entities, 2,031 properties, and 3,398 signatures. The number of reified relation statements remains unchanged at 75,870 for Mistral and 51,657 for OpenAI, indicating that fusion primarily changes normalization and representation rather than statement count. JSON validity is 100% in all four settings, and class coverage is 99.97% for Mistral and 99.99% for OpenAI. Property coverage improves from 82.51% to 96.42% for Mistral and from 81.52% to 85.11% for OpenAI after fusion. Exact signature compliance is lower: it rises from 49.86% to 72.61% for Mistral and from 56.94% to 61.03% for OpenAI. The paper reports 39 inconsistent signatures in the fused Mistral graph and 52 in the fused OpenAI graph. Competency-question SPARQL tests retrieve actor roles and legal justifications, but no retrieval accuracy, answer completeness, or comparison with alternative graph-construction methods is reported. The baselines are effectively the same systems without fusion or with the alternative model/ontology variant, not independent contemporary extraction or ontology-engineering baselines; the tested scale is a substantial corpus of 6,370 articles but not a demonstrated deployment or stress test at 10–100 times that scale. Novelty Classification The contribution is primarily NEW METHOD, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, with a domain-specific NEW FORMULATION of ontology refinement through observed relation signatures: the workflow integrates known LLM extraction, embeddings, RDF/RML, and ontology constraints in a French maintenance-regulation setting, while its more substantive finding is that unseen domain–range signatures, rather than mostly unseen predicates, are the dominant remaining alignment problem. It does not introduce a new general-purpose language-model architecture, benchmark, or formally new ontology-learning algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility The paper evaluates four structural metrics—JSON validity, class coverage, property coverage, and exact signature compliance—and includes a qualitative inspection of inconsistent signatures plus competency-question SPARQL tests. It compares GPT-4.1 with mistral-large-2512 under temperature-zero prompting and reports both fused and unfused outputs. However, it provides no human gold-standard annotations, relation/entity precision or recall, error bars, multiple-seed analysis, significance tests, or independent legal-expert validation. The ablation is limited to the presence or absence of fusion; it does not isolate entity fusion from predicate fusion, test the 0.7 threshold, compare open extraction with alternative ontology-induction procedures, or evaluate formal validation and repair. Code and prompt templates are stated to be available at https://github.com/gmontenegrou/LegiMaintLex, and datasets are stated to be available at https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1GfJPdJiGv_dZuC9utOgCTyzmeYb5lYU0?usp=drive_link. The graphs and ontology artifacts are not clearly identified as downloadable releases. Prompt-level constraints are not formally enforced, and the evaluation metrics can reward reuse of the induced ontology without establishing semantic correctness. Because the ontology is induced from one sample of the same corpus later used for graph construction, the evaluation is exposed to corpus-specific adaptation and possible Goodhart effects. Deployability: (4-property check) Profile: EMPIRICAL and SYSTEMS. Practical: The workflow uses Python, RDF/RML tooling, and commercially accessible OpenAI or Mistral model APIs, so it is technically runnable on ordinary infrastructure, although API cost, latency, licensing, and data-governance requirements are not measured. Efficient: Fusion reduces entity counts by 71.9% for Mistral and 28.7% for OpenAI and reduces Mistral property counts by 81.1%, but the paper reports no extraction runtime, token usage, monetary cost, memory footprint, or comparison with cheaper alternatives. Effective: The evidence establishes structured-output validity and ontology alignment, and competency queries retrieve some target information, but it does not establish legally accurate extraction or safe compliance decisions because no gold-standard semantic evaluation is provided. Scalable: The method runs on 6,370 articles, but the paper does not test 10×–100× scale, incremental updates, long-document behavior, rate-limit handling, or ontology drift as regulations evolve. The work delivers code and prompts, a corpus-derived RDF knowledge graph, and two induced ontology variants; it stops short of a validated production tool or maintained update pipeline. Strengths - The open-extraction-to-closed-extraction design addresses a real tension between discovering domain vocabulary and enforcing downstream structural consistency. - The paper separates predicate coverage from signature compliance, exposing that existing predicates can still be misused with new class combinations; this is more informative than reporting only vocabulary overlap. - The evaluation covers a nontrivial corpus of 6,370 French regulatory articles and preserves relation evidence and provenance through RDF reification, Web Annotation, and PROV-compatible representations. - The comparison between GPT-4.1 and Mistral reveals a meaningful qualitative difference: OpenAI induces a broader, more fine-grained vocabulary, while Mistral produces a smaller vocabulary focused on normative and compliance relations. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly identify the need for iterative ontology refinement that validates and integrates newly observed domain–range signatures, improved entity and predicate fusion, and formal validation or repair mechanisms such as SHACL. They also state that future work must evaluate GraphRAG-based consultation and updating when legal provisions change. The qualitative analysis acknowledges entity-typing errors, incorrect target-type expectations, modality and polarity encoded in predicates, French predicates appearing despite English-label instructions, and the danger that over-normalization can hide legally important distinctions. These limitations are confronted directly as future engineering priorities, but the paper does not quantify their impact on legal correctness. Analyst-Identified Gaps The principal gap is the absence of an independently labeled evaluation set and human or expert assessment of extraction correctness; consequently, 100% JSON validity and high class coverage cannot support claims of reliable legal knowledge. The paper does not compare against a fixed manually engineered ontology, supervised legal information-extraction system, retrieval-augmented extraction baseline, or a simpler LLM pipeline without ontology induction. It also does not report precision loss caused by fusion, despite acknowledging that merging predicates may erase distinctions such as obligation, prohibition, responsibility, and condition. The ontology sample and full-corpus evaluation are drawn from the same regulatory collection, with no held-out topics, later legal amendments, other French legal sources, or non-French transfer test. Prompt-level signatures are not checked by SHACL or repaired, and the reported property/signature metrics lack a clear gold reference; in particular, low signature compliance may reflect ontology incompleteness, extraction errors, or legitimate polysemy, but the experiments do not disentangle these causes. Finally, the paper does not measure downstream CMMS utility, compliance decision quality, query precision/recall, update latency, or operational cost. Bottom Line This is a useful systems-oriented workflow and diagnostic study for researchers constructing ontology-grounded legal KGs, but practitioners should not treat it as evidence of production-ready regulatory understanding until expert-validated accuracy, independent baselines, formal constraint checking, and downstream compliance evaluations are added.

Problem & Motivation The paper addresses semantic test-oracle generation for black-box REST APIs in industrial CI/CD environments. QA engineers must validate business-level properties such as enumerations, temporal relationships, types, and required fields, but many rapidly evolving services lack accurate OpenAPI specifications and newly deployed endpoints lack enough execution history for invariant mining. Existing schema-based methods depend on documentation, dynamic inference methods depend on many traces, and general-purpose LLMs can be too costly, slow, or prone to generating weak or flaky assertions. The targeted gap is the single-sample, zero-specification setting in which only one request–response pair is available and the system must infer which fields matter and which constraints are likely to generalize. Key Idea The central insight is to turn expert-derived semantic perturbations into execution-based reinforcement-learning feedback rather than treating assertion generation as token-level imitation. For each observed response, Restor labels business-critical fields and constructs valid and invalid variants; generated assertion code is rewarded when it passes the original and valid variants, rejects invalid variants, and accesses relevant rather than dynamic fields. This makes the model optimize behavioral discrimination and field coverage instead of reproducing one canonical assertion syntax. The individual ingredients—LLM fine-tuning, expert labels, mutation-based testing, and GRPO—are known, but their combination targets the unusually cold single-traffic oracle-generation setting. Methodology Restor has two phases. First, it collects a production request, response, and endpoint identifier; three ByteDance QA engineers label key fields using entity, domain-logic, and operational-status criteria while excluding dynamic fields such as timestamps and trace IDs. The same annotators infer natural-language constraints and create three positive and three negative replacements per key field, producing augmented response bodies. Second, a lightweight internal Doubao-Seed-1.6-flash model generates groups of Python assertion programs conditioned on the API context. Each candidate must execute successfully on the original response or receives a reward of -1. Otherwise, the reward combines key-field identification, computed from precision and recall against the labeled field set, with semantic accuracy, computed as weighted negative-sample kill rate minus weighted positive-sample kill rate and clipped to [-1, 1]. GRPO samples eight outputs per prompt, normalizes rewards within each group into token-level advantages, applies a clipped policy objective, and regularizes against a reference model using KL divergence. Critical design decisions are the expert-defined field set, the positive/negative mutation scheme, and the reward gate requiring validity on the original response; the paper motivates each, but does not empirically justify their relative contributions. Training uses two epochs, a learning rate of 1e-6, KL coefficient 0.001, and clip ratio 0.2, with all training and evaluation run once. Key Results The main dataset contains more than 2,300 anonymized traces from over 1,500 REST APIs, 246 services, 15 business lines, and a random 80:10:10 train/validation/test split; the held-out test set contains 229 samples. Restor obtains 81.30% precision, 96.15% recall, and 85.42% F1 for key-field identification. The base Doubao-Seed-1.6-flash obtains 68.54% precision and 77.29% F1, while DeepSeek-V3.1-Terminus obtains 67.57% precision and higher 98.64% recall but lower F1; one-tailed Wilcoxon tests over 229 samples report p < 0.001 for Restor's precision and F1 improvements over both baselines. In assertion categorization, Restor produces 663 exact matches, 22 partial matches, 15 overly general assertions, 28 not-validated fields, and 45 incorrect assertions, compared with 622 exact matches for DeepSeek and 549 for base Doubao; the paper's narrative emphasizes reduced omissions, although the reported “incorrect” count is not zero. In a separate 48-case industrial study involving 13 QA engineers across 11 business lines, Restor reaches 60.27% precision, 94.54% recall, and 69.91% F1, with 216 exact matches, 43 partial matches, 24 overly general assertions, 3 incorrect assertions, and 30 not-validated fields. Production adoption rose from 74.1% before deployment to 92.6% in the first post-deployment interval and 97.2% in the final reported interval; core lines BL02 and BL03 achieved 97.0% over 1,064 tasks and 93.2% over 117 tasks. The strongest baselines are general LLM prompting, not specialized systems such as AGORA/AGORA+, SATORI, Tratto, or LlamaRestTest, and no latency, cost, throughput, defect-detection, or CI failure-rate numbers are reported. Novelty Classification The contribution is primarily NEW PROBLEM, NEW METHOD, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL: it applies GRPO with execution-based rewards to semantic REST API oracle generation from a single trace and reports deployment evidence; the underlying components and model-training algorithm are standard, and the paper does not introduce a new RL algorithm, formal oracle semantics, or publicly reusable benchmark. Rigor & Reproducibility The paper uses held-out endpoints, expert majority voting, a separate 48-case industrial evaluation, and a nonparametric significance test for key-field metrics. However, it reports no ablations for GRPO versus supervised fine-tuning or prompt engineering under matched compute, no ablations for reward terms or mutation counts, no multiple training seeds, confidence intervals, inter-rater agreement, or independent external labeling. The field labels, inferred constraints, and positive/negative samples are produced by three ByteDance QA engineers, and the evaluation categories appear to depend on the same organizational notion of correctness, creating potential evaluator and reward-model alignment bias. The strongest comparisons are omitted, including direct evaluations against specialized oracle-generation methods. Source code, raw data, and trained weights are not released because the dataset and model are proprietary; no public repository or reproducibility package is provided. The production adoption metric is self-reported by the authors' internal platform and measures human acceptance or commit behavior rather than fault detection or assertion correctness. Deployability: (4-property check) Profile: EMPIRICAL, with a deployed SYSTEMS component. - Practical: The model runs in ByteDance's internal CI/CD test-generation platform on commercially available infrastructure, but hardware requirements, inference latency, and deployment cost are not reported. - Efficient: The lightweight model is intended to be cheaper and faster than DeepSeek-V3.1-Terminus, but the paper supplies no parameter count, tokens-per-second, memory use, latency, or cost comparison. - Effective: Evidence supports improved field-selection metrics, assertion categories, and human adoption, but it measures proxy quality and acceptance rather than the number of real regressions detected or the reduction in escaped defects. - Scalable: The system was used across 1,500 APIs and production business lines, but the paper does not test 10x–100x scale, long-term distribution shift, concurrent CI load, or payloads beyond the acknowledged approximately 400-field edge cases. The work delivers an internal test-generation platform integration and a trained model, but neither the library, model, dataset, nor source code is reusable outside ByteDance; it does not stop at paper form, yet external deployment is not directly reproducible. Strengths - It isolates a consequential and under-addressed cold-start setting: generating semantic oracles from one request–response pair without specifications, source code, or historical logs. - The reward directly evaluates executable behavior on valid and invalid variants, which is better aligned with oracle quality than token-level similarity or purely structural checks. - The evaluation spans offline held-out samples, noisier user cases, and a production workflow, with meaningful evidence that the method reduces omissions and dynamic-field assertions relative to the selected baselines. - The production results are operationally relevant: adoption increased from 74.1% to 97.2% over the reported intervals, and the system was exercised across 246 services, although the causal interpretation remains limited. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly report verbosity and assertion-density problems for 3 of 48 cases with more than 400 response fields, compared with a typical training distribution below 100 fields. They acknowledge that highly specialized business rules, including complex proprietary billing calculations, cannot always be inferred from a single black-box sample. They also acknowledge that all generated assertions are Python-specific and that the data and model are proprietary. Their threats-to-validity section discusses human annotation bias, possible adoption-metric bias, ByteDance-specific conventions, and limited cross-organization generalizability, but argues that the underlying methodology should transfer with new constraint definitions. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The paper does not demonstrate that GRPO is responsible for the gains: there is no ablation against SFT, supervised constraint classification, reward components, mutation-based data augmentation, group size, or model scale. - The evaluation ground truth is partly circular: the same three internal QA engineers define key fields and constraints, construct the mutations used for training and reward evaluation, and participate in expert assessment; independent annotators or inter-rater statistics are absent. - The single-sample premise is weakened by training on a large collection of related internal traffic and by using organizational conventions that may make fields and constraints easier to infer than in genuinely cold external APIs. - Comparisons exclude the most relevant specialized oracle-generation baselines and do not establish whether Restor detects more real API regressions than AGORA+, SATORI, Tratto, schema-based tools, or carefully engineered non-LLM methods. - The assertion-accuracy categories and production adoption rate do not measure test effectiveness, such as mutation score, real fault detection, escaped-defect reduction, flaky-test rate, review time, or CI runtime. - The reported production improvement is observational and coincides with deployment, onboarding, workload changes, and possibly other platform changes; no controlled rollout or per-task paired analysis supports a causal attribution to GRPO. - The paper does not report the model's parameter count, inference latency, training compute, financial cost, sample-selection policy in deployment, or the frequency with which generated assertions are edited before adoption. Bottom Line Restor is a useful and technically plausible production-oriented treatment of single-trace REST oracle generation, but its strongest claims should be treated as organization-specific empirical evidence rather than a fully validated advance until ablations, independent evaluation, stronger specialized baselines, and fault-detection measurements are provided.

Problem & Motivation The paper addresses the difficulty of integrating generative AI and intelligent agents into technical and vocational education and training (TVET) classrooms where teaching must connect academic instruction, industrial standards, heterogeneous equipment, vocational assessment, and workshop safety. The problem affects dual teachers, enterprise engineering experts, students, and administrators in secondary and higher vocational institutions. Existing work often treats AI adoption or teacher-perceived usefulness as a proxy for teaching efficiency and commonly studies teachers alone. The paper argues that this misses the labor and risk created when AI-generated content requires technical validation, adaptation to local equipment, interpretation for students, and compliance review against industrial and safety standards. The stated gap is therefore an insufficiently multi-stakeholder and context-sensitive account of how AI changes work in dual-teacher classrooms, particularly in computing, Internet of Things, and big-data training. Key Idea The core insight is that intelligent-agent efficiency in safety-sensitive TVET is not net time savings but bounded, task-dependent redistribution of professional judgment. AI can assist with standardized drafting, sorting, and preliminary screening, but human teachers and industry experts must retain authority over technical reasoning, industrial compliance, safety judgment, and final assessment. The CMEO framework organizes this insight as a closed loop: contextual constraints generate human–AI coping mechanisms, institutional and infrastructure enablers make those mechanisms sustainable, and the resulting outcomes concern workload redistribution and value-oriented evaluation. The framework is a contextual synthesis rather than a demonstrated algorithm or general theory. Methodology The study uses a qualitative interpretivist design based on 15 one-on-one semi-structured interviews: five on-campus dual teachers, three industry engineering experts, four vocational students, and three teaching administrators. Participants came from secondary, higher, and adult vocational settings, although the reported institutional sample comprises seven secondary and eight higher-vocational participants, covering IoT, computer application, and big-data majors. Interviews lasted 30–60 minutes, were conducted in Chinese, recorded with written consent, fully transcribed and anonymized, and translated into English with AI assistance. English working transcripts were imported into NVivo 14 for inductive open, axial, and selective coding; ambiguous passages, technical terms, and quotations were checked against the Chinese originals. The output is an 18-code CMEO framework: seven constraints, four mechanisms, five enablers, and two outcomes. Key design decisions include purposive multi-role sampling, explanation-first assessment in which technical reasoning precedes acceptance of AI outputs, and human–AI task division in which agents perform standardized aggregation or preliminary scoring while teachers and experts perform final review. The sampling logic and workflow are described, but the paper does not report a formal interview protocol in full, coder agreement statistics, independent coding by specified researchers, or a clear operational rule for determining saturation beyond the claim that the final three interviews added no new primary categories. The study does not implement or experimentally test an intelligent-agent system; mechanisms such as private deployment, edge inference, evidence-chain diagnosis, and learning analytics are reported as participant-described practices or recommendations rather than evaluated interventions. Key Results The main empirical result is qualitative: participants reported limited benefits for repetitive tasks such as courseware drafting, exercise sorting, material generation, and error screening, but no participant reported an overall productivity increase. Respondents described seven constraints: restricted access to authentic enterprise data; a gap between tool operation and technical reasoning; cognitive overload from large volumes of AI-generated material; mismatch with local equipment and workshop conditions; hallucinated or unsafe technical guidance; student over-reliance on automated fault diagnosis; and mismatch between uniform AI pacing and differentiated student ability. Four reported or proposed coping mechanisms were explanation-first rubrics, teacher–expert–AI co-assessment, evidence-chain diagnostic training, and interpretable learning analytics for targeted tutoring. Five enabling conditions were tiered teacher training with secure data sandboxes, private campus deployment and edge inference, governance guardrails, shared accountability for abnormal AI cases, and alignment among industry resources, courses, and certification standards. The study reports no accuracy, F1, time, throughput, cost, learning-gain, safety-incident, retention, or statistically tested outcome measures. It compares its interpretation primarily with prior literature and the technology acceptance model rather than with competing systems or empirical baselines. The evidence scale is a bounded, purposive sample of 15 interviews across Jiangsu vocational institutions, not a standard-scale or stress-scale evaluation. The most notable finding is counter to simple automation narratives: AI reportedly accelerates local routine tasks while increasing total cross-role obligations for validation, adaptation, interpretation, and risk control. Novelty Classification NEW FORMULATION, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and contextual analytical framework. The paper’s genuine contribution is the multi-stakeholder formulation of AI efficiency as workload redistribution and professional judgment under TVET-specific equipment, industrial, and safety constraints, supported by interviews spanning teachers, experts, students, and administrators; the CMEO structure itself is largely a standard thematic organization of constraints, responses, enabling conditions, and outcomes rather than a technically new method or validated general theory. Rigor & Reproducibility The paper provides a participant table, interview duration, sampling rationale, coding trail, 18-code codebook, reflexive journals, audit-trail claims, negative-case retention, cross-role comparison, ethics procedures, and manual checks of AI-translated quotations against Chinese transcripts. These practices support qualitative transparency, but the paper reports no multiple-seed analogue, inter-coder reliability, member checking, external audit, systematic negative-case analysis, or evidence showing how many participants endorsed each theme. The study explicitly acknowledges moderate rather than maximal credibility and relies on self-reported perceptions rather than observed classroom behavior. AI translation formed the primary coding corpus, creating a possible interpretation risk despite quotation-level cross-checking. Full transcripts are not public; the interview guide, selected deidentified excerpts, and codebook may be available from the authors upon reasonable request, with no URL or repository stated. No software, model weights, dataset, or implementable intelligent-agent artifact is released. The evaluation is not a direct benchmark comparison, and the paper lacks objective baseline measurements for the claimed efficiency gains or workload increases. Deployability (4-property check) Profile: EMPIRICAL, because the paper reports interview-based findings rather than a deployed system or formal theory. Practical: The recommended practices could in principle run on commercially available hardware, but the paper does not implement or measure a concrete system, and private model deployment or edge inference may require institution-specific infrastructure. Efficient: No compute, memory, latency, staffing, or total-workload measurements compare local deployment, public agents, or human-only workflows; the evidence instead suggests that automation of routine tasks can be offset by validation and adaptation costs. Effective: The interviews support perceived usefulness for drafting and screening and identify plausible safeguards, but they do not establish improved student competency, industrial employability, safety judgment, or net teaching efficiency. Scalable: The study covers 15 participants from Jiangsu institutions and three related majors; it does not test 10×–100× growth in users, institutions, data, classes, or model workload, and its conclusions are explicitly not generalizable without cross-regional and cross-major validation. The work stops at a paper-based framework and governance recommendations; it does not deliver a reusable library, CLI, tool, dataset, or trained model. Strengths - It broadens the unit of analysis beyond teachers by incorporating five dual teachers, three industry experts, four students, and three administrators, making visible workload and legitimacy concerns that a teacher-only study could miss. - It identifies concrete TVET-specific failure modes—equipment mismatch, enterprise-data restrictions, industrial-standard deviation, unsafe guidance, and loss of systematic troubleshooting—rather than discussing AI risk only at an abstract ethical level. - It links constraints, coping practices, institutional conditions, and outcomes in one framework, producing actionable governance implications such as explanation-first assessment, human final authority, secure sandboxes, and task-specific restrictions. - It is appropriately cautious in its stated scope: the authors characterize the findings as subjective, bounded, and applicable primarily to computing and IoT-related dual-teacher classrooms in Jiangsu rather than claiming universal validity. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly state that the findings rely on subjective practitioner accounts and cannot validate long-term institutional or student learning outcomes. They acknowledge moderate rather than maximal qualitative credibility, possible semantic misalignment between Chinese originals and English working transcripts, the small localized sample, and the inability to generalize the CMEO framework across regions, majors, or vocational systems without further verification. They also state that the framework is context-specific and recommend large-sample surveys, intervention studies with long-term classroom tracking, and cross-regional comparisons. These limitations are confronted directly in the discussion and conclusion rather than hidden behind claims of universal applicability. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The paper does not establish whether total workload rises, falls, or remains unchanged in measured terms; statements about redistribution and the absence of productivity gains are based on interview accounts, with no time-on-task logs, workload scales, or before/after comparison. - The proposed mechanisms are not separated from the observed findings: the paper does not show that explanation-first rubrics, evidence-chain training, private deployment, or governance guardrails caused better learning, safer practice, lower verification cost, or higher adoption. - The sample is narrow and potentially clustered by institution or professional network; the paper does not report recruitment rates, participant refusals, institutional counts by site, or meaningful variation in actual agent exposure and usage intensity. - The literature comparison is largely conceptual and does not provide strong empirical baselines, competing governance frameworks, or systematic evidence that prior TVET studies are single-perspective in the precise way claimed. - The use of AI-translated English as the primary coding corpus remains a methodological concern because translation can alter culturally and technically situated meanings; quotation-level checking does not demonstrate that the full thematic analysis is invariant to coding in Chinese. - The discussion sometimes uses causal language such as “mechanisms,” “enablers,” and “offset” although the cross-sectional interview design can support perceived relationships and plausible explanations, not causal effects. Bottom Line This is a useful qualitative scoping and governance paper for researchers and TVET administrators concerned with safe human–AI collaboration, but it is not evidence that intelligent agents improve vocational teaching and should not be ranked as a validated efficiency method or deployable system.

DualG-MRAG: Decoupling Macro-Reasoning and Micro-Matching for Multimodal Retrieval-Augmented Generation

J Tao, Q Sun, H Yuan, Z Zhang, J Li · arxiv.org · 10 new citations to your articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces DualG-MRAG, a multimodal RAG system that separates global cross-document reasoning from local visual-evidence matching using coupled Macro and Micro knowledge graphs. - Why it's important: Multimodal QA systems often retrieve semantically related fragments but fail to connect evidence across images, tables, and text, causing errors on multi-hop questions and increasing hallucination risk. - How it does it: It uses Micro-Graph subgraph matching to activate query-relevant entities, query-conditioned NBFNet-style message passing over a Macro Graph to rank evidence, and dynamic programming over message flows to serialize explicit reasoning paths for the MLLM. - The good: On the reported benchmarks, the method improves MMQA R@5 from 42.1% for MMGraphRAG to 61.9% and improves MMQA exact match with Qwen3-VL-4B from 37.2% for ViDoRAG to 44.2%. - The missing: The paper does not establish how the GNN is trained, report statistical variation or multiple seeds, release the proposed implementation, or isolate the contribution of its many heuristic scoring and graph-construction choices. - Read it or not: Researchers working on multimodal GraphRAG should read it for the macro/micro decomposition and path-extraction design, but should treat its efficiency and generalization claims as provisional until the training protocol and larger-scale evaluations are disclosed.

Problem & Motivation: The work targets knowledge-intensive multimodal question answering over heterogeneous text, images, and tables, especially questions requiring multiple evidence hops across documents. Dense vector retrieval and conventional multimodal RAG flatten evidence into independent chunks, while unified multimodal graphs face a granularity trade-off: fine-grained visual nodes increase graph size and retrieval noise, whereas coarse entities lose local visual details needed for verification. Existing graph retrievers also often use query-agnostic propagation and expose node scores rather than explicit evidence chains, leaving the downstream MLLM to reconstruct cross-modal relationships. Key Idea: The central insight is to decouple two retrieval functions that have conflicting granularity requirements: use a compact Macro Graph for global topological routing and a separate Micro Graph for fine-grained, document-local matching. Query-matched micro-facts activate macro entities, allowing global reasoning to proceed without inserting all local visual details into the global topology; the GNN's message-flow computation is then reused to decode an explicit reasoning path rather than only producing document scores. Methodology: Offline, the system constructs a Macro Graph by applying Qwen3-VL-8B-based image captioning and OpenIE to textual and image content, then adds equivalence edges when all-mpnet-v2 entity cosine similarity exceeds 0.8. It constructs a Micro Graph of image/table-local facts represented as tuples <node, relation, node, document pointer>, and aligns micro nodes to macro entities first by exact matching and then by ColBERT semantic linking. At inference, an LLM parses the query into constraint triples, target entities, and a visual budget; approximate top-3 candidate retrieval followed by heuristic branch-and-bound subgraph matching produces graph-level micro evidence, while a separate node-level nearest-neighbor branch supplies document boosting without expanding the GNN seed set. The resulting seed mask initializes an NBFNet-style, six-layer query-driven GNN using all-mpnet-v2 query embeddings; relational messages use layer-specific relation transformations and DistMult-style scoring, and node states are updated by summed incoming messages followed by a linear layer. Macro node scores are projected to text and image documents, min-max normalized separately, combined with micro scores using reported weights alpha=0.1 and beta=0.9, decayed for documents lacking micro evidence, and fused using a max operation. Finally, local flow probabilities are computed from message/state dot products with temperature 1.0, and a Viterbi-like dynamic program extracts maximum-probability paths from active seeds to high-scoring targets; aligned source snippets are serialized into prompts for the downstream MLLM. The paper does not clearly specify the GNN training objective, supervision source, optimization procedure, or whether the retriever is trained jointly with any component, which is a major methodological omission. The dual-tier representation is motivated conceptually, but the fixed thresholds, max-based fusion, score weights, visual decay, parser constraints, and heuristic search choices receive limited justification. Key Results: On 1,000 sampled MMQA validation queries and 1,000 sampled WebQA validation queries, with corpus sizes of 17.6K and 30.3K documents respectively, DualG-MRAG obtains MMQA EM/F1 of 44.20/47.57% with Qwen3-VL-4B and 46.00/51.19% with Qwen3-VL-8B; WebQA ROUGE-L/BERTScore are 50.10/70.58% and 48.92/69.74%. For comparison, the strongest listed MMQA EM baselines are ViDoRAG at 37.20% with the 4B backbone and MMGraphRAG at 39.50% with the 8B backbone; WebQA results are more mixed, with DualG-MRAG leading the listed methods on ROUGE-L but only narrowly improving or not improving BERTScore relative to the strongest baseline. Retrieval recall reaches 49.4%/61.9% at R@2/R@5 on MMQA versus MMGraphRAG's 31.8%/42.1%, and 37.0%/58.2% on WebQA, where VLM2Vec-V2.0 leads at R@2 with 38.1% but falls below DualG-MRAG at R@5 with 54.6%. On ScienceQA's 4,241 test questions, the method reports 90.99% average accuracy, compared with 89.06% for HM-RAG, 88.96% for zero-shot Qwen3-VL-8B, and 88.12% for VLM2Vec-V2.0; it reaches 91.52% on image-context questions and 87.87% on grades 7–12. The reported average retrieval latency is approximately 0.44 seconds, compared with approximately 0.09 seconds for VLM2Vec-V2.0 and 40.5 seconds for MMGraphRAG. Ablations show that removing the Micro Graph lowers MMQA/WebQA R@5 to 54.3%/40.0%, removing the Macro Graph lowers it to 21.8%/33.8%, and removing path injection reduces Qwen3-VL-4B MMQA EM from 44.2% to 41.8%; however, path injection slightly hurts Qwen3-VL-8B MMQA EM, from 46.0% to 46.5% when removed. These results are on standard but relatively small sampled/localized evaluation settings rather than demonstrated 10x–100x stress scales. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION, NEW METHOD, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING: the macro/micro graph decomposition and reuse of query-conditioned GNN message flows for explicit path decoding constitute the main claimed methodological contribution, while the individual ingredients—knowledge-graph extraction, dense entity linking, NBFNet-style propagation, heuristic subgraph matching, and dynamic programming—are established techniques combined for multimodal RAG rather than wholly new primitives. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper includes component ablations, two MLLM backbone sizes, retrieval metrics, latency comparisons, three datasets, and fine-grained ScienceQA breakdowns. It does not report error bars, confidence intervals, significance tests, or multiple random seeds. The evaluation uses strong-looking contemporary baselines, including MMGraphRAG, HM-RAG, ViDoRAG, VLM2Vec-V2.0, and CoRe-MMRAG, but the paper does not provide enough detail to verify that all systems use comparable retrieval budgets, indexing pipelines, context lengths, or preprocessing. MMQA and WebQA evaluation samples are drawn from validation sets and use local corpora built from associated documents, which may substantially simplify retrieval relative to open-corpus deployment; the paper does not evaluate on an independently collected or adversarial corpus. ScienceQA uses the training set to build the knowledge base and the test set for evaluation, but the special protocol allowing models to generate answers with and without retrieval and choose the more logical answer may confound retrieval evaluation. The proposed GNN training loss, data splits for graph construction/training, graph sizes after extraction, parsing/linking accuracy, and failure rates are not stated. No code, dataset, model weights, or repository for DualG-MRAG is reported; URLs are provided for several baselines and Qwen3-VL. The complexity analysis treats dense indexing as O(log N) and assumes an unspecified active subgraph much smaller than the full graph, so its asymptotic efficiency argument does not establish end-to-end complexity. Deployability (4-property check): EMPIRICAL profile. Practical: The reported system runs on NVIDIA A100 hardware, which demonstrates feasibility on commercially available accelerators, but the required Qwen3-VL-8B graph-construction pass, graph indexes, MLLM generation, and unspecified retriever training/storage costs are not fully quantified. Efficient: Retrieval latency is reported as approximately 0.44 seconds per query, substantially below MMGraphRAG's approximately 40.5 seconds but above VLM2Vec-V2.0's approximately 0.09 seconds; 59.95% of the internal latency is attributed to Micro Matching and 39.40% to Macro Reasoning, with no memory or total preprocessing measurements. Effective: The method improves reported retrieval recall and QA scores on MMQA, WebQA, and ScienceQA, but these benchmarks and the local-corpus setup measure benchmark QA performance rather than hallucination reduction, factuality under noisy retrieval, or reliable evidence attribution. Scalable: The paper claims localized subgraph computation and tests corpora of only 12.7K–30.3K candidate documents; it provides no 10x–100x scale experiment, graph-size curve, index-memory analysis, or evidence that graph construction and entity resolution remain manageable at web scale. The work describes a research system and reusable graph-retrieval/path-decoding procedure, but no software artifact or trained model release is stated. Strengths: - The macro/micro separation addresses a real multimodal graph-design tension and gives local visual evidence a document pointer without forcing every visual detail into the global routing graph. - The system connects retrieval and generation structurally: path decoding uses intermediate GNN message flow to provide explicit cross-document evidence chains rather than only a ranked chunk list. - Ablations support the functional distinction between the two graph tiers: removing the Macro Graph sharply reduces MMQA R@5 from 61.9% to 21.8%, while removing the Micro Graph sharply reduces WebQA R@5 from 58.2% to 40.0%. - The paper evaluates both retrieval and end-to-end generation, includes two backbone sizes, and reports a meaningful latency comparison rather than only accuracy. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The paper explicitly acknowledges the granularity/noise trade-off, the NP-hardness of exact subgraph matching, the need for heuristic approximation, and the possibility that path injection over-constrains larger MLLMs: removing path injection slightly improves Qwen3-VL-8B MMQA EM from 46.0% to 46.5%. It does not provide a dedicated limitations section or systematically discuss parser errors, graph-extraction errors, modality coverage, hallucinated graph facts, domain transfer, or memory/preprocessing cost. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The most serious gap is the missing training specification for the GNN retriever: the paper gives inference equations but no loss, supervision labels, negative sampling, optimization schedule, or training/evaluation separation, making the reported retriever difficult to reproduce and raising the possibility of hidden benchmark-specific tuning. The method relies heavily on Qwen3-VL-8B for image captioning, OpenIE, fine-grained visual parsing, and query parsing, so improvements may partly reflect a large proprietary-to-the-paper preprocessing pipeline rather than the proposed graph architecture; extraction quality and cost are not measured. The local-corpus construction from associated documents makes retrieval recall comparisons less representative of open-domain retrieval, and the paper does not compare against stronger contemporary multimodal or graph-retrieval variants under matched budgets. The ablations remove entire graph tiers but do not isolate path decoding from prompt formatting, micro-score fusion, visual decay, seed expansion, relation extraction, or the max fusion rule. The complexity claims assume bounded query graphs and small active neighborhoods without reporting actual graph statistics, worst-case behavior, memory use, or latency as corpus size grows. Finally, evidence recall does not establish that retrieved paths are correct, faithful, or causally responsible for the answer; no grounding, citation accuracy, calibration, hallucination, or human evaluation is provided. Bottom Line: The paper offers a useful and plausibly effective multimodal GraphRAG architecture, but its strong benchmark gains are not yet sufficient for top-tier confidence because training details, controlled component comparisons, evidence faithfulness, reproducibility, and scale validation remain underdeveloped.

High performance computing machine learning architecture for the LISA Global Fit

TM de Figueiredo Sarmento · repositorio-aberto.up.pt · inference optimize llm faster inference throughput - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a dual-branch feed-forward neural surrogate that predicts the log-likelihood of a single Galactic Binary from eight waveform parameters and 1,556 frequency-domain LISA TDI features in the 2.95–3.00 mHz band. - Why it's important: Replacing repeated physics-based likelihood evaluations could reduce the computational cost of the MCMC-based LISA Global Fit, although the demonstrated end-to-end saving is only 2× and the experiment covers a highly simplified subproblem. - How it does it: It encodes physical parameters and magnitude/phase representations of the A and E TDI channels through separate multilayer perceptrons, fuses their latent vectors, and trains the regressor with MSE on diverse synthetic backgrounds. - The good: Increasing background diversity from 2,000 to 40,000 unique realizations at fixed 200,000-sample training size improved global test MSE from 4.42×10^6 to 1.48×10^6 and top-5%-error R² from 0.36 to 0.82. - The missing: The work does not establish robustness on noisy, multi-source, full-band, trans-dimensional Global Fit workloads, nor does it report repeated-seed uncertainty, sampler convergence diagnostics, or a rigorous posterior-distance analysis. - Read it or not: Read it for the empirical analysis of dataset diversity and the practical JAX–PyTorch integration bottleneck; skip it if you need evidence for mission-scale LISA deployment or a substantially new surrogate-learning algorithm.

Problem & Motivation The work addresses the computational cost of Bayesian inference for LISA, whose signal-dominated data will contain many overlapping Galactic Binary and other gravitational-wave sources. In Global Fit pipelines, MCMC repeatedly evaluates expensive waveform-based likelihoods while fitting source parameters and updating residuals. The specific gap targeted is the lack of a demonstrated likelihood surrogate integrated into an active LISA Global Fit implementation. The thesis is a master's dissertation dated July 22, 2026 rather than a peer-reviewed conference or journal paper, and it narrows the operational problem to one Galactic Binary in a 2.95–3.00 mHz band with 5–10 additional simulated binary backgrounds. Key Idea The central insight is that generalization depends more on diversity of background TDI realizations than on balancing the highly skewed likelihood target distribution. Reusing many parameter evaluations for the same background causes the signal encoder to memorize background-specific offsets; using only five target evaluations per background, yielding 40,000 backgrounds for 200,000 samples, forces the network toward a more transferable mapping. The dual-branch architecture itself is largely a standard multimodal MLP design rather than a fundamentally new learning mechanism. Methodology The pipeline samples eight Galactic Binary parameters—amplitude, inclination, initial phase, polarization, frequency, frequency derivative, ecliptic longitude, and latitude—from stated priors, maps them to unit-hypercube coordinates, generates 90-day synthetic TDI data at 5-second cadence, injects 5–10 additional binaries, and computes analytical A/E-channel log-likelihood targets. Training examples contain an eight-dimensional parameter vector, a 1,556-dimensional feature vector from 389 frequency bins across real/imaginary A and E components, and the corresponding log-likelihood. The feature pipeline converts complex spectra to magnitude and phase, standardizes magnitudes using training-set statistics, and leaves phase values in [-π, π]. The parameter branch uses fully connected layers 8→256→512→256; the data branch uses 1,556→256→128→64; their 320-dimensional concatenation enters a 320→256→256→128 regression trunk with batch normalization, ReLU, dropout 0.4, and a 320→128 residual projection before scalar output. The model minimizes MSE with Adam, uses early stopping, and sweeps learning rates {10^-4, 5×10^-4, 10^-3} and batch sizes {128, 256, 512}. The thesis also compares low-, medium-, and high-diversity datasets and downsampling, oversampling, and 20-bin stratified sampling. These design choices are operationally plausible, but several are weakly justified: the architecture is selected without comparison to a single-branch MLP, CNN, kernel method, or simpler parameter-only/data-only ablation; MSE is chosen from preliminary runs without reported controlled results against MAE or Huber; and raw phase rather than periodic sin/cos encoding is used despite the acknowledged discontinuity. Key Results The high-diversity 200,000_5 model, trained on 200,000 samples from 40,000 unique backgrounds and evaluated on a 24,000-example test set, achieves MSE 1.48×10^6, global R² 0.97, top-10%-error MSE 9.39×10^6 and R² 0.87, and top-5%-error MSE 1.35×10^7 and R² 0.82. The low-diversity 200,000_100 model, based on 2,000 backgrounds, achieves MSE 4.42×10^6, global R² 0.91, and top-5%-error R² 0.36; the intermediate 200,000_15 model achieves MSE 1.87×10^6 and global R² 0.96. The reported hyperparameter winner uses batch size 512 and learning rate 0.001, with test MSE 1.30×10^6, MAE 759.24, and R² 0.9746 on the high-diversity dataset. Downsampling, oversampling, and stratified binning perform worse than the raw training distribution, with reported MSE values of 2.7392×10^6, 2.91×10^6, and approximately 3.4678×10^6, respectively. On the subset with log-likelihood greater than -20,000 (22,003 examples), the champion model reports MSE 1.0×10^6, MAE 711, and R² 0.95 overall; its worst 10% and 5% subsets have R² 0.67 and 0.37. Isolated likelihood inference takes 0.002 seconds for the surrogate versus 0.01 seconds for the analytical baseline, a reported 5× speedup. In the integrated ensemble MCMC experiment—one noisy SNR 40.97 source, six months of data, 100 walkers, 10 temperatures, 200 burn-in and 200 production iterations—the end-to-end speedup is approximately 2×. Posterior plots broadly align but show biases in amplitude, inclination, and initial phase and an overconfident, narrower frequency-derivative posterior. The baselines are the authors' analytical likelihood implementation and a physical MCMC run, not a broad comparison against current neural likelihood, normalizing-flow, GPU-native, or surrogate-assisted MCMC alternatives. The tested scale is a single source and narrow band, not a stress-scale Global Fit. Novelty Classification The contribution is primarily NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION: it provides a prototype surrogate and reports that background-realization diversity dominates target-based likelihood balancing in this setup, while the dual-branch network, MSE regression, magnitude/phase preprocessing, and JAX callback integration are standard techniques combined for a new LISA Global Fit setting rather than a new learning formulation. Rigor & Reproducibility The thesis uses independent training, validation, and test partitions of 200,000, 24,000, and 24,000 examples and evaluates global, high-likelihood, p90, and p95 error subsets. It includes a small grid sweep over learning rate and batch size and compares three resampling strategies. However, it reports no multiple random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, statistical significance tests, calibration metrics, effective sample sizes, acceptance rates, autocorrelation times, or formal posterior-distance measures. Architecture ablations are absent, and the claimed usefulness of the surrogate for stationary MCMC is not isolated from its observed posterior bias. The training backgrounds contain injected binaries but explicitly omit instrumental noise, while the final integration uses noisy data; this distribution shift is not systematically evaluated. The text names wrapper classes and cached .npz datasets but gives no public code, dataset, model-weight URL, or repository. The test-set construction is not fully specified with respect to background disjointness, and the fixed test ratio of 50 evaluations per signal differs from the training ratios, making the generalization protocol difficult to assess. The likelihood baseline is also the generator of all labels and the comparison target, so the experiment measures approximation to the simulator rather than accuracy against real LISA observations. Deployability: (4-property check) Profile: SYSTEMS, because the thesis builds and integrates a surrogate into an MCMC pipeline and measures end-to-end execution, although the evaluation remains prototype-scale. Practical: The model can run on commercially available CPU/GPU hardware, and the reported PyTorch implementation runs on GPU hardware, but the deployment requires a compatible JAX–PyTorch environment and a pipeline-specific wrapper. Efficient: Isolated inference improves from 0.01 to 0.002 seconds per likelihood evaluation, but serialization, host-to-device transfers, and Python sampler control reduce the measured end-to-end speedup to approximately 2×; memory footprint and energy consumption are not quantified. Effective: On synthetic data the surrogate approximately preserves the broad posterior structure, but localized parameter biases and frequency-derivative uncertainty underestimation show that scientific equivalence to the physical likelihood is not established. Scalable: Scalability beyond one source, one narrow frequency band, and one active MCMC experiment is not tested; the proposed GPU-native JAX implementation and full multi-source Global Fit scaling remain future work rather than demonstrated results. The work delivers a prototype software artifact consisting of a trained neural surrogate, a data-generation pipeline, and a GBSurrogateLik integration wrapper; it does not state that code, data, or weights are publicly released. Strengths - The controlled comparison of 2,000, approximately 13,334, and 40,000 unique backgrounds at fixed sample count exposes a concrete memorization failure mode and links it to measurable degradation in tail performance. - The thesis evaluates both standalone inference latency and end-to-end MCMC runtime, correctly showing that a nominal 5× model speedup becomes only 2× after framework and device-transfer overheads. - It tests the surrogate inside an operational sampler rather than stopping at regression metrics, and it explicitly reports posterior biases and uncertainty underestimation instead of presenting the posterior plots as exact agreement. - The narrow-band scope is clearly stated, which prevents the prototype result from being mistaken for a full solution to trans-dimensional, multi-source LISA inference. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly limit the study to a single Galactic Binary in a 2.95–3.00 mHz band and acknowledge that it does not solve the full Global Fit. They acknowledge omission of noise during training, the gap between isolated and end-to-end speedups, JAX pure-callback serialization, host-to-device transfer latency, and Python-hosted MCMC control. They also identify posterior biases, uncertainty underestimation, the need for native JAX/XLA execution and on-device sampling, and the need for active learning, alternative architectures, and periodic phase encoding. These limitations are confronted directly, although the conclusion still uses feasibility language that extends beyond the tested regime. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The central scientific claim is trained and evaluated on highly synthetic data: the training data omit instrumental noise, the background consists only of a small number of injected Galactic Binaries, and no Sangria or other full-complexity challenge result is reported. - The experiment does not test robustness to unseen noise spectra, waveform-model mismatch, observation durations, frequency bands, source amplitudes, source counts, or multiple resolvable targets; consequently, the 5× and 2× speedup claims cannot support mission-scale extrapolation. - No baseline ablation establishes that the dual-branch design, residual connection, magnitude/phase conversion, dropout, or 1,556-dimensional representation outperforms simpler alternatives. The statement that shallow models are incapable of approximating the target is asserted from parameter correlations rather than experimentally demonstrated. - MCMC validity is under-evaluated: one injected source, one sampler configuration, 200 burn-in iterations, and 200 production iterations do not establish convergence or unbiased posterior recovery. Acceptance rates, effective sample sizes, chain mixing, repeated injections, and quantitative posterior divergences are missing. - The thesis reports conflicting or insufficiently controlled runtime contexts: the analytical baseline, surrogate batch size, device synchronization, compilation warm-up, precision, and number of evaluations are not fully specified, so the reported 0.01-, 0.002-, 5×-, and 2× figures are difficult to reproduce or compare. - There is no public artifact link, no seed specification, and no independent replication, which substantially limits reproducibility for a systems result whose main value lies in integration behavior. Bottom Line This is a useful engineering proof-of-concept and a credible study of background-diversity effects, but practitioners should treat it as preliminary: its strongest contribution is diagnosing why a narrow-band surrogate can generalize poorly and why framework integration erases theoretical speedups, not demonstrating a deployable acceleration of the LISA Global Fit.

Investigating Coastal Classification with Multi-Modal Large Language Models

H de Heer · repository.tudelft.nl · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper builds and evaluates a coastal-classification pipeline that compares a 12-channel ResNet-50, prompted GPT-4o/LLaMA-3.2/Qwen2.5 models, and a Qwen2.5-VL-7B model modified and fine-tuned to ingest multispectral and elevation data. - Why it's important: Reliable automated coastal typology could support large-scale erosion, flooding, habitat, and adaptation monitoring, where manual expert interpretation is expensive and difficult to scale. - How it does it: It combines group-wise cross-validation, structured zero-/few-shot prompting with diversity-balanced example selection, and replacement of Qwen2.5's RGB patch-embedding layer with a 12-channel input interface trained using LoRA. - The good: The strongest evidence is that the 12-channel ResNet-50 reaches average F1 0.720 versus 0.662 for its RGB version, while fine-tuned Qwen2.5 improves from 0.686 to 0.700 with additional channels and GPT-4o reaches 0.689 with few-shot prompting. - The missing: The study does not provide a clean, independently held-out test set or sufficiently controlled few-shot protocol, so claims about generalization and prompting benefits may be optimistic, especially given that CoastBench was still private and Europe-only. - Read it or not: Read it for an early empirical study of multimodal models on coastal remote sensing and for its practical non-RGB Qwen2.5 adaptation, but do not treat its rankings or deployment claims as established without stronger external evaluation.

Problem & Motivation The work addresses automated classification of coastal environments from satellite and elevation data for environmental monitoring, coastal-hazard assessment, and adaptation planning. The target application involves four related labels: eight coastal geomorphology classes, five shore-material classes, binary built-environment presence, and binary coastal-defence presence. Existing approaches include expert interpretation, pixel-based classifiers, and CNNs trained on imagery or geospatial features; they generally do not provide a unified treatment of these labels or exploit pretrained vision-language knowledge. The paper targets the gap between conventional image classifiers and multimodal models that can accept structured prompts and produce human-readable outputs, while also addressing the mismatch between MLLMs' usual RGB inputs and remote-sensing data containing infrared, spectral-index, and elevation channels. Key Idea The central technical insight is that MLLMs can be made more useful for coastal classification through two complementary forms of task-specific adaptation: carefully selected, diverse and class-balanced few-shot examples for pretrained models, and direct architectural expansion of a pretrained vision encoder to accept non-RGB satellite channels. The work also argues, based on expert disagreement, that label ambiguity rather than model capacity may impose a practical ceiling near F1 0.70. The few-shot selection method itself is a straightforward greedy combination of coverage and inverse-frequency balancing rather than a fundamentally new learning paradigm. Methodology CoastBench contains 1,090 European coastal transects in the 2025-01-27 version, each represented by a 200 x 200 pixel, 10 m-resolution patch covering approximately 8 km². Inputs comprise six Sentinel-2 reflectance bands, two elevation products (Copernicus DEM and DeltaDTM), and four indices (NDVI, NDWI, MNDWI, and NDMI); labels are concatenated across the four prediction dimensions. The supervised CNN uses a ResNet-50 encoder, robust min-max normalization, random rotations/flips, sigmoid outputs, binary cross-entropy loss, and five-fold group cross-validation by transect. Its configuration was selected through a 195-run Bayesian hyperparameter sweep. For pretrained MLLMs, GPT-4o, Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, and LLaMA-3.2-11B-Vision-Instruct receive RGB images and structured prompts under three conditions: V1 structured zero-shot, V1.1 zero-shot plus reasoning text, and V2 multimodal few-shot prompting. Few-shot subsets contain 10 examples and are selected randomly, by brute-force diversity, greedily by unseen label values, or by a greedy-balanced score combining label coverage with inverse-frequency rewards. For Qwen2.5 fine-tuning, the first vision patch-embedding layer is replaced to accept either three or twelve channels, RGB weights are copied, new channels use He initialization, the Hugging Face data pipeline is modified for NumPy arrays, and LoRA is applied to the vision side while the language model and most pretrained components remain frozen. The fine-tuned model uses five-fold grouped cross-validation, 60 epochs, and default Qwen training settings. Finally, CNN feature ablations remove individual channels or groups and report mean F1 changes over five folds and two seeds, with paired t-tests. Key Results The 12-channel ResNet-50 obtains F1 scores of 0.578 for coastal type, 0.700 for shore type, 0.860 for built environment, and 0.825 for defence, for average F1 0.720; the RGB ResNet-50 obtains 0.465, 0.653, 0.861, and 0.784, respectively, for average F1 0.662. The best prompted GPT-4o result is average F1 0.689 with 10 few-shot examples selected by the greedy-balanced method, compared with 0.638 in zero-shot and 0.636 with the zero-shot reasoning variant; it therefore exceeds the RGB CNN baseline but not the full 12-channel CNN. GPT-4o's few-shot component scores are 0.465 coastal, 0.605 shore, 0.823 built, and 0.830 defence. Qwen2.5 and LLaMA perform substantially worse in prompted settings, with best reported average F1 values of 0.543 and 0.326, respectively. Fine-tuned Qwen2.5 reaches average F1 0.700 with 12 channels versus 0.686 with RGB; coastal F1 rises from 0.503 to 0.556 and shore F1 from 0.618 to 0.659, but built F1 falls from 0.813 to 0.789 and defence F1 from 0.811 to 0.793. The largest class-specific gain is reported for the Inlet coastal class, approximately +0.18, and the No Sediment shore class improves by approximately +0.10. CNN grouped ablations show drops of 0.020 for removing infrared (p=0.007), 0.016 for removing RGB (p=0.070), 0.014 for removing spectral indices (p=0.149), and 0.014 for removing elevation (p=0.026). At the individual-channel level, removing Blue or NDWI produces an average-F1 drop of 0.020, with p=0.002 and p=0.030, respectively. Two Deltares experts independently label 50 diverse transects and obtain average F1 around 0.68–0.70, below the CNN's 0.72, but this benchmark uses broader spatial context and domain knowledge and is too small to establish a reliable human ceiling. The reported scale is standard for a small remote-sensing benchmark, not a global or operational stress test. Novelty Classification NEW METHOD, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION: the paper's most credible novel contribution is an empirical demonstration and implementation of Qwen2.5-VL fine-tuning with 12-channel coastal remote-sensing input, including modified patch embedding and data handling; the balanced few-shot sampler and use of standard ResNet, LoRA, prompting, and ablation techniques are primarily combinations of existing ideas applied to a new coastal setting. The claim of being the first MLLM coastal-classification study is plausible from the cited literature but is not independently established by a broad comparison. Rigor & Reproducibility The study uses transect-grouped five-fold cross-validation, reports class-wise F1, provides confusion matrices, repeats CNN ablations over two seeds, and includes uncertainty estimates and paired t-tests for ablations. The ablations are useful for identifying modality contributions, although the effects are small and several tests are non-significant. The main reproducibility weaknesses are substantial: CoastBench was actively under development and not yet publicly released, the paper does not state that code, trained weights, or a fixed data snapshot are publicly available, and the repository link is only a general TU Delft repository URL. The CNN is selected through a large hyperparameter sweep using the same overall cross-validation framework, with no clearly separated outer test loop, creating a risk of validation overfitting. The few-shot experiments also do not clearly establish that support examples are drawn exclusively from a training partition disjoint from evaluated samples; if examples were selected from the full dataset, the comparison is contaminated by task-specific label and image exposure. GPT-4o is a proprietary, potentially nondeterministic API, and API version, decoding parameters, cost, latency, and repeated-run protocol are not stated. The paper compares against a ResNet-50 baseline but does not include stronger modern remote-sensing CNN/Transformer baselines, GeoChat or other domain-adapted remote-sensing MLLMs, or a conventional multispectral transformer. The reported correlations between few-shot diversity/balance and F1 are observational and based on few selection conditions, not causal evidence. Deployability (4-property check) Profile: EMPIRICAL, with a partial SYSTEMS component. Practical: The supervised models and fine-tuned 7B Qwen2.5 can run on commercially available GPUs—the CNN was trained on an RTX 3090 and Qwen2.5 on an H100—while GPT-4o requires an external commercial API. Efficient: Training cost is reported as approximately one hour per CNN run on an RTX 3090 and one hour per Qwen cross-validation fold on an H100, but inference latency, memory footprint, API cost, throughput, and comparison with smaller remote-sensing models are not evaluated. Effective: The models achieve average F1 between 0.326 and 0.720 on the benchmark, and the full-channel CNN is the strongest measured system, but the evidence addresses static classification labels rather than demonstrated improvement in a real coastal-management workflow. Scalable: The experiments cover only 1,090 European transects and 8 km² patches; there is no 10×–100× scale test, global geographic holdout, temporal shift test, sensor shift test, or operational mapping experiment. The thesis includes a Gradio interaction demonstration and a modified training pipeline, but it does not establish a released reusable library, CLI, dataset, or trained model artifact. Strengths - The paper frames a concrete and underexplored remote-sensing task with four complementary coastal attributes rather than a single coarse land-cover label. - The controlled RGB-versus-12-channel comparisons provide useful evidence that infrared, spectral-index, and elevation information improves geomorphological classification, even though gains are uneven across labels. - The Qwen2.5 architectural modification is technically relevant: the paper identifies that naïvely copying RGB weights to elevation channels causes convergence problems and reports an empirical improvement from He initialization. - The study does not hide label problems; expert disagreement and concrete mislabeled or ambiguous examples expose a fundamental limitation of the benchmark and temper claims about further model improvements. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly acknowledge that CoastBench contains only European coastlines, is relatively small, and has inconsistent or ambiguous labels. They report an approximate performance ceiling near F1 0.70, recommend multi-expert or probabilistic labeling, and note that additional contextual metadata and larger global coverage are needed. They also acknowledge possible memorization in qualitative out-of-distribution examples, inconsistent multi-turn behavior of fine-tuned Qwen2.5, the need for better non-RGB initialization and hyperparameter tuning, and the absence of ground truth for the OOD demonstrations. These limitations are confronted directly in the discussion, although the conclusion still uses broad language about scalability and interpretability that is not fully measured. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The evaluation lacks a clearly independent geographic or temporal test set; group cross-validation by transect prevents local leakage but does not establish transfer to unseen countries, coastal regimes, sensors, or years. - The dataset's private and evolving status prevents independent verification and makes the reported snapshot difficult to reproduce; the paper does not state a code or weights release. - Few-shot support-set construction is not described with enough partition discipline to rule out test contamination, and the selection algorithm is evaluated mainly through correlations rather than a clean nested experiment with fixed support pools. - Hyperparameter tuning and model selection appear to use the same cross-validation evidence later used for headline reporting, which can inflate the best CNN score. - The claimed interpretability benefit of MLLMs is not evaluated with faithfulness tests, expert assessment of explanations, or comparison to saliency/feature attribution from the CNN; structured text output is not itself evidence of interpretability. - The human benchmark uses only two experts and 50 samples selected for diversity, does not report inter-annotator agreement in detail, and is not directly comparable to model evaluation because experts can inspect broader context. - No calibration, confidence, abstention, uncertainty, cost-sensitive evaluation, or error analysis by geography and class prevalence is provided, despite the intended hazard-management use case. - The strongest system is a conventional 12-channel CNN, while the paper's MLLM motivation is not supported by a demonstrated operational advantage in accuracy, cost, robustness, or user utility. Bottom Line This is a useful early benchmark and engineering study for coastal multimodal remote sensing—especially the 12-channel Qwen2.5 adaptation and label-quality analysis—but practitioners should prefer the full-channel ResNet-50 for the reported task and wait for public data, independent geographic testing, and leakage-controlled comparisons before adopting the MLLM approach.

CAPEval: A Decoupled Caption Evaluation across Understanding and Generation (20 ▲ )

Zhipeng Liu, Haochen Wang, Zhaoxiang Zhang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 5 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces CAPEval, a caption-evaluation benchmark that separates caption Coverage—the fraction of visual checklist facts mentioned—from Precision—the fraction of mentioned facts that are correct—and relates both measures to downstream multimodal training utility. - Why it's important: Caption quality affects large-scale VLM and text-to-image training, but a single quality score cannot tell practitioners whether to prioritize descriptive breadth or factual reliability for a given objective. - How it does it: It combines human-written long captions and approximately 14,965 manually verified atomic facts across 300 images with Qwen2.5-72B checklist judging, then trains matched VLM and T2I pipelines while varying only the caption source. - The good: Across ten controlled captioners, Coverage significantly predicts understanding performance in both VLM pipelines, while Precision significantly predicts generation performance in both T2I pipelines. - The missing: The central correlations rely on only ten captioners and a single text-only LLM judge, without reported judge-agreement statistics, uncertainty across training seeds, or ablations separating caption length, domain, and other confounds from Coverage and Precision. - Read it or not: Read it if you curate image-text data for VLM or T2I training and need a useful task-dependent diagnostic, but treat the causal and generality claims as preliminary rather than established.
