Problem & Motivation Automated penetration testing must cover a contextual, multi-stage workflow spanning authorization, reconnaissance, vulnerability analysis, exploitation, privilege escalation, lateral movement, persistence, and reporting. Existing evaluations make it difficult to determine what LLM agents can actually do because they mix single-flag CTFs, containerized tasks, multi-host cyber ranges, live-network experiments, peer-reviewed studies, official evaluations, preprints, and vendor self-reports. The central gap is therefore not merely insufficient model capability, but weak comparability and external validity: success on an isolated challenge does not establish reliable performance in an enterprise network with identities, defenders, operational noise, and business constraints. Key Idea The core insight is to separate two dimensions that prior surveys often conflate: how realistic the evaluated environment is and how trustworthy the supporting evidence is. R1–R4 ranges from static or single-challenge CTFs to live enterprise or campus networks, while A–D ranges from peer-reviewed, transparent evidence to opaque author or vendor self-reports. The paper combines this matrix with a Type A/Type B failure distinction: Type A failures arise from engineering deficiencies such as poor tool schemas, context overflow, or incomplete retrieval, whereas Type B failures arise from long-horizon planning, causal consistency, and state-management limitations. Methodology The paper presents a critical narrative review with structured evidence charting rather than a systematic review. It searches Web of Science, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, arXiv, OpenReview, USENIX, ACL Anthology, and selected NIST, AISI, MITRE, OWASP, vendor, and project sources over January 2023–May 11, 2026, while retaining DeepExploit and AutoPentest-DRL as historical anchors. Inclusion requires a direct connection to automated penetration testing, agent-based offensive security, cyber ranges, or CTF solving; traceable methodology; quantitative results; and mapping to PTES, MITRE ATT&CK, or the proposed realism framework. The review claims deduplication and disputed-item rechecking, and charts system, benchmark, publication type, PTES stage, ATT&CK mapping, realism, tool coupling, human baseline, metric, cost, evidence grade, and source, but does not report the candidate count, final included count, screening flow, or inter-rater agreement. The main analytical stages are: reconstruct the evolution from rules and reinforcement learning to LLM agents; describe a common eight-layer agent architecture covering operator, planning, reasoning, multi-agent coordination, tools, memory, safety/audit, and environment; organize benchmark results along R1–R4; assess PTES-stage maturity; and map failure types to mitigations. The key design decisions—using an ordinal realism scale, using a separate evidence grade, and comparing capabilities by PTES stage—are intuitively useful but only partially justified, because the paper does not validate the scales against independent judgments or outcomes. It does not define a mathematical objective or train a model. Key Results The review reports that D-CIPHER achieves 22.0% on NYU CTF Bench and 44.0% on an HTB subset, while Claude 3.5 Sonnet obtains approximately 17.5% on Cybench and GPT-4o obtains 21.21% on AutoPenBench, all largely R1 or R1–R2 evidence. On the AISI 95-task expert tier, GPT-5.5, Claude Mythos, GPT-5.4, and Opus 4.7 reportedly achieve 71.4%, 68.6%, 52.4%, and 48.6% task-pass rates, respectively; the paper grades this evidence B because it comes from an official evaluation rather than peer review. xOffense, using a domain-tuned Qwen3-32B model with chain-of-thought fine-tuning, reports 79.17% completion on AutoPenBench subtasks, while HackingBuddyGPT raises Linux privilege-escalation success from 33% to 83% with guidance and Reflexion, compared with a cited 75% human baseline. These gains are task- and scaffold-specific and are not directly comparable to end-to-end completion. On the R3 AISI TLO task, GPT-5.5 completes the 32-step chain in 2 of 10 attempts and Claude Mythos Preview in 3 of 10; GPT-5.4 and Opus 4.7 reportedly achieve 0 of 10. On the R4 ARTEMIS study, an agent evaluated on an approximately 8,000-host, 12-subnet university network ranks second overall against 10 human professionals and six public agents, submits nine valid vulnerabilities, and receives an 82% acceptance rate. The reported cost for some ARTEMIS configurations is approximately USD 18 per hour versus roughly USD 60 per hour for human testers. Additional cited findings include 20–40% performance on attack-and-defense CTFs, up to 2.6× performance variation from changing the agent scaffold, and a 9.5-percentage-point solve-rate improvement from a Kali tool stack over Ubuntu across 200 NYU CTF tasks. The most important cross-benchmark pattern is a realism-performance gap: bounded reconnaissance, reporting, Web exploitation, and Linux privilege escalation are substantially stronger than binary exploitation, long-horizon attack chains, AD lateral movement, persistence, and defender-present operation. The evidence is concentrated in R1–R2 settings; R3–R4 conclusions rely heavily on official evaluations and one B-grade ARTEMIS study. Novelty Classification The contribution is primarily NEW FORMULATION and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING in the form of a structured synthesis: the R1–R4 realism scale crossed with A–D evidence grading, together with the claim that reported capability decays as realism and task horizon increase. It also offers a useful NEW FAILURE TAXONOMY/SYNTHESIS through the Type A/Type B distinction, but the underlying agent mechanisms—ReAct, Reflexion, RAG, multi-agent orchestration, tool calling, and reinforcement-learning post-training—are standard techniques borrowed from the reviewed literature rather than methods introduced by this paper. The work does not introduce a new dataset, trained model, benchmark implementation, or evaluated system. Rigor & Reproducibility The paper improves transparency by publishing database queries, inclusion and exclusion criteria, evidence-grade definitions, realism definitions, and the variables used for charting. It explicitly distinguishes solve rate, pass rate, subtask completion, end-to-end attempts, and live-network metrics rather than treating them as interchangeable. However, it does not report the number of retrieved, screened, excluded, or included records; provide a PRISMA-style flow; identify all coded studies in a machine-readable table; report inter-rater agreement; preregister the protocol; or perform sensitivity analysis for alternative realism and evidence assignments. No meta-analysis, confidence intervals across studies, significance tests, or systematic effect-size aggregation is provided. The review frequently relies on preprints, official technical evaluations, open-source project documentation, and vendor-associated reports, although it labels them with grades. The A–D scheme combines source authority, methodological disclosure, and independent reproducibility into one ordinal label, which may obscure important tradeoffs. The cited ARTEMIS and AISI results have small evaluation samples, incomplete deployment or training disclosure, no active defender or EDR in the ARTEMIS network, and limited independent replication. The paper itself does not release a dataset, code repository, annotation file, or software artifact; no URL for a review corpus or coding tool is mentioned. Potential benchmark contamination is acknowledged for Cybench through public-writeup exposure, but comparable contamination checks are not established across all reviewed benchmarks. Deployability: (4-property check) Profile: EMPIRICAL, but the paper is a literature review rather than an empirical evaluation of a system built by the authors. * Practical: The reviewed LLM-agent systems generally run through commercially available cloud or local compute and standard security tooling such as Kali, Nmap, Metasploit, CALDERA, Docker, and MCP, but the paper does not provide a reproducible implementation of its own. * Efficient: The review cites approximately USD 18 per hour for some ARTEMIS configurations versus approximately USD 60 per hour for human testers, but it does not provide a standardized cost, latency, token, retry, or memory comparison across systems; long-horizon tasks may incur substantial tool-call and retry costs. * Effective: Evidence supports useful performance on reconnaissance, reporting, bounded Web exploitation, and selected Linux privilege-escalation tasks, but only 2/10 or 3/10 completion on the 32-step TLO range and weak AD lateral movement show that the evidence does not establish reliable autonomous end-to-end penetration testing. * Scalable: ARTEMIS was evaluated on an approximately 8,000-host university network, but the study lacked active defenders and full deployment disclosure; no 10×–100× stress test, multi-organization replication, or defender-present enterprise evaluation demonstrates scalability beyond the reported setting. The work delivers a reusable conceptual evidence-classification framework and a PTES/failure-mode synthesis, not a library, CLI, tool, dataset, trained model, or independently runnable benchmark. Strengths - The R1–R4 realism distinction directly addresses a central evaluation error: treating single-challenge CTF performance as evidence of enterprise red-team capability. - The A–D evidence grading forces the review to distinguish peer-reviewed benchmarks from official evaluations, preprints, and vendor self-reports instead of aggregating them into a single leaderboard. - The PTES-stage matrix is more operationally useful than a model-level score because it identifies reconnaissance and reporting as relatively mature, Web exploitation and bounded privilege escalation as supportive, and AD lateral movement and persistence as weak. - The Type A/Type B distinction provides a practical interpretation of failure causes: tool schemas, retrieval, summarization, and context partitioning can address some failures, whereas long-horizon causal planning and state consistency require more than prompt engineering. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly state that the review is narrative rather than fully PRISMA-compliant, lacks preregistration and dual independent screening, may contain selection bias, and represents only a snapshot through May 11, 2026. They acknowledge that official evaluations and vendor system cards lack anonymous peer review, that vendor conflicts of interest may affect results, and that many R3 evaluations lack active defenders. They also identify ARTEMIS limitations: no active defender or EDR, host-organization judging of submissions, incomplete training and deployment disclosure, and a human baseline of only 10 testers. The paper openly states that cross-benchmark metrics are not directly comparable and that fully autonomous red-teaming is not yet mature. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The review presents the realism and evidence scales as operational frameworks but does not test their reliability, predictive validity, or sensitivity to alternate coding decisions. - It does not disclose the size or composition of the reviewed corpus, making coverage and publication-selection bias impossible to assess despite broad database queries. - The evidence grade may over-credit official or government evaluations relative to transparent peer-reviewed studies because source authority, reproducibility, and methodological detail are collapsed into one label; conversely, an A grade is not evidence that a result generalizes beyond its benchmark. - The review sometimes draws broad capability conclusions from narrow studies, such as inferring the value of domain fine-tuning from xOffense's 79.17% AutoPenBench subtask result without a matched cross-domain evaluation. - The claim that increasing reasoning-token budget suggests an engineering rather than fundamental bottleneck is not established by the review: monotonic scaling on one evaluation does not separate compute limitations from model-reasoning limitations. - The ARTEMIS R4 result is influential but effectively a single, B-grade, host-judged study; the absence of defenders, EDR, independent replication, and full system disclosure substantially limits claims about production competence. - The paper does not systematically separate human-assisted, semi-autonomous, and fully autonomous systems when comparing scores, despite human hints and intervention being major determinants of penetration-testing success. - Several quantitative comparisons omit standardized uncertainty, cost denominators, retry budgets, tool permissions, and intervention counts, even though the paper correctly identifies these as important confounders. Bottom Line This is a useful critical orientation paper for researchers and practitioners who need to audit claims about LLM penetration agents, but its conceptual framework and literature synthesis are not rigorous enough to replace a preregistered systematic review, an independently validated meta-benchmark, or direct replication of the headline R3–R4 results.

Agentic AI Autonomy Assessment: A Decision-Support Framework Towards Governed Supply Chain Systems

L Trumpler, RF de Assis, ER da Silva… · arxiv.org · generating environments for agent testing in enterprises - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces the Agentic AI Autonomy Assessment (AAAA) framework, which measures task-level autonomy from delegation, consultation, and collaboration interactions across an agentic system’s lifecycle. - Why it’s important: Supply-chain organizations need to govern how much decision authority AI systems exercise without assuming that greater autonomy improves operational performance. - How it does it: It computes an Autonomy Score as a weighted combination of internally generated tasks and the absence of consultation events, then applies the score to LLM-controlled players in a simulated beer distribution game. - The good: The paper separates autonomy from capability and reports a position-dependent association between autonomy and cost: distributor cost decreases with autonomy while retailer cost increases, with coefficients of -211.14 euros and +68.45 euros respectively. - The missing: The study does not establish construct validity against human ratings or alternative autonomy measures, and its prompt-based autonomy manipulation produces a narrow, highly skewed score range rather than controlled L1-L5 conditions. - Read it or not: Supply-chain governance and human-AI collaboration researchers should read it for the task-level measurement proposal, but readers seeking validated autonomy metrics or deployment evidence should treat it as an early conceptual and simulation study.

Problem & Motivation: Agentic AI systems increasingly interpret goals, decompose them into tasks, coordinate with other entities, and execute supply-chain decisions with limited human involvement. Existing autonomy taxonomies generally provide discrete levels, depend on subjective assessment, and do not monitor changes during development, runtime, and end-of-life. The resulting gap concerns governance rather than simply automation: organizations lack an objective way to identify how decision ownership, authority, and execution responsibility are distributed across humans, agents, tools, and organizational systems. The application domain is decentralized, uncertain, multi-echelon supply-chain decision-making, where autonomy can alter inventory, ordering, coordination, cost, service levels, and bullwhip dynamics. Key Idea: Measure autonomy at the executable-task level rather than treating it as an intrinsic property of an agent or a fixed system category. Each task is characterized by observable responsibility allocation through delegation, consultation, or collaboration. The framework interprets internally generated tasks as evidence of autonomous initiative and consultation-dependent execution as evidence of retained external control; it then combines these quantities into a scalar score. This is the paper’s central insight, although the specific metrics are simple ratios and the conceptual distinction overlaps with prior adjustable-autonomy and human-agent delegation work. Methodology: AAAA models an agentic system as a perception-reasoning-action loop containing state, goals, hierarchical tasks, actions, external interactions, and an operational environment. The implementation records a task store containing predefined high-level goals and dynamically created subtasks. The Initiative Rate is IR = N_I/N, where N_I is the number of internally generated tasks and N is the total number of executable tasks. The Consultation Rate is CR = N_C/N, where N_C is the number of tasks requiring external consultation. The composite score is AS = w_1 IR + w_2(1 - CR), with nonnegative weights summing to one; the experiment does not report a sensitivity analysis over these weights. Collaboration is defined conceptually but excluded from the quantitative score. The empirical system uses LangGraph with a main game graph and parallel player subgraphs, each using a ReAct-style local LLM loop that alternates model reasoning and tool execution. Available tools include ordering, shipment creation, task creation and updates, task removal, consultation requests, and termination. Four LLM-controlled tiers play a 10-week beer distribution game with starting inventory of 16 units, demand sequence [4, 8, 12, 8, 4, 2, 4, 8, 12, 8], two-week information and shipping lead times, holding cost of 1 euro per unit, and backlog cost of 2 euros per unit. Five system-prompt configurations, L1 through L5, instruct the agent to behave respectively as operator, collaborator, consultant, approver, or observer. For each tier and prompt level, the authors run 12 repetitions, giving 60 runs per tier and 240 tier-level observations overall. The user consultation function always approves requests, so consultation frequency is measured without changing subsequent actions. The critical design decisions—task-level measurement, prompt-based autonomy manipulation, and a fixed approval oracle—are plausible for a prototype but only weakly justified as controls for the intended construct. Key Results: Observed autonomy scores range from 0.33 to 0.97 with mean 0.83; the distribution is left-skewed (skewness -1.465, p < 0.0001), indicating concentration at high autonomy despite the intended five-level manipulation. Mean total costs are 308.49 euros for the factory, 211.24 euros for the distributor, 190.15 euros for the wholesaler, and 157.11 euros for the retailer, with standard deviations of 196.16, 157.60, 169.53, and 47.06 euros. OLS cost slopes against autonomy are -195.64 euros for the factory (p = 0.167), -211.14 euros for the distributor (p = 0.028), +60.04 euros for the wholesaler (p = 0.573), and +68.45 euros for the retailer (p = 0.018). A pooled regression of the tier-specific slopes reports a positive tier-gradient coefficient of +109.6 euros (p = 0.015). Mean fill rates are 82.04% for the factory, 56.75% for the distributor, 64.24% for the wholesaler, and 29.00% for the retailer. Fill-rate OLS slopes are not significant for the factory (-13.58 percentage points, p = 0.423), distributor (+16.16, p = 0.388), or wholesaler (-15.27, p = 0.340); the retailer has a significant negative slope of -9.60 percentage points (p = 0.030), also reported by a Tobit model with p = 0.030. The evidence therefore supports a cost association that differs by tier, not a general performance improvement from autonomy. The simulation is a small, standard-scale demonstration rather than a stress test or real-world deployment, and no comparison with non-LLM heuristics, centralized optimization, human players, or fixed-autonomy controllers is reported. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and potentially NEW SYSTEM/TOOL: the paper formulates autonomy as a task-interaction measurement problem and reports a preliminary tier-dependent autonomy-cost association, but the underlying ingredients—delegation, consultation, task decomposition, adjustable autonomy, and weighted behavioral ratios—largely combine established ideas rather than introducing a fundamentally new measurement theory or algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper reports repeated runs, descriptive statistics, OLS regressions, p-values, error bands, and a Tobit analysis for some fill-rate outcomes, but it does not report random seeds, confidence intervals numerically for the main estimates, effect-size uncertainty beyond plotted bands, power analysis, multiple-comparison correction, or robustness to alternative regression specifications. It provides no ablation isolating Initiative Rate from Consultation Rate, no sensitivity analysis for w_1 and w_2, no human or expert annotation study, no inter-rater comparison, and no test of whether the score agrees with the five prompt labels. The 12 repetitions per condition appear to be stochastic LLM runs, but the paper does not establish independence or quantify model-output variance separately from simulation variance. The prompt is both the treatment and the mechanism used to induce autonomy, creating possible confounding between autonomy, reasoning style, verbosity, task generation, and decision quality. The score distribution shows that the manipulation did not produce well-separated levels. The simulation, local LLM identity and version, model parameters, prompts beyond the summarized augmentations, code, data, and model weights are not stated as publicly released; no URL or repository is mentioned. The absence of standard supply-chain baselines is a major limitation for interpreting the performance findings. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS, because the paper builds an executable LangGraph agentic workflow and evaluates it in a simulation, although it does not demonstrate production deployment. Practical: The architecture uses a local LLM, LangGraph, and a REST-based simulator, so a prototype can plausibly run on commercially available hardware, but hardware requirements, inference latency, model size, and operational integration costs are not stated. Efficient: No compute, memory, token, latency, or cost comparison with alternative agent architectures or optimization policies is reported. Effective: The evidence shows that the framework can log task interactions and that autonomy scores correlate with simulated tier costs in some regressions, but it does not show improved supply-chain outcomes or validated governance risk detection. Scalable: The experiment covers four tiers, 10 weeks, and 240 tier-level runs; behavior at 10x to 100x the number of tiers, tasks, time steps, agents, or concurrent workflows is not tested, despite claims of lifecycle monitoring and heterogeneous-system applicability. The work delivers a prototype agentic workflow and a conceptual measurement framework, but it does not state that a reusable library, CLI, dataset, trained model, or monitoring package is released. Strengths: - The task-centric abstraction addresses a real weakness of system-level autonomy labels: it can in principle aggregate measurements from individual tasks to agents, teams, and workflows while remaining independent of a particular agent framework. - The paper explicitly distinguishes autonomy from intelligence, reasoning quality, and performance, avoiding the common assumption that more independent execution is automatically better. - The framework connects autonomy measurement to concrete governance controls, including acceptable autonomy ranges, runtime monitoring, and differentiated policies across supply-chain tiers. - The simulation produces a potentially useful counterpoint to monotonic-autonomy narratives: the observed cost slopes reverse from upstream to downstream tiers, while fill-rate results remain mostly nonsignificant. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that the beer distribution game does not capture the complexity and variability of real supply chains; prompt manipulation may not reliably control autonomy because LLM behavior is stochastic; the observed autonomy range is narrow and sensitivity is limited; and collaboration is conceptualized but not included in the quantitative metrics. They call for industry validation, stronger experimental controls, incorporation of collaboration and multi-agent coordination, and evaluation of robustness, adaptability, decision quality, and cross-tier interactions. The authors confront these scope limits directly, but the discussion still presents governance and lifecycle-monitoring implications more broadly than the empirical evidence supports. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The proposed score has unresolved construct-validity and identification problems. A high score can result from internally generating many trivial subtasks or avoiding consultation, neither of which necessarily indicates meaningful decision authority; conversely, a capable agent may consult frequently for safety reasons and receive a low score. The treatment of collaboration as an unmeasured third interaction type undermines the claim that the framework captures distributed autonomy. The formulas count tasks equally even though tasks differ substantially in risk, authority, duration, reversibility, and consequence, and the paper does not define how nested tasks, repeated consultations, removed tasks, or partially completed tasks are counted. The fixed approval oracle removes the behavioral effect of oversight and may not represent human governance. Prompt levels are not experimentally validated, scores overlap heavily, and the high-autonomy skew makes comparisons across nominal levels difficult. The regression analysis does not appear to control for demand realization, random seeds, cross-tier dependence, repeated measures, or the fact that changing one tier’s prompt may alter system-wide dynamics; the paper also does not establish whether the pooled slope model is statistically appropriate. Multiple tier-by-metric tests are reported without correction. Most importantly, there is no strong baseline or counterfactual showing that AAAA detects autonomy more objectively or usefully than existing autonomy taxonomies, human assessments, action-authority logs, or direct policy constraints. The causal language around upstream benefits and downstream harm should therefore be treated as exploratory association from one short simulation. Bottom Line: The paper is worth reading as an early, concrete framing of autonomy monitoring for supply-chain governance and as a source of testable hypotheses about tier-dependent effects, but its metric and empirical claims are not yet validated enough to displace established adjustable-autonomy concepts or support deployment decisions.

Foundation Models and Fine-Tuning: Toward a New Generation of Models for Time Series Forecasting

M Laglil, B Pracca, E Devijver, E Gaussier · arxiv.org · 10 new citations to your articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper reviews time-series foundation-model architectures and evaluates full fine-tuning, LoRA fine-tuning, and few-shot LoRA adaptation for Chronos 2 and TTM-R3-PT across the GIFT-Eval forecasting benchmark. - Why it's important: Practitioners need to know when adapting a pretrained forecaster improves accuracy enough to justify downstream data, compute, and overfitting risk. - How it does it: It compares zero-shot inference with full-parameter updates and rank-8 LoRA updates under full-data and 20%-data regimes, using normalized MAPE and MWQL/CRPS-related probabilistic scores. - The good: On Chronos 2, LoRA-full-shot improves normalized MWQL from 0.364 to 0.357 on medium datasets and from 0.310 to 0.301 on large datasets, while avoiding the substantial degradation caused by full fine-tuning. - The missing: The study evaluates only two publicly fine-tunable models, uses a single fixed hyperparameter configuration per model, and does not establish whether the reported gains survive stronger baselines, dataset-specific tuning, or leakage-free evaluation. - Read it or not: Read it if you deploy time-series foundation models and need practical adaptation heuristics; skip it as evidence of a general fine-tuning law because the experimental comparison is narrow and partly contaminated by pretraining overlap.

Problem & Motivation: Time-series forecasting systems must operate across domains, frequencies, series dimensions, and forecast horizons, often with limited labeled history for each target dataset. Conventional models generally require dataset-specific architecture and hyperparameter choices, while zero-shot foundation models promise reuse across tasks but may underperform when target distributions differ from pretraining data. The specific gap is the limited empirical understanding of post-pretraining adaptation: whether full fine-tuning or parameter-efficient LoRA adaptation helps, how much target data is needed, and how the answer changes with model size, domain, horizon, and probabilistic versus point-forecasting objectives. Key Idea: The central insight is an empirical adaptation rule rather than a new forecasting architecture: large foundation models such as Chronos 2 may benefit from low-rank updates that preserve pretrained weights and limit overfitting, whereas compact models such as TTM-R3-PT can often be updated directly. The paper also organizes time-series foundation models around architecture, pretraining, and adaptation, but this taxonomy largely synthesizes existing model designs rather than introducing a new formulation. Methodology: The review covers Transformer encoder-decoder, decoder-only, encoder-only, recurrent sLSTM, MLP-Mixer, and sparse-MoE time-series foundation models, including Chronos, TimesFM, Moirai, TOTO, Chronos 2, Moirai 2.0, TiRex, TTM-R3-PT, and Timer-S1. The experiments use Chronos 2 and TTM-R3-PT because they were publicly available for fine-tuning and were reported as free of test leakage at model-selection time. For each target dataset, the pipeline applies zero-shot inference, full fine-tuning of all parameters, rank-8 LoRA with all target training data, and rank-8 LoRA using 20% of the training data. Full fine-tuning uses 4,000 gradient steps; LoRA uses frozen pretrained weights plus low-rank updates with alpha 16; learning rates are 1e-4 for Chronos 2 full fine-tuning, 1e-3 for TTM full fine-tuning, and 1e-5 for both LoRA settings. Quantile loss is the optimization objective, with point forecasts evaluated by median-based MAPE and probabilistic forecasts evaluated by normalized MWQL, used as a discrete approximation to CRPS. The three main design decisions are the fixed per-model hyperparameters across datasets, the use of LoRA rank 8 without dataset-specific rank selection, and normalization against Seasonal Naive before arithmetic aggregation; the first improves operational realism but confounds method quality with tuning quality, the second is insufficiently justified, and the third improves cross-dataset comparability but can obscure absolute errors and is problematic for series with small or zero values. Key Results: The benchmark contains 15 univariate and 8 multivariate datasets spanning 7 domains and 10 frequencies, with approximately 144,000 series, 177 million observations, and 95 dataset-frequency-horizon configurations. For Chronos 2, normalized MWQL by dataset size is 0.423 zero-shot, 0.577 full fine-tuning, 0.477 LoRA-full-shot, and 0.471 LoRA-few-shot on small datasets; 0.364, 0.387, 0.357, and 0.394 on medium datasets; and 0.310, 0.322, 0.301, and 0.330 on large datasets. Thus LoRA-full-shot improves over zero-shot by about 1.9% on medium data and 2.9% on large data, whereas full fine-tuning degrades performance. For Chronos 2 normalized MAPE, LoRA-few-shot is best on small datasets at 0.612, LoRA-full-shot is best on medium datasets at 0.722, and LoRA-few-shot is best on large datasets at 0.931, compared with zero-shot values of 0.544, 0.703, and 1.006 respectively. For TTM-R3-PT, full fine-tuning gives only a modest large-dataset MWQL improvement from 0.355 to 0.350; LoRA is worse at 0.352. Results vary materially by domain: Chronos 2 zero-shot is best for Energy MWQL at all reported horizons (0.520 short, 0.255 medium, 0.225 long), while LoRA-few-shot is best for Energy MAPE (0.916, 0.870, and 1.364). In Nature, Chronos 2 full fine-tuning increases short-horizon MAPE from 0.677 to 0.939, a 38.7% relative increase. In Transport, Chronos 2 full fine-tuning improves medium-horizon MWQL from 0.146 to 0.138. The paper reports three-seed means and standard deviations for fine-tuned variants, but most differences are small and no significance tests or aggregate confidence intervals are provided. The experiments are standard-scale rather than stress-scale: they use existing benchmark datasets and models up to 120M parameters, not 8.3B Timer-S1 or deployment-scale workloads. Novelty Classification: The contribution is primarily NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING and SURVEY/SYNTHESIS, with a limited ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION component: the paper systematically compares adaptation strategies for two pretrained forecasters across GIFT-Eval, but its methods—full fine-tuning, LoRA, quantile loss, and zero-shot evaluation—are standard combinations rather than a new algorithm, dataset, or theoretical formulation. Rigor & Reproducibility: The study reports three seeds for full fine-tuning and LoRA and publishes exact principal hyperparameters, dataset sources, evaluation metrics, and the repository used for TTM-R3-PT; it also identifies AutoGluon-TimeSeries as the Chronos 2 implementation. The paper does not state that its own code, checkpoints, complete experiment logs, or processed benchmark splits are released beyond the cited upstream repositories. There are no component ablations for LoRA rank, target layers, alpha, learning rate, number of steps, or which model modules are adapted, and no dataset-specific hyperparameter sweep. The zero-shot comparison is not fully leakage-free because Chronos 2 and TTM-R3-PT were pretrained on a subset of GIFT-Eval training data; the authors acknowledge this and compare each model mainly against its own adapted version, but this still limits claims about generalization. The benchmark is also the basis for model selection and contains pretraining-overlapping data, creating a potential Goodhart and contamination concern. Standard strong forecasting baselines such as seasonal naive, classical statistical methods, supervised deep models, and other current foundation models are not included in the adaptation experiment, so the results establish relative adaptation effects rather than overall forecasting superiority. Reported standard deviations are often near zero, but the paper does not explain whether variability comes from seed changes, fixed test windows, or aggregation across datasets, and it does not report statistical significance. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL. - Practical: Chronos 2 and TTM-R3-PT can run on commercially available hardware in principle, but the paper does not report hardware, wall-clock training time, peak memory, or inference latency. - Efficient: LoRA reduces the number of trainable parameters and can merge into the base weights without inference overhead, but the paper does not quantify parameter counts trained, GPU-hours, memory savings, or speed relative to full fine-tuning. - Effective: The evidence supports conditional gains—especially Chronos 2 LoRA on medium and large datasets—but not universal improvement; zero-shot inference remains best in several domains and fine-tuning can sharply worsen error. - Scalable: The evaluation reaches 120M parameters and benchmark-scale datasets but does not test 10x–100x larger downstream datasets, longer contexts, higher-dimensional covariates, or deployment throughput; scalability beyond the tested setting is therefore not evaluated. The work delivers an empirical study and a review, not a new standalone software artifact, dataset, trained model, or reusable proof technique; it relies on upstream AutoGluon and IBM TTM repositories. Strengths: - It isolates a practically important decision—whether and how to adapt a pretrained forecaster—rather than merely reporting another zero-shot leaderboard result. - It evaluates both point and probabilistic forecasting across 95 dataset-frequency-horizon configurations, with domain, horizon, and dataset-size breakdowns that expose cases where aggregate averages conceal failure. - It identifies a useful model-scale interaction: LoRA is more effective for the 120M-parameter Chronos 2 model, while direct full fine-tuning is at least competitive for compact TTM-R3-PT. - It explicitly reports contamination risk and the limitations of fixed hyperparameters, which makes the conclusions more credible than an unqualified claim that fine-tuning always helps. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that the target benchmark overlaps with the pretraining data of Chronos 2 and TTM-R3-PT, limiting the rigor of zero-shot comparisons. They also acknowledge that they use one fixed hyperparameter set per model rather than dataset-specific tuning, that this may disadvantage full fine-tuning, and that fine-tuning is not universally beneficial. In the conclusion, they note the scarcity and proprietary nature of time-series data and the lack of theoretical and empirical understanding of foundation-model generalization. These limitations are confronted directly, although the conclusion still describes fine-tuning as generally improving zero-shot performance despite several substantial degradations. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The main unacknowledged weakness is the narrow experimental treatment: only two publicly fine-tunable models are tested, both selected from the same benchmark ecosystem, and no contemporary pretrained model is evaluated under the same adaptation protocol. The paper does not compare against retraining smaller supervised models, classical baselines beyond the normalization reference, or strong domain-specific fine-tuning pipelines. It does not report absolute MAPE or MWQL, training/inference costs, hardware, parameter-count reductions, or calibration diagnostics, so practical efficiency and probabilistic quality remain largely inferred. The fixed 4,000-step budget and model-specific learning rates may systematically favor some strategies, while the absence of early stopping, validation-based selection, LoRA placement ablations, or rank sweeps prevents attributing gains specifically to low-rank adaptation. The use of MAPE is also fragile for zero or near-zero observations, but the paper does not discuss this issue. Finally, the paper claims that fine-tuning can particularly improve long-term forecasts, yet several tables show small or inconsistent gains and the evidence does not establish a statistically reliable horizon-dependent effect. Bottom Line: This preprint is a useful practitioner-oriented study of Chronos 2 and TTM-R3-PT adaptation on GIFT-Eval, especially for its warning that LoRA can outperform full fine-tuning on larger Chronos 2 targets, but it does not justify broad conclusions about time-series foundation-model fine-tuning because of contamination, limited model coverage, missing cost analysis, and weak baseline and tuning controls.

Towards Live Refactoring of Microservices Architectures

JPD Fernandes · repositorio-aberto.up.pt · simulation environments for business processes - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper builds Vivactor-M, a web-based microservice architecture refactoring prototype that interactively edits a Service Endpoint Call Graph, emulates the resulting topology with template-driven Docker containers, detects architecture smells, and applies automated structural refactorings. - Why it's important: Microservice architectures accumulate architectural erosion, while existing tools mainly support monolith-to-microservice decomposition and impose batch-oriented edit-compile-run feedback, limiting exploratory maintenance of deployed service topologies. - How it does it: It represents services, endpoints, databases, calls, languages, and shared libraries in a JSON intermediate representation, regenerates a Docker Compose emulation after graph changes, and runs deterministic smell detectors/refactoring rules, with Gemini used for Wrong Cuts classification and restructuring. - The good: An eight-person task study measured a mean SUS score of 81.56 (SD 8.86), median 82.5, and a mean completion time of 13:18 (SD 2:59), while participants consistently rated real-time visualization positively. - The missing: The study does not compare Vivactor-M against a non-live baseline, does not measure actual maintainability/coupling/cohesion or behavioral preservation after refactoring, and evaluates a manually prepared abstraction rather than automated recovery and transformation of real source repositories. - Read it or not: Read it for a candid prototype-level exploration of live architectural visualization and its UX requirements; skip it as evidence of production-grade automated microservice refactoring or causal benefits of liveness.

Problem & Motivation Microservice teams must maintain service boundaries, endpoint dependencies, data ownership, and deployment independence as systems evolve. Architectural erosion increases coupling, maintenance effort, and technical debt, but existing academic refactoring tools largely target initial monolith decomposition rather than ongoing changes to an already-microservice architecture. The dissertation frames liveness—continuous, low-latency feedback during architectural edits—as a way to reduce cognitive overhead and encourage structural exploration. Its literature review searches IEEE Xplore, Scopus, ScienceDirect, and ACM using four query families, reducing 896 retrieved records to 29 selected studies and adding 14 externally identified references. However, live software development/live refactoring was not actually included in the systematic search and was instead covered through supervisor-selected references, weakening the evidential basis for the claimed research gap. Key Idea The central insight is to make the architecture itself, rather than the complete application implementation, the live refactoring object. Vivactor-M uses a Service Endpoint Call Graph as a lightweight intermediate representation and compiles it into black-box Docker service templates. This preserves service topology, endpoint calls, databases, and selected metadata while avoiding the dependency and configuration complexity of executing arbitrary repositories. The approach is an integration of known graph visualization, Docker emulation, smell detection, and automated refactoring ideas; its distinctive aspect is their combination into an interactive, feedback-oriented environment for post-decomposition microservice architecture editing. Methodology The pipeline begins with architecture recovery, but the implemented study bypasses automated recovery and manually supplies a JSON graph. The representation stores service nodes with type, language, magnitude, and port; directed HTTP edges with endpoint, call definition, and method; and system-level business-domain and self-managed-library metadata. React/Vite and Reagraph provide graph rendering and manipulation, while a Go backend orchestrates parsing, smell detection, refactoring, template generation, and Docker Engine interaction. Graph changes generate language-specific service templates and Dockerfiles, a docker-compose configuration, health checks, and Compose Watch updates; major topology changes require rebuilding the emulation. The engine implements 10 of Taibi and Lenarduzzi’s 11 smells, omitting ESB Usage. Detectors use endpoint-string checks for API versioning, graph traversal for cycles, port checks for hard-coded endpoints, naming-based database ownership heuristics for service intimacy, node-size rules for Microservice Greedy, a 50-node threshold for API Gateway absence, shared-library membership, database fan-in for Shared Persistency, language diversity for Too Many Standards, and an external Gemini call for Wrong Cuts. Refactoring rules inject version prefixes, add gateways, replace hard-coded routing with Traefik service discovery, merge or split nodes, create service wrappers, provision per-service databases, standardize templates, and generate LLM-based domain groupings. The design decisions to abstract execution, use a graph-centered IR, and use smell rules instead of quality metrics are pragmatic and explicitly motivated by implementation constraints, but the paper provides limited correctness justification for several rules and does not formalize preservation of behavior or architectural invariants. Key Results The primary empirical evaluation involved eight participants: five master’s students and three PhD-level participants; four reported prior familiarity with liveness, and one had prior experience with microservice refactoring tools. Participants loaded a prepared PiggyMetrics intermediate representation, launched emulation, fixed a hard-coded endpoint, manually added two services and two edges to create a cyclic dependency, refactored the cycle, performed one additional refactoring, stopped emulation, and exported the graph. Completion times ranged from 11:30 to 20:30, with a mean of 13:18, standard deviation of 2:59, and median of 12:36. SUS scores ranged from 67.5 to 92.5, averaging 81.56 with standard deviation 8.86; the authors map this to an “Excellent” rating. A four-item, author-defined liveness subscale averaged 85.16 (SD 5.73), but it is not a validated psychometric measure and the paper acknowledges that its mapping to SUS adjective categories is only approximate. Questionnaire responses showed positive perceptions of real-time visualization and liveness, but latency received comparatively weaker ratings. A separate survey intended to assess smell-remediation effectiveness obtained only 11 responses and was excluded from formal hypothesis testing. No quantitative execution latency values, graph sizes, throughput, memory use, build cost, refactoring correctness rates, baseline comparisons, or measured changes in maintainability, coupling, cohesion, availability, or performance are reported. Novelty Classification NEW SYSTEM/TOOL; NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING; ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. Vivactor-M contributes a prototype that combines a Service Endpoint Call Graph, template-driven Docker emulation, interactive topology editing, architecture-smell detection, and low-latency feedback for ongoing microservice refactoring. The graph representation, Docker containers, Reagraph visualization, standard smell catalog, DFS cycle detection, API Gateway pattern, and LLM classification are existing or standard components; the genuinely new element is their application as a live, topology-level refactoring workflow together with initial UX observations about transparency and feedback requirements, not a new refactoring algorithm or validated quality model. Rigor & Reproducibility The dissertation reports the participant-level SUS and task-time values, includes the questionnaire, task instructions, demographic summaries, qualitative feedback, and an explicit threats-to-validity section. It also candidly reports major scope reductions, including manual architecture recovery, emulation rather than execution, omission of ESB Usage, discarded quality metrics, UI bugs, and the failed 11-response remediation survey. There are no component ablations, repeated-seed experiments, significance tests, confidence intervals, controlled comparisons, or non-live baselines. The evaluation uses one manually prepared benchmark abstraction and a highly guided workflow; seven of eight participants completed the task within a narrow range, but the study does not establish that liveness caused the observed completion time or usability score. The paper does not state that source code, Docker images, datasets, model weights, or a repository URL are publicly released. The use of Gemini creates an external dependency and potential privacy/reproducibility issue for Wrong Cuts. The SLR is only partially reproducible because live-refactoring literature was excluded from the database queries and 14 references were added through snowballing or external search. Deployability: (4-property check) Profile: SYSTEMS, with empirical user evaluation. Practical: The prototype uses React/Vite, Go, Docker, Docker Compose, and commercially available Windows hardware, so the demonstrated emulation workflow is technically runnable, but deployment against arbitrary production repositories is not supported because recovery is manual and business logic is abstracted. Efficient: The authors claim low-latency feedback and use Compose Watch, but report no measured latency, CPU, memory, container-build time, or comparison with direct execution, batch refactoring, or existing tools; major changes require a rebuild. Effective: The system detects and transforms graph-level instances of 10 catalogued smells and users completed the prescribed workflow, but the evidence does not show that the transformations improve maintainability, preserve behavior, or solve the underlying smells in real code. Scalable: Scalability is asserted as a design goal through abstraction and Go concurrency, but no experiment evaluates larger graphs, production-scale service counts, 10×–100× growth, concurrent users, or high-frequency topology changes; the interface already reports layout congestion for highly connected graphs. The work delivers a software artifact: a web prototype with Docker-based emulation, an intermediate JSON representation, graph visualization/manipulation, smell detection, and automated template-level refactoring. No public artifact URL or repository is stated. Strengths - The dissertation identifies a concrete and underexplored workflow gap—continuous feedback for refactoring existing microservice topologies—and implements an end-to-end prototype rather than stopping at a conceptual proposal. - The architecture/emulation pivot is technically pragmatic: abstracting internal service logic makes heterogeneous repositories tractable while retaining endpoint and dependency structure needed for topology-level experimentation. - The work provides explicit detection and remediation rules for 10 smells, including graph algorithms, database and library topology handling, service discovery, and template regeneration, making the prototype’s behavior inspectable at a high level. - The qualitative findings are useful despite limited scope: participants repeatedly requested source-level diffs, change logs, explanations of applied patterns, stable graph layouts, smell/refactoring proximity, and the ability to dismiss contextually acceptable smells. These observations refine liveness from mere responsiveness toward transparency and user control. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly acknowledge the eight-person, academically homogeneous sample; instructional and Hawthorne effects; manual architecture recovery; use of emulation rather than production execution; dependence on a manually constructed intermediate representation; prototype bugs and unstable graph layout; weak latency evaluation; lack of measured maintainability outcomes; omission of ESB Usage; simplistic database-ownership heuristics; ambiguity in the target user population; and the insufficient 11-response survey for RQ1. They also identify theoretical weaknesses in the smell catalog, including overlap between Inappropriate Service Intimacy and Shared Persistency, context-dependent validity of Microservice Greedy, and unsupported or ambiguous remediation guidance for Cyclic Dependency. The authors generally confront these issues directly and classify the hypothesis as only partially validated. Analyst-Identified Gaps - There is no controlled A/B comparison against a conventional edit-compile-run workflow, an offline graph editor, or existing tools, so positive liveness effects are based on within-prototype perceptions rather than causal evidence. - The prescribed task is not an independent test of smell detection or remediation: participants are told which smells to fix, work from a prepared graph, and receive substantial conceptual scaffolding. This measures learnability and perceived usability more than autonomous architectural diagnosis. - The tool’s refactoring semantics are not validated against source code, tests, runtime traces, or expert-authored gold transformations. Some operations, such as merging services, replacing shared libraries with network services, forcing database-per-service, or inserting an API Gateway into a cycle, can create substantial trade-offs and are not universally valid. - The custom liveness scale uses four positively worded, author-defined items and is transformed with an ad hoc formula; the analysis does not report item-level means, reliability, ordinal treatment, or uncertainty, and therefore should not support strong claims about liveness as a construct. - The literature comparison omits or underweights recent automated refactoring work such as SABER in the direct empirical comparison, and the claim that existing tools lack live refactoring is not established through a systematic search of live-refactoring literature. - The paper does not report graph topology, number of services, number of edges, Docker image/build characteristics, exact update latency, or failure behavior, preventing assessment of the claimed low-latency and scalable design. - The use of Gemini for Wrong Cuts is neither benchmarked against human labels nor evaluated for stability, prompt sensitivity, privacy, or cost; the resulting refactoring may be non-deterministic and difficult to reproduce. Bottom Line This dissertation is worth reading as a candid prototype study that surfaces important transparency and interaction requirements for live architectural visualization, but it does not yet provide reliable evidence that Vivactor-M performs correct, scalable, or beneficial automated refactoring of real microservice systems.

Problem & Motivation The paper addresses coordination across manufacturing networks involving multiple plants, firms, logistics nodes, and national jurisdictions. These networks must reconcile production capacity, inventory, quality, transport, energy, compliance, and disruption information at different temporal and organizational scales. Prior work covers asset-level digital twins, cyber-physical production systems, supply-chain twins, and edge analytics, but the paper identifies a gap in handling real-time cross-company data quality, semantic heterogeneity, model uncertainty, security, and authority over consequential decisions. The target users are manufacturers, supply-chain operators, logistics providers, and governance or compliance stakeholders responsible for network-level decisions that cannot safely be delegated to a monolithic or opaque optimizer. Key Idea The central insight is to treat a manufacturing-network twin as a governed federation of purpose-bounded partial twins rather than as a single comprehensive replica. The framework makes data provenance, semantic validity, uncertainty, and decision authority first-class architectural concerns. Its most consequential design move is to place a policy and authorization boundary between analytical recommendations and executable actions: local controllers retain authority over safety-critical operations, while network services coordinate allocation, inventory, and disruption responses subject to explicit escalation rules. Methodology The paper develops a focused conceptual synthesis from standards, reviews, and foundational studies covering manufacturing digital-twin architectures, cyber-physical production systems, supply-chain resilience, and edge-enabled analytics. The resulting pipeline has five layers: L1 captures timestamped machine, quality, inventory, and logistics observations with source identity and calibration metadata; L2 performs local range, rate-of-change, unit, duplicate, and signal-quality checks, produces local features and state estimates, and activates bounded fallback behavior during connectivity loss; L3 maps local tags and business events to canonical, versioned concepts with unit metadata and event-time semantics; L4 maintains connected but separate plant, asset, product, and logistics twins and produces predictions, scenarios, uncertainty estimates, and optimization recommendations; L5 applies policy, safety, contractual, access, and jurisdictional checks before human approval or restricted automated execution. Three assurance planes apply across the layers: provenance and auditability, separate treatment of measurement/model/scenario uncertainty, and security, privacy, and policy enforcement. The paper does not specify a concrete predictive model, optimizer, loss function, ontology, protocol, or implementation technology. Critical design decisions include purpose-bounded fidelity, mandatory validated semantic mappings before decision use, local autonomy within approved operating envelopes, and mandatory human authorization for material safety, workforce, regulatory, or cross-company consequences. These choices are argued conceptually but are not quantitatively justified. Key Results The paper reports no experimental, simulated, hardware-in-the-loop, pilot, or field results, and therefore provides no accuracy, F1, latency, throughput, cost, resilience, parameter-count, or statistical-significance measurements. It defines four testable propositions instead: versioned mappings may reduce reconciliation errors; edge validation and fallback envelopes may reduce latency and service interruption; uncertainty-aware scenario ranking may reduce infeasible or unstable recommendations under drift and delayed events; and provenance-linked authorization may improve explainability and reduce unauthorized actions, potentially at the cost of approval latency and workarounds. The proposed validation plan covers replay data and synthetic faults, hardware-in-the-loop testing, a prospective single-site pilot with a contemporaneous baseline, and transfer across at least two heterogeneous sites. These are future evaluation plans, not results. No baseline architecture or competing system is actually implemented or compared. Novelty Classification NEW FORMULATION; NEW SYSTEM/TOOL at the conceptual-design level; NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING: not present. The genuine contribution is a governance-centered formulation that integrates purpose-bounded federated twins, semantic/version control, uncertainty handling, and authority-aware decision orchestration; the underlying layers and individual controls largely combine established ideas from digital twins, edge computing, cyber-physical systems, supply-chain resilience, security, and human oversight rather than introducing a new algorithm or validated system. Rigor & Reproducibility The paper is transparent that it uses a purposive conceptual synthesis rather than a systematic review or empirical case study, and it acknowledges that relevant sector-specific evidence may be omitted. It presents no ablations, formal analysis, error bars, multiple seeds, significance tests, implementation details, benchmark protocol, or measured comparison. The proposed metrics and reporting requirements are useful as an evaluation specification, but they are not applied to data. The data statement says that data will be made available on request, although no dataset is used or released, and no code, model weights, ontology, schema mappings, simulator, or repository URL is provided. The source base mixes established peer-reviewed work with several recent or practice-oriented references, including sources whose relevance to transnational manufacturing is indirect; the review method does not establish systematic coverage or assess source quality in a reproducible way. The paper avoids claiming quantified industrial benefits, but its architecture-level claims remain untested. Deployability: (4-property check) Profile: THEORETICAL/CONCEPTUAL — the paper presents a formalized architecture and propositions but no proof, executable system, or primary experiment. - Sound: The requirements are internally coherent and assumptions such as bounded autonomy, explicit semantics, provenance, and human authorization are stated, but there is no formal model or proof establishing that the architecture guarantees safety, consistency, privacy, or resilience. - General: The framework is intended for heterogeneous multi-plant and cross-border networks, but its applicability under legacy equipment, weak instrumentation, incompatible legal regimes, small suppliers, and severe disruptions is asserted as a design goal rather than demonstrated. - Tight: Not applicable in the usual bound-comparison sense; the paper supplies no quantitative bound or formal performance guarantee, and its propositions remain qualitative. - Implementable: The staged agenda suggests a practical path through replay, hardware-in-the-loop, pilot, and multi-site testing, but the paper does not specify enough algorithms, interfaces, schemas, policies, or infrastructure to implement the framework directly. The work delivers a reusable conceptual architecture and evaluation checklist, not a software artifact, dataset, trained model, library, CLI, or reusable proof technique. Strengths - It identifies a substantive systems-level gap between asset or plant digital twins and accountable decisions spanning independent firms and jurisdictions. - It makes semantics and provenance governable artifacts, requiring versioned mappings, owners, tests, change histories, and traceability of both numerical values and their meanings. - It distinguishes recommendations from authorized actions and assigns safety-critical and time-critical authority to local controllers, a useful separation for cyber-physical deployments. - It proposes evaluation dimensions beyond prediction accuracy, including node-level burden transfer, fallback behavior, approval latency, policy exceptions, operator overrides, and audit completeness. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly state that the work is conceptual and has not been validated in a live multi-site network. They acknowledge the purposive, non-exhaustive review; sensor drift; semantic heterogeneity; delayed logistics events; jurisdictional restrictions; uncertainty-transfer problems; approval latency; informal workarounds; uneven adoption among small and medium-sized enterprises; and possible selection bias toward plants with mature instrumentation. They also state that the framework does not establish reductions in emissions, water use, logistics cost, or sensor drift, and that such claims require domain-specific boundaries, credible baselines, prospective evaluation, and reporting of unsuccessful deployments. These limitations are confronted directly rather than hidden, which improves the paper's credibility, although it also confirms that the contribution remains a research agenda rather than validated evidence. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The paper does not define a concrete conflict-resolution mechanism for local versus network objectives; it calls for escalation rules but provides no policy language, optimization formulation, priority semantics, or proof of consistency. - It does not specify how uncertainty should be calibrated, propagated across federated twins, or converted into scenario rankings, so the central uncertainty-aware decision claim cannot yet be reproduced. - It lacks a systematic comparison with existing reference architectures, industrial interoperability standards, federated-learning or data-space designs, digital supply-chain twins, and policy-enforcement systems. - It does not quantify the maintenance cost of versioned ontologies, provenance logs, policy testing, recalibration, edge fallback models, or cross-border data governance, despite presenting these as central operational requirements. - Security is reduced to baseline controls such as least privilege, segmentation, signed artifacts, and logging; there is no threat model, adversarial evaluation, privacy analysis, or evidence that these controls prevent unauthorized cross-boundary actions. - The review includes several indirect or weakly connected sources and does not explain inclusion criteria, search strings, screening, or evidence weighting, limiting confidence in the claimed literature gap. - The framework does not address how operators, suppliers, and logistics firms negotiate data ownership, incentives, liability, or refusal to share information, even though these issues may determine whether federation is feasible. Bottom Line This is a useful governance-oriented conceptual position and design checklist for researchers planning manufacturing digital-twin deployments, but it is not competitive evidence of a working method or system and should not be relied on for claims about operational benefit until the proposed staged evaluations are conducted.

Reassessing Code Authorship Attribution in the Era of Language Models

A Kumar Dipongkor, Z Yao, K Moran · dl.acm.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper presents an empirical evaluation of seven pretrained code language models for code authorship attribution, covering six datasets, interpretability analyses, and functionality-preserving adversarial attacks. - Why it's important: Reliable attribution supports software maintenance, forensics, plagiarism detection, and security, but real-world code is multilingual, imbalanced, short, and vulnerable to deliberate style changes. - How it does it: The study fine-tunes transformer classifiers with cross-entropy, compares them with the path-based PbNN baseline, analyzes token and embedding attributions, and evaluates 28 GPT-4-generated code transformations validated for functionality. - The good: Across the reported benchmarks, LMs substantially outperform PbNN, with DeepSeek-Coder reaching 0.74 accuracy on LeetCode and 0.98–1.00 accuracy on several monolingual datasets, while contrastively pretrained models show lower attack success rates. - The missing: The evaluation relies mainly on an old baseline and random cross-validation within datasets, without strong contemporary baselines or project/time-separated tests that establish whether models generalize beyond benchmark-specific author and problem cues. - Read it or not: Read it for the broad empirical characterization of model size, code length, stylometric variation, and adversarial robustness; skip it as evidence of deployable authorship attribution unless its generalization and leakage concerns are resolved.

Novelty (60) and Non-Obviousness (62) are moderate: the breadth of model, interpretability, and adversarial analyses is useful, but the classifiers and most analyses are established and the central robustness mechanism remains correlational.
