Problem & Motivation: The paper addresses sustainable supply-chain design for industrial and e-commerce-oriented logistics systems facing demand variation, incomplete or inconsistent information, disruptions, environmental constraints, and competing financial objectives. The intended users are supply-chain managers, policymakers, and organizations designing procurement, warehousing, distribution, fulfillment, last-mile, and reverse-logistics operations. The claimed gap is the absence of a universal framework covering alternatives across multiple logistics functions and management levels. The motivation is reasonable, but the literature review does not establish that such frameworks are absent, nor does it clearly distinguish the proposed scope from existing sustainable supply-chain network-design, fuzzy/neutrosophic MCDM, digital-twin, and multi-objective optimization work. Key Idea: The central idea is a configurable “logistics builder”: represent supply-chain design as a hierarchy of functional areas, attributes, and discrete alternatives, then attach conventional logistics models and uncertainty-aware decision methods to the relevant choices. Neutrosophic logic is intended to encode truth, indeterminacy, and falsity in evaluations, while the holistic view links material, information, financial, service, and reverse flows. The tabular architecture is the most identifiable contribution; the paper does not show that neutrosophic reasoning itself produces decisions that conventional fuzzy, probabilistic, robust, or deterministic methods cannot produce. Methodology: The framework begins with Table 1, which lists procurement and distribution attributes such as ownership, sourcing centralization, warehouse automation, warehouse specialization, transportation mode, inventory availability, fulfillment, delivery speed, eco-friendly delivery, vehicle type, vertical/horizontal integration, and return processing. It then maps selected decisions to established models. The make-or-buy threshold is expressed as Q_i = F/(C_i − V_i), with outsourcing recommended below the threshold and insourcing above it. The adjusted EOQ formulation incorporates demand, ordering cost, storage cost, limited working capital, borrowing cost, alternative investment returns, a loan period, and a stochastic replenishment coefficient; the reported EOQ values are 276 and 206 units for Products A and B. Facility allocation is illustrated using a capacitated warehouse-location formulation and a coordinate-distance objective, with distance calculated as Manhattan distance. The neutrosophic component defines truth, indeterminacy, and falsity memberships, proposes a weighted score S_i = Σ_j w_j(T_ij − F_ij + I_ij), and gives a resource-allocation model that maximizes Σ_i,j T_ij x_ij subject to capacity constraints. Three critical design decisions are insufficiently justified: the choice and semantics of neutrosophic membership values, the aggregation rule that rewards indeterminacy, and the assumption that increased inventories, vertical integration, parallel process organization, and fuel-free delivery generally improve sustainability or resilience. Manufacturing is explicitly excluded from the tabular framework despite the paper framing the problem as whole supply-chain design, and the relationship between the framework, the models, and an actual optimization procedure is not specified as an executable pipeline. Key Results: The paper reports one numerical facility-allocation example with three suppliers, five customers, total delivery volume of 14,000 units, and manually specified coordinates. Using the stated transportation-work calculation, it selects customer point C5 at coordinates (78, 67), reporting a minimum value of 742,900 tonne-km among the listed candidate points; no comparison is made with a multi-facility, capacitated, routing, or emissions-aware optimum. A second illustrative calculation assumes an 18% annual loan rate, investment returns of 15% and 20%, storage-cost share of 0.2, replenishment coefficient 0.5, and a two-year loan period, producing EOQs of 276 units for Product A and 206 for Product B, with delivery frequencies of 51 and 49. These are calculations on synthetic or unspecified illustrative inputs, not measured outcomes from an industrial deployment. No accuracy, cost reduction, emissions reduction, service-level improvement, disruption-recovery metric, runtime, scalability result, or statistically supported comparison is reported. The abstract and conclusion claim simulation-based validation and mention AnyLogic, deep learning, causal inference, reinforcement learning, and digital twins, but the body presents none of those experiments or results. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (conceptual), and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION are the closest categories; the genuinely distinctive element is the proposed cross-functional attribute–option table that organizes supply-chain design alternatives alongside financial and sustainability considerations, whereas the neutrosophic sets, MCDM score, linear programming, EOQ, make-or-buy, and facility-allocation components are standard methods combined without a demonstrated new algorithmic result. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper contains no component ablations, sensitivity analysis, multiple scenarios, error bars, repeated trials, statistical tests, or comparison against deterministic MCDM, fuzzy MCDM, robust optimization, stochastic programming, or modern sustainable supply-chain network-design baselines. The numerical example uses a very small manually specified instance and does not provide a real enterprise dataset, data collection protocol, membership elicitation procedure, criterion weights, or code. No software, dataset, model weights, implementation repository, or URL is reported. The proposed neutrosophic optimization model uses only truth-membership values in its objective and does not operationalize indeterminacy or falsity in the constraints or objective. The weighted score S_i = T_i − F_i + I_i is not justified and can rank more-indeterminate alternatives more favorably, which conflicts with the stated purpose of representing uncertainty unless a specific decision-theoretic rationale is supplied. The facility example also appears to select a customer location as a warehouse site without modeling fixed opening costs, capacity, supplier-to-customer assignment, multiple facilities, or demand fulfillment constraints. Consequently, the examples demonstrate arithmetic application of formulas rather than validation of the claimed framework. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL, because the paper includes numerical experiments and claims validation, although the evidence is primarily illustrative rather than empirical deployment. * Practical: The individual calculations could run on commercially available hardware, but the paper does not provide an implementation of the full framework or specify how an organization would collect, normalize, and maintain neutrosophic assessments. * Efficient: Computational cost is not measured; the displayed models are small and standard, but the cost of searching the combinatorial attribute space, integrating multiple models, and performing uncertainty analysis is not established. * Effective: The evidence does not show that the framework improves cost, emissions, resilience, customer retention, or sustainability relative to existing methods; it only produces one selected location and two EOQ values from assumed inputs. * Scalable: No experiment tests larger networks, more facilities, more products, disruption scenarios, or 10×–100× scale; scalability is asserted in the abstract and conclusion but not demonstrated. The work stops at paper form: it does not deliver a library, CLI, decision-support system, dataset, trained model, or other reusable software artifact. Strengths: - The table covers a broad set of operational decisions, including reverse logistics, last-mile delivery, fulfillment, outsourcing, inventory, and information integration, which is more system-oriented than papers focused on a single routing or facility-location problem. - It explicitly connects financial constraints and alternative investment returns to inventory decisions through an adjusted EOQ formulation, an uncommon but potentially useful managerial perspective. - The paper identifies several practical tensions—such as inventory versus shipment frequency, vertical integration versus outsourcing, and centralization versus flexibility—that deserve multi-objective treatment in sustainable supply-chain design. - The numerical inputs and reported intermediate outputs make the small illustrative calculations at least partly inspectable, although they do not constitute validation. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The paper briefly acknowledges data generalization and reliance on aggregated enterprise data covering an entire manufacturing cycle, although the presented numerical example does not document such a dataset. It also notes limitations of the make-or-buy formula, including economic shocks, long-term effects, short-term stagnation, and labor shortages. The conclusion calls for future work on a universal decision-support tool combining neutrosophic optimization, fuzzy AHP, Bayesian reasoning, hybrid AI, reinforcement learning, and digital twins. These acknowledgments are directionally appropriate, but they do not confront the missing validation, ambiguous neutrosophic specification, or mismatch between the claimed simulation/AI validation and the experiments actually described. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The paper claims “real-world simulation-based validation” and later invokes AnyLogic, deep learning, and causal inference, but reports no simulation design, real data, trained model, causal estimand, or validation result. - The neutrosophic framework is not actually used in the numerical example: no truth, indeterminacy, falsity memberships, criterion weights, alternative rankings, or neutrosophic optimization solution are provided. - The proposed MCDM aggregation formula is theoretically and decision-theoretically under-motivated because it adds indeterminacy rather than penalizing or separately reporting it. - Sustainability is mostly asserted rather than measured; the paper reports no lifecycle emissions, energy use, waste, social indicators, carbon accounting boundary, or trade-off between economic and environmental objectives. - The facility-allocation example is too small and structurally incomplete to support claims about supply-chain design: it lacks facility fixed costs, capacity, assignment decisions, routing, inventory effects, service constraints, and comparison with standard location-allocation solutions. - Several recommendations are presented as generally preferable—vertical integration, higher inventory, parallel processes, warehouses near consumers, and fuel-free delivery—without modeling their costs, feasibility, rebound effects, disruption exposure, or domain-specific counterexamples. - The framework claims coverage of supply-chain design but excludes manufacturing, and the treatment of social sustainability and stakeholder preferences is largely nominal rather than operational. - The literature review does not systematically compare the framework with established sustainable network-design and fuzzy/neutrosophic MCDM methods, so the claimed universal gap remains unsubstantiated. Bottom Line: The paper offers a readable taxonomy and systems-integration perspective for sustainable logistics design, but practitioners gain no validated decision procedure or evidence of improvement over standard supply-chain optimization methods, making it substantially weaker than a methodologically complete empirical or optimization study.

Problem & Motivation The paper addresses the difficulty of making operational and strategic decisions in business systems characterized by uncertainty, stochastic behavior, dynamic interactions, and interdependent processes. The intended users are organizations involved in logistics, manufacturing, energy, e-commerce, and business-process reengineering, where testing alternative configurations in the real world can be costly or risky. It identifies a gap in the fragmented treatment of discrete-event simulation, system dynamics, agent-based modeling, and hybrid simulation, arguing that existing work lacks a generalized workflow integrating these approaches with optimization for prescriptive decision-making. The paper frames simulation as a way to conduct controlled virtual experimentation, but it does not establish through a literature review or empirical comparison that such an integration gap is genuinely unresolved. Key Idea The core idea is to treat prescriptive analytics as an iterative lifecycle rather than as a single optimization algorithm: define the decision problem, conceptualize the system, construct and calibrate a simulation model, design and run experiments, validate the model, analyze sensitivity, generate alternative scenarios, and integrate the results into a digital decision-support platform. The substantive insight is organizational and methodological—linking established simulation paradigms and lifecycle steps—but the paper does not introduce a new mathematical mechanism, search strategy, coupling protocol, or formal criterion for selecting among simulation paradigms. Methodology The study uses a conceptual and methodological design based on established operations-research and simulation literature. Its workflow begins with problem formulation and objective/project-plan definition; proceeds to conceptual modeling, in which system components, relationships, variables, constraints, and the choice among discrete-event, agent-based, system-dynamics, or hybrid models are specified; and then develops parallel digital and data models. Data may come from electronic records, observation, or expert assessment, with statistical analysis used to fit input distributions. The workflow next performs experimental design, specifies run duration, iteration count, and input variation, executes repeated stochastic simulations, records model parameters and outputs, and iterates through model and data calibration. Verification and validation are proposed, followed by sensitivity analysis, preparation of alternative scenarios, documentation, and industrial deployment. The paper claims that optimization is integrated after or alongside simulation to identify favorable parameter configurations, but it gives no objective function, decision variables, constraints, optimization algorithm, coupling strategy, or convergence criterion. The three critical design decisions—choice of simulation paradigm, use of hybrid models, and integration of simulation with optimization—are motivated only at a general level and are not operationally justified for a concrete application. Key Results No quantitative results are reported. The stated result is a generalized flowchart containing problem definition, objective setting, conceptualization, digital and data modeling, experiment design, iterative simulation, calibration, approval checks, sensitivity analysis, scenario preparation, reporting, and industrial application. The paper claims that simulation enables risk-free scenario evaluation, that optimization improves efficiency, cost, and service quality, and that hybrid models can represent complex systems more comprehensively. It does not report a dataset, a simulated business case, number of scenarios, model size, runtime, accuracy, cost reduction, throughput, service-level change, statistical uncertainty, or comparison with a conventional decision process or competing prescriptive-analytics method. Consequently, the claims of improved decision accuracy, operational efficiency, adaptability, and scalability are not measured. The work is tested at no experimental scale; its examples concern possible applications in logistics, manufacturing, energy, and e-commerce rather than evaluated deployments. Novelty Classification NEW FORMULATION; ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION are the closest classifications, although the contribution is primarily a synthesis of established simulation lifecycle practices rather than a new technical method. The paper’s potentially distinctive element is the explicit framing of multiple simulation paradigms, optimization, validation, sensitivity analysis, and digital-platform integration as one generalized workflow; however, it does not demonstrate that this formulation differs materially from established simulation methodology and cross-paradigm modeling frameworks. Rigor & Reproducibility The paper includes no ablations, controlled comparisons, repeated experimental results, error bars, statistical tests, or sensitivity results despite prescribing these activities in its workflow. There is no implemented model, source code, dataset, trained model, software repository, or executable artifact; the DOI points to Zenodo, but no release contents or repository URL are specified. The evaluation is entirely conceptual and relies on broad assertions supported by references, many of which are foundational or older simulation sources. It lacks current prescriptive-analytics baselines, formal comparison against existing simulation-optimization workflows, and a concrete case study. The paper also has a serious evidence mismatch: it labels the conceptual framework’s description as “results” and concludes that it improves decision quality and efficiency without presenting measurements that could support those claims. Deployability (4-property check) Profile used: EMPIRICAL, with the qualification that the paper reports a conceptual methodology and no empirical execution. * Practical: The proposed workflow could in principle run on commercially available hardware using tools such as AnyLogic, FlexSim, or AutoMod, but no implementation or hardware requirements are provided. * Efficient: Computational and modeling costs are not measured; the paper acknowledges that simulation development may require substantial expertise and computational resources but gives no comparison with alternative methods. * Effective: The framework plausibly supports scenario analysis, but the paper does not show that it improves any operational metric or solves a specified business decision problem beyond a general proxy claim. * Scalable: Scalability is mentioned as a consideration, but no model size, workload, runtime, stress test, or 10×–100× scale experiment is reported. The work does not deliver a software artifact, library, CLI, dataset, trained model, or reusable formal proof technique; it stops at a paper-level workflow and flowchart. Strengths - The workflow covers several important simulation-engineering stages that conceptual papers often omit, including input-data modeling, calibration, verification, validation, stochastic replication, and sensitivity analysis. - It correctly recognizes that operational, strategic, and behavioral phenomena may require different simulation abstractions and that hybrid modeling can be relevant when a single paradigm is insufficient. - It identifies the organizational integration problem—connecting models to decision-makers and digital platforms—rather than treating simulation as an isolated offline analysis. - The paper states practical barriers involving data quality, expertise, computational resources, and end-user participation, which are credible constraints on simulation-based decision support. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly acknowledge that simulation-model development is complex and time-consuming, requires expertise and computational resources, depends on data availability and quality, and may fail to deliver value if end users are not involved or cannot interpret model outputs. They also note that hybrid modeling and AI/ML integration create opportunities but do not discuss concrete failure modes, validation burdens, or governance risks in detail. These limitations are acknowledged qualitatively, but the paper does not quantify their effects or show how the proposed workflow mitigates them. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The paper does not define a concrete decision problem, so the proposed algorithm cannot be judged against a real objective, constraint set, or operational requirement. - “Optimization” is underspecified: there is no objective function, algorithm, treatment of stochastic simulation outputs, multi-objective formulation, or method for proving or estimating optimality. - The claimed integration of DES, ABM, system dynamics, and hybrid models is not implemented; the paper provides no coupling architecture, synchronization semantics, model-selection rule, or example showing that hybridization improves fidelity or decisions. - There is no empirical validation, numerical outcome, baseline, ablation, uncertainty interval, or deployment evidence, making the results section a restatement of expected benefits rather than research findings. - The literature gap is asserted rather than demonstrated. Prior work on cross-paradigm simulation, simulation optimization, digital twins, business-process simulation, and decision-support systems is not systematically reviewed or compared. - The paper makes broad claims about real-time integration, industrial applicability, sustainable competitive advantage, and improved accuracy without addressing latency, data drift, model misspecification, organizational adoption, or causal validity. - Several references appear weakly aligned with the technical claims, including citations on mobile-food-ordering satisfaction and consumer behavior used in a simulation-methodology context; the paper does not explain how these sources support the proposed algorithm. Bottom Line This paper is a readable high-level synthesis of simulation-project best practices, but it offers little research value for a top-tier technical audience because its generalized algorithm is not operationalized, compared, or empirically evaluated.

These papers collectively examine how AI is moving from isolated automation toward autonomous, agentic systems that coordinate decisions, workflows, and actions across enterprise contexts.
